context_brief: characteristic factors for commuting polynomial averages
original_question: Suppose p1, ..., pℓ ∈ Z[t] are pairwise independent polynomials. Do there exist an integer d and Host–Kra factors Zd,T1, ..., Zd,Tℓ such that these factors are characteristic for the commuting-transformation averages (1/N) Σ T1^{p1(n)} f1 · ... · Tℓ^{pℓ(n)} fℓ?
self_contained_problem:
Let $(X,\mathcal{B},\mu)$ be a probability space and let $T_1,\dots,T_\ell:X\to X$ be commuting invertible measure-preserving transformations. For an invertible measure-preserving transformation $T$ on $(X,\mathcal{B},\mu)$ and an integer $d\ge 0$, let $Z_{d,T}$ denote the $d$-th Host–Kra factor of the system $(X,\mathcal{B},\mu,T)$ (the factor characterized by the Gowers–Host–Kra seminorm $\|\cdot\|_{U^{d+1}(T)}$, so that $\mathbb{E}(f\mid Z_{d,T})=0$ iff $\|f\|_{U^{d+1}(T)}=0$).

Two polynomials $p,q\in\mathbb{Z}[t]$ are called independent if they are linearly independent over $\mathbb{Q}$ together with the constant polynomial $1$; a family $p_1,\dots,p_\ell\in\mathbb{Z}[t]$ is pairwise independent if any two of its members are independent.

Given $f_1,\dots,f_\ell\in L^\infty(\mu)$, consider the multiple ergodic averages
$$A_N(f_1,\dots,f_\ell)=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N} (T_1^{p_1(n)}f_1)\cdots(T_\ell^{p_\ell(n)}f_\ell).$$

A tuple of factors $(\mathcal{Y}_1,\dots,\mathcal{Y}_\ell)$ is called characteristic for these averages if
$$\lim_{N\to\infty}\bigl\|A_N(f_1,\dots,f_\ell)-A_N(\mathbb{E}(f_1\mid\mathcal{Y}_1),\dots,\mathbb{E}(f_\ell\mid\mathcal{Y}_\ell))\bigr\|_{L^2(\mu)}=0$$
for all $f_1,\dots,f_\ell\in L^\infty(\mu)$.

Prove or disprove: for every pairwise independent family $p_1,\dots,p_\ell\in\mathbb{Z}[t]$, there exists an integer $d\ge 0$ (depending only on $p_1,\dots,p_\ell$) such that the factors $Z_{d,T_1},\dots,Z_{d,T_\ell}$ are characteristic for the averages $A_N(f_1,\dots,f_\ell)$ in $L^2(\mu)$.
status_search_result: The problem appears to have been resolved by Frantzikinakis and Kuca in "Joint ergodicity for commuting transformations and applications to polynomial sequences" (arXiv:2207.12288, published in Inventiones Mathematicae, 2024/2025). They establish that for pairwise independent polynomial iterates with commuting measure-preserving transformations, the Host–Kra factors of suitable degree are characteristic, using a "seminorm smoothing" technique that resolves several conjectures of this type.

original_question: In the special case where T1, ..., Tℓ are weak mixing and p1, ..., pℓ are pairwise independent integer polynomials, must the averages (1/N) Σ T1^{p1(n)} f1 · ... · Tℓ^{pℓ(n)} fℓ converge in L2(µ) to the product of the integrals ∫f1 dµ · ... · ∫fℓ dµ?
self_contained_problem:
Let $(X,\mathcal{B},\mu)$ be a probability space, and let $T_1,\ldots,T_\ell:X\to X$ be invertible measure-preserving transformations of $(X,\mathcal{B},\mu)$. Recall that a measure-preserving transformation $T$ on $(X,\mathcal{B},\mu)$ is weak mixing if for every $f,g\in L^2(\mu)$,
$$\lim_{N\to\infty}\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}\Big|\int (T^n f)\, g\, d\mu-\int f\,d\mu\int g\,d\mu\Big|=0.$$
A finite collection of polynomials $p_1,\ldots,p_\ell\in\mathbb{Z}[t]$ is called pairwise independent if every $p_i$ and every difference $p_i-p_j$ ($i\neq j$) is non-constant.

Assume that each transformation $T_i$ is weak mixing (the transformations are not assumed to commute or to be related in any other way), and that $p_1,\ldots,p_\ell\in\mathbb{Z}[t]$ are pairwise independent. Prove or disprove: for every $f_1,\ldots,f_\ell\in L^\infty(\mu)$,
$$\lim_{N\to\infty}\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}\big(T_1^{p_1(n)}f_1\big)\cdots\big(T_\ell^{p_\ell(n)}f_\ell\big)=\int f_1\,d\mu\;\cdots\;\int f_\ell\,d\mu$$
in $L^2(\mu)$.
status_search_result: Recent work by Frantzikinakis and Kuca (Inventiones, 2024; arXiv:2207.12288) establishes joint ergodicity criteria for commuting transformations with pairwise independent polynomial iterates and, in particular, proves convergence to the product of integrals when the transformations are weak mixing and commute. The general problem stated for not-necessarily-commuting weak mixing transformations does not appear to be fully settled in this generality, so the problem is regarded as partially solved.

original_question: If p1, ..., pℓ ∈ Z[t] are rationally independent, are the rational Kronecker factors K_rat(T1), ..., K_rat(Tℓ) characteristic for the commuting-transformation averages (1/N) Σ T1^{p1(n)} f1 · ... · Tℓ^{pℓ(n)} fℓ?
self_contained_problem:
Let $(X,\mathcal{B},\mu)$ be a probability space and let $T_1,\dots,T_\ell:X\to X$ be commuting invertible measure-preserving transformations. For each $i$, let $\mathcal{K}_{\mathrm{rat}}(T_i)\subseteq L^2(\mu)$ denote the rational Kronecker factor of $T_i$, defined as the closed linear span of all eigenfunctions of $T_i$ with rational eigenvalues; equivalently, $f\in\mathcal{K}_{\mathrm{rat}}(T_i)$ iff the orbit $\{T_i^n f:n\in\mathbb{Z}\}$ generates a finite-dimensional $T_i$-invariant subspace of $L^2(\mu)$ on which $T_i$ acts with rational spectrum.

Let $p_1,\dots,p_\ell\in\mathbb{Z}[t]$ be polynomials that are rationally independent, meaning that no nontrivial rational linear combination $c_1 p_1+\cdots+c_\ell p_\ell$ with $(c_1,\dots,c_\ell)\in\mathbb{Q}^\ell\setminus\{0\}$ is a constant polynomial.

For $f_1,\dots,f_\ell\in L^\infty(\mu)$, consider the multiple ergodic averages
$$A_N(f_1,\dots,f_\ell) \;=\; \frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N} (T_1^{p_1(n)} f_1)\cdot (T_2^{p_2(n)} f_2)\cdots (T_\ell^{p_\ell(n)} f_\ell).$$

Show that the factors $\mathcal{K}_{\mathrm{rat}}(T_1),\dots,\mathcal{K}_{\mathrm{rat}}(T_\ell)$ are characteristic for these averages: that is, if $\mathbb{E}(f_i\mid \mathcal{K}_{\mathrm{rat}}(T_i))=0$ for some $i\in\{1,\dots,\ell\}$, then
$$\lim_{N\to\infty} \big\| A_N(f_1,\dots,f_\ell)\big\|_{L^2(\mu)} \;=\; 0.$$
category_tag: multiple ergodic averages and characteristic factors
status_search_result: Subsequent work on joint ergodicity for commuting transformations and polynomial sequences (Frantzikinakis–Kuca, 2022, arXiv:2207.12288) establishes that for linearly independent integer polynomials the rational Kronecker factor is characteristic and derives Khintchine-type lower bounds. Related work (e.g., arXiv:2102.09967) addresses joint ergodicity of polynomial sequences. The full statement under the precise rational-independence hypothesis appears largely resolved in this line of work, though formulations and full generality may differ slightly from the originally posed problem.

context_brief: optimal lower bounds for polynomial recurrence
original_question: Suppose p1, ..., pℓ ∈ Z[t] are rationally independent and have zero constant term. For every measurable set A and every ε > 0, must there exist n ∈ N such that µ(A ∩ T1^{p1(n)} A ∩ ... ∩ Tℓ^{pℓ(n)} A) ≥ µ(A)^{ℓ+1} - ε?
self_contained_problem:
Let $(X,\mathcal{B},\mu)$ be a probability space and let $T_1,\dots,T_\ell\colon X\to X$ be commuting invertible measure-preserving transformations. Let $p_1,\dots,p_\ell\in\mathbb{Z}[t]$ be polynomials with zero constant term that are rationally independent (meaning that no nontrivial rational linear combination of $p_1,\dots,p_\ell$ is the zero polynomial; equivalently, $p_1,\dots,p_\ell$ are linearly independent over $\mathbb{Q}$).

Prove or disprove: for every measurable set $A\in\mathcal{B}$ and every $\varepsilon>0$, there exists $n\in\mathbb{N}$ such that
$$\mu\bigl(A\cap T_1^{-p_1(n)}A\cap T_2^{-p_2(n)}A\cap\cdots\cap T_\ell^{-p_\ell(n)}A\bigr)\;\geq\;\mu(A)^{\ell+1}-\varepsilon.$$
status_search_result: Web search did not return a definitive resolution of this specific optimal lower bound for polynomial multiple recurrence with rationally independent polynomials and several commuting transformations. Related results by Frantzikinakis and others address mean convergence and recurrence along independent polynomials, but a complete proof of the sharp $\mu(A)^{\ell+1}-\varepsilon$ lower bound in this generality does not appear to be confirmed in the search evidence.

original_question: If {p1, ..., pℓ} is an intersective family of integer-valued polynomials, meaning that for every r ∈ N there exists n with each pi(n) divisible by r, then for every system (X, X, µ, T1, ..., Tℓ) and every A ∈ X with µ(A) > 0, must there exist n ∈ N such that µ(A ∩ T1^{p1(n)} A ∩ ... ∩ Tℓ^{pℓ(n)} A) > 0?
self_contained_problem:
Call a finite family $\{p_1, \dots, p_\ell\}$ of integer-valued polynomials in one variable an intersective family if for every $r \in \mathbb{N}$ there exists $n \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $r \mid p_i(n)$ for all $i = 1, \dots, \ell$.

Let $(X, \mathcal{X}, \mu)$ be a probability space and let $T_1, \dots, T_\ell : X \to X$ be invertible measure-preserving transformations (which may be assumed to commute). Prove or disprove the following statement:

For every intersective family of integer-valued polynomials $\{p_1, \dots, p_\ell\}$ and every $A \in \mathcal{X}$ with $\mu(A) > 0$, there exists $n \in \mathbb{N}$ such that
$$\mu\bigl(A \cap T_1^{p_1(n)} A \cap T_2^{p_2(n)} A \cap \cdots \cap T_\ell^{p_\ell(n)} A\bigr) > 0.$$
status_search_result: For a single transformation ($\ell$ transformations all equal), the polynomial Szemerédi/PSZ characterization by Bergelson–Leibman–Lesigne shows that joint intersectivity is equivalent to the recurrence property. For several commuting transformations along distinct polynomials, recurrence is known under strong hypotheses (e.g., distinct degrees, or polynomials with zero constant term via Bergelson–Leibman), but the general case for arbitrary intersective families with multiple commuting transformations does not appear to be settled in the literature surveyed; recent works on rings of integers and non-commuting transformations explicitly leave the rationally dependent / general intersective case open.

original_question: For every system (X, X, µ, T, S) and bounded functions f, g, do the commuting-transformation averages (1/N) Σ f(T^n x) g(S^n x) converge pointwise almost everywhere?
self_contained_problem:
Let $(X,\mathcal{X},\mu)$ be a standard probability space, and let $T,S\colon X\to X$ be two commuting invertible measure-preserving transformations (i.e., $T\circ S = S\circ T$, and both preserve $\mu$). For any $f,g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, define the bilinear ergodic averages
$$A_N(f,g)(x) \;=\; \frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N} f(T^n x)\, g(S^n x), \qquad N\ge 1.$$
Prove or disprove: for every such system $(X,\mathcal{X},\mu,T,S)$ and every choice of $f,g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, the sequence $A_N(f,g)(x)$ converges as $N\to\infty$ for $\mu$-almost every $x\in X$.
status_search_result: The pointwise almost-everywhere convergence of the bilinear averages $\frac{1}{N}\sum f(T^n x) g(S^n x)$ for two general commuting measure-preserving transformations is a well-known open problem. Mean (L^2) convergence is known (Conze–Lesigne, and more generally Tao for any number of commuting transformations). Pointwise convergence has been established only in special cases, e.g. for distal systems and for certain related cubic averages by Huang, Shao and Ye, but the general case remains open as of recent literature.

context_brief: optimal error term in nilsequence decomposition
original_question: For commuting transformations T1, ..., Tℓ and bounded functions f0, ..., fℓ, does every correlation sequence ∫ f0 · T1^n f1 · ... · Tℓ^n fℓ dµ admit a decomposition ψ(n) + e(n) where ψ is an ℓ-step nilsequence and the Cesàro average of |e(n)| tends to 0?
self_contained_problem:
Let $(X,\mathcal{B},\mu)$ be a probability space and let $T_1,\ldots,T_\ell:X\to X$ be commuting invertible measure-preserving transformations. For bounded measurable functions $f_0,f_1,\ldots,f_\ell\in L^\infty(\mu)$, define the multiple correlation sequence
$$a(n)=\int_X f_0\cdot (T_1^n f_1)\cdot (T_2^n f_2)\cdots (T_\ell^n f_\ell)\,d\mu,\qquad n\in\mathbb{Z}.$$
A bounded sequence $(\psi(n))_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}$ is called an $\ell$-step nilsequence if there exist an $\ell$-step nilmanifold $G/\Gamma$ (with $G$ a connected, simply connected nilpotent Lie group of nilpotency class $\ell$ and $\Gamma$ a uniform discrete subgroup), a continuous function $F:G/\Gamma\to\mathbb{C}$, an element $g\in G$, and a point $x\in G/\Gamma$ such that $\psi(n)=F(g^n x)$ for all $n$.

Question: Is it true that for every choice of commuting transformations $T_1,\ldots,T_\ell$ and bounded functions $f_0,\ldots,f_\ell$ as above, the sequence $a(n)$ admits a decomposition
$$a(n)=\psi(n)+e(n)$$
where $(\psi(n))$ is an $\ell$-step nilsequence and the error term satisfies
$$\lim_{N\to\infty}\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}|e(n)|=0\,?$$
status_search_result: The problem was answered affirmatively by Frantzikinakis (arXiv:1407.0631, "Multiple correlation sequences and nilsequences"), where it is proved that any multiple correlation sequence for commuting measure-preserving transformations with linear iterates decomposes as an ℓ-step nilsequence plus an error term that is small in uniform density. Subsequent refinements and extensions (e.g., decompositions along primes, polynomial iterates) have appeared.

context_brief: noncommuting polynomial recurrence with extra variable
original_question: Let T1, ..., Tℓ be arbitrary invertible measure preserving transformations, and let p1, ..., pℓ be distinct polynomials with zero constant term. Must every measurable set A of positive measure contain a pattern of the form A ∩ T1^{m+p1(n)} A ∩ ... ∩ Tℓ^{m+pℓ(n)} A with positive measure for some m, n ∈ N?
self_contained_problem:
Let $(X,\mathcal{X},\mu)$ be a probability space and let $T_1,\dots,T_\ell\colon X\to X$ be invertible measure preserving transformations (no commutativity is assumed). Let $p_1,\dots,p_\ell\in\mathbb{Z}[x]$ be distinct polynomials with zero constant term. Prove or disprove: for every $A\in\mathcal{X}$ with $\mu(A)>0$, there exist $m,n\in\mathbb{N}$ such that
$$\mu\!\left(A\cap T_1^{\,m+p_1(n)}A\cap T_2^{\,m+p_2(n)}A\cap\cdots\cap T_\ell^{\,m+p_\ell(n)}A\right)>0.$$
status_search_result: A theorem of Frantzikinakis (J. London Math. Soc., 2023; arXiv:1302.5571) establishes the desired multiple recurrence in the two-variable form $m+p_i(n)$ under the stronger hypothesis that the polynomials $p_1,\dots,p_\ell$ are rationally independent (with zero constant term), for arbitrary, possibly non-commuting, invertible measure preserving transformations. The general case of merely distinct polynomials does not appear to be resolved in the literature, so the problem is partially solved.

$$\frac{|a(t)-c\,p(t)|}{\log t}\;\longrightarrow\;\infty\qquad\text{as }t\to\infty.$$

$$\lim_{N\to\infty}\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N} (T^{[a_1(n)]}f_1)\cdots(T^{[a_\ell(n)]}f_\ell)\;=\;\int f_1\,d\mu\,\cdots\,\int f_\ell\,d\mu,$$

original_question: Can one find a Hardy-field function a(t) with super-polynomial growth, meaning a(t)/t^k → ∞ for every k, such that the integer sequence [a(n)] is good for multiple recurrence and multiple convergence of powers?
self_contained_problem:
Let H denote a Hardy field, that is, a field (closed under differentiation) of germs at +∞ of real-valued functions defined on a half-line [c, ∞), such that every nonzero element is eventually monotone and of constant sign. Say that a sequence of integers (b_n)_{n∈ℕ} is good for multiple recurrence of powers if for every k ∈ ℕ, every invertible measure-preserving system (X, 𝒳, μ, T), and every set A ∈ 𝒳 with μ(A) > 0, there exists n ∈ ℕ such that
  μ(A ∩ T^{-b_n} A ∩ T^{-2 b_n} A ∩ ⋯ ∩ T^{-k b_n} A) > 0.
Say that (b_n) is good for multiple convergence of powers if for every k ∈ ℕ, every such system (X, 𝒳, μ, T), and all f_1, …, f_k ∈ L^∞(μ), the averages
  (1/N) ∑_{n=1}^{N} (T^{b_n} f_1)(T^{2 b_n} f_2) ⋯ (T^{k b_n} f_k)
converge in L^2(μ) as N → ∞.

Question: Does there exist a function a ∈ H satisfying a(t)/t^k → ∞ as t → ∞ for every k ∈ ℕ (i.e., a has super-polynomial growth) such that the integer sequence b_n = ⌊a(n)⌋ is good for both multiple recurrence and multiple convergence of powers?

Research on Hardy field sequences (Frantzikinakis; Frantzikinakis–Kuca; Bergelson–Moreira–Richter) has primarily handled polynomial growth and certain non-polynomial polynomially bounded cases. Recent work has resolved several conjectures of Frantzikinakis in the polynomial-growth regime, but the existence of a super-polynomial Hardy field example good for multiple recurrence and convergence of powers does not appear to have been established in the literature surveyed.

original_question: If c is a positive noninteger and p_n denotes the nth prime, is the sequence [p_n^c] good for multiple recurrence and multiple convergence of powers?
self_contained_problem:
Let $c>0$ be a non-integer real number, let $(p_n)_{n\ge 1}$ denote the increasing sequence of prime numbers, and let $\lfloor\cdot\rfloor$ denote the floor function. A sequence $(a_n)_{n\ge 1}$ of integers is said to be good for multiple recurrence of powers if, for every invertible measure preserving system $(X,\mathcal{B},\mu,T)$, every integer $k\ge 1$, and every set $A\in\mathcal{B}$ with $\mu(A)>0$, there exists $n\ge 1$ such that
$$\mu\bigl(A\cap T^{-a_n}A\cap T^{-2a_n}A\cap\cdots\cap T^{-k a_n}A\bigr)>0.$$
The sequence is said to be good for multiple convergence of powers if, for every invertible measure preserving system $(X,\mathcal{B},\mu,T)$, every integer $k\ge 1$, and all $f_1,\dots,f_k\in L^\infty(\mu)$, the averages
$$\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N} f_1(T^{a_n}x)\,f_2(T^{2a_n}x)\cdots f_k(T^{k a_n}x)$$
converge in $L^2(\mu)$ as $N\to\infty$.

Prove that the sequence $a_n=\lfloor p_n^{c}\rfloor$ is good for both multiple recurrence of powers and multiple convergence of powers.

original_question: Is the oscillatory sequence [n sin n] good for multiple recurrence and multiple convergence of powers?
self_contained_problem:
Let $(X,\mathcal{B},\mu,T)$ be an invertible measure-preserving system on a probability space, and for a real number $x$ let $\lfloor x\rfloor$ denote its integer part. Consider the integer sequence $a(n) = \lfloor n\sin n\rfloor$ for $n\in\mathbb{N}$.

Call a sequence $(a(n))_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\subset\mathbb{Z}$ good for multiple recurrence of powers if, for every invertible measure-preserving system $(X,\mathcal{B},\mu,T)$, every set $A\in\mathcal{B}$ with $\mu(A)>0$, and every integer $k\geq 1$, there exists $n\in\mathbb{N}$ with
$$\mu\bigl(A\cap T^{-a(n)}A\cap T^{-2a(n)}A\cap\cdots\cap T^{-k\,a(n)}A\bigr)>0.$$
Call $(a(n))$ good for multiple convergence of powers if, for every such system, every $k\geq 1$, and all $f_1,\dots,f_k\in L^\infty(\mu)$, the averages

converge in $L^2(\mu)$ as $N\to\infty$.

original_question: If c > 1 is not an integer, is the sequence [n^c] good for multiple recurrence and multiple convergence of commuting transformations? More strongly, for every system (X, X, µ, T1, ..., Tℓ) and bounded functions f1, ..., fℓ, is the L2-limit of (1/N) Σ T1^[n^c] f1 · ... · Tℓ^[n^c] fℓ equal to the L2-limit of the linear averages (1/N) Σ T1^n f1 · ... · Tℓ^n fℓ?

$$\lim_{N\to\infty}\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}T_1^{a_n}f_1\cdots T_\ell^{a_n}f_\ell$$

original_question: Let (a_n(ω)) be a random non-lacunary sequence built by independently selecting n with probability σ_n, where σ_n decreases and nσ_n → ∞. Almost surely, is (a_n(ω)) good for multiple recurrence and multiple convergence of commuting transformations, and do the averages (1/N) Σ T1^{a_n(ω)} f1 · ... · Tℓ^{a_n(ω)} fℓ always converge in L2 to the same limit as the linear averages (1/N) Σ T1^n f1 · ... · Tℓ^n fℓ?
self_contained_problem:
Let $(\sigma_n)_{n\ge 1}$ be a non-increasing sequence of real numbers with $0\le \sigma_n\le 1$ and $n\sigma_n\to\infty$. On a probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ let $(X_n)_{n\ge 1}$ be independent $\{0,1\}$-valued random variables with $\mathbb P(X_n=1)=\sigma_n$. For $\omega\in\Omega$ let $(a_n(\omega))$ be the increasing enumeration of $\{n\in\mathbb N : X_n(\omega)=1\}$ (almost surely an infinite, non-lacunary subset of $\mathbb N$).

Let $\ell\in\mathbb N$. Show that almost surely the sequence $(a_n(\omega))$ has the following two properties.

(i) (Multiple recurrence and convergence for commuting transformations.) For every probability space $(X,\mathcal X,\mu)$ and every family $T_1,\dots,T_\ell$ of commuting invertible measure-preserving transformations of $(X,\mathcal X,\mu)$, and every $A\in\mathcal X$ with $\mu(A)>0$,
$$\liminf_{N\to\infty}\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\mu\big(A\cap T_1^{-a_n(\omega)}A\cap\cdots\cap T_\ell^{-a_n(\omega)}A\big)>0,$$
and for all $f_1,\dots,f_\ell\in L^\infty(\mu)$ the averages
$$\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N} T_1^{a_n(\omega)}f_1\cdot T_2^{a_n(\omega)}f_2\cdots T_\ell^{a_n(\omega)}f_\ell$$
converge in $L^2(\mu)$ as $N\to\infty$.

(ii) (Same limit as the linear averages.) The $L^2(\mu)$-limit in (i) coincides with the $L^2(\mu)$-limit of the linear averages
$$\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N} T_1^{n}f_1\cdot T_2^{n}f_2\cdots T_\ell^{n}f_\ell.$$
category_tag: multiple ergodic averages along random sequences
status_search_result: For a single transformation ($\ell=1$), analogous results for random non-lacunary sequences with $n\sigma_n\to\infty$ are known via work of Bourgain and of Frantzikinakis–Lesigne–Wierdl on random ergodic theorems. For commuting transformations ($\ell\ge 2$), partial progress on multiple ergodic averages along random sequences has been obtained (e.g., Frantzikinakis on pointwise convergence of multiple averages along random sequences), but a search did not turn up a definitive published resolution of the full problem as stated for general commuting systems and arbitrary $\ell$. Status is therefore reported as unknown.

original_question: For a random sequence (a_n(ω)) selected with nσ_n → ∞, is it almost surely true that for every system (X, X, µ, T, S) and bounded functions f, g, the averages (1/N) Σ T^n f · S^{a_n(ω)} g converge in L2 to E(f | I_T) · E(g | I_S)? If σ_n = n^{-a} with a ∈ (0,1), does the convergence also hold almost everywhere?
self_contained_problem:
Let $(\sigma_n)_{n\ge 1}$ be a sequence of real numbers with $0 \le \sigma_n \le 1$ and $n\sigma_n \to \infty$. On some probability space, let $(\xi_n)_{n\ge 1}$ be independent $\{0,1\}$-valued random variables with $\mathbb{P}(\xi_n=1)=\sigma_n$, and define the random subset $\{n : \xi_n(\omega)=1\}=\{a_1(\omega)<a_2(\omega)<\cdots\}$ of the positive integers (so $(a_n(\omega))$ is the increasing enumeration of indices with $\xi_n=1$).

Consider any measure-preserving system $(X,\mathcal X,\mu,T,S)$, where $T,S\colon X\to X$ are commuting (or arbitrary) invertible measure-preserving transformations of the probability space $(X,\mathcal X,\mu)$, and let $\mathcal I_T,\mathcal I_S$ denote the $\sigma$-algebras of $T$- and $S$-invariant sets, with $\mathbb E(\cdot\mid\mathcal I_T)$, $\mathbb E(\cdot\mid\mathcal I_S)$ the corresponding conditional expectations.

(a) Show that almost surely in $\omega$, for every such system $(X,\mathcal X,\mu,T,S)$ and every $f,g\in L^\infty(\mu)$,
$$\lim_{N\to\infty}\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N} T^n f \cdot S^{a_n(\omega)} g \;=\; \mathbb E(f\mid\mathcal I_T)\cdot \mathbb E(g\mid\mathcal I_S)$$
in $L^2(\mu)$.

(b) If moreover $\sigma_n = n^{-a}$ for some $a\in(0,1)$, show that the convergence in (a) also holds pointwise $\mu$-almost everywhere.

original_question: Let (a_n(ω)) and (b_n(ω)) be two independent random sequences built from selection probabilities n^{-a} and n^{-b} with a, b ∈ (0,1) and a ≠ b. Is it almost surely true that for every system (X, X, µ, T, S) and bounded functions f, g, the averages (1/N) Σ T^{a_n(ω)} f · S^{b_n(ω)} g converge, in L2 or pointwise, to E(f | I_T) · E(g | I_S)?

original_question: A system with multiplicative structure is a quadruple (X, X, µ, T_n) where T_0 = T_1 = id and T_m ◦ T_n = T_{mn}. In every such system and for every measurable set A of positive measure, do there exist integers m > n ≥ 1 such that µ(T_{2mn} A ∩ T_{(m-n)(m+n)} A) > 0?
self_contained_problem:
Let $(X,\mathcal{X},\mu)$ be a probability space, and let $(T_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ be a family of invertible measure-preserving transformations of $(X,\mathcal{X},\mu)$ satisfying
\[
T_0 = T_1 = \mathrm{id}, \qquad T_m \circ T_n = T_{mn} \quad \text{for all } m,n\in\mathbb{N}.
\]
Such a quadruple $(X,\mathcal{X},\mu,(T_n))$ is called a measure-preserving system with multiplicative structure.

Question: Is it true that for every such system and for every $A\in\mathcal{X}$ with $\mu(A) > 0$, there exist integers $m > n \geq 1$ such that
\[
\mu\bigl(T_{2mn}\, A \,\cap\, T_{(m-n)(m+n)}\, A\bigr) > 0\,?
\]
(Here $(2mn,\, m^2-n^2,\, m^2+n^2)$ is the standard parametrization of Pythagorean triples, so the question concerns simultaneous multiplicative recurrence along the legs of a Pythagorean triple.)
status_search_result: Recent work by Frantzikinakis, Klurman and Moreira (2023, published in Forum of Mathematics, Pi, 2025) established partition regularity of Pythagorean pairs in the combinatorial sense, and a 2025 preprint by Frantzikinakis on decomposition results for multiplicative actions develops further tools for multiplicative recurrence along quadratic patterns. None of the located sources claim that the ergodic recurrence question for measure-preserving systems with multiplicative structure along $(2mn, m^2-n^2)$ has been settled, and surveys list multiplicative recurrence along Pythagorean configurations as an outstanding challenge.

original_question: In noncommutative group-based cryptography, what is the most appropriate choice of platform group?

original_question: In noncommutative group-based cryptography, should the underlying group platform be finite or infinite?
self_contained_problem:
In noncommutative group-based cryptography, a "platform group" is a (finitely generated, finitely presented) group G in which certain algorithmic problems (such as the conjugacy search problem, the word problem, the membership problem, or variants of the Diffie–Hellman problem) are used to construct cryptographic primitives. The security of such schemes depends on the existence of efficiently computable normal forms together with computationally hard search problems on G.

Determine, with justification, whether the platform group G used in noncommutative group-based cryptographic protocols should be taken to be finite or infinite. Specifically:

(a) Identify advantages and disadvantages of using a finite group G as a platform (in terms of presence of hard search problems, key-space size, efficiency of group operations, and resistance to known attacks such as length-based and linear-algebraic attacks).

(b) Identify advantages and disadvantages of using an infinite group G as a platform (in terms of the same criteria, including the need for an efficiently computable normal form and bounds on element representation length).

(c) Decide which class — finite groups or infinite groups — provides a more suitable platform for noncommutative group-based cryptography, or give criteria under which one class is preferable to the other.
status_search_result: This is a foundational design question in noncommutative group-based cryptography rather than a precisely formulated mathematical conjecture. The literature reflects ongoing debate: most early proposals (e.g., Anshel–Anshel–Goldfeld, Ko–Lee using braid groups) use infinite groups, while later proposals have explored finite nonabelian groups. No consensus answer has been established, so the question remains open as a matter of cryptographic design.

original_question: Can additional public-key constructions for noncommutative cryptography be built from other search problems and decision problems in combinatorial group theory?
self_contained_problem:
Background. In noncommutative (group-based) public-key cryptography, the security of a protocol typically rests on the conjectured computational hardness of a search problem or a decision problem in a finitely presented (generally nonabelian) group G. Classical examples include:

- The Conjugacy Search Problem: given g, h ∈ G with h = x⁻¹gx for some x ∈ G, find such an x. This underlies the Ko–Lee key-exchange and the Anshel–Anshel–Goldfeld key-exchange when G is taken to be a braid group Bₙ.
- The Word Problem, the Membership Problem, the Subgroup Conjugacy Problem, the Twisted Conjugacy Search Problem, the Power Conjugacy Problem, the Geodesic Length Problem, the Simultaneous Conjugacy Search Problem, the Decomposition Search Problem, etc.

A "public-key construction based on a problem P in combinatorial group theory" means a key-establishment scheme, public-key encryption scheme, or digital signature scheme whose IND-CPA / one-wayness / unforgeability can be reduced (in the standard cryptographic sense) to the assumed average-case hardness of P over an explicitly specified family of group presentations, together with an efficient key-generation, encryption/decryption (or signing/verification) algorithm running in polynomial time in the security parameter.

Problem. Construct new public-key cryptographic primitives for noncommutative cryptography from search problems and decision problems in combinatorial group theory other than those already exploited (e.g., other than the conjugacy search problem in braid groups underlying the Ko–Lee and Anshel–Anshel–Goldfeld protocols). Specifically:

(a) Identify a search or decision problem P in combinatorial group theory, together with a family {Gₙ} of finitely presented groups (with efficiently sampleable instances), such that P is conjectured to be hard on average over this family.

(b) Design an efficient public-key construction (key exchange, encryption, or signature) whose security provably reduces to the average-case hardness of P over {Gₙ}.

(c) Show that the construction is not equivalent (under polynomial-time reductions) to existing braid-group-based or conjugacy-search-based protocols, thereby yielding genuinely new public-key constructions.
status_search_result: The question of building further public-key constructions from additional search/decision problems in combinatorial group theory remains an active research direction. Surveys and monographs (e.g., Myasnikov–Shpilrain–Ushakov's "Non-Commutative Cryptography and Complexity of Group-Theoretic Problems" and the AMS survey "Applications of Group Theory in Cryptography") continue to propose new schemes (e.g., based on decomposition search, complete decomposition, twisted conjugacy, extra-special groups), but no single resolution closes the open-ended program; new constructions continue to be proposed and cryptanalyzed. The question is therefore best classified as an ongoing open research program rather than a settled problem.

original_question: How can the security of these noncommutative group-based cryptographic protocols be analyzed rigorously?
self_contained_problem:
Let G be a finitely presented noncommutative (nonabelian) group, given by a finite presentation with efficient algorithms for multiplication, inversion, and normal form computation. Several public-key cryptographic protocols have been proposed whose security relies on computational problems in such groups, including:

(i) the Anshel–Anshel–Goldfeld commutator key exchange, in which two parties publish tuples of conjugates of public generators and derive a shared key from a commutator;
(ii) the Ko–Lee (and related Diffie–Hellman type) key exchange, whose security is based on variants of the conjugacy search problem in G, e.g. given (g, h) with h = x^{-1} g x for some x in a specified subgroup A ≤ G, recover a suitable conjugator;
(iii) ElGamal-type and other encryption/signature schemes built over noncommutative platforms (braid groups, polycyclic groups, Thompson's group, matrix groups over group rings, etc.).

Develop a rigorous security framework for such protocols. Specifically:

(a) Formulate precise computational and decisional hardness assumptions (e.g. conjugacy search, simultaneous conjugacy search, subgroup-restricted conjugacy, commutator key exchange problem, decomposition problem, membership search) over a chosen platform group G with prescribed distributions on keys and parameters.

(b) Give formal definitions of security (e.g. IND-CPA, IND-CCA, key-indistinguishability against passive/active adversaries) appropriate for these protocols.

(c) Provide reductions proving that breaking the protocol implies solving the underlying group-theoretic problem, or conversely exhibit polynomial-time algorithms (such as length-based, linear centralizer, linear decomposition, or quotient attacks) that break the protocol.

The problem is to carry out such a rigorous security analysis: identify platform groups and parameter distributions for which the underlying problems are provably hard (under standard complexity assumptions), and produce protocols together with proofs of security in a well-defined adversarial model.
status_search_result: The general question of rigorously analyzing the security of noncommutative group-based cryptographic protocols remains an active research area with many open subproblems. Significant partial progress has been made: e.g., a linear centralizer attack provides provable polynomial-time cryptanalysis of the Anshel–Anshel–Goldfeld commutator key exchange on its original braid-group platform, and length-based, linear decomposition, and quotient attacks break many concrete proposals. However, surveys note that provable-security treatments (with formal reductions) of braid- and polycyclic-group cryptosystems remain sparse, and the broader program of giving rigorous security proofs across noncommutative platforms is still open.

original_question: What notion of security should be used for noncommutative group-based cryptography: practicality, worst-case complexity, average-case complexity, generic complexity, or some other measure?
self_contained_problem:
In group-based (noncommutative) cryptography, cryptographic protocols are built on computationally hard algorithmic problems in infinite (often nonabelian) groups, such as the conjugacy search problem, the word problem, the membership problem, or the decomposition problem in classes of groups like braid groups, polycyclic groups, Thompson's group, or small-cancellation groups. The "security" of such a protocol depends on what notion of computational hardness is required of the underlying algorithmic problem. Several candidate notions exist:

1. Practicality: actual running times of all known attacks on instances of cryptographic size are infeasible.
2. Worst-case complexity: there is no polynomial-time algorithm that solves every instance of the underlying problem.
3. Average-case complexity: there is no algorithm whose expected running time over a natural distribution on inputs is polynomial.
4. Generic-case complexity: there is no algorithm that runs in polynomial time on a subset of inputs whose density (with respect to a natural stratification, e.g., by word length) tends to 1.
5. Some other (yet to be formulated) measure tailored to cryptographic use, e.g., asymptotic density-based hardness, smoothed complexity, or a measure incorporating the distribution of keys actually produced by the protocol.

Problem. Determine the appropriate notion of security/hardness on which the design and analysis of noncommutative group-based cryptographic schemes should be based. Specifically, formulate a rigorous definition of "secure underlying problem" for group-based cryptography that:

(a) rules out attacks that succeed on a non-negligible fraction of keys actually generated by realistic key-generation procedures;
(b) is robust under the standard reductions used in cryptography (e.g., search-to-decision, hybrid arguments);
(c) correctly reflects observed cryptanalytic successes (such as length-based attacks and linear-algebra attacks against certain Anshel–Anshel–Goldfeld and Ko–Lee type schemes), in the sense that any underlying problem deemed "secure" by the definition is in fact not broken by these attacks;
(d) is at least as strong a guarantee as worst-case hardness, average-case hardness, and generic-case hardness, or alternatively, justify which of these (or which combination) is the right one to adopt.

Equivalently: among practicality, worst-case complexity, average-case complexity, generic-case complexity, or another measure, which one (or which precise combination) should serve as the definition of security for noncommutative group-based cryptography?
status_search_result: The question of which complexity measure should serve as the foundation of security for noncommutative group-based cryptography remains an active research topic. Generic-case complexity has been advocated as more cryptographically meaningful than worst-case or average-case complexity, and is widely used in cryptanalysis of group-based schemes; however, no consensus on a single definitive security definition (combining practicality, worst-case, average-case, and generic-case considerations) has been reached, and surveys continue to list this as an open foundational problem.

original_question: What authentication schemes should be developed for noncommutative group-based cryptography?
self_contained_problem:
Develop and analyze authentication schemes for noncommutative group-based cryptography. Concretely: let $G$ be a finitely presented noncommutative group given by an efficient presentation (so that the word problem is efficiently solvable but the conjugacy search problem, the simultaneous conjugacy search problem, or some related algorithmic problem is conjecturally hard). Design an interactive identification protocol between a prover $P$ (holding a secret $s \in G$ or a secret tuple of group elements) and a verifier $V$ (holding the corresponding public information, e.g.\ a conjugate $w^s = s^{-1}ws$ for a public $w \in G$, or other public data derived from $s$) such that:

(a) (Completeness) An honest prover knowing $s$ is accepted with probability $1$.
(b) (Soundness) Any probabilistic polynomial-time prover not knowing $s$ is accepted with negligible probability, under a clearly stated computational assumption on $G$ (e.g.\ hardness of the conjugacy search problem, the membership search problem, the decomposition problem, or a related noncommutative group-theoretic problem).
(c) (Zero-knowledge or witness-indistinguishability) The transcript of the interaction reveals no efficiently extractable information about $s$ beyond what is implied by the public data.

The task is to propose such schemes, identify candidate platform groups (e.g., braid groups, Thompson's group, polycyclic groups, small cancellation groups, matrix groups over noncommutative rings) on which the underlying hardness assumption is plausible, and rigorously prove the completeness, soundness, and zero-knowledge properties, as well as resistance to known attacks (length-based attacks, linear-algebra attacks, quotient attacks).
status_search_result: Several authentication/identification schemes based on noncommutative groups have been proposed (e.g., Sibert–Dehornoy–Girault braid-group identification, schemes based on the conjugacy/decomposition search problems, Dehornoy's LD-system based authentication, and more recent constructions using extra special groups and polycyclic groups). However, the broader research program of designing and rigorously analyzing secure, efficient authentication schemes in noncommutative group-based cryptography remains an active area, with many proposed schemes broken by length-based or linear-algebra attacks. The question is therefore best described as an ongoing research program, partially addressed but not closed.

original_question: For polycyclic-group-based cryptography, which commuting subgroups should be chosen so that the described schemes remain secure?
self_contained_problem:
Let $G$ be a polycyclic group, that is, a group admitting a subnormal series $G = G_0 \trianglerighteq G_1 \trianglerighteq \cdots \trianglerighteq G_n = \{1\}$ in which each successive quotient $G_i/G_{i+1}$ is cyclic. Suppose two subgroups $A, B \leq G$ are publicly chosen which commute elementwise, i.e. $ab = ba$ for every $a \in A$ and every $b \in B$. Such a pair $(A,B)$ underlies non-commutative key-exchange protocols of commutator/Ko–Lee type: with a public element $w \in G$, Alice picks a secret $a \in A$ and publishes $w^a$, Bob picks a secret $b \in B$ and publishes $w^b$, and the shared key is $w^{ab} = w^{ba}$.

Determine criteria for choosing the polycyclic group $G$ together with the commuting subgroups $A, B \leq G$ so that the resulting key-exchange (and related conjugacy/commutator-based) schemes are provably secure: namely, identify a class of polycyclic platform groups $G$ and pairs of commuting subgroups $(A,B)$ for which
(i) the conjugacy search problem (given $w$ and $w^x$ with $x \in A$ or $x \in B$, recover $x$) and the simultaneous/commutator variants are computationally hard,
(ii) known cryptanalytic techniques (length-based attacks, linear/decomposition attacks, quotient and Hirsch-length based attacks) do not succeed in subexponential time, and
(iii) elements of $A$ and $B$ admit efficient sampling and normal-form computation in $G$.

Equivalently: characterize the appropriate choice of commuting subgroups $A, B$ inside polycyclic groups $G$ which renders these schemes secure.
status_search_result: Subsequent surveys on polycyclic group-based cryptography (notably the 2016 survey on the status of polycyclic group-based cryptography and the 2022 survey on group-based cryptography in the quantum era) continue to list the choice of commuting subgroups (and platform polycyclic groups) for commutator/Ko–Lee-type schemes as an unresolved design question. While particular proposed classes have been broken by length-based and linear decomposition attacks, no general criterion guaranteeing security has been established.

original_question: What is the computational complexity of the search conjugacy problem in polycyclic groups?
self_contained_problem:
A group $G$ is called polycyclic if it admits a subnormal series
$$\{1\}=G_0\trianglelefteq G_1\trianglelefteq\cdots\trianglelefteq G_n=G$$
in which every quotient $G_{i+1}/G_i$ is cyclic. Every polycyclic group is finitely presented and admits a polycyclic presentation, with respect to which elements have a unique normal form whose bit-length serves as the natural input size measure.

The conjugacy decision problem for $G$ asks, given two elements $u,v\in G$ (in normal form), to decide whether there exists $g\in G$ such that $g^{-1}ug=v$. The search conjugacy problem asks for an algorithm that, given such $u,v\in G$ which are known (or verified) to be conjugate, outputs a specific conjugating element $g\in G$ with $g^{-1}ug=v$.

Determine the computational complexity of the search conjugacy problem in polycyclic groups: provide tight upper and lower bounds (as a function of the input length, and uniformly or non-uniformly in the group $G$) on the time complexity required to produce a conjugator $g$, and on the bit-length of a smallest such $g$ that always exists.
status_search_result: The decision version of the conjugacy problem in polycyclic groups has been shown to be NP-complete in the uniform setting (Cavallo–Kahrobaei, 2014), and reductions show the search version is at least as hard as subset-sum-style problems. However, no precise tight complexity classification of the search conjugacy problem for polycyclic groups (including uniform upper bounds, conjugator length bounds, and matching lower bounds) appears to be established; the question remains open and is the subject of ongoing investigation.

original_question: What is the computational complexity of the decision conjugacy problem in polycyclic groups, for example for the Eick-Ostheimer algorithm?
self_contained_problem:
A group $G$ is called polycyclic if it admits a subnormal series $G = G_0 \trianglerighteq G_1 \trianglerighteq \cdots \trianglerighteq G_n = \{1\}$ in which every quotient $G_i/G_{i+1}$ is cyclic. Every polycyclic group is finitely presented and admits a polycyclic presentation, with respect to which elements have a unique normal form. The decision conjugacy problem for a polycyclic group $G$ asks: given two elements $u,v \in G$ (specified in normal form with respect to a fixed polycyclic presentation), decide whether there exists $g \in G$ such that $g^{-1} u g = v$. It is known that this problem is decidable on polycyclic groups, and an explicit algorithm (the Eick–Ostheimer algorithm) has been described that reduces conjugacy testing to computations involving unit groups of orders in algebraic number fields.

Determine the computational complexity of the decision conjugacy problem in polycyclic groups, given as input two elements in normal form together with a polycyclic presentation of the group. In particular, analyze the worst-case time complexity of the Eick–Ostheimer algorithm as a function of the input size (e.g., the bit-length of the inputs and the Hirsch length of the group).
status_search_result: Subsequent work has established partial complexity results: the uniform conjugacy problem over a family of polycyclic groups has been shown to be NP-complete (reduced from subset sum), and empirical studies on metabelian polycyclic groups suggest the Eick–Ostheimer algorithm scales very poorly (over 100 hours for Hirsch length 14). However, a precise worst-case complexity analysis of the Eick–Ostheimer algorithm itself, and a tight complexity classification of the decision conjugacy problem for general polycyclic groups, do not appear to have been fully resolved.

original_question: What is the computational complexity of the collection algorithm used to compute normal forms of elements in polycyclic groups?
self_contained_problem:
A polycyclic group $G$ is a group that admits a subnormal series
$$G = G_1 \trianglerighteq G_2 \trianglerighteq \cdots \trianglerighteq G_{n+1} = \{1\}$$
in which every quotient $G_i/G_{i+1}$ is cyclic. Choose generators $g_i \in G_i$ such that $g_i G_{i+1}$ generates $G_i/G_{i+1}$, and let $r_i \in \{2,3,\ldots\} \cup \{\infty\}$ be the order of $g_i G_{i+1}$. The group $G$ then admits a polycyclic (consistent) presentation on $g_1,\ldots,g_n$ with power relations $g_i^{r_i} = w_{i,i}$ (when $r_i$ is finite) and conjugation relations $g_j^{g_i} = w_{i,j}$ and $g_j^{g_i^{-1}} = w'_{i,j}$ for $1 \le i < j \le n$, where each right-hand side is a normal word $g_{i+1}^{e_{i+1}} \cdots g_n^{e_n}$ with $0 \le e_k < r_k$ when $r_k$ is finite. Every element of $G$ has a unique normal form $g_1^{a_1} g_2^{a_2} \cdots g_n^{a_n}$ with $0 \le a_i < r_i$ when $r_i$ is finite and $a_i \in \mathbb{Z}$ otherwise. The collection algorithm takes an arbitrary word in the generators $g_1^{\pm 1},\ldots,g_n^{\pm 1}$ and, by repeatedly applying the power and conjugation relations to move smaller-indexed generators to the left, produces this normal form.

Determine the worst-case computational complexity of the collection algorithm for computing the normal form of an input word of length $\ell$ in a polycyclic group of Hirsch length $n$ given by a consistent polycyclic presentation, as a function of $\ell$, $n$, and the bit-length of exponents appearing in the relations and the input.
status_search_result: Several partial results exist. Improved collection algorithms (e.g., Gebhardt's "Efficient Collection in Infinite Polycyclic Groups", J. Symb. Comp. 2002) give better bounds in terms of exponents in collected words but no closed-form complexity for the general polycyclic case. For the special case of finitely generated nilpotent groups, Mal'cev-coordinate methods (Macdonald–Miasnikov–Nikolaev–Vassileva, and the logspace/compressed-word work of Macdonald et al., arXiv:1503.03888) yield logspace and quasilinear-time normal-form algorithms. A general sharp complexity bound for collection in arbitrary polycyclic groups does not appear to be established, so the question seems only partially resolved.

original_question: What is the computational complexity of the twisted search conjugacy problem in polycyclic groups?
self_contained_problem:
Let $G$ be a polycyclic group, given by a finite polycyclic presentation. Recall that $G$ is polycyclic if it has a subnormal series $G = G_0 \triangleright G_1 \triangleright \cdots \triangleright G_n = \{1\}$ with each quotient $G_i/G_{i+1}$ cyclic. Given an endomorphism $\varphi : G \to G$ (specified by the images of the polycyclic generators), two elements $u, v \in G$ are said to be $\varphi$-twisted conjugate if there exists $g \in G$ such that $v = g^{-1} u\, \varphi(g)$.

The twisted search conjugacy problem is: given as input a polycyclic presentation of $G$, an endomorphism $\varphi$, and two elements $u, v \in G$ that are known to be $\varphi$-twisted conjugate, compute an explicit element $g \in G$ such that $v = g^{-1} u\, \varphi(g)$.

Determine the computational complexity of this twisted search conjugacy problem over the class of polycyclic groups (e.g., establish tight upper and lower bounds, or determine whether it is solvable in polynomial time, NP-complete, or harder).
status_search_result: Recent work has produced practical algorithms for deciding twisted conjugacy in polycyclic-by-finite groups (Tertooy and others, 2020 and 2025) and has studied complexity of ordinary conjugacy search in polycyclic groups, showing for instance that the uniform conjugacy problem can be NP-complete in some polycyclic families. However, no precise complexity classification of the twisted search conjugacy problem in polycyclic groups appears in the literature; the problem is still posed as an open question.

original_question: What is the computational complexity of the Reidemeister-Schreier rewriting algorithm in free groups?
self_contained_problem:
Let $F$ be a finitely generated free group with free generating set $X$, and let $H \leq F$ be a subgroup of finite index given by a Schreier transversal $T$ (a set of coset representatives closed under taking prefixes). The Reidemeister–Schreier rewriting procedure produces, from a word $w \in F$ representing an element of $H$, an expression of $w$ as a word in the Schreier generators $\{\, t x \cdot \overline{tx}^{\,-1} : t \in T,\ x \in X,\ tx \notin T\,\}$ of $H$, where $\overline{g}$ denotes the coset representative of $g$ in $T$.

Determine the computational complexity of the Reidemeister–Schreier rewriting algorithm in free groups. More precisely, give tight upper and lower bounds (as a function of the length $|w|$ of the input word, the rank $|X|$ of $F$, and the index $[F:H]$ together with the size of the Schreier transversal) on the time required to rewrite an arbitrary input word $w \in H$ as a word in the Schreier generators of $H$.
status_search_result: Standard references note that the Reidemeister–Schreier rewriting algorithm can have worse-than-exponential complexity in the rank/index, motivating alternative rewriting methods. However, no precise tight complexity bound (matching upper and lower bounds) for the rewriting algorithm in free groups appears to be established in the literature surveyed; the question of its precise complexity seems to remain open.

original_question: What is the generic-case complexity of the search conjugacy problem in polycyclic groups?

original_question: For polycyclic groups, both finite and infinite, can quantum algorithms be designed for the decision problems used in cryptography?
self_contained_problem:
A group $G$ is called polycyclic if it admits a subnormal series
$$\{1\} = G_0 \triangleleft G_1 \triangleleft \cdots \triangleleft G_n = G$$
in which every quotient $G_{i+1}/G_i$ is cyclic. Polycyclic groups (both finite and infinite) have been proposed as platforms for group-based cryptography, where security relies on the presumed hardness of certain algorithmic decision problems, such as the conjugacy (search) problem, the twisted conjugacy problem, the word problem in specific quotients, the subgroup membership problem, and the conjugacy decomposition problem.

Design quantum algorithms (running in time polynomial in the input size on a quantum Turing machine / quantum circuit model) that solve these decision problems on polycyclic groups, covering both the finite and the infinite cases. Concretely: for each cryptographically used decision problem on a finitely presented polycyclic group $G$, either
(a) exhibit a polynomial-time quantum algorithm that decides the problem on inputs given as words in a fixed polycyclic generating sequence of $G$, or
(b) prove that no such quantum algorithm exists under standard complexity assumptions.
status_search_result: Recent surveys on post-quantum group-based cryptography (Kahrobaei–Flores, 2022; Kahrobaei et al., AMS Surveys vol. 278) continue to highlight that the quantum complexity of decision problems used in polycyclic-group cryptography (conjugacy search, twisted conjugacy, subgroup membership, etc.) is largely open, and indeed part of the rationale for proposing infinite polycyclic groups is the absence of known efficient quantum attacks. No general polynomial-time quantum algorithm for these decision problems is known, so the question remains open.

original_question: Is there a quantum algorithm for the search conjugacy problem in a polycyclic group that lowers the complexity of solving that problem?
self_contained_problem:
A group $G$ is called polycyclic if it admits a subnormal series
$$G = G_0 \trianglerighteq G_1 \trianglerighteq \cdots \trianglerighteq G_n = \{1\}$$
in which every quotient $G_i/G_{i+1}$ is cyclic. The search conjugacy problem in $G$ is the following algorithmic problem: given two elements $u, v \in G$ that are known to be conjugate (i.e., there exists $x \in G$ with $x^{-1} u x = v$), produce an explicit element $x \in G$ that conjugates $u$ to $v$.

The classical complexity of the search conjugacy problem in general polycyclic groups is conjectured to be exponential, and this hardness underlies several proposed group-based cryptographic schemes.

Question: Does there exist a quantum algorithm that solves the search conjugacy problem in an arbitrary polycyclic group with strictly lower (e.g., subexponential or polynomial) computational complexity than the best known classical algorithm?
status_search_result: Recent surveys on polycyclic group-based cryptography in the quantum era (e.g., Kahrobaei–Flores 2022 and the Gryak–Kahrobaei survey on the status of polycyclic group-based cryptography) continue to list the existence of efficient quantum algorithms for the (search) conjugacy problem in polycyclic groups as an open question. While Grover-type speedups and partial results for nil-2 groups via the hidden subgroup problem are known, no quantum algorithm is known to reduce the complexity of the general search conjugacy problem in polycyclic groups.

original_question: How can the proposed noncommutative group-based cryptosystems be implemented in practice?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the following two public-key key-exchange protocols built on a finitely generated noncommutative group $G$ (for instance, a braid group $B_n$):

(a) Ko–Lee protocol. Fix two commuting subgroups $A, B \le G$ (so that $ab = ba$ for every $a \in A$, $b \in B$) and a public element $w \in G$. Alice picks a secret $a \in A$ and publishes $a^{-1} w a$; Bob picks a secret $b \in B$ and publishes $b^{-1} w b$. The shared key is $a^{-1} b^{-1} w b a = b^{-1} a^{-1} w a b$.

(b) Anshel–Anshel–Goldfeld protocol. Public tuples $\bar{x} = (x_1,\dots,x_n)$ and $\bar{y} = (y_1,\dots,y_m)$ in $G$ are fixed. Alice's secret is a word $a$ in the $x_i$ and she publishes $(a^{-1} y_1 a,\dots, a^{-1} y_m a)$; Bob's secret is a word $b$ in the $y_j$ and he publishes $(b^{-1} x_1 b,\dots, b^{-1} x_n b)$. Each party then reconstructs the commutator $[a,b] = a^{-1} b^{-1} a b$ as the shared key.

Security relies on hardness of conjugacy-search and related problems in $G$.

Problem. Provide a concrete and practical implementation of these noncommutative group-based cryptosystems. Specifically:

1. Choose a platform group $G$ together with an explicit finite presentation, a normal form for elements, and efficient algorithms for multiplication, inversion, and reduction to normal form.
2. Specify how public parameters (the element $w$ or the tuples $\bar{x}, \bar{y}$, and the relevant subgroups) are generated so that known attacks (length-based attacks, linear-algebra/linear-representation attacks, summit-set attacks, etc.) are infeasible.
3. Specify how secret keys are sampled from a distribution that yields hard instances of the underlying conjugacy-search or simultaneous-conjugacy-search problem.
4. Give parameter sizes and complexity estimates ensuring a prescribed security level while keeping key sizes and protocol running times competitive with standard number-theoretic systems.

Either exhibit such an implementation with rigorous justification of its security and efficiency, or prove that no such implementation is possible under stated assumptions.
status_search_result: The implementation of noncommutative (especially braid-group) cryptosystems remains an active area without a settled, widely-deployed practical solution. Length-based and linear-representation attacks (Cheon–Jun, Hughes–Tannenbaum, Garber et al.) have repeatedly broken concrete proposed parameter sets for the Ko–Lee and AAG protocols, while research continues on alternative platform groups (Thompson's group, polycyclic groups, matrix groups) and parameter regimes. No standardized practical implementation of these schemes has been adopted, so the question of how to implement them practically and securely remains open.

original_question: Can the computer algebra system GAP be used to build cryptographic implementations that are both practical and secure?
self_contained_problem:
GAP (Groups, Algorithms, Programming) is a free, open-source computer algebra system specialized for computational discrete algebra, with particular emphasis on computational group theory. It provides a high-level programming language, a library of algorithms for groups, rings, fields, algebras, and combinatorial structures, and an extensive database of finite groups and related objects.

A cryptographic implementation is considered practical if it can perform key generation, encryption/decryption (or signing/verification, etc.) on standard inputs within times comparable to mainstream cryptographic libraries (e.g., on the order of milliseconds to seconds for typical parameter sizes). It is considered secure if it correctly implements a cryptographic primitive whose security is supported by accepted hardness assumptions, and if the implementation itself avoids well-known classes of vulnerabilities (such as exploitable side channels through timing variation, faulty randomness, or incorrect arithmetic).

Determine whether GAP, as a programming environment and library, can be used to construct cryptographic implementations that simultaneously satisfy the practicality and security criteria above. More precisely: exhibit either (a) a concrete cryptographic scheme together with a GAP implementation meeting both criteria, with quantitative benchmarks and a security analysis of the implementation, or (b) a justified argument identifying intrinsic obstacles in GAP (e.g., interpreter overhead, lack of constant-time primitives, randomness sources, memory model) that prevent any GAP implementation of standard cryptographic primitives from meeting these criteria.
status_search_result: The question is open-ended and informally posed; no definitive published result establishes that GAP either is or is not suitable for practical and secure cryptography. GAP has been used for prototyping group-based cryptographic schemes (e.g., via packages related to combinatorial group theory), but these are typically research prototypes rather than production-grade implementations, and no authoritative source resolves the question in general.

context_brief: Fractal Weyl law for resonance counting
original_question: For an open chaotic quantum scattering system with hyperbolic trapped set of Minkowski dimension 1 + 2 nu, what is the sharp asymptotic counting law for long-living resonances? Equivalently, in a fixed high-frequency window [k, k + W] - i[0, gamma] or in the semiclassical strip [E - C hbar, E + C hbar] - i[0, gamma hbar], is the number of resonances of order hbar^(-nu), and does there exist a nontrivial profile F(gamma) such that the count equals C F(gamma) hbar^(-nu) + o(hbar^(-nu))?
self_contained_problem:
Consider an open chaotic quantum scattering system whose semiclassical Schrödinger operator P(ℏ) has a hyperbolic trapped set K_E at energy E whose Minkowski (box-counting) dimension equals 1 + 2ν, with 0 ≤ ν < (n-1)/2 in dimension n. Let Res P(ℏ) denote the set of quantum resonances of P(ℏ), regarded as poles of the meromorphic continuation of the resolvent (P(ℏ) − z)^{-1} from the upper half-plane to a conic neighborhood of the real axis.

(Strong fractal Weyl law conjecture.) Prove or disprove: there exists a nondecreasing, not identically vanishing function F : (0, ∞) → [0, ∞) such that, for every C > 0 and every γ > 0,
   #{ z ∈ Res P(ℏ) : Re z ∈ [E − Cℏ, E + Cℏ], −Im z ∈ [0, γℏ] } = C · F(γ) · ℏ^{−ν} + o(ℏ^{−ν})   as ℏ → 0.

(Weak form.) Equivalently, for hyperbolic trapped sets of dimension 1 + 2ν, establish a two-sided bound of the form c_γ ℏ^{−ν} ≤ #{ z ∈ Res P(ℏ) : Re z ∈ [E − Cℏ, E + Cℏ], −Im z ∈ [0, γℏ] } ≤ C_γ ℏ^{−ν} for some constants 0 < c_γ ≤ C_γ depending on γ > 0.

In a high-frequency formulation: for fixed width W > 0 and depth γ > 0, determine the asymptotic count of resonances inside the rectangle [k, k+W] − i[0, γ] of the complex frequency plane as k → ∞.
status_search_result: The fractal Weyl law conjecture remains open in general. Sharp upper bounds of order ℏ^{-ν} are established in hyperbolic settings, but no matching general lower bound (weak form) is known, and the strong asymptotic with profile F(γ) is unproved. Recent work (2025) even provides counterexamples to certain formulations of the law for semiclassical resonances, and numerical studies continue to test the conjecture in specific systems such as three-disk scattering and open quantum maps.

original_question: For open chaotic scattering systems with hyperbolic trapped sets, does there exist a resonance-free strip of depth gamma > 0 below the real axis at high frequency, and what is the optimal value of that gap? In particular, for obstacle scattering, can the asymptotic resonance gap be as large as gamma_cl / 2, or must it be strictly smaller?
self_contained_problem:
Consider an open chaotic scattering system in $\mathbb{R}^n$, for instance the exterior Dirichlet Laplacian $-\Delta$ on $\mathbb{R}^n \setminus \mathcal{O}$, where $\mathcal{O}$ is a finite union of strictly convex smooth obstacles satisfying Ikawa's non-eclipse condition (so that the broken geodesic flow has a hyperbolic, fractal trapped set $K$). Resonances are the poles of the meromorphic continuation of the cutoff resolvent $\chi(-\Delta - k^2)^{-1}\chi$ from $\{\Im k > 0\}$ to the lower half-plane $\{\Im k \le 0\}$. Define the classical decay rate $\gamma_{cl}$ as the (minimal) transverse Lyapunov exponent (equivalently, half the topological entropy of the unstable Jacobian) of the flow restricted to $K$. A "resonance gap" is a number $\gamma > 0$ such that for some $k_0$ the rectangle $\{k \in \mathbb{C} : \Re k \ge k_0,\ -\gamma \le \Im k \le 0\}$ contains no resonances.

(a) Prove that under the above hypotheses there exists $\gamma > 0$ giving a resonance gap at high frequency, and determine the supremum $\gamma_{\max}$ of admissible values of $\gamma$.

(b) For obstacle scattering with hyperbolic trapped set, decide whether the asymptotic resonance gap can attain the value $\gamma_{cl}/2$, or whether one must always have $\gamma_{\max} < \gamma_{cl}/2$.
status_search_result: The existence of some resonance gap for obstacle scattering with hyperbolic trapped sets is known (e.g., via topological-pressure bounds of Ikawa, Gaspard–Rice, Nonnenmacher–Zworski, and via the fractal uncertainty principle in dimension 2 by Vacossin (arXiv:2201.08259)). However, the optimal value of the gap, and in particular whether it can reach the conjectural bound $\gamma_{cl}/2$ (analogous to the conjecture for hyperbolic surfaces) or must be strictly smaller, remains an open problem. Recent works (e.g., Dyatlov–Zahl, Bourgain–Dyatlov, Jakobson–Naud) have improved gaps for hyperbolic surfaces but have not settled the optimal asymptotic gap for obstacles.

context_brief: Phase cancellations for sharper spectral bounds
original_question: Can one rigorously prove enough cancellation among the phases accumulated along different classical paths in the quantum monodromy expansion so that the off-diagonal terms behave as if the phases were random, yielding the sharper spectral-radius bound rsp(M(alpha, hbar)) <= exp(P(-phi^+ + 2 log |alpha|)/2 + eps)?
self_contained_problem:
Setup. Consider a smooth open chaotic Hamiltonian flow on a phase space, restricted to a neighbourhood of its trapped set K, and its semiclassical quantization through a quantum monodromy operator M(α, ℏ), where α = α_1 α_2 ⋯ α_n ranges over symbolic words of length n that label the classical orbits (paths) reflected/encoded by a symbolic dynamics. To each such symbolic path α one associates a classical action θ_α and a "weight" coming from the unstable Jacobian; standard semiclassical analysis yields, for the matrix elements of an iterate L_s^n of the associated transfer operator (or of M(α, ℏ)),

   ⟨e_α' , L_s^n e_α⟩ ≈ J_{αα'} · e^{ i (θ_α − θ_{α'}) / ℏ },

with J_{αα'} a real, positive, slowly varying amplitude. Let φ^+ denote the (positive) topological pressure functional associated with the unstable Jacobian on K, evaluated at the relevant value, and let P(·) denote the topological pressure functional for the classical flow on the trapped set. Define the spectral radius

   r_sp(M(α, ℏ)) := lim_{n → ∞} ‖M(α, ℏ)^n‖^{1/n}.

The diagonal contribution to ‖L_s^n‖^2 is controlled by the standard pressure sum

   ∑_α e^{−n φ^+(α) + 2n log|α|},   (∗)

giving an immediate "trivial" spectral bound. The off-diagonal contribution involves the oscillating factors e^{i(θ_α − θ_{α'})/ℏ}.

Problem. Prove that the phases {θ_α / ℏ}, considered as α varies over symbolic words of length n in the semiclassical limit ℏ → 0 with n ≍ |log ℏ|, exhibit cancellation at least as strong as that of independent uniformly distributed random phases, in the following quantitative sense: the off-diagonal sums 

   ∑_{α ≠ α'} J_{αα'} e^{i(θ_α − θ_{α'})/ℏ}

are, with controlled error, of the same order of magnitude as the diagonal sum (∗); and consequently establish the sharper spectral-radius bound

   r_sp(M(α, ℏ)) ≤ exp( P(−φ^+ + 2 log|α|)/2 + ε )

for every ε > 0, in the semiclassical limit ℏ → 0.
status_search_result: The conjectured "pressure-half" spectral bound for quantum monodromy operators in open chaotic systems, which would follow from genuine pseudo-randomness of the classical actions (phases) along symbolic orbits, remains open. It is the well-known fractal-Weyl/pressure-gap conjecture in semiclassical resonance theory; only the trivial bound (without the factor 1/2) and partial improvements under additional assumptions (e.g., specific symmetry/arithmetic settings or under a normal hyperbolicity / pressure < 0 assumption giving resonance gaps) are currently known. No proof of the full pseudo-random cancellation has been published.

original_question: For obstacle scattering in the high-frequency limit, given an infinite sequence of long-living resonances k_j with Re k_j -> infinity, what spatial or phase-space structure do the associated metastable states have? More specifically, can one prove in the obstacle setting that these metastable states microlocalize near the outgoing tail K^+ and are described by semiclassical measures that are invariant under the flow up to global decay?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathcal{O} \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ ($n \geq 2$) be a smooth, bounded obstacle with $\mathbb{R}^n \setminus \mathcal{O}$ connected, and consider the Dirichlet Laplacian $-\Delta$ on the exterior domain $\Omega = \mathbb{R}^n \setminus \mathcal{O}$. The associated outgoing resolvent $R(k) = (-\Delta - k^2)^{-1}$, defined for $\mathrm{Im}\, k > 0$, admits a meromorphic continuation to the lower half-plane (or to the logarithmic cover when $n$ is even); its poles $k_j \in \mathbb{C}$ with $\mathrm{Im}\, k_j < 0$ are the scattering resonances. To each resonance $k_j$ is associated a metastable state (resonant eigenfunction) $u_j$, satisfying $(-\Delta - k_j^2) u_j = 0$ in $\Omega$ with Dirichlet boundary conditions and outgoing radiation behaviour at infinity.

Let $\Phi^t$ denote the broken billiard (geodesic) flow on the cosphere bundle of $\Omega$ corresponding to free propagation in $\Omega$ with specular reflection at $\partial \mathcal{O}$. Define the trapped set
$$ K = \{ \rho \in S^* \Omega : \Phi^t(\rho) \text{ remains in a bounded set for all } t \in \mathbb{R} \}, $$
and the outgoing tail
$$ K^+ = \{ \rho \in S^* \Omega : \Phi^t(\rho) \text{ remains in a bounded set for all } t \leq 0 \}. $$

Suppose there exists an infinite sequence of resonances $(k_{j_\ell})$ with $\mathrm{Re}\, k_{j_\ell} \to \infty$ and $|\mathrm{Im}\, k_{j_\ell}|$ uniformly bounded (long-living resonances). Normalize the corresponding metastable states $u_{j_\ell}$ (e.g. on a fixed bounded region containing $\mathcal{O}$).

Prove or disprove the following microlocalization statement: any semiclassical defect measure $\mu$ obtained as a weak-$*$ limit of the Wigner distributions of $u_{j_\ell}$ (rescaled so that $h_\ell = 1/\mathrm{Re}\, k_{j_\ell}$) is supported in the outgoing tail $K^+$, and is invariant under the billiard flow $\Phi^t$ up to a global exponential decay rate determined by $\lim_\ell \mathrm{Im}\, k_{j_\ell}$, i.e. $(\Phi^t)_* \mu = e^{-2 \alpha t} \mu$ for the appropriate constant $\alpha \geq 0$.
status_search_result: Rigorous results on microlocalization of long-living metastable states on the outgoing tail and their description via flow-invariant semiclassical measures (up to global decay) have been established for smooth Hamiltonian flows and open quantum maps (e.g., work of Nonnenmacher–Zworski and subsequent literature, including recent results on chaotic scattering as of 2024), but no analogous rigorous result is known for obstacle scattering with billiard dynamics. The problem appears to remain open.

original_question: Fix Lambda >= 0 and a sequence of resonances z(hbar) whose imaginary parts satisfy Im z(hbar) / hbar -> -Lambda / 2. Which Lambda-eigenmeasures can occur as semiclassical measures of the corresponding metastable states, and is there a favored or even unique limiting measure?
self_contained_problem:
Setup. Let $(M,g)$ be a Riemannian manifold (or, more generally, the configuration space of a Hamiltonian scattering system) on which a self-adjoint semiclassical Schrödinger-type operator $P(\hbar) = -\hbar^2 \Delta/2 + V$ is defined, whose classical Hamiltonian flow $\Phi^t$ on phase space $T^*M$ admits a hyperbolic (chaotic) trapped set $K$. Resonances of $P(\hbar)$ are the poles $z(\hbar) \in \mathbb{C}$, $\operatorname{Im} z(\hbar) \le 0$, of the meromorphic continuation of the resolvent $(P(\hbar) - z)^{-1}$, with associated metastable (resonant) states $u_\hbar$.

Given $\Lambda \ge 0$, a $\Lambda$-eigenmeasure is a Radon measure $\mu$ on phase space supported on the outgoing tail of the trapped set such that, for every $t \ge 0$ and every continuous compactly supported observable $a$,
$$\int (a \circ \Phi^t)\, d\mu = e^{-\Lambda t} \int a\, d\mu,$$
i.e., $\mu$ is conditionally invariant under the classical flow with decay rate $\Lambda$.

A semiclassical measure of a sequence $(u_\hbar)$ of normalized resonant states is any weak-$*$ limit point of the Wigner distributions $W_\hbar[u_\hbar]$ as $\hbar \to 0$. It is known that under the assumption
$$\frac{\operatorname{Im} z(\hbar)}{\hbar} \longrightarrow -\frac{\Lambda}{2} \qquad (\hbar \to 0),$$
every such semiclassical measure is a $\Lambda$-eigenmeasure.

Problem. Fix $\Lambda \ge 0$ and consider all sequences of resonances $z(\hbar)$ satisfying the asymptotic decay condition above, together with associated normalized metastable states.

(a) Characterize precisely which $\Lambda$-eigenmeasures arise as semiclassical measures of such sequences.

(b) Determine whether there exists a distinguished ("favored") $\Lambda$-eigenmeasure that is selected in this semiclassical limit, and in particular whether the semiclassical measure is unique (independent of the choice of resonance sequence) for chaotic open systems.
status_search_result: The general classification problem appears to remain open, but several partial results exist. Ingremeau (2017) showed that, under a no-resonance-strip assumption, distorted plane waves in chaotic scattering admit a unique semiclassical measure. More recent work (Ketzmerick–Clauß et al., 2024–2025) proposes selection criteria via generalized Ulam approximations of the Perron–Frobenius operator that pick out a particular conditionally invariant measure of given decay rate, with numerical evidence that resonance states converge to it. A complete characterization of all attainable Lambda-eigenmeasures and a proof of uniqueness in full generality have not been established.

original_question: Given an incoming scattering state u_E,in at energy E > 0 for a semiclassical scattering Hamiltonian, what is the spatial or phase-space structure of the full solution u_E inside the interaction region? In particular, how are that structure and its visible patterns influenced by trajectories that spend a long time near the trapped set K_E or remain forever on the incoming tail K_E^-?
self_contained_problem:
Let $P(h) = -h^2 \Delta + V(x)$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$, with $V \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$ (or more generally a smooth short-range potential), and fix an energy $E > 0$ that is non-trapping at infinity in the usual semiclassical sense. Let $p(x,\xi) = |\xi|^2 + V(x)$ denote the classical Hamiltonian, and let $\Phi^t$ be its Hamiltonian flow on the energy shell $\Sigma_E = p^{-1}(E)$. Define the trapped set at energy $E$ by
$$K_E = \{(x,\xi) \in \Sigma_E : \Phi^t(x,\xi) \text{ remains in a compact set for all } t \in \mathbb{R}\},$$
and the incoming and outgoing tails by
$$K_E^\pm = \{(x,\xi) \in \Sigma_E : \Phi^t(x,\xi) \text{ remains in a compact set for all } \mp t \ge 0\}.$$

For an incoming asymptotic data $u_{E,\mathrm{in}}$ at energy $E$, let $u_E$ denote the corresponding generalized eigenfunction of $P(h)$ with $(P(h)-E)u_E = 0$ whose incoming part equals $u_{E,\mathrm{in}}$ (defined via the standard scattering / Eisenstein construction).

Describe, in the semiclassical limit $h \to 0$, the spatial and phase-space structure of $u_E$ inside the interaction region (i.e., on the support of $V$ and a neighborhood of $K_E$). Specifically, characterize:

(a) the semiclassical wavefront set / Lagrangian structure of $u_E$ in terms of $u_{E,\mathrm{in}}$ and the forward flow-out of its wavefront set under $\Phi^t$;

(b) how classical trajectories that spend a long transient time near $K_E$, and trajectories that lie in the incoming tail $K_E^-$, contribute to the amplitude, concentration, and visible interference patterns of $u_E$ in the interior;

(c) quantitative estimates (in $h$) for the local mass and microlocal concentration of $u_E$ near $K_E$ and along $K_E^-$ as functions of properties of $K_E$ (e.g. its topological pressure, dimension, or hyperbolicity).
status_search_result: The problem is a broad research question concerning the fine semiclassical structure of scattering eigenfunctions in the presence of a (typically fractal/hyperbolic) trapped set. context_brief: Ampleness of the maximal abelian extension of Q
original_question: Is the maximal abelian extension Qab of the rational numbers Q an ample field, where a field K is called ample when every smooth K-curve with a K-rational point has infinitely many K-rational points, equivalently when K satisfies the other equivalent conditions listed in Proposition 2.1?
self_contained_problem:
A field $K$ is called ample (also known as large) if every smooth $K$-curve that has at least one $K$-rational point has infinitely many $K$-rational points. Equivalent characterizations include: $K$ is existentially closed in the Laurent series field $K((t))$; every smooth, geometrically integral $K$-variety with a $K$-rational point has a Zariski-dense set of $K$-rational points; and $K$ is existentially closed in some Henselian non-trivially valued extension of $K$.

Let $\mathbb{Q}^{\mathrm{ab}}$ denote the maximal abelian extension of the field of rational numbers $\mathbb{Q}$, that is, the compositum inside a fixed algebraic closure $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ of all finite Galois extensions of $\mathbb{Q}$ with abelian Galois group (equivalently, by the Kronecker–Weber theorem, $\mathbb{Q}^{\mathrm{ab}} = \mathbb{Q}(\mu_\infty)$, the field obtained by adjoining all roots of unity to $\mathbb{Q}$).

Determine whether $\mathbb{Q}^{\mathrm{ab}}$ is an ample field.
status_search_result: The question of whether $\mathbb{Q}^{\mathrm{ab}}$ is an ample/large field appears to remain open. It is known (work of Pop, Harbater) that if $\mathbb{Q}^{\mathrm{ab}}$ were ample, Shafarevich's conjecture on the freeness of $\mathrm{Gal}(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}/\mathbb{Q}^{\mathrm{ab}})$ would follow, and Shafarevich's conjecture itself remains open over number fields. Recent literature on "big fields that are not large" continues to discuss this as an outstanding problem.

original_question: Is the maximal solvable Galois extension Qsolv of Q pseudo algebraically closed, meaning that every absolutely irreducible Q-variety has a Qsolv-rational point? Equivalently, does every absolutely irreducible Q-variety admit a solvable rational point?

context_brief: Whether Qtot,S intersect Qsolv is PSC
original_question: Fix a finite set S of places of Q, and let Qtot,S be the maximal extension of Q in which every place in S is totally split. Is the field Qtot,S intersected with Qsolv pseudo S-closed (PSC), where a subfield K of Qtot,S is PSC if every smooth Q-variety that has a point over Qp for each p in S (with Q_infinity = R) has a K-rational point?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathbb{Q}$ be the field of rational numbers, with algebraic closure $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$. The set of places of $\mathbb{Q}$ consists of the prime numbers together with the archimedean place $\infty$, and we set $\mathbb{Q}_\infty := \mathbb{R}$. Fix a finite set $S$ of places of $\mathbb{Q}$.

Define the field of totally $S$-adic numbers
$$\mathbb{Q}_{\mathrm{tot},S} \;=\; \bigcap_{p\in S}\;\bigcap_{\sigma\in\mathrm{Gal}(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}/\mathbb{Q})}\sigma(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}\cap \mathbb{Q}_p^{\mathrm{alg}}),$$
the maximal algebraic extension of $\mathbb{Q}$ inside $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ in which every place $p\in S$ is totally split. Let $\mathbb{Q}_{\mathrm{solv}}$ denote the maximal solvable extension of $\mathbb{Q}$ in $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ (the compositum of all finite Galois extensions of $\mathbb{Q}$ with solvable Galois group).

A subfield $K \subseteq \mathbb{Q}_{\mathrm{tot},S}$ is called pseudo $S$-adically closed (PSC) if every smooth geometrically integral $\mathbb{Q}$-variety $V$ which has a $\mathbb{Q}_p$-rational point for every $p\in S$ has a $K$-rational point.

Question: Is the field $\mathbb{Q}_{\mathrm{tot},S}\cap \mathbb{Q}_{\mathrm{solv}}$ PSC?
