original_question: (Well-known problem). Does there exist a finitely presented(infinite) simple group of finite cohomological dimension greater than 2?

original_question: An isometric action of a group G on a metric space S is called acylindrical if for every ε > 0 there exist R, N > 0 such that for every two points x, y with d(x, y) ⩾ R, there are at most N elements g ∈ G satisfying d(x, gx) ⩽ ε and d(y, gy) ⩽ ε. A group is said to be acylindrically hyperbolic if it is not virtually cyclic and admits an acylindrical action on a hyperbolic space with unbounded orbits. Is the automorphism group of a finitely generated acylindrically hyperbolic group also acylindrically hyperbolic?
self_contained_problem:
Definitions. An isometric action of a group $G$ on a metric space $(S,d)$ is called acylindrical if for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there exist constants $R, N > 0$ such that for any two points $x, y \in S$ with $d(x,y) \geq R$, the number of elements $g \in G$ satisfying simultaneously $d(x, gx) \leq \varepsilon$ and $d(y, gy) \leq \varepsilon$ is at most $N$. A group $G$ is called acylindrically hyperbolic if $G$ is not virtually cyclic and $G$ admits an acylindrical isometric action on a (Gromov-)hyperbolic metric space with unbounded orbits.

Question. Let $G$ be a finitely generated acylindrically hyperbolic group. Is the automorphism group $\operatorname{Aut}(G)$ also acylindrically hyperbolic?
status_search_result: The general question appears to remain open. Significant partial results are known: Genevois (2021) proved that the automorphism group of any infinitely-ended finitely generated group is acylindrically hyperbolic; analogous results hold for Aut(F_n) (n≥2), for automorphism groups of one-ended hyperbolic groups, and for relatively hyperbolic groups (with a finite collection of finitely generated proper peripheral subgroups). However, no source confirms a full positive (or negative) answer for arbitrary finitely generated acylindrically hyperbolic groups.

$$T \cap G' = T \cap H',$$
where $G'$ and $H'$ denote the derived subgroups of $G$ and $H$, respectively?

Background context: For every prime $p \geq 5$ such a nontrivial characteristic subgroup is known to exist in any finite $p$-group $T$. For $p = 3$ it is known that there exist two nontrivial characteristic subgroups $K_1, K_2$ of $T$ such that, with $H_i = N_G(K_i)$,
$$T \cap G' = (T \cap H_1')(T \cap H_2').$$
The symmetric group $S_4$ shows that the analogous statement can fail for $p = 2$ in some Sylow 2-subgroups. The question asks whether, for $p = 3$, a single characteristic subgroup suffices.

original_question: Let p be a prime, and P a finite p-group. (a) Suppose that P has an abelian subgroup of order pn. For which n does P necessarily have a normal abelian subgroup of order pn? (b) Suppose that P has an elementary abelian subgroup of order pn. For which n does P necessarily have a normal elementary abelian subgroup of order pn? It is easy to see that for p = 2, the answer to(b) is “yes” only for n = 1. The answer to both questions is “yes” for n < (p + 2)/2(G. G. Glauberman, J. Algebra, 319, no. 2(2008), 800–805), as well as for n ⩽ 5 when p ̸= 2(M. Konvisser, D. Jonah, J. Algebra, 34(1975), 309–330). The answer to both questions is “no” for n ⩾ (p+9)/2 when p ⩾ 5(for p ⩾ 7 due to G. Glauberman, Contemp. Math., 524(2010), 61–65; for p = 3, 5 due to Ya. G. Berkovich, J. Algebra, 248, no. 2(2002), 472–553). Thus, the only open cases for p ⩾ 5 are n = 6 for p = 5, and n = (p + 3)/2, (p + 5)/2, (p + 7)/2 for p > 5.
self_contained_problem:
Let p be an odd prime with p ≥ 5, and let P be a finite p-group. Determine, for the values of n listed below, whether each of the following implications holds for every such P:

(a) If P contains an abelian subgroup of order p^n, then P contains a normal abelian subgroup of order p^n.

(b) If P contains an elementary abelian subgroup of order p^n (i.e., an abelian subgroup of exponent p), then P contains a normal elementary abelian subgroup of order p^n.

The cases to resolve are:
- p = 5 and n = 6;
- p > 5 and n ∈ {(p+3)/2, (p+5)/2, (p+7)/2}.

(It is known that the answer is "yes" whenever n < (p+2)/2 or n ≤ 5 with p ≠ 2, and "no" whenever n ≥ (p+9)/2 with p ≥ 5; the problem asks to settle the remaining values of n above.)

original_question: Let L be a finite non-abelian simple group, and let D be a conjugacy class of involutions in L. Consider the complete graph Γ with vertex set D. Define an equivalence relation ∼ (graph coloring) on the set of edges as follows: (a, b) ∼ (c, d) if and only if |ab| = |cd|. An automorphism of the coloured graph Γ is a permutation τ ∈ SD such that(a, b) ∼ (aτ, bτ) for every edge(a, b). Is it true that the automorphism group of Γ is a subgroup of Aut(L)?
self_contained_problem: Let $L$ be a finite non-abelian simple group, and let $D$ be a conjugacy class of involutions in $L$. Form the complete graph $\Gamma$ with vertex set $D$, and colour its edges by the following equivalence relation: for edges $(a,b)$ and $(c,d)$, declare $(a,b)\sim(c,d)$ if and only if the orders of the products satisfy $|ab|=|cd|$. An automorphism of the edge-coloured graph $\Gamma$ is a permutation $\tau\in\mathrm{Sym}(D)$ such that $(a,b)\sim(a^{\tau},b^{\tau})$ for every edge $(a,b)$; equivalently, $|ab|=|a^{\tau}b^{\tau}|$ for all $a,b\in D$. The group $L$ acts on $D$ by conjugation, and this action extends to an action of $\mathrm{Aut}(L)$ on $D$ by colour-preserving permutations, giving a natural embedding of $\mathrm{Aut}(L)/C_{\mathrm{Aut}(L)}(D)$ into the automorphism group $\mathrm{Aut}(\Gamma)$ of the coloured graph. Determine whether $\mathrm{Aut}(\Gamma)$ always equals (is contained in) the image of $\mathrm{Aut}(L)$; that is, decide whether for every finite non-abelian simple group $L$ and every conjugacy class $D$ of involutions of $L$, the automorphism group of the coloured complete graph $\Gamma$ described above is a subgroup of $\mathrm{Aut}(L)$.

original_question: Let G be a finite soluble group with triality, which means that G admits a group of automorphisms S isomorphic to the symmetric group of degree 3 given by the presentation S = ⟨σ, ρ | σ 2 = ρ3 = 1; σρσ = ρ2 ⟩ such that m · mρ · mρ = 1 for all m in the set of commutators M(G):= {[g, σ] | g ∈ G}. Suppose in addition that G = [G, S], the group G is generated by d elements of M(G) and their images under S, and xn = 1 for all x ∈ M(G). Is it true that the Fitting height of G is bounded in terms of d and n? An affirmative answer would provide a reduction of the analogue of the Restricted Burnside Problem for Moufang loops to the nilpotent case.
self_contained_problem:
Let $S = \langle \sigma, \rho \mid \sigma^2 = \rho^3 = 1,\ \sigma\rho\sigma = \rho^2 \rangle$ denote the symmetric group of degree 3. A finite group $G$ is said to be a group with triality if $S$ acts on $G$ by automorphisms in such a way that 
$$m \cdot m^{\rho} \cdot m^{\rho^2} = 1$$
for every element $m$ of the set
$$M(G) := \{[g,\sigma] : g \in G\} = \{g^{-1} g^{\sigma} : g \in G\}.$$
Assume that:
1. $G$ is finite and soluble;
2. $G$ is a group with triality with respect to $S$ as above;
3. $G = [G,S]$;
4. $G$ is generated by $d$ elements of $M(G)$ together with all of their images under the action of $S$;
5. there is a positive integer $n$ such that $x^n = 1$ for every $x \in M(G)$.

The Fitting height (nilpotent length) $h(G)$ of $G$ is the smallest integer $h$ such that the iterated Fitting series
$$1 = F_0(G) \le F_1(G) \le \cdots \le F_h(G) = G$$
reaches $G$, where $F_{i+1}(G)/F_i(G) = F(G/F_i(G))$ is the Fitting subgroup of $G/F_i(G)$.

Question: Must $h(G)$ be bounded by a function depending only on $d$ and $n$?

original_question: Let q be a power of a prime p, and let mn(q) be the maximum p-length of p-solvable subgroups of GL(n, q). Is it true that lim mn(q)/ log2 n = 1? İ. Güloğlu n→∞
self_contained_problem:
Let $p$ be a prime and let $q$ be a power of $p$. Recall that a finite group $G$ is called $p$-solvable if it admits a normal series whose factors are either $p$-groups or $p'$-groups (groups of order coprime to $p$); the $p$-length $\ell_p(G)$ is the minimum number of $p$-group factors that appear in such a series. For each integer $n \geq 1$, define
$$m_n(q) = \max\{\ell_p(H) : H \leq \mathrm{GL}(n,q),\ H \text{ is } p\text{-solvable}\},$$
where $\mathrm{GL}(n,q)$ is the group of invertible $n \times n$ matrices over the finite field with $q$ elements. Determine whether
$$\lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{m_n(q)}{\log_2 n} = 1.$$

original_question: Let ℓ(X) denote the composition length of a finite group X. Let A be a finite nilpotent group acting by automorphisms on a finite soluble group G. Let c(G, A) be the number of trivial A-modules in a given A-composition series of G. (Note that c(G, A) = ℓ(CG(A)) if(|A|, |G|) = 1.) Conjecture: there are absolute constants C1 and C2 such that the Fitting height of G is at most C1 ℓ(A) + C2 c(G, A). İ. Güloǧlu
self_contained_problem:
For a finite group $X$, let $\ell(X)$ denote its composition length (the number of factors in any composition series of $X$). Let $A$ be a finite nilpotent group acting by automorphisms on a finite soluble group $G$. An $A$-composition series of $G$ is a chain $1 = G_0 \triangleleft G_1 \triangleleft \cdots \triangleleft G_n = G$ of $A$-invariant subgroups of $G$ such that each factor $G_{i+1}/G_i$ admits no proper nontrivial $A$-invariant subgroup; each such factor is regarded as an $A$-module (in the generalized sense). Define $c(G, A)$ to be the number of factors $G_{i+1}/G_i$ in such a series on which $A$ acts trivially. (When $\gcd(|A|, |G|) = 1$, this number coincides with $\ell(C_G(A))$, the composition length of the fixed-point subgroup.) Let $h(G)$ denote the Fitting height (Fitting length) of $G$, i.e. the length of the shortest normal series of $G$ with nilpotent factors.

Prove or disprove: there exist absolute constants $C_1$ and $C_2$ such that for every finite nilpotent group $A$ acting by automorphisms on every finite soluble group $G$,
$$h(G) \le C_1\, \ell(A) + C_2\, c(G, A).$$
category_tag: Fitting height of soluble groups under coprime/nilpotent action
status_search_result: The conjecture appears as a recently proposed problem attributed to İ. Güloğlu. Related work by Ercan, Güloğlu and collaborators has established Fitting-height bounds in special cases (e.g., good actions, coprime/odd-order settings, and cases where $A$ is cyclic), but no general proof of the stated linear bound $h(G) \le C_1 \ell(A) + C_2 c(G,A)$ for arbitrary finite nilpotent $A$ acting on a finite soluble $G$ is found in the literature. The problem appears to remain open.

original_question: Let X be a non-empty class of finite groups of odd order closed under taking subgroups, homomorphic images, and extensions. Let H be an X-maximal subgroup of a finite group G, and N a normal subgroup of G. Must H ∩ N be an X-maximal subgroup of N?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathfrak{X}$ be a non-empty class of finite groups of odd order that is closed under taking subgroups, homomorphic images, and group extensions (i.e., if $1 \to A \to B \to C \to 1$ is exact with $A, C \in \mathfrak{X}$, then $B \in \mathfrak{X}$). For a finite group $G$, call a subgroup $K \le G$ an $\mathfrak{X}$-maximal subgroup of $G$ if $K \in \mathfrak{X}$ and $K$ is maximal (with respect to inclusion) among subgroups of $G$ that belong to $\mathfrak{X}$.

Let $G$ be a finite group, let $H$ be an $\mathfrak{X}$-maximal subgroup of $G$, and let $N$ be a normal subgroup of $G$. Determine whether $H \cap N$ is necessarily an $\mathfrak{X}$-maximal subgroup of $N$.

original_question: We say that a product XY = {xy | x ∈ X, y ∈ Y } of two subsets X, Y of a group G is direct if for every z ∈ XY there are unique x ∈ X, y ∈ Y such that z = xy. Is there an infinite group G such that every subset A ⊆ G satisfies the following property: all the maximal subsets B for which the product AB is direct have the same cardinality? Note that for checking the property for a given infinite group G, it suffices to consider only those subsets A ⊆ G for which |A| = |G \ A|. Indeed, the property is equivalent to A−1 A ∩ BB −1 = {1} and A−1 AB = G, and these imply |G| = |A||B|, since G is infinite. Now, if |A| < |G \ A|, then |A| < |G|, and so |B| = |G|; and if |A| > |G \ A|, then A−1 A = G, and so |B| = 1, for all B satisfying the property.
self_contained_problem:
Let $G$ be a group. For subsets $X, Y \subseteq G$, define their product $XY = \{xy : x \in X,\ y \in Y\}$, and say the product $XY$ is direct if for every $z \in XY$ there exist unique $x \in X$ and $y \in Y$ with $z = xy$ (equivalently, $X^{-1}X \cap YY^{-1} = \{1\}$). For a subset $A \subseteq G$, call a subset $B \subseteq G$ an $A$-complement if $AB$ is direct and $B$ is maximal (with respect to inclusion) among subsets with this property.

Question: Does there exist an infinite group $G$ with the property that for every subset $A \subseteq G$, all maximal $A$-complements $B \subseteq G$ have the same cardinality?

(Equivalently, for an infinite $G$, the condition that $AB$ is direct and $B$ is maximal is equivalent to $A^{-1}A \cap BB^{-1} = \{1\}$ together with $A^{-1}AB = G$, which forces $|G| = |A|\cdot|B|$. Hence the property only needs to be checked for those $A$ with $|A| = |G \setminus A|$.)

original_question: For a finite group G, let χ1(G) denote the totality of the degrees of all irreducible complex characters of G with allowance for their multiplicities. Suppose that H is a finite group with χ1(H) = χ1(G). a) If G is an almost simple group, must H be isomorphic to G? b) If G is a quasisimple group, must H be isomorphic to G? This is true if G is a simple group(see 11.8(a) in Archive).
self_contained_problem:
For a finite group $G$, let $\chi_1(G)$ denote the multiset of degrees of all irreducible complex characters of $G$, counted with their multiplicities (equivalently, $\chi_1(G)$ records, for each positive integer $d$, the number of irreducible complex characters of $G$ of degree $d$). Recall that a finite group $G$ is called:
- almost simple if there exists a non-abelian finite simple group $S$ such that $S \trianglelefteq G \le \mathrm{Aut}(S)$ (equivalently, $G$ has a unique minimal normal subgroup, which is non-abelian simple);
- quasisimple if $G$ is perfect (i.e., $G = [G,G]$) and $G/Z(G)$ is non-abelian simple.

Let $H$ be a finite group with $\chi_1(H) = \chi_1(G)$ (equality of multisets of irreducible character degrees).

(a) If $G$ is almost simple, must $H \cong G$?

(b) If $G$ is quasisimple, must $H \cong G$?

The analogous statement for non-abelian simple groups is known to hold (resolving the corresponding earlier Kourovka question 11.8(a) by work on alternating, sporadic, and Lie-type simple groups), and partial results characterize many quasisimple classical groups by their complex group algebras, but the full almost-simple and quasisimple cases as posed appear to remain open.

original_question: Let G be a finite group, Z(p) the localization at p, and Fp the field of p elements. Let X be the class of Fp G-modules obtained by reduction of simple QG-modules. Is it true that Z(p) G is semiperfect if and only if each projective indecomposable Fp G-module can be written as an N-linear combination of modules in X inside the Grothendieck group of Fp G? The “only if” direction is proved, and the affirmative answer is obtained if p does not divide |G| (D. Johnston, D. Rumynin, J. Algebra, 687, no. 1(2026), 776–791).
self_contained_problem:
Let $G$ be a finite group and $p$ a prime. Denote by $\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}$ the localization of $\mathbb{Z}$ at the prime ideal $(p)$, and by $\mathbb{F}_p$ the field with $p$ elements. Consider the group rings $\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}G$, $\mathbb{Q}G$, and $\mathbb{F}_p G$.

For every simple $\mathbb{Q}G$-module $V$, choose a $G$-invariant $\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}$-lattice $L\subseteq V$ (such a lattice exists, and although it is not unique, the resulting class of $\mathbb{F}_p G$-modules is well-defined up to the relations used below). Let $\mathcal{X}$ denote the class of all $\mathbb{F}_p G$-modules of the form $L/pL$ obtained in this way (the "reductions modulo $p$" of simple $\mathbb{Q}G$-modules).

Recall that a ring $R$ is called semiperfect if $R/J(R)$ is semisimple and idempotents lift modulo the Jacobson radical $J(R)$. Let $K_0(\mathbb{F}_p G)$ denote the Grothendieck group of finitely generated $\mathbb{F}_p G$-modules with respect to short exact sequences.

Question: Is it true that $\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}G$ is semiperfect if and only if every projective indecomposable $\mathbb{F}_p G$-module can be expressed as an $\mathbb{N}$-linear combination of classes of modules from $\mathcal{X}$ inside $K_0(\mathbb{F}_p G)$?

It is known that the "only if" direction holds, and that the equivalence holds when $p\nmid |G|$. Determine whether the equivalence holds in general.

original_question: For a fixed(finitely generated free)-by-cyclic group G = Fn ⋊ Z, is there an algorithm that, given a finite subset S of G, finds a finite presentation for the subgroup H = ⟨S⟩? Cf. 4.8 in Archive.
self_contained_problem:
Let $n\ge 2$ and let $F_n$ denote the free group of rank $n$. Fix an automorphism $\varphi\in\mathrm{Aut}(F_n)$ and form the (finitely generated free)-by-cyclic group
$$G \;=\; F_n\rtimes_\varphi \mathbb{Z},$$
i.e.\ the semidirect product in which a chosen generator of $\mathbb{Z}$ acts on $F_n$ via $\varphi$. The group $G$ is given by an explicit finite presentation.

Decide whether there exists an algorithm with the following specification: the input is a finite subset $S\subseteq G$ (each element given as a word in the generators of $G$), and the output is a finite presentation $\langle X\mid R\rangle$ of the subgroup $H=\langle S\rangle\le G$ generated by $S$. original_question: Is the uniform subgroup membership problem decidable for(finitely generated free)-by-cyclic groups? That is, for a fixed group G = Fn ⋊ Z, is there an algorithm that, given elements w, h1,..., hk ∈ G, decides whether or not w belongs to the subgroup H = ⟨h1,..., hk ⟩?
self_contained_problem:
Let $n \geq 2$ and let $F_n$ be the free group of rank $n$. A (finitely generated free)-by-cyclic group is a semidirect product $G = F_n \rtimes_\varphi \mathbb{Z}$, where $\varphi \in \mathrm{Aut}(F_n)$ specifies the action of the generator of $\mathbb{Z}$ on $F_n$ by conjugation.

The uniform subgroup membership problem for a fixed group $G$ is the following decision problem: given as input a finite list of elements $w, h_1, \ldots, h_k \in G$ (each represented as a word in a fixed finite generating set of $G$), decide whether $w \in \langle h_1, \ldots, h_k \rangle$, the subgroup of $G$ generated by $h_1, \ldots, h_k$.

Question: Is the uniform subgroup membership problem decidable for every (finitely generated free)-by-cyclic group $G = F_n \rtimes \mathbb{Z}$? Equivalently, does there exist, for each such $G$, an algorithm which on input $(w, h_1, \ldots, h_k)$ correctly decides whether $w$ belongs to $\langle h_1, \ldots, h_k \rangle$?
status_search_result: The problem appears as a new entry in the 2026 Kourovka Notebook of unsolved problems in group theory, which lists open problems. Decidability of the subgroup membership problem for free-by-cyclic groups in general is not established in the literature; only partial decidability results exist for special subclasses (e.g. certain one-relator or surface-related cases), while membership in various related families of groups is known to be undecidable. No source claims a full positive or negative resolution for arbitrary $F_n \rtimes \mathbb{Z}$.

original_question: (E. Zelmanov). Let F be a field of characteristic p > 0, and let Γ be the principal congruence subgroup of Aut(F [x1,..., xn ]) consisting of all automorphisms that send each variable xi to xi modulo terms of higher degree. Then Γ is a residuallyp group. Does Γ satisfy a pro-p identity?
self_contained_problem:
Let $F$ be a field of characteristic $p>0$, and let $F[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ be the polynomial ring in $n$ commuting variables over $F$. Let $\mathrm{Aut}(F[x_1,\dots,x_n])$ denote its group of $F$-algebra automorphisms, and let $\Gamma$ be the principal congruence subgroup consisting of all automorphisms $\varphi$ such that, for every $i\in\{1,\dots,n\}$, $\varphi(x_i) \equiv x_i$ modulo terms of degree $\ge 2$ (i.e.\ $\varphi(x_i)-x_i$ lies in the square of the augmentation ideal $(x_1,\dots,x_n)$). It is known that $\Gamma$ is a residually-$p$ group, so it has a pro-$p$ completion $\widehat{\Gamma}_p$. Recall that a pro-$p$ group $G$ is said to satisfy a pro-$p$ identity if there exists a nontrivial element $w$ in the free pro-$p$ group $F_k$ on some finite number $k$ of generators such that $w$ vanishes under every continuous homomorphism $F_k\to G$. 

Question: Does $\Gamma$ satisfy a pro-$p$ identity (equivalently, does its pro-$p$ completion satisfy a pro-$p$ identity)?

original_question: Is it true that if a normal subgroup A of a Sylow p-subgroup of a p-soluble finite group G has exponent pe, then the normal closure of A in G has(p, e)-bounded(or even e-bounded) p-length?
self_contained_problem:
Let $p$ be a prime and let $G$ be a finite $p$-soluble group, i.e., a finite group all of whose composition factors are either $p$-groups or $p'$-groups. Recall that the $p$-length $\ell_p(G)$ of $G$ is the number of $p$-factors in a shortest normal series of $G$ whose factors are either $p$-groups or $p'$-groups. Suppose that $P$ is a Sylow $p$-subgroup of $G$ and that $A \trianglelefteq P$ is a normal subgroup of $P$ of exponent dividing $p^{e}$ (so every element of $A$ has order at most $p^{e}$). Let $A^{G} = \langle A^{g} : g \in G\rangle$ denote the normal closure of $A$ in $G$.

Determine whether the $p$-length $\ell_p(A^{G})$ of the normal closure $A^{G}$ is bounded above by a function depending only on $p$ and $e$ (a $(p,e)$-bounded quantity). More strongly, decide whether $\ell_p(A^{G})$ can be bounded above by a function of $e$ alone, independent of $p$ and of $G$.

original_question: Suppose that φ is an automorphism of a finite soluble group G. Must G contain a subgroup of index bounded in terms of |φ| and |CG(φ)| whose Fitting height is bounded(a) in terms of |φ|? (b) or even in terms of the composition length of ⟨φ⟩? An affirmative answer to part(b) is known when |φ| is a prime power(B. Hartley– V. Turau), or when(|G|, |φ|) = 1(A. Turull, B. Hartley–I. M. Isaacs). Also cf. 19.43.
self_contained_problem:
Let G be a finite soluble group and let φ be an automorphism of G. Denote by |φ| the order of φ, by C_G(φ) = {g ∈ G : φ(g) = g} the fixed-point subgroup of φ in G, and by ⟨φ⟩ the cyclic subgroup generated by φ in Aut(G); the composition length of ⟨φ⟩ is the number of prime factors of |φ| counted with multiplicity. Recall that the Fitting height (nilpotent length) h(H) of a finite soluble group H is the length of the shortest normal series of H all of whose factors are nilpotent.

Decide each of the following.

(a) Does there exist a function f₁ depending only on |φ|, and a function g₁ depending only on |φ| and |C_G(φ)|, such that G always contains a subgroup H with [G : H] ≤ g₁(|φ|, |C_G(φ)|) and h(H) ≤ f₁(|φ|) ?

(b) Does there exist a function f₂ depending only on the composition length c(|φ|) of ⟨φ⟩, and a function g₂ depending only on |φ| and |C_G(φ)|, such that G always contains a subgroup H with [G : H] ≤ g₂(|φ|, |C_G(φ)|) and h(H) ≤ f₂(c(|φ|)) ?

It is known that part (b) (and hence (a)) holds in the special cases when |φ| is a prime power, and when gcd(|G|, |φ|) = 1. The problem is to settle the general case.

original_question: Suppose that A is a nilpotent group of automorphisms of a finite soluble group G. Is the Fitting height of G bounded in terms of |A| and |CG(A)|? An affirmative answer is known when(|G|, |A|) = 1(J. G. Thompson, even for soluble A, with improved bounds in subsequent papers of H. Kurzweil, A. Turull, B. Hartley–I. M. Isaacs), when A is cyclic(see 19.43), or when CG(A) = 1(E. C. Dade). Note that for any non-nilpotent finite group A there are finite soluble groups G of unbounded Fitting height with CG(A) = 1(S. D. Bell–B. Hartley).
self_contained_problem:
Let $G$ be a finite soluble group and let $A$ be a finite nilpotent group acting on $G$ by automorphisms. The Fitting height (nilpotent length) $h(G)$ of $G$ is the length of the shortest normal series
$$1 = F_0 \le F_1 \le \cdots \le F_h = G$$
in which each quotient $F_{i+1}/F_i$ is nilpotent. Let $C_G(A) = \{g \in G : g^a = g \text{ for all } a \in A\}$ denote the fixed-point subgroup.

Question: Does there exist a function $f : \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ such that 
$$h(G) \le f(|A|,\,|C_G(A)|)$$
for every finite soluble group $G$ and every finite nilpotent group $A$ acting on $G$ by automorphisms?

(It is known that the answer is affirmative in each of the following cases: when $\gcd(|G|,|A|)=1$; when $A$ is cyclic; and when $C_G(A)=1$. Conversely, for every non-nilpotent finite group $A$ there exist finite soluble groups $G$ of arbitrarily large Fitting height admitting $A$ as a fixed-point-free group of automorphisms, so the nilpotency hypothesis on $A$ is essential.)

Let $G$ be a finite soluble group and let $\varphi$ be an automorphism of $G$. Denote by $|\varphi|$ the order of $\varphi$, by $C_G(\varphi)=\{g\in G:\varphi(g)=g\}$ the fixed-point subgroup of $\varphi$ in $G$, and by $r$ the Prüfer rank of $C_G(\varphi)$ (that is, the least integer such that every finitely generated subgroup of $C_G(\varphi)$ can be generated by $r$ elements). original_question: A finite group G is said to be semi-abelian if it has a sequence of subgroups 1 = G0 ⩽ G1 ⩽ · · · ⩽ Gn = G such that for every i the subgroup Gi+1 is isomorphic to a quotient of a semidirect product Ai ⋊ Gi for some abelian group Ai. Conjecture: Semi-abelian finite groups are monomial.
self_contained_problem:
Definitions. Let G be a finite group.

(a) G is called monomial (or an M-group) if every irreducible complex character of G is induced from a linear (one-dimensional) character of some subgroup of G.

(b) G is called semi-abelian if there exists a chain of subgroups
   1 = G_0 ≤ G_1 ≤ G_2 ≤ ... ≤ G_n = G
such that for each i ∈ {0, 1, ..., n-1}, the group G_{i+1} is isomorphic to a quotient of a semidirect product A_i ⋊ G_i for some abelian group A_i (with some action of G_i on A_i).

Conjecture. Every semi-abelian finite group is monomial.

Prove or disprove this conjecture.

original_question: Is there an algorithm deciding if a given one-relator group is hyperbolic?
self_contained_problem:
A one-relator group is a group given by a finite presentation of the form G = ⟨ x_1, …, x_n | r ⟩, where r is a single nontrivial cyclically reduced word in the free group F(x_1, …, x_n). A finitely generated group is called (Gromov-)hyperbolic if its Cayley graph (with respect to some, equivalently any, finite generating set) is a δ-hyperbolic metric space for some δ ≥ 0, i.e. every geodesic triangle has each side contained in the δ-neighbourhood of the union of the other two.

Question: Does there exist an algorithm which, on input a finite presentation ⟨ x_1, …, x_n | r ⟩ of a one-relator group, decides in finite time whether the group it defines is hyperbolic?
status_search_result: The decidability of hyperbolicity for one-relator groups appears to be an open problem. Recent surveys on the theory of one-relator groups discuss the conjecture that a one-relator group is hyperbolic iff it contains no Baumslag–Solitar subgroup, and report partial results (e.g., Louder–Wilton/Linton's work on one-relator groups with negative immersions being hyperbolic), but a general decision algorithm is not known.

original_question: A group G is called an orientable Poincaré duality group of dimension n over a ring R if it is of type FP over R and Hi(G; RG) = 0 for i ̸= n, while Hn(G; RG) = R as an RG-module, where the action on R is trivial. (Note that G is not required to be finitely presented.) If G is an orientable Poincaré duality group of dimension n over all fields, is it an orientable Poincaré duality group over the integers?
self_contained_problem:
Let $G$ be a (discrete) group and $R$ a commutative ring. Recall that $G$ is said to be of type $\mathrm{FP}$ over $R$ if the trivial $RG$-module $R$ admits a finite-length resolution by finitely generated projective $RG$-modules. Recall further that $G$ is called an orientable Poincaré duality group of dimension $n$ over $R$ if $G$ is of type $\mathrm{FP}$ over $R$ and the cohomology of $G$ with coefficients in the group ring satisfies
\[ H^i(G; RG) = 0 \text{ for } i \neq n, \qquad H^n(G; RG) \cong R \]
as $RG$-modules, where the $G$-action on the right-hand $R$ is trivial. (Note that $G$ is not assumed to be finitely presented.)

Suppose $G$ is an orientable Poincaré duality group of dimension $n$ over every field. Must $G$ then be an orientable Poincaré duality group of dimension $n$ over the ring of integers $\mathbb{Z}$?

original_question: For a ring R, we say that a group G is of type FL(R) if the trivial RG-module R admits a finite resolution by finitely generated free modules. If R is a field, we define the Euler characteristic of G over R to be the alternating sum of R-ranks of homology groups Hi(G; R). Does there exist a group of type FL(Fi) for two fields F1 and F2 such that the Euler characteristics of the group over the fields F1 and F2 differ?
self_contained_problem:
Let R be a (unital, associative) ring and let G be a group. Denote by RG the group ring of G over R, and view R as the trivial RG-module (with G acting trivially). The group G is said to be of type FL(R) if there exists a finite resolution

  0 → F_n → F_{n-1} → ··· → F_1 → F_0 → R → 0

of the trivial RG-module R by finitely generated free RG-modules F_i.

When R is a field, define the Euler characteristic of G over R by
  χ_R(G) = Σ_{i ≥ 0} (-1)^i dim_R H_i(G; R),
where H_i(G; R) is the i-th homology group of G with coefficients in the trivial RG-module R (the sum is finite when G is of type FL(R)).

Question: Does there exist a group G together with two fields F_1 and F_2 such that G is of type FL(F_1) and of type FL(F_2), but χ_{F_1}(G) ≠ χ_{F_2}(G)?

original_question: We say that a group is a Tarski monster if it is finitely generated, not cyclic, and all of its proper non-trivial subgroups are isomorphic to each other. a) Do there exist amenable torsion-free Tarski monsters? b) Do there exist amenable Tarski monsters of prime exponent?
self_contained_problem:
Call a group $G$ a Tarski monster if $G$ is finitely generated, not cyclic, and all proper non-trivial subgroups of $G$ are pairwise isomorphic. Recall that a group is amenable if it admits a finitely additive, left-invariant probability measure defined on all of its subsets (equivalently, satisfies the Følner condition).

(a) Does there exist a torsion-free amenable Tarski monster?

(b) Does there exist an amenable Tarski monster of prime exponent (that is, a Tarski monster $G$ such that $g^p = e$ for every $g \in G$ for some fixed prime $p$, which is amenable)?
status_search_result: The classical Tarski monsters constructed by Olshanskii are well-known examples of non-amenable groups without free subgroups, and the question of whether amenable Tarski monsters exist (either torsion-free or of prime exponent) does not appear resolved. original_question: Is the conjugacy problem in CT(Z) algorithmically decidable? See the definition of CT(Z) in 17.57.
self_contained_problem:
A residue class of $\mathbb{Z}$ is a set of the form $r(m) = \{n \in \mathbb{Z} : n \equiv r \pmod{m}\}$ with $m \in \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ and $0 \le r < m$. Given two disjoint residue classes $r_1(m_1)$ and $r_2(m_2)$, the associated class transposition $\tau_{r_1(m_1),\, r_2(m_2)}$ is the involution of $\mathbb{Z}$ that interchanges these two classes via the unique affine bijection $r_1 + km_1 \leftrightarrow r_2 + km_2$ ($k \in \mathbb{Z}$) and fixes every other integer pointwise. Let
$$\mathrm{CT}(\mathbb{Z}) := \langle \tau_{r_1(m_1),\, r_2(m_2)} : r_1(m_1) \cap r_2(m_2) = \varnothing \rangle$$
be the subgroup of $\mathrm{Sym}(\mathbb{Z})$ generated by all class transpositions. Each element $g \in \mathrm{CT}(\mathbb{Z})$ admits a finite description as a residue-class-wise affine permutation, so finite words in class transpositions provide an effective input encoding.

Decide: Is the conjugacy problem in $\mathrm{CT}(\mathbb{Z})$ algorithmically decidable? That is, does there exist an algorithm that, given two elements $g, h \in \mathrm{CT}(\mathbb{Z})$ (each presented as a finite product of class transpositions), determines whether there exists $x \in \mathrm{CT}(\mathbb{Z})$ with $x^{-1} g x = h$?

No published solution was located in the search; Kohl's RCWA package documentation and related papers discuss algorithmic aspects but do not announce a decidability result for conjugacy in CT(Z).

original_question: Is it algorithmically decidable whether a given element g ∈ CT(Z) (a) permutes a nontrivial partition of Z into residue classes? (b) has only finite cycles? (c) has no finite cycles?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathbb{Z}$ denote the ring of integers. A *residue class* in $\mathbb{Z}$ is a set of the form $r(m) := \{r + km : k \in \mathbb{Z}\}$ for integers $m \geq 1$ and $0 \leq r < m$. Given two disjoint residue classes $r_1(m_1)$ and $r_2(m_2)$, the *class transposition* $\tau_{r_1(m_1),r_2(m_2)}$ is the permutation of $\mathbb{Z}$ that interchanges $r_1 + k m_1$ with $r_2 + k m_2$ for every $k \in \mathbb{Z}$ and fixes all other integers. Let $\mathrm{CT}(\mathbb{Z})$ be the subgroup of $\mathrm{Sym}(\mathbb{Z})$ generated by all class transpositions. Every element $g \in \mathrm{CT}(\mathbb{Z})$ admits a finite description as a word in class transpositions (equivalently, as a residue-class-wise affine bijection of $\mathbb{Z}$ specified by finite data).

A *partition of $\mathbb{Z}$ into residue classes* is a finite partition $\mathbb{Z} = \bigsqcup_{i=1}^{n} r_i(m_i)$ where each block is a residue class; it is *nontrivial* if $n \geq 2$. An element $g \in \mathrm{CT}(\mathbb{Z})$ is said to *permute* such a partition if $g$ maps the set of blocks to itself. A *cycle* of $g$ is an orbit of $\langle g \rangle$ on $\mathbb{Z}$; it is *finite* if its length is finite.

Decide whether each of the following decision problems, taking as input a finite description of an element $g \in \mathrm{CT}(\mathbb{Z})$, is algorithmically decidable:

(a) Does $g$ permute some nontrivial partition of $\mathbb{Z}$ into residue classes?

(b) Are all cycles of $g$ on $\mathbb{Z}$ finite?

(c) Does $g$ have no finite cycles on $\mathbb{Z}$?
status_search_result: The class transposition group CT(ℤ) (introduced by Kohl) is known to be a simple group, and its finitely generated subgroups can have unsolvable membership problem. Decision problems concerning cycle structure and invariant residue-class partitions of individual elements are tied to Collatz-type dynamics and are listed as new open problems in the 2026 edition of the Kourovka Notebook; recent literature (e.g., on horizontal class transpositions and orders of products) does not report a resolution of (a)–(c).

original_question: Given two distinct sets P1 and P2 of odd primes none of which is a subset of the other, is it true that ⟨CTP1(Z), CTP2(Z)⟩ ⪇ CTP1 ∪P2(Z)? See the definition of CTP(Z) in 17.60.
self_contained_problem:
Let Sym(Z) denote the symmetric group on the set Z of integers. For integers m ≥ 1 and 0 ≤ r < m write r(m) := r + mZ for the residue class of r modulo m. Two residue classes r1(m1) and r2(m2) are called disjoint if (r1+m1Z) ∩ (r2+m2Z) = ∅. Given disjoint residue classes r1(m1) and r2(m2), the associated class transposition τ_{r1(m1), r2(m2)} ∈ Sym(Z) is the involution that interchanges, for every k ∈ Z, the integers r1 + k m1 and r2 + k m2 (in the natural order-preserving bijection between the two classes) and fixes all other integers.

Let CT(Z) denote the subgroup of Sym(Z) generated by all class transpositions. For any set P of odd primes, define
   CT_P(Z) := ⟨ τ_{r1(m1), r2(m2)} : r1(m1), r2(m2) disjoint, every prime divisor of m1·m2 lies in P ∪ {2} ⟩,
i.e. the subgroup of CT(Z) generated by those class transpositions whose moduli have all odd prime divisors in P.

Question. Let P1 and P2 be two distinct sets of odd primes such that neither is contained in the other (so P1 ⊄ P2 and P2 ⊄ P1). Is the inclusion
   ⟨ CT_{P1}(Z), CT_{P2}(Z) ⟩  ⊊  CT_{P1 ∪ P2}(Z)
necessarily strict? Equivalently, prove or disprove that the subgroup of CT(Z) generated by CT_{P1}(Z) and CT_{P2}(Z) is always a proper subgroup of CT_{P1 ∪ P2}(Z).
status_search_result: The problem is one of Stefan Kohl's questions on class transposition groups recorded in the Kourovka Notebook. Kohl's publication list and recent papers (2024–2025) on class transposition groups by Pan, Bardakov, Iskra and others address related problems (e.g. orders of products of class transpositions, the horizontal class transposition group), but no source found resolves this specific comparison of ⟨CT_{P1}(Z), CT_{P2}(Z)⟩ with CT_{P1∪P2}(Z); it appears to remain open.

original_question: Let σ = (σij), 1 ⩽ i ̸= j ⩽ n, be an irreducible elementary net(carpet) of order n ⩾ 3 over a field K(see 19.48). The net σ is said to be closed if the elementary net subgroup E(σ) does not contain new elementary transvections. The net σ is said to be completable if its diagonal can be supplemented with subgroups to a complete net. Completable elementary nets are closed. It is known that over fields of characteristic 0 and 2 there exist irreducible closed elementary nets that are not completable(V. A. Koibaev, Trudy Inst. Mat. Mekh. Ural Div. Ross. Akad. Nauk, 17, no. 4(2011), 134–141(Russian); V. A. Koibaev, Siberian Math. J., 62, no. 2(2021), 262–266). Do there exist irreducible closed elementary nets of order n ⩾ 3 over a field of odd characteristic that are not completable?
self_contained_problem:
Let $K$ be a field and $n\geq 3$. An (elementary) net (or carpet) of order $n$ over $K$ is a collection $\sigma=(\sigma_{ij})_{1\le i\ne j\le n}$ of additive subgroups $\sigma_{ij}\subseteq K$ satisfying the carpet conditions $\sigma_{ir}\sigma_{rj}\subseteq \sigma_{ij}$ for all distinct indices $i,r,j$. A full net additionally specifies additive subgroups $\sigma_{ii}\subseteq K$ on the diagonal with $\sigma_{ij}\sigma_{jj}\subseteq\sigma_{ij}$ and $\sigma_{ii}\sigma_{ij}\subseteq\sigma_{ij}$. The net $\sigma$ is called irreducible if every off-diagonal subgroup $\sigma_{ij}$ is nonzero.

For an elementary net $\sigma$, let $E(\sigma)$ denote the elementary net subgroup, that is, the subgroup of $\mathrm{GL}_n(K)$ generated by all elementary transvections $t_{ij}(\alpha)=I+\alpha e_{ij}$ with $\alpha\in\sigma_{ij}$ and $i\ne j$. The net $\sigma$ is said to be closed if $E(\sigma)$ contains no elementary transvections $t_{ij}(\alpha)$ with $\alpha\notin\sigma_{ij}$ (no "new" elementary transvections). The net $\sigma$ is called completable if there exist additive subgroups $\sigma_{ii}\subseteq K$ ($i=1,\dots,n$) such that the resulting full collection $(\sigma_{ij})_{1\le i,j\le n}$ is a (full) net. Every completable elementary net is closed.

It is known that over fields of characteristic $0$ and characteristic $2$ there exist irreducible closed elementary nets of order $n\ge 3$ that are not completable.

Question: Does there exist a field $K$ of odd characteristic and an integer $n\ge 3$ admitting an irreducible closed elementary net $\sigma$ of order $n$ over $K$ that is not completable?
status_search_result: The problem appears in the 2026 Kourovka Notebook list of new problems on group theory. No published solution was found in web searches; the question is posed as an open problem, with known existence results only in characteristics 0 and 2 (Koibaev, 2011 and 2021).

original_question: Let d be an integer that is not divisible√by n-th powers of primes, let xn − d be an irreducible polynomial over Q, let θ = n d, and let K = Q(θ) be the radical extension of degree n of the field Q. The multiplicative group K ∗ of the field K is canonically embedded into the group AutQ(K) of all invertible Q-linear mappings of the Q-space K; let T be the image of K ∗ under this embedding. In the natural basis 1, θ, θ2,..., θn−1 of the Q-space K the group AutQ(K) corresponds to G = GL(n, Q), and the subgroup T to a subgroup T(d) (unsplit maximal torus). Every subgroup H of G containing T(d) and some one-dimensional transformation is rich in elementary transvections(V. A. Koibaev, St. Petersbg. Math. J., 21, no. 5(2010), 731–742) and thus defines a net σ = σ(H) (V. A. Koibaev, A. V. Shilov, J. Math. Sci. New York 171, no. 3(2010), 380–385). Let E(σ) denote the subgroup generated by all transvections in the net group G(σ). Is it true that H ⩽ NG(E(σ))? This inclusion was proved in the case n = 2(V. A. Koibaev, Dokl. Math., 41, no. 3(1990), 414–416).
self_contained_problem:
Let $n \geq 2$ be an integer and let $d \in \mathbb{Z}$ be an integer not divisible by the $n$-th power of any prime, and assume that the polynomial $x^n - d$ is irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}$. Set $\theta = \sqrt[n]{d}$ and let $K = \mathbb{Q}(\theta)$, a radical extension of $\mathbb{Q}$ of degree $n$. The multiplicative group $K^{*}$ acts on $K$ by multiplication, giving a canonical embedding $K^{*} \hookrightarrow \mathrm{Aut}_{\mathbb{Q}}(K)$. Identifying $\mathrm{Aut}_{\mathbb{Q}}(K)$ with $G = \mathrm{GL}(n,\mathbb{Q})$ via the basis $1, \theta, \theta^{2}, \ldots, \theta^{n-1}$, let $T(d) \leq G$ be the image of $K^{*}$ (an unsplit maximal torus of $G$).

A subgroup $H \leq G$ is said to be rich in elementary transvections if for every pair $i \neq j$ the set $\{\alpha \in \mathbb{Q} : I + \alpha e_{ij} \in H\}$ generates the additive group used in defining the associated net. To any such $H$ one associates a net (carpet) of additive subgroups $\sigma = \sigma(H) = (\sigma_{ij})$ of $\mathbb{Q}$, and the net group $G(\sigma) \leq G$ consists of matrices whose $(i,j)$-entry lies in $\sigma_{ij}$ off the diagonal (with appropriate diagonal conditions). Let $E(\sigma) \leq G(\sigma)$ be the subgroup generated by all elementary transvections $I + \alpha e_{ij}$ with $\alpha \in \sigma_{ij}$, $i \neq j$.

Now suppose $H \leq G$ contains $T(d)$ and at least one one-dimensional transformation (a transvection). Then $H$ is rich in elementary transvections and so determines such a net $\sigma = \sigma(H)$ and subgroup $E(\sigma)$.

Question: Is it always true that
$$H \leq N_{G}(E(\sigma))?$$

(The inclusion is known to hold for $n = 2$.)

original_question: Let p be a prime and let G be a pro-p group. Suppose that all of the(continuous Galois) cohomology groups H n(G, Fp) of G with coefficients in the field of p elements are finite. Does it necessarily follow that the cohomology ring H ∗ (G, Fp) is finitely generated? The answer is known to be ‘yes’ if G is abelian-by-(p-adic analytic), as follows from(J. King, Commun. Algebra, 27, no. 10(1999), 4969–4991).
self_contained_problem:
Let $p$ be a prime number and let $G$ be a pro-$p$ group. Consider the continuous cohomology groups $H^n(G,\mathbb{F}_p)$ of $G$ with coefficients in the trivial discrete module $\mathbb{F}_p$ (the field with $p$ elements), and assemble them into the graded $\mathbb{F}_p$-algebra $H^*(G,\mathbb{F}_p)=\bigoplus_{n\ge 0}H^n(G,\mathbb{F}_p)$ under cup product.

Assume that $H^n(G,\mathbb{F}_p)$ is finite for every $n\ge 0$. Must the graded $\mathbb{F}_p$-algebra $H^*(G,\mathbb{F}_p)$ be finitely generated?

(It is known that the answer is affirmative when $G$ is abelian-by-($p$-adic analytic).)

original_question: Let G be a finitely generated group with a fixed finite generating set S and the corresponding word metric LS(∗). An element g is said to be distorted in G if LS(g n)/n → 0 as n → ∞; this notion is independent of the choice of the generating set S. For any, not necessarily finitely generated, group H, an element g ∈ H is said to be distorted if there is a finitely generated subgroup G of H containing g in which g is distorted. Do there exist finitely generated left-orderable groups in which every nontrivial element is distorted? Note that it is straightforward to construct countable(not finitely generated) left-orderable groups with this property using HN N-extensions and applying results of V. V. Bludov and A. M. W. Glass.
self_contained_problem:
Definitions. Let G be a finitely generated group with a fixed finite generating set S, and let L_S: G → ℤ_{≥0} denote the corresponding word length (word metric from the identity). An element g ∈ G is called distorted in G if

    lim_{n→∞} L_S(g^n)/n = 0.

This property does not depend on the choice of the finite generating set S. For an arbitrary (not necessarily finitely generated) group H, an element g ∈ H is called distorted in H if there exists a finitely generated subgroup G ≤ H with g ∈ G such that g is distorted in G.

A group H is called left-orderable if there exists a total order ≤ on H that is invariant under left multiplication: for all a, b, c ∈ H, a ≤ b implies ca ≤ cb.

Question. Does there exist a finitely generated left-orderable group H such that every nontrivial element g ∈ H is distorted in H?

original_question: Do there exist finitely generated left-orderable groups with only one nontrivial conjugacy class? A positive answer to this question implies a positive answer to 21.78. Note that D. Osin constructed torsion-free finitely generated groups with only one nontrivial conjugacy class; see 9.10 in Archive.
self_contained_problem:
A group $G$ is called left-orderable if there exists a total order $\le$ on $G$ that is invariant under left multiplication, i.e., $a \le b$ implies $ga \le gb$ for all $g, a, b \in G$. The conjugacy class of an element $x \in G$ is the set $\{gxg^{-1} : g \in G\}$; the identity always forms a conjugacy class by itself. A group has "only one nontrivial conjugacy class" if all non-identity elements are pairwise conjugate, i.e., $G \setminus \{1\}$ is a single conjugacy class.

Question: Does there exist a finitely generated left-orderable group $G$ such that all non-identity elements of $G$ are conjugate to one another?

original_question: (J. Wiegold). Let Γ be a finite simple group and let Nn(Γ) denote the set of normal subgroups of the free group Fn of rank n whose quotient is isomorphic to Γ. be the set of normal subgroups of $F_n$ whose quotient is isomorphic to $\Gamma$. The group $\mathrm{Aut}(F_n)$ acts on $N_n(\Gamma)$ by $\varphi \cdot N := \varphi(N)$.

original_question: The function dn(σ, τ) = (1/n)·|{x ∈ {1,..., n} | σ(x) ̸= τ (x)}| is a distance on the symmetric group Sn. For a finitely generated group G, an almost-homomorphism is a sequence of set-theoretic maps fn: G → Sn satisfying dn(fn(g)fn(h), fn(gh)) → 0 as n → ∞ for all g, h ∈ G. An almost-homomorphism {fn } is said to be close to a homomorphism if there is a sequence of group homomorphisms ρn: G → Sn such that dn(ρn(g), fn(g)) → 0 as n → ∞ for all g ∈ G. The group G is said to be permutation stable if every almost-homomorphism of G is close to a homomorphism. Conjecture: Metabelian groups are permutation-stable.
self_contained_problem:
For each positive integer $n$, let $S_n$ denote the symmetric group on $\{1,2,\dots,n\}$, and define the normalized Hamming distance on $S_n$ by
$$d_n(\sigma,\tau) = \frac{1}{n}\,\bigl|\{x \in \{1,\dots,n\} : \sigma(x) \neq \tau(x)\}\bigr|.$$
Let $G$ be a finitely generated group. A sequence of (set-theoretic) maps $f_n : G \to S_n$ is called an almost-homomorphism if for every $g,h \in G$,
$$d_n\bigl(f_n(g)\,f_n(h),\ f_n(gh)\bigr) \longrightarrow 0 \quad \text{as } n \to \infty.$$
The almost-homomorphism $\{f_n\}$ is said to be close to a homomorphism if there exists a sequence of group homomorphisms $\rho_n : G \to S_n$ such that for every $g \in G$,
$$d_n\bigl(\rho_n(g),\ f_n(g)\bigr) \longrightarrow 0 \quad \text{as } n \to \infty.$$
The group $G$ is permutation stable if every almost-homomorphism of $G$ is close to a homomorphism. (Recall that a group is metabelian if its commutator subgroup is abelian.)

Prove or disprove: every finitely generated metabelian group is permutation stable.
status_search_result: The conjecture (attributed to Levit–Lubotzky) is, in general, still open. Significant partial progress is known: Levit and Lubotzky proved permutation stability of permutational wreath products of finitely generated abelian groups, and the lamplighter group has all invariant random subgroups co-sofic (hence is permutation stable). Ishikura (arXiv:2301.07586) proved that all finitely generated free metabelian groups are permutation stable. The general metabelian case has not been resolved.

original_question: For σ ∈ Sn and τ ∈ Sm, where n ⩽ m, let dflex n(σ, τ) = (1/n) · (|{x ∈ {1,..., n} | σ(x) ̸= τ (x)}| + (m − n)). An almost-homomorphism {fn } is said to be flexibly close to a homomorphism if there is a sequence of group homomorphisms ρn: G → Smn with n ⩽ mn such that dflex n(ρn(g), fn(g)) → 0 as n → ∞ for all g ∈ G. The group G is said to be flexibly permutation stable if every almost-homomorphism of G is flexibly close to a homomorphism. Is SLn(Z) flexibly permutation-stable?
self_contained_problem:
Let $S_k$ denote the symmetric group on $\{1,2,\dots,k\}$. For positive integers $n \le m$, $\sigma \in S_n$, and $\tau \in S_m$, define the flexible normalized Hamming distance
$$d^{\mathrm{flex}}_n(\sigma,\tau) \;=\; \frac{1}{n}\Bigl(\,\bigl|\{x\in\{1,\dots,n\} : \sigma(x)\neq \tau(x)\}\bigr| \;+\; (m-n)\Bigr).$$
Let $G$ be a finitely generated group. A sequence $\{f_n\}$ with $f_n \colon G \to S_n$ is called an almost-homomorphism if for every $g,h \in G$,
$$\frac{1}{n}\bigl|\{x \in \{1,\dots,n\} : f_n(gh)(x) \neq f_n(g)f_n(h)(x)\}\bigr| \longrightarrow 0 \quad \text{as } n\to\infty.$$
The almost-homomorphism $\{f_n\}$ is said to be flexibly close to a homomorphism if there exist integers $m_n \ge n$ and group homomorphisms $\rho_n \colon G \to S_{m_n}$ such that $d^{\mathrm{flex}}_n(\rho_n(g), f_n(g)) \to 0$ as $n\to\infty$ for every $g \in G$.

The group $G$ is called flexibly permutation-stable if every almost-homomorphism of $G$ is flexibly close to a homomorphism in this sense.

Question: For each integer $n \ge 2$, is the special linear group $\mathrm{SL}_n(\mathbb{Z})$ flexibly permutation-stable?
status_search_result: The flexible permutation stability of SL_n(Z) (equivalently PSL_n(Z)) is a well-known open problem. Bowen and Burton (2019) showed that flexible stability of PSL_d(Z) for some d ≥ 5 would imply the existence of a non-sofic group, but the question itself remains unresolved. No published result establishes or refutes flexible permutation stability of SL_n(Z).

original_question: Is a flexibly permutation-stable group always permutation-stable?
self_contained_problem:
Let $G$ be a countable discrete group with a finite or countable generating set, and let $S_n$ denote the symmetric group on $n$ letters, equipped with the normalized Hamming (permutation) metric $d_n(\sigma,\tau) = \tfrac{1}{n}\,|\{i : \sigma(i) \ne \tau(i)\}|$.

A sequence of maps $\varphi_n : G \to S_{k_n}$ (with $k_n \to \infty$) is called an asymptotic homomorphism in permutations if for every $g,h \in G$,
$$\lim_{n\to\infty} d_{k_n}\bigl(\varphi_n(gh),\,\varphi_n(g)\varphi_n(h)\bigr) = 0.$$

The group $G$ is said to be permutation-stable (P-stable) if for every asymptotic homomorphism $\varphi_n : G \to S_{k_n}$ there exists a sequence of genuine homomorphisms $\psi_n : G \to S_{k_n}$ such that $\lim_{n\to\infty} d_{k_n}(\varphi_n(g),\psi_n(g)) = 0$ for every $g \in G$.

The group $G$ is said to be flexibly permutation-stable if for every asymptotic homomorphism $\varphi_n : G \to S_{k_n}$ there exist integers $m_n \ge k_n$ with $(m_n - k_n)/k_n \to 0$, and genuine homomorphisms $\psi_n : G \to S_{m_n}$, such that, identifying $\{1,\dots,k_n\} \subset \{1,\dots,m_n\}$ and viewing each $\varphi_n(g)$ as an element of $S_{m_n}$ fixing the additional points,
$$\lim_{n\to\infty} d_{m_n}\bigl(\varphi_n(g),\,\psi_n(g)\bigr) = 0 \quad \text{for every } g \in G.$$

Question: Must every flexibly permutation-stable group be permutation-stable?
status_search_result: The question of whether flexible permutation stability implies (strict) permutation stability is a recognized open problem in the theory of group stability. Recent literature (e.g., works on surface groups being flexibly stable, and on virtually free / free metabelian groups being permutation stable) treats the two notions as a priori distinct, with no known proof that flexible stability implies stability. No published resolution was found.

original_question: Assume that a finite group G has a family of d-generator subgroups whose indices have no common divisor. Is it true that G can be generated by d + 1 elements? The answer is positive if G is solvable(L. G. Kovács, H.-S. Sim, Indag. Math., 2(1991), 229–232). For an arbitrary finite group G it is proved that G can be generated by d + 2 elements(A. Lucchini, Commun. Algebra, 28, no. 4(2000), 1875–1880).
self_contained_problem:
Let $G$ be a finite group and $d$ a positive integer. Assume that $G$ has a family of subgroups $\{H_i\}_{i\in I}$ such that:
(i) each $H_i$ can be generated by $d$ elements, and
(ii) the indices $[G:H_i]$ have no nontrivial common divisor, i.e. $\gcd_{i\in I}[G:H_i]=1$.

The minimal number of generators $d(G)$ of $G$ is known to satisfy $d(G)\le d+2$ for every such $G$, and $d(G)\le d+1$ whenever $G$ is solvable.

Question: Is it true that, for every finite group $G$ as above, $G$ can be generated by $d+1$ elements?
status_search_result: The problem appears in the Kourovka Notebook list of unsolved problems. The solvable case was settled by Kovács and Sim (1991), and Lucchini (2000) proved the general bound $d(G)\le d+2$. No source found indicating the $d+1$ bound has been established for arbitrary finite groups, so the question remains open.

original_question: Let Γ be a graph of diameter d. For i ∈ {1, 2,..., d}, let Γi be the graph on the same vertex set as Γ with vertices u, w adjacent in Γi if and only if dΓ (u, w) = i. Does there exist a Q-polynomial distance-regular graph Γ of diameter 3 such that Γ2 and Γ3 are strongly regular? A. A. Makhnëv
self_contained_problem:
Let Γ be a finite connected simple graph of diameter d, and let d_Γ(·,·) denote the graph distance in Γ. For each i ∈ {1, 2, …, d} define Γ_i to be the graph on the same vertex set as Γ in which two distinct vertices u, w are adjacent if and only if d_Γ(u, w) = i.

Recall that Γ is called distance-regular if for all i ∈ {0,1,…,d} and all vertices u, w with d_Γ(u, w) = i, the numbers
  c_i = |{x : d_Γ(u, x) = i−1, d_Γ(x, w) = 1}|,
  a_i = |{x : d_Γ(u, x) = i, d_Γ(x, w) = 1}|,
  b_i = |{x : d_Γ(u, x) = i+1, d_Γ(x, w) = 1}|
depend only on i (not on the particular pair u, w). A distance-regular graph of diameter d is Q-polynomial (with respect to some ordering E_0, E_1, …, E_d of its primitive idempotents) if there exist scalars such that, in the Bose–Mesner algebra under entrywise multiplication, E_1 ∘ E_j is a linear combination of E_{j−1}, E_j, E_{j+1} for each j, equivalently if the dual eigenvalue sequence makes the dual intersection numbers tridiagonal.

A graph on v vertices is strongly regular with parameters (v, k, λ, μ) if it is k-regular, every two adjacent vertices have exactly λ common neighbours, and every two non-adjacent vertices have exactly μ common neighbours.

Question: Does there exist a Q-polynomial distance-regular graph Γ of diameter 3 such that both Γ_2 and Γ_3 are strongly regular?

original_question: (W. Willems). Conjecture: The sum of squares of the degrees of the irreducible p-Brauer characters of a finite group G is at least the p′-part of |G|. This is known to be true for p = 2(G. Malle, Adv. Math., 380(2021), Paper no. 107609, 15 pp.).
self_contained_problem:
Let $G$ be a finite group and $p$ a prime. Let $\mathrm{IBr}_p(G)$ denote the set of irreducible $p$-Brauer characters of $G$, and let $|G|_{p'}$ denote the $p'$-part of $|G|$ (i.e., the largest divisor of $|G|$ coprime to $p$). Prove or disprove that
$$\sum_{\varphi \in \mathrm{IBr}_p(G)} \varphi(1)^2 \;\ge\; |G|_{p'}$$
holds for every finite group $G$ and every prime $p$.
status_search_result: The conjecture remains open in general. It is known to hold for p = 2 (Malle, Adv. Math. 380 (2021), 107609), and earlier results of Willems established it for p-solvable groups (groups with a p-complement). Tong-Viet has reduced the conjecture to a statement about quasi-simple groups, and partial verifications exist for certain families of quasi-simple groups at odd primes, but no full proof is known.

original_question: (M. Herzog, J. Schönheim). Let G be a group and let k ⩾ 2. self_contained_problem: Let $G$ be a group and let $k \geq 2$ be an integer. original_question: The Gruenberg–Kegel graph(or the prime graph) GK(G) of a finite group G is a labelled graph with vertex set consisting of all prime divisors of the order of G in which different vertices p and q are adjacent if and only if G contains an element of order pq. Let GK(G) denote the abstract graph obtained from GK(G) by removing all labels. A finite group G is said to be recognizable by the isomorphism type of its Gruenberg–Kegel graph if there are no finite groups H not isomorphic to G with GK(H) isomorphic to GK(G). Are there infinitely many(pairwise non-isomorphic) finite groups which are recognizable by the isomorphism type of the Gruenberg–Kegel graph?
self_contained_problem:
For a finite group $G$, the Gruenberg–Kegel graph (or prime graph) $\mathrm{GK}(G)$ is the labelled graph whose vertex set is the set of prime divisors of $|G|$, where two distinct vertices $p$ and $q$ are joined by an edge if and only if $G$ contains an element of order $pq$. Let $\widetilde{\mathrm{GK}}(G)$ denote the underlying abstract (unlabelled) graph obtained from $\mathrm{GK}(G)$ by forgetting the prime labels on the vertices. A finite group $G$ is said to be recognizable by the isomorphism type of its Gruenberg–Kegel graph if there is no finite group $H$ with $H \not\cong G$ such that $\widetilde{\mathrm{GK}}(H)$ is isomorphic (as an abstract graph) to $\widetilde{\mathrm{GK}}(G)$.

Question: Do there exist infinitely many pairwise non-isomorphic finite groups that are recognizable by the isomorphism type of their Gruenberg–Kegel graph?
status_search_result: Recent work (2024–2025) on recognition by isomorphism type of Gruenberg–Kegel graphs lists only finitely many known examples (certain sporadic simple groups, some $E_8(q)$, ${}^2E_6(2)$, ${}^2G_2(27)$, etc.), and a 2022 result of Cameron and coauthor shows any such group must be almost simple. Recent surveys explicitly pose related problems and treat the existence of infinitely many such groups as not settled.

original_question: Is there an almost simple but not simple group which is recognizable by the isomorphism type of its Gruenberg–Kegel graph? Note that if a group G is recognizable by the isomorphism type of its Gruenberg– Kegel graph, then G is recognizable by its Gruenberg–Kegel graph, and therefore G is almost simple(P. J. Cameron, N. V. Maslova, J. Algebra, 607(2022), 186–213).
self_contained_problem:
For a finite group $G$, the Gruenberg–Kegel graph (or prime graph) $\Gamma(G)$ is the simple undirected graph whose vertex set is the set $\pi(G)$ of prime divisors of the order $|G|$, and in which two distinct primes $p$ and $q$ are joined by an edge if and only if $G$ contains an element of order $pq$.

A finite group $G$ is said to be recognizable by its Gruenberg–Kegel graph if every finite group $H$ with $\Gamma(H) = \Gamma(G)$ (equality of labeled graphs on the prime vertex set) satisfies $H \cong G$.

A finite group $G$ is said to be recognizable by the isomorphism type of its Gruenberg–Kegel graph if every finite group $H$ such that $\Gamma(H)$ is isomorphic to $\Gamma(G)$ as an abstract (unlabeled) graph satisfies $H \cong G$.

A finite group $G$ is called almost simple if there exists a non-abelian finite simple group $S$ such that $S \trianglelefteq G \le \mathrm{Aut}(S)$.

It is known that any finite group recognizable by the isomorphism type of its Gruenberg–Kegel graph is almost simple.

Question: Does there exist a finite almost simple group that is not simple and is recognizable by the isomorphism type of its Gruenberg–Kegel graph?
status_search_result: A 2025 preprint on characterization of groups by the isomorphism type of the Gruenberg–Kegel graph explicitly lists this as an open problem ("Problem 2"). Known results establish that groups recognizable in this sense must be almost simple, and the recognized examples investigated so far (e.g., certain exceptional groups of Lie type such as ${}^2E_6(2)$ and $E_8(q)$) are all simple. No almost simple non-simple example has been exhibited.

original_question: Is it true that a periodic group containing an involution is locally finite if the centralizer of every element of even order is locally finite?
self_contained_problem:
A group $G$ is called periodic if every element of $G$ has finite order. The centralizer of an element $g \in G$ is $C_G(g) = \{x \in G : xg = gx\}$. A group is called locally finite if every finitely generated subgroup is finite. An involution is an element of order $2$.

Determine whether the following statement is true: Every periodic group $G$ that contains an involution and has the property that the centralizer $C_G(g)$ is locally finite for every element $g \in G$ of even order is itself locally finite.
status_search_result: The problem is posed as a new entry in a recent edition of a well-known collection of unsolved problems in group theory. Related results (e.g., Shunkov-type theorems, Hartley–Kuzucuoğlu results on periodic groups with involutions of finite centralizer) address weaker or different hypotheses, but no source was found establishing or refuting the precise statement under the assumption that centralizers of all even-order elements are locally finite. Status appears unresolved based on available sources.

original_question: (M. Tărnăuceanu). Is it true that for every positive rational number r there exists a finite group G such that | Aut(G)|/|G| = r? A similar question is answered in the positive for graphs, monoids, partial groups, and posets(R. Molinier, Preprint, 2025, https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.21059). It is also known that the set {| Aut(G)|/|G| | G is a finite abelian group} is dense in [0, +∞) (M. Tărnăuceanu, Elemente Math. (2025), https://ems.press/journals/ em/articles/14298544).
self_contained_problem:
For a finite group $G$, let $\operatorname{Aut}(G)$ denote its automorphism group. Determine whether the following statement holds: for every positive rational number $r \in \mathbb{Q}_{>0}$, there exists a finite group $G$ such that
$$\frac{|\operatorname{Aut}(G)|}{|G|} = r.$$
Equivalently, is the set $\left\{\dfrac{|\operatorname{Aut}(G)|}{|G|} : G \text{ is a finite group}\right\}$ equal to $\mathbb{Q}_{>0}$?
status_search_result: The problem appears as a newly posed question in the 2026 edition of a well-known problem collection in group theory. Related results are known: the analogous statement for graphs, monoids, partial groups, and posets has been proven (Molinier, 2025), and the set of ratios |Aut(G)|/|G| for finite abelian G is known to be dense in [0,∞) (Tărnăuceanu, 2025). However, no resolution for the full finite-group case has been found in the literature.

original_question: Let w be a multilinear commutator word, and assume that G is a group where the set of w-values is covered by finitely many cyclic subgroups. Is it true that the verbal subgroup w(G) is finite-by-cyclic? This is true for lower central words(G. Cutolo, C. Nicotera, J. Algebra, 324, no. 7(2010), 1616–1624).
self_contained_problem:
A multilinear commutator word (or outer commutator word) is a word obtained from a sequence of distinct variables by nested commutation; equivalently, it is defined recursively by setting w = x for a single variable, and given multilinear commutator words u(x_1,...,x_s) and v(x_{s+1},...,x_{s+t}) on disjoint sets of variables, declaring w(x_1,...,x_{s+t}) = [u(x_1,...,x_s), v(x_{s+1},...,x_{s+t})] to be a multilinear commutator word. Examples include the lower central words γ_k and the derived words δ_k.

For a group G and a word w(x_1,...,x_n), the set of w-values in G is G_w = { w(g_1,...,g_n) : g_i ∈ G }, and the verbal subgroup w(G) is the subgroup of G generated by G_w.

A group H is called finite-by-cyclic if H has a finite normal subgroup N such that H/N is cyclic.

Question: Let w be an arbitrary multilinear commutator word, and let G be a group such that the set of w-values G_w is contained in the union of finitely many cyclic subgroups of G. Must the verbal subgroup w(G) be finite-by-cyclic?

(It is known that the answer is affirmative when w is a lower central word γ_k.)
category_tag: Verbal subgroups and word values in groups
status_search_result: The question, posed for general multilinear commutator words, generalizes a 2010 theorem of Cutolo and Nicotera handling lower central words. Subsequent work by Detomi, Morigi, and Shumyatsky and others has studied related coverings of w-values (countable coverings, periodic subgroups, BFC-type conditions, ranks), but no source located confirms a positive resolution for arbitrary multilinear commutator words under coverings by finitely many cyclic subgroups. The problem appears to remain open.

original_question: Conjecture: If G is a transitive permutation group on a finite set Ω, then for any distinct α, β in Ω there is an element g ∈ G with αg = β whose number of fixed points is different from 1. P. Müller
self_contained_problem:
Let $G$ be a transitive permutation group acting on a finite set $\Omega$. For $g\in G$ and $\alpha\in\Omega$, write $\alpha^g$ for the image of $\alpha$ under $g$, and let $\mathrm{fix}(g)=|\{\omega\in\Omega:\omega^g=\omega\}|$ denote the number of fixed points of $g$ on $\Omega$.

Prove or disprove: for every transitive permutation group $G$ on a finite set $\Omega$ and for every pair of distinct elements $\alpha,\beta\in\Omega$, there exists $g\in G$ such that $\alpha^g=\beta$ and $\mathrm{fix}(g)\neq 1$.
status_search_result: The conjecture appears as a newly posed problem in the 2026 update of the Kourovka Notebook. Web searches return no published resolution of this specific statement; related work concerns Thompson's problem (asking for an element with $\alpha^g=\beta$ and no fixed points), to which P. Müller produced a counterexample, but that does not settle the present weaker conjecture allowing any number of fixed points other than 1. No evidence of a proof or counterexample was located.

original_question: Suppose that A and G are finite groups such that A acts coprimely on G by automorphisms. Let C = CG(A) be the fixed-point subgroup, and let C ′ denote its derived subgroup. Is it true that the number of A-invariant irreducible characters χ of G whose restriction χC is never zero is exactly |C/C ′ |? This would follow if one could show that χC is never zero if and only if the Glauberman–Isaacs correspondent χ∗ of χ is linear.
self_contained_problem:
Let $A$ and $G$ be finite groups of coprime order such that $A$ acts on $G$ by automorphisms. Denote by $C = C_G(A)$ the subgroup of fixed points of $A$ in $G$, and by $C'$ the derived subgroup of $C$. By the Glauberman–Isaacs correspondence, there is a canonical bijection $\chi \mapsto \chi^*$ between the set $\operatorname{Irr}_A(G)$ of $A$-invariant irreducible complex characters of $G$ and the set $\operatorname{Irr}(C)$ of irreducible complex characters of $C$.

For $\chi \in \operatorname{Irr}_A(G)$, write $\chi_C$ for the restriction of $\chi$ to $C$, and say that $\chi_C$ is "never zero" if $\chi(c) \neq 0$ for every $c \in C$.

(a) Prove or disprove: the number of characters $\chi \in \operatorname{Irr}_A(G)$ such that $\chi_C$ is never zero equals $|C : C'|$.

(b) Prove or disprove the following stronger statement, which would imply (a): for $\chi \in \operatorname{Irr}_A(G)$, the restriction $\chi_C$ is never zero if and only if the Glauberman–Isaacs correspondent $\chi^* \in \operatorname{Irr}(C)$ is a linear character.
status_search_result: The problem is posed as a new entry in the 2026 edition of the Kourovka Notebook of unsolved problems in group theory. A web search located related work on the Glauberman–Isaacs correspondence and on vanishing/non-vanishing of restricted characters under coprime action, but no published proof or counterexample to the stated equivalence or counting statement was found. The problem appears to be currently open.

original_question: Which finite almost simple groups are the automorphism groups of regular polytopes of rank 3? In other words, which finite almost simple groups are generated by three involutions two of which commute? This question has been answered for finite simple groups; see 7.30 in Archive. Ya.
self_contained_problem:
A finite group $G$ is called almost simple if there exists a non-abelian finite simple group $S$ such that $S \trianglelefteq G \leq \mathrm{Aut}(S)$ (identifying $S$ with its group of inner automorphisms). An abstract regular polytope of rank $3$ has automorphism group generated by three involutions $\rho_0, \rho_1, \rho_2$ such that $\rho_0$ and $\rho_2$ commute (the "string C-condition" in rank 3 reduces to this commuting relation together with the intersection condition on the parabolic subgroups $\langle \rho_0,\rho_1\rangle$ and $\langle \rho_1,\rho_2\rangle$).

Equivalently, classify all finite almost simple groups $G$ that can be generated by three involutions $a, b, c \in G$ with $ac = ca$, and that arise as the full automorphism group of some abstract regular polytope of rank $3$.

Problem: Determine explicitly which finite almost simple groups are the automorphism groups of abstract regular polytopes of rank $3$.
category_tag: Almost simple groups and regular polytopes
status_search_result: The analogous question for finite simple groups has been answered. For finite almost simple groups, the problem has been resolved for several specific infinite families (e.g. PSL(2,q) and PGL(2,q), groups of type PGL(3,q), Suzuki and Ree groups), and an "atlas" of small almost simple groups has been compiled, but a complete classification across all finite almost simple groups does not appear in the literature. The status is therefore best described as partially solved.

original_question: Let V be a variety generated by a finite group, and let f(n)p be the order of the free group in V on n generators. Is it true that the sequence n log f(n) has a limit as n → ∞, and this limit is an integer?
self_contained_problem:
Let $V$ be a variety of groups generated by a finite group (so that $V$ is locally finite). For each positive integer $n$, let $F_V(n)$ denote the free group of $V$ of rank $n$, and set 
$$f(n) = |F_V(n)|,$$ 
which is finite. Determine whether the sequence
$$\frac{\log\log f(n)}{n}$$
necessarily converges as $n \to \infty$, and, when it does, whether the limit is always an integer.

original_question: (V. V. Uspenskii). A Hausdorff topological group G is called minimal if it does not admit a strictly coarser Hausdorff group topology. A topological group is called Raikov complete if its two-sided uniform structure is complete. It is known that a finite direct product of Raikov complete minimal topological groups is again minimal. Is it true that an arbitrary Cartesian product of Raikov complete minimal topological groups remains minimal? It is known that an arbitrary Cartesian product of centre-free minimal topological groups is minimal(M. Megrelishvili, Topology Appl., 62, no. 1(1995), 1–19).
self_contained_problem:
A Hausdorff topological group $(G,	au)$ is called minimal if there is no Hausdorff group topology $	au'$ on $G$ with $	au' \subsetneq 	au$. The two-sided (Roelcke) uniformity on a topological group $G$ is the supremum of its left and right uniformities; $G$ is called Raikov complete if it is complete with respect to this two-sided uniformity. It is known that:

(a) any finite direct product of Raikov complete minimal Hausdorff topological groups, equipped with the product topology, is again a minimal topological group;
(b) any (possibly infinite) Cartesian product of centre-free minimal Hausdorff topological groups is minimal.

Question: Is it true that for an arbitrary family $\{G_i\}_{i \in I}$ of Raikov complete minimal Hausdorff topological groups, the Cartesian product $\prod_{i \in I} G_i$ endowed with the product topology is also a minimal topological group?
status_search_result: The problem is posed by V. V. Uspenskii as a new entry in the 2026 (current) Kourovka-style problem list of unsolved problems. Web searches return only related work (e.g., perfect local minimality, products of locally minimal groups, Megrelishvili's centre-free case) but no announcement of a resolution of the general Cartesian-product question for Raikov complete minimal groups, so the problem appears to remain open.

original_question: For a group word w(x1,..., xn) on n letters, define e0(x1,..., xn) = x1 and ek+1(x1,..., xn) = w(ek(x1,..., xn),..., xn) for all k ∈ N. A group G is said to satisfy the Engel type iterated identity w if for all x1,..., xn ∈ G there exists m ∈ N such that em(x1,..., xn) = 1. Conjecture: For every non-trivial word w, if a finitely generated branch group G(see 15.12) satisfies the iterated identity w, then G is a torsion group. This is true in the case of the commutator word w = [x1, x2 ] (G. Fernández- Alcober, M. Noce, G. Tracey, J. Algebra, 554(2020), 54–77).
self_contained_problem:
Let $w(x_1,\dots,x_n)$ be a group word on $n$ letters. For a group $G$, define iterates $e_0,e_1,\dots\colon G^n\to G$ by
$$e_0(x_1,\dots,x_n)=x_1, \qquad e_{k+1}(x_1,\dots,x_n)=w\bigl(e_k(x_1,\dots,x_n),\,x_2,\dots,x_n\bigr) \quad (k\ge 0).$$
The group $G$ is said to satisfy the Engel-type iterated identity $w$ if for every $x_1,\dots,x_n\in G$ there exists $m=m(x_1,\dots,x_n)\in\mathbb N$ such that $e_m(x_1,\dots,x_n)=1$.

Recall that a group $G$ acting faithfully on an infinite spherically homogeneous rooted tree $T$ is called a branch group if it acts transitively on each level of $T$ and, for every $n\ge 0$, the rigid level stabilizer (the direct product of the rigid stabilizers of all vertices at level $n$) has finite index in $G$.

Prove or disprove: for every non-trivial word $w$, if a finitely generated branch group $G$ satisfies the Engel-type iterated identity $w$, then $G$ is a torsion group.

(It is known that this holds for the commutator word $w(x_1,x_2)=[x_1,x_2]$.)
status_search_result: The conjecture appears in the Kourovka Notebook as a new problem. It is established for the commutator word $w=[x_1,x_2]$ (Fernández-Alcober, Noce, Tracey, J. Algebra 554 (2020), 54–77, with related work on Engel elements in weakly branch groups). No reference verifying the full conjecture for arbitrary non-trivial words could be found, so the general case appears to remain open.

original_question: (D. Segal). A group word w is said to be concise in a class C of groups if for every group G in C such that the set Gw of word values of w in G is finite, the verbal subgroup w(G) = ⟨Gw ⟩ is also finite(see also Archive 2.45). Is every word concise in the class of residually finite groups? See(D. Segal, Words. Notes on verbal width in groups, Cambridge Univ. Press, 2009) for a partial solution.
self_contained_problem:
A group word is an element $w = w(x_1, \ldots, x_n)$ of the free group $F_n$ on free generators $x_1, \ldots, x_n$. For a group $G$, the set of $w$-values in $G$ is
$$G_w = \{\, w(g_1, \ldots, g_n)^{\pm 1} : g_1, \ldots, g_n \in G \,\},$$
and the verbal subgroup of $G$ corresponding to $w$ is $w(G) = \langle G_w \rangle$.

A word $w$ is said to be concise in a class $\mathcal{C}$ of groups if, for every group $G \in \mathcal{C}$ with $G_w$ finite, the verbal subgroup $w(G)$ is also finite.

A group $G$ is residually finite if for every nontrivial $g \in G$ there exists a normal subgroup $N \trianglelefteq G$ of finite index with $g \notin N$.

Question: Is every group word $w$ concise in the class of residually finite groups? That is, must $w(G)$ be finite whenever $G$ is residually finite and $G_w$ is finite?
category_tag: Conciseness of words in residually finite groups
status_search_result: The general question of whether every word is concise in the class of residually finite groups remains open. Partial results exist for various families (e.g., Engel-type words, multilinear commutator words, generalizations of Engel words), and an active ERC/Horizon project ("GroupConciseness") and recent papers (2018–2025) continue to address the conjecture, but no full solution or counterexample is known.

original_question: A first order formula φ(x) in the group language with one free variable is said to be concise in a class C of groups if for every group G in C such that the set Gφ of elements in G satisfying φ is finite, the subgroup φ(G) generated by Gφ is also finite(cf. 21.105 and Archive 2.45). Is every formula with one free variable concise in the class of residually finite groups?
self_contained_problem:
Work in the first-order language of groups (one binary operation, one unary operation for inverse, and a constant for the identity). Let φ(x) be a first-order formula in this language with a single free variable x. For any group G, write
  G_φ = { g ∈ G : G ⊨ φ(g) },
and let φ(G) denote the subgroup of G generated by G_φ.

Given a class C of groups, the formula φ(x) is said to be concise in C if for every group G ∈ C the finiteness of G_φ implies the finiteness of φ(G).

A group G is called residually finite if for every nonidentity element g ∈ G there exists a finite group F and a homomorphism π : G → F with π(g) ≠ 1.

Question: Is every first-order formula φ(x) (in the group language, with one free variable) concise in the class of residually finite groups?
category_tag: Concise formulae in residually finite groups

original_question: A sequence {Fn } of pairwise disjoint finite subsets of a topological group is called expansive if for every open subset U there is a number m such that Fn ∩ U ̸= ∅ for all n > m. Suppose that a countable group G can be partitioned into countably many dense subsets. Is it true that in G there exists an expansive sequence? Cf. 15.80.
self_contained_problem:
Let G be a countable group endowed with a (Hausdorff) topological group structure (or, more generally, regarded as a topological group via some group topology). A sequence {F_n}_{n∈ℕ} of pairwise disjoint finite subsets of a topological group is called expansive if for every nonempty open subset U there exists m ∈ ℕ such that F_n ∩ U ≠ ∅ for all n > m.

Suppose that the countable group G can be partitioned into countably many dense subsets (with respect to its topology). Must G contain an expansive sequence of pairwise disjoint finite subsets?
