original_question: For a finite group G let Cod(G) denote the set of irreducible character codegrees of G(see 20.78). Define σ(G) = max{|π(m)|: m ∈ Cod(G)}, where π(m) denotes the set of prime divisors of an integer m. It is proved that there exists a constant k such that |π(G)| ⩽ k · σ(G) for every finite group G(Y. Yang, G. Qian, J. Algebra, 478(2017), 215–219), but the estimate provided for k is very crude. Can the constant k be taken as 4?
self_contained_problem:
Let G be a finite group. For an irreducible complex character χ of G, define its codegree by cod(χ) = |G : ker(χ)| / χ(1), and let Cod(G) = { cod(χ) : χ ∈ Irr(G) }. For a positive integer m, let π(m) denote the set of prime divisors of m, and write π(G) = π(|G|). Define
   σ(G) = max{ |π(m)| : m ∈ Cod(G) }.
It is known that there is an absolute constant k such that |π(G)| ≤ k · σ(G) for every finite group G. Determine whether one may take k = 4; that is, does the inequality
   |π(G)| ≤ 4 · σ(G)
hold for every finite group G?
status_search_result: Searches reveal active recent research on character codegrees of finite groups (including work by Qian and collaborators), but no source establishes the optimal constant k = 4 in the inequality |π(G)| ≤ k · σ(G). The Yang–Qian result (J. Algebra 478, 2017) gives only a crude k, and no later paper found resolves whether k = 4 suffices. The problem appears to remain open.

original_question: Conjecture: The derived length of a finite solvable group G does not exceed |Cod(G)| − 1. The Fitting height of G is known to be at most min{|Cod(G)|−1, |Cod(G)|/2+1} (G. Qian, Y. Zeng, J. Group Theory, to appear).
self_contained_problem:
For a finite group $G$, let $\mathrm{Irr}(G)$ denote the set of complex irreducible characters of $G$. For $\chi \in \mathrm{Irr}(G)$, define the codegree of $\chi$ by
$$\mathrm{cod}(\chi) = \frac{[G:\ker\chi]}{\chi(1)},$$
and set
$$\mathrm{Cod}(G) = \{\mathrm{cod}(\chi) : \chi \in \mathrm{Irr}(G)\}.$$
Let $G$ be a finite solvable group, and let $dl(G)$ denote its derived length, i.e., the smallest non-negative integer $n$ such that the $n$-th term $G^{(n)}$ of the derived series is trivial.

Prove or disprove the following: for every finite solvable group $G$,
$$dl(G) \le |\mathrm{Cod}(G)| - 1.$$
category_tag: character codegrees of finite solvable groups
status_search_result: Recent literature on character codegrees treats the bound $dl(G) \le |\mathrm{Cod}(G)|-1$ for solvable groups as an open conjecture. Partial results bound the Fitting height by $\min\{|\mathrm{Cod}(G)|-1, |\mathrm{Cod}(G)|/2+1\}$ (Qian–Zeng), and related codegree analogues of Huppert's conjectures are actively studied, but no general proof of the derived-length bound has been published.

original_question: Let S be a nonabelian finite simple group, and x a nonidentity automorphism of S. Let α(x) be the smallest number of conjugates of x in G = ⟨x, Inn S⟩ that generate G. The values of α(x) had been studied in(R. Guralnick, J. Saxl, J. Algebra, 268, no. 2(2003), 519–571). (a) (R. Guralnick, J. Saxl). Conjecture: If S is an exceptional group of Lie type, then α(x) ⩽ 5 for every nonidentity automorphism x of S. (b) For each exceptional group S of Lie type, find the largest value of α(x).
self_contained_problem:
Let $S$ be a nonabelian finite simple group and let $x$ be a nonidentity automorphism of $S$. Identify $S$ with the inner automorphism group $\operatorname{Inn} S$ and set $G = \langle x, \operatorname{Inn} S\rangle$, an almost simple group with socle $S$. Define
$$\alpha(x) = \min\{\, k \in \mathbb{Z}_{>0} : \text{there exist } g_1,\ldots,g_k \in G \text{ with } \langle x^{g_1},\ldots,x^{g_k}\rangle = G \,\}.$$

Restrict attention to the case in which $S$ is an exceptional group of Lie type (i.e. $S$ is one of $G_2(q)$, $F_4(q)$, $E_6(q)$, ${}^2E_6(q)$, $E_7(q)$, $E_8(q)$, ${}^2B_2(q)$, ${}^2G_2(q)$, ${}^3D_4(q)$, or ${}^2F_4(q)$, in their simple versions).

(a) Prove or disprove: for every nonidentity automorphism $x$ of $S$, $\alpha(x) \leq 5$.

(b) For each exceptional simple group $S$ of Lie type, determine the exact value of $\max_{x} \alpha(x)$, where the maximum is taken over all nonidentity automorphisms $x$ of $S$.
category_tag: Generation of finite simple groups by conjugates
status_search_result: The Guralnick–Saxl conjecture on the bound α(x) ≤ 5 for exceptional groups of Lie type, and the determination of the exact maximum of α(x) for each such group, appear to remain open. Recent activity (e.g. work on sporadic socle cases settling α ≤ 4 with Fischer-group exceptions, and ongoing studies of generation by regular unipotent elements in groups of Lie type from 2024–2025) treats related cases and partial results, but no source verifying the conjecture in full or computing the maximum α(x) for all exceptional types was found.

original_question: Let S be a finite simple nonabelian group that is not isomorphic to any group 2B2(q). A nonidentity automorphism x of S is called a τ-automorphism if every two conjugates of x in ⟨x, Inn(S)⟩ generate a subgroup of order not divisible by 3. If S admits a τ-automorphism, we call S a τ-group. (a) List all τ-groups up to isomorphism. (b) Do τ-automorphisms of odd order exist?
self_contained_problem:
Let $S$ be a finite nonabelian simple group, and assume that $S$ is not isomorphic to any Suzuki group $\,^{2}B_{2}(q)$. Identify $S$ with its group of inner automorphisms $\operatorname{Inn}(S) \le \operatorname{Aut}(S)$. A nonidentity automorphism $x \in \operatorname{Aut}(S)$ is called a $\tau$-automorphism of $S$ if for every two conjugates $x_1, x_2$ of $x$ in the subgroup $\langle x, \operatorname{Inn}(S) \rangle \le \operatorname{Aut}(S)$, the order of the subgroup $\langle x_1, x_2 \rangle$ is not divisible by $3$. A finite nonabelian simple group $S$ (not isomorphic to any $\,^{2}B_{2}(q)$) is called a $\tau$-group if it admits at least one $\tau$-automorphism.

(a) Determine, up to isomorphism, all $\tau$-groups $S$.

(b) Decide whether there exists a $\tau$-group $S$ that admits a $\tau$-automorphism of odd order.

original_question: A nonempty class X of finite groups is said to be complete if X is closed under taking subgroups, homomorphic images, and extensions. The symmetric boundary of a complete class X other than the class of all finite groups is defined as the largest integer n such that Sn ∈ X. Every positive integer n ̸= 3 coincides with the symmetric boundary of some complete class. It is proved(mod CFSG, D. O. Revin, Algebra i Analiz, 37, no. 1(2025), 141–176(Russian)) that, for every complete class X, there exists a nonnegative integer m with the following property: for every finite group G and each conjugacy class D of G, if every m elements of D generate a subgroup belonging to X, then ⟨D⟩ ∈ X. The smallest such m is called the Baer–Suzuki width of X denoted by BS(X). It is also proved(mod CFSG, ibid.) that, for a complete class X of symmetric boundary n, the value of BS(X) is at least n and is bounded above in terms of n. For every positive integer n ̸= 3, let f+ (n) and f− (n) be respectively the maximum and the minimum of BS(X), where X runs over all complete classes of symmetric boundary n. (a) Find f+ (n) for n = 4, 5, 6. It is known that f+ (1) = 2, f+ (2) = 3, and f+ (n) = 2(n − 1) for n ⩾ 7. (b) Is it true that f− (n) = n for all n ̸= 3? This is known to be true for n = 1, 2, 4.
self_contained_problem:
Call a nonempty class X of finite groups complete if it is closed under taking subgroups, homomorphic images, and extensions. For a complete class X different from the class of all finite groups, define its symmetric boundary to be the largest integer n such that the symmetric group S_n belongs to X. (Every positive integer n ≠ 3 arises as the symmetric boundary of some complete class.) 

Assume the following result: for every complete class X there exists a smallest nonnegative integer m, denoted BS(X) and called the Baer–Suzuki width of X, with the property that, for every finite group G and every conjugacy class D of G, if every m-element subset of D generates a subgroup belonging to X, then the subgroup ⟨D⟩ generated by D belongs to X. Assume further that, for any complete class X with symmetric boundary n, one has BS(X) ≥ n and BS(X) is bounded above by a function of n.

For each positive integer n ≠ 3, let
   f_+(n) = max { BS(X) : X is a complete class of symmetric boundary n },
   f_−(n) = min { BS(X) : X is a complete class of symmetric boundary n }.

It is known that f_+(1) = 2, f_+(2) = 3, and f_+(n) = 2(n − 1) for all n ≥ 7, and that f_−(n) = n for n = 1, 2, 4.

(a) Determine the values of f_+(n) for n = 4, 5, 6.
(b) Decide whether f_−(n) = n holds for every positive integer n ≠ 3.

original_question: Let G be a finite group and p be a prime. Let Ψp,G be the class function of G which vanishes on all p-singular elements of G and whose value at each p-regular element x of G is the number of p-elements of CG(x). (a) Is it true that Ψp,G is a character of G? (b) If yes, can Ψp,G be afforded by a projective RG-module, where R is a complete discrete valuation ring of characteristic zero such that the field of fractions of R is a splitting field for G and its subgroups, and the residue field R/J(R) is a splitting field of characteristic p for G and its subgroups? It is known that Ψp,G is a character when G ≅ Sn for any positive integer n and any prime p(T. Scharf, J. Algebra, 139, no. 2(1991), 446–457).
self_contained_problem:
Let $G$ be a finite group and let $p$ be a prime number. An element of $G$ is called a $p$-element if its order is a power of $p$, and a $p$-regular element if its order is coprime to $p$; otherwise it is called $p$-singular. For each $x \in G$, let $C_G(x)$ denote the centralizer of $x$ in $G$. Define the class function $\Psi_{p,G}: G \to \mathbb{Z}$ by
$$\Psi_{p,G}(x) = \begin{cases} \#\{y \in C_G(x) : y \text{ is a } p\text{-element}\}, & \text{if } x \text{ is } p\text{-regular},\\ 0, & \text{if } x \text{ is } p\text{-singular}.\end{cases}$$

(a) Is $\Psi_{p,G}$ a character of $G$ (i.e., the character of some finite-dimensional complex representation of $G$)?

(b) Assuming the answer to (a) is yes, let $R$ be a complete discrete valuation ring of characteristic zero whose field of fractions $K$ is a splitting field for $G$ and all its subgroups, and whose residue field $R/J(R)$ has characteristic $p$ and is a splitting field for $G$ and all its subgroups. Can $\Psi_{p,G}$ be afforded by a projective $RG$-module?

(It is known that $\Psi_{p,G}$ is a character whenever $G$ is isomorphic to a symmetric group $S_n$, for every positive integer $n$ and every prime $p$.)

original_question: A finite group G is called weakly ab-maximal if |H: [H, H]| ⩽ |G: [G, G]| for all H ⩽ G. Do weakly ab-maximal groups have bounded derived length? It is known that weakly ab-maximal groups are direct products of weakly abmaximal p-groups(F. Lisi, L. Sabatini, J. Group Theory, 27(2024), 1203–1217).
self_contained_problem:
Call a finite group $G$ weakly ab-maximal if for every subgroup $H \le G$ one has
$$|H:[H,H]| \;\le\; |G:[G,G]|,$$
where $[X,X]$ denotes the commutator subgroup of $X$. (It is known that every weakly ab-maximal finite group is a direct product of weakly ab-maximal $p$-groups.)

Question: Does there exist a constant $d$ (independent of $G$) such that every weakly ab-maximal finite group $G$ has derived length at most $d$? Equivalently, is the derived length of weakly ab-maximal finite groups bounded?
status_search_result: The problem is posed as a new question in the 2026 Kourovka Notebook of unsolved problems in group theory. Related work by Lisi–Sabatini (J. Group Theory 27 (2024)) establishes the direct product decomposition into p-group factors, and a subsequent arXiv preprint (2502.05821) constructs extremal ab-maximal p-groups answering related questions of González-Sánchez–Klopsch and Lisi–Sabatini, but no source found resolves the boundedness of the derived length for weakly ab-maximal groups. The problem appears to remain open.

original_question: Let C1,..., Cn be(left or right) cosets of a finite group G such that U:= C1 ∪ · · · ∪ Cn is not G. Is it always true that |G \ U | ⩾ |G|/2n? Affirmative answers are known in some special cases(B. Sambale, M. Tărnăuceanu, J. Algebraic Combin., 55(2022), 979–987).
self_contained_problem:
Let $G$ be a finite group and let $C_1, C_2, \ldots, C_n$ be cosets of subgroups of $G$ (each $C_i$ is a left or right coset $g_iH_i$ for some subgroup $H_i \le G$ and some $g_i \in G$). Set
$$U := C_1 \cup C_2 \cup \cdots \cup C_n,$$
and assume $U \neq G$. Determine whether the inequality
$$|G \setminus U| \;\ge\; \frac{|G|}{2^n}$$
necessarily holds for every such configuration.
status_search_result: The conjecture has been verified in special cases. Sambale and Tărnăuceanu (J. Algebraic Combin. 55 (2022), 979–987) proved a weaker bound |G\U| ≥ |G|/(2·n!) in general, and established the sharp bound |G|/2^n for elementary abelian groups (via an Alon–Füredi linear algebra argument) and obtained results for cyclic groups linked to a number-theoretic problem of Erdős. The full conjecture for arbitrary finite groups appears to remain open.

original_question: A group is boundedly acyclic if its bounded cohomology with trivial real coefficients vanishes in all positive degrees. Is every branch group boundedly acyclic?
self_contained_problem:
A group $G$ is called boundedly acyclic if its bounded cohomology with trivial real coefficients vanishes in all positive degrees, that is, $H_b^n(G;\mathbb{R}) = 0$ for every $n \geq 1$.

Recall that a branch group is a group $G$ acting faithfully and level-transitively by automorphisms on an infinite spherically homogeneous rooted tree $T$ such that, for every level $n \geq 0$, the rigid level stabilizer $\mathrm{Rist}_G(n)$ — defined as the direct product over all vertices $v$ at level $n$ of the rigid vertex stabilizers $\mathrm{Rist}_G(v) = \{g \in G : g \text{ fixes every vertex of } T \text{ not lying below } v\}$ — has finite index in $G$.

Question: Is every branch group boundedly acyclic?
status_search_result: The question appears as a newly posed problem in the 2026 Kourovka Notebook. Recent literature on bounded acyclicity (e.g., works on binate groups, lamplighters, and Thompson-like groups) provides many new examples of boundedly acyclic groups, but no source located identifies branch groups in general as boundedly acyclic or refutes this. The problem appears to be open.

original_question: (a) Does there exist a finitely generated simple group that is of exponential growth but not of uniformly exponential growth? (b) Does there exist a finitely generated hereditarily just-infinite group that is of exponential growth but not of uniformly exponential growth?
self_contained_problem:
Let G be a finitely generated group with finite generating set S, and let B_S(n) denote the set of elements of G expressible as words of length at most n in S ∪ S^{-1}. The exponential growth rate of G with respect to S is

  ω(G,S) := lim_{n→∞} |B_S(n)|^{1/n} ≥ 1.

The group G is said to have exponential growth if ω(G,S) > 1 for some (equivalently, every) finite generating set S, and to have uniformly exponential growth if

  ω(G) := inf { ω(G,S) : S a finite generating set of G } > 1.

Recall that a group is simple if it has no proper nontrivial normal subgroups, and that an infinite group G is just-infinite if every proper quotient of G is finite; G is hereditarily just-infinite if every finite-index subgroup of G is just-infinite.

Questions:
(a) Does there exist a finitely generated simple group that has exponential growth but does not have uniformly exponential growth?
(b) Does there exist a finitely generated hereditarily just-infinite group that has exponential growth but does not have uniformly exponential growth?
status_search_result: Wilson (2004) constructed finitely generated groups of exponential but non-uniformly exponential growth, and later examples include branch groups of this type. However, no construction is known to produce such groups that are simple, or hereditarily just-infinite. The literature on uniform exponential growth (Breuillard, Mann, Osin, Wilson, and others) does not record a resolution to either part, so both questions appear to remain open.

original_question: (A. Thom). Is there any group which is not isomorphic to the quotient of a residually finite group by an amenable normal subgroup?
self_contained_problem:
A group $G$ is called residually finite if for every non-identity element $g \in G$ there exists a finite group $F$ and a homomorphism $\varphi: G \to F$ such that $\varphi(g) \neq 1$. A group $A$ is called amenable if there exists a finitely additive, left-translation-invariant probability measure defined on all subsets of $A$.

Determine whether there exists a group $Q$ that is not isomorphic to $R/N$ for any residually finite group $R$ and any amenable normal subgroup $N \trianglelefteq R$. Equivalently, is every group a quotient of some residually finite group by an amenable normal subgroup?
status_search_result: The question, attributed to A. Thom, appears in a recent collection of new open problems in group theory (Kourovka Notebook). A search did not turn up any published resolution; the question relates to extensions/quotients involving sofic-like properties (since residually-finite-by-amenable groups are sofic), and no example of a group failing to be such a quotient is known. The status appears to be open.

original_question: Does there exist a group G that contains a family(Gn)n∈N of finite-index subgroups such that for every n there is a homomorphism fn: Gn → Z whose kernel is of type Fn, but not of type Fn+1?
self_contained_problem:
Recall that a group H is said to be of type F_n if there exists a K(H,1) Eilenberg–MacLane CW-complex with finite n-skeleton; equivalently, H admits a classifying space whose n-skeleton has only finitely many cells. Type F_1 means finitely generated and type F_2 means finitely presented. A group is of type F_n but not of type F_{n+1} if the n-skeleton can be made finite but no classifying space has finite (n+1)-skeleton.

Question: Does there exist a group G together with a family (G_n)_{n∈ℕ} of finite-index subgroups of G such that for every positive integer n there is a homomorphism f_n : G_n → ℤ whose kernel ker(f_n) is of type F_n but not of type F_{n+1}?

original_question: A pro-p group is(relatively) strictly finitely presented if it is the pro-p completion of a group that is finitely presented(respectively, finitely presented in some finitely-based variety of groups). A pro-p group is finitely axiomatizable if it is determined up to isomorphism by a single sentence in the first-order language of group theory. (a) Does there exist a(relatively) strictly finitely presented pro-p group that is not finitely axiomatizable in the class of all pro-p groups? (b) In particular, is every finitely generated free pro-p group finitely axiomatizable? See(A. Nies, K. Tent, D. Segal, Proc. London Math. Soc. (3), 123(2021), 597– 635; D. Segal, Preprint, 2025, https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.04816).
self_contained_problem:
Work in the first-order language of group theory (with signature consisting of multiplication, inversion, and the identity element).

Definitions.
- A pro-p group is the inverse limit of a system of finite p-groups; equivalently, a profinite group in which every open normal subgroup has index a power of p.
- The pro-p completion of an abstract group G is the inverse limit of the finite p-group quotients of G.
- A variety of groups is the class of all groups satisfying a given set of group identities (laws). A variety is finitely based if it can be defined by finitely many such identities.
- A pro-p group P is called strictly finitely presented if there exists a finitely presented abstract group G whose pro-p completion is isomorphic to P.
- A pro-p group P is called relatively strictly finitely presented if there exists an abstract group G that is finitely presented in some finitely based variety of groups, and whose pro-p completion is isomorphic to P.
- A pro-p group P is finitely axiomatizable in the class of all pro-p groups if there exists a single first-order sentence φ in the language of groups such that, for every pro-p group Q, one has Q ≅ P if and only if Q ⊨ φ.

Questions.
(a) Does there exist a (relatively) strictly finitely presented pro-p group that is not finitely axiomatizable in the class of all pro-p groups?
(b) In particular, is every finitely generated free pro-p group finitely axiomatizable in the class of all pro-p groups?
status_search_result: The problem is posed as a new entry in the 2026 Kourovka Notebook and references a 2025 preprint by Segal as the most recent work. No source found establishes finite axiomatizability of finitely generated free pro-p groups or resolves part (a); the question appears to remain open.

original_question: Let p be a prime number. A group Γ is called p-Jordan if there exist constants J and e such that any finite subgroup G ⊂ Γ contains a normal abelian subgroup of order coprime to p and of index at most J · |G(p) |e. (For example by the results of Brauer–Feit and Larsen–Pink, for any field K of characteristic p the group GLn(K) is p-Jordan with e = 3.) Let the p-Jordan exponent e(Γ) of the group Γ be the infimum of all constants e for which the above bound holds for some constant J = J(e). a) Is it true that this infimum is always attained? b) Is it true that e(Γ) ⩽ 3 for any p-Jordan group Γ?
self_contained_problem:
Let $p$ be a prime number. For a finite group $G$, denote by $|G(p)|$ the order of a Sylow $p$-subgroup of $G$ (equivalently, the largest power of $p$ dividing $|G|$). A group $\Gamma$ is called $p$-Jordan if there exist constants $J \ge 1$ and $e \ge 0$ such that every finite subgroup $G \subset \Gamma$ contains a normal abelian subgroup $A \trianglelefteq G$ whose order is coprime to $p$ and whose index satisfies
$$[G : A] \le J \cdot |G(p)|^{e}.$$
(By the theorems of Brauer–Feit and Larsen–Pink, for any field $K$ of characteristic $p$ the group $\mathrm{GL}_n(K)$ is $p$-Jordan with $e = 3$.) Define the $p$-Jordan exponent of $\Gamma$ by
$$e(\Gamma) := \inf\{ e \ge 0 : \text{there exists } J = J(e) \text{ such that the bound above holds for all finite } G \subset \Gamma \}.$$

(a) Is the infimum $e(\Gamma)$ always attained, i.e., is there always a constant $J$ such that the bound $[G:A] \le J \cdot |G(p)|^{e(\Gamma)}$ holds for every finite subgroup $G \subset \Gamma$?

(b) Is it true that $e(\Gamma) \le 3$ for every $p$-Jordan group $\Gamma$?

original_question: Let w be a group word, and G a profinite group. Is it true that the cardinality of the set of w-values in G is either finite or at least continuum? An affirmative answer is known for several important words; see(E. Detomi, B. Klopsch, P. Shumyatsky, J. London Math. Soc. (2), 102(2020), 977–993).
self_contained_problem:
A profinite group is a topological group that is isomorphic to an inverse limit of finite groups; equivalently, a compact, Hausdorff, totally disconnected topological group. A group word is an element $w = w(x_1, \dots, x_n)$ of the free group on countably many generators $x_1, x_2, \dots$. For a group $G$, the set of $w$-values in $G$ is
$$G_w = \{\, w(g_1, \dots, g_n) : g_1, \dots, g_n \in G \,\}.$$

Question: Let $w$ be a group word and let $G$ be a profinite group. Is it true that the cardinality $|G_w|$ is either finite or at least $2^{\aleph_0}$ (the cardinality of the continuum)?
status_search_result: The question is the "strong conciseness" problem for profinite groups. It has been confirmed for several important classes of words — most notably for multilinear commutator words and for power words $x^q$ in the class of all profinite groups (Detomi–Klopsch–Shumyatsky, J. London Math. Soc. 102 (2020), 977–993), and for all words in nilpotent profinite groups. Subsequent work (e.g., Detomi–Klopsch–Shumyatsky, Math. Nachr. 2023; "On profinite groups admitting a word with only few values", arXiv:2401.15707) has extended the list of words for which it is known. The general case for an arbitrary word in an arbitrary profinite group remains open.

original_question: Is it true that the extension of the A. Agrachev–R. Gamkrelidze construction of groups from pre-Lie rings in(J. Soviet Math., 17(1981), 1650–1675) suggested in Definition 66 of(A. Smoktunowicz, J. Pure Appl. Algebra, 229, no. 12(2025), 108128) produces groups from pre-Lie rings? If this extended construction does give a group, then it also gives a brace, and so an affirmative answer to this question would have consequences for the theory of set-theoretic solutions of the Yang–Baxter equation and for the theory of braces.
self_contained_problem:
Background. A (left) pre-Lie ring is an abelian group $(A,+)$ equipped with a biadditive operation $\cdot:A\times A\to A$ satisfying the left pre-Lie identity
$$ (a\cdot b)\cdot c - a\cdot(b\cdot c) \;=\; (b\cdot a)\cdot c - b\cdot(a\cdot c)\qquad(a,b,c\in A). $$
The commutator $[a,b]:=a\cdot b-b\cdot a$ then turns $A$ into a Lie ring.

A (left) brace is an abelian group $(B,+)$ together with a second binary operation $\circ$ such that $(B,\circ)$ is a group and
$$ a\circ(b+c)+a \;=\; a\circ b+a\circ c\qquad(a,b,c\in B). $$
Braces provide non-degenerate involutive set-theoretic solutions of the Yang–Baxter equation.

The classical Agrachev–Gamkrelidze construction associates to a pre-Lie ring $A$ in which a suitable formal exponential/Magnus-type series converges (e.g. $A$ nilpotent, or a complete filtered $\mathbb Q$-pre-Lie algebra) a group structure $\circ$ on $A$ given by
$$ a\circ b \;=\; a+b+\Omega(a,b), $$
where $\Omega$ is a universal series of iterated pre-Lie products built from the pre-Lie operation, recovering on the Lie quotient the Baker–Campbell–Hausdorff formula. Together with the additive structure this yields a brace $(A,+,\circ)$.

Extended construction. Replace the convergence/nilpotence requirement by a purely formal definition: for an arbitrary (not necessarily nilpotent, not necessarily $\mathbb Q$-divisible) pre-Lie ring $A$, define a partial binary operation $\circ$ on $A$ (where defined) by the same universal expression as in the Agrachev–Gamkrelidze formula, interpreted in $A$ via the pre-Lie product alone, with the symmetric brace-style identities used to extend it to all of $A$.

Question. Does this extended construction always produce a group? Equivalently: for every pre-Lie ring $A$, is the operation $\circ$ defined as above a well-defined associative operation on $A$ admitting two-sided inverses and the additive identity as neutral element, so that $(A,+,\circ)$ is a brace (and hence yields a set-theoretic solution of the Yang–Baxter equation)?

original_question: A group G is said to be virtually special if G has a finite-index subgroup isomorphic to the fundamental group of a special complex(in the sense of F. Haglund, D. T. Wise, Geom. Funct. Anal., 17, no. 5(2008), 1551–1620; cf 20.60.) A group G is called a CAT(0) group if it acts properly discontinuously and cocompactly by isometries on a CAT(0) metric space. a) Is every CAT(0) free-by-cyclic group virtually special? b) A weaker question: does every CAT(0) free-by-cyclic group virtually embed into a right-angled Artin group?
self_contained_problem:
Definitions.

(1) A nonpositively curved cube complex X is called special (in the sense of Haglund–Wise) if its hyperplanes satisfy: each hyperplane is two-sided, no hyperplane self-intersects, no hyperplane self-osculates, and no two hyperplanes inter-osculate.

(2) A group G is called virtually special if G contains a finite-index subgroup isomorphic to the fundamental group of a compact special cube complex. Equivalently, G has a finite-index subgroup that embeds into a right-angled Artin group.

(3) A right-angled Artin group on a finite simplicial graph Γ with vertex set V and edge set E is A(Γ) = ⟨V | [v,w] = 1 for {v,w} ∈ E⟩.

(4) A group G is a CAT(0) group if there exists a CAT(0) geodesic metric space on which G acts properly discontinuously and cocompactly by isometries.

(5) A group G is free-by-cyclic if there is a short exact sequence 1 → F → G → Z → 1 with F a finitely generated free group; equivalently G ≅ F ⋊_φ Z for some automorphism φ of F.

Problem. Let G be a CAT(0) free-by-cyclic group.

(a) Must G be virtually special?

(b) (Weaker form.) Must G virtually embed in a right-angled Artin group, i.e., must G contain a finite-index subgroup isomorphic to a subgroup of some right-angled Artin group A(Γ)?

No source found resolving the question in full generality, including non-hyperbolic, non-tubular CAT(0) free-by-cyclic groups.

original_question: (M. Bridson). Let Fm be a free group of rank m and let ϕ ∈ Aut(Fm) be a polynomially growing automorphism of maximal degree m − 1, which means that for some(equivalently, any) free basis {x1,..., xm } of Fm, the sequence maxi |ϕn(xi)| grows at the rate of nm−1, where |g| denotes the minimal length of g in the xi and their inverses. a) Is the free-by-cyclic group Fm ⋊ϕ Z virtually special? b) In particular, are the Hydra groups Gm = Fm ⋊ Z = ⟨a1,..., am, t | t−1 a1 t = a1, t−1 ai t = ai ai−1 for all i > 1⟩ virtually special?
self_contained_problem:
Let $m \geq 2$ and let $F_m$ denote the free group of rank $m$ with free basis $\{x_1,\dots,x_m\}$. For $g\in F_m$ let $|g|$ be the word length of $g$ with respect to $\{x_1^{\pm 1},\dots,x_m^{\pm 1}\}$. An automorphism $\varphi\in\mathrm{Aut}(F_m)$ is said to be polynomially growing of degree $d$ if, for some (equivalently any) free basis, the sequence $\max_{1\le i\le m}|\varphi^n(x_i)|$ grows like $n^d$ as $n\to\infty$. A finitely generated group is called virtually special if it has a finite-index subgroup that embeds in a right-angled Artin group (equivalently, a finite-index subgroup is the fundamental group of a special cube complex in the sense of Haglund–Wise).

(a) Suppose $\varphi\in\mathrm{Aut}(F_m)$ is polynomially growing of maximal degree $m-1$. Is the free-by-cyclic group $F_m\rtimes_\varphi \mathbb{Z}$ virtually special?

(b) In particular, is the Hydra group
$$G_m=\langle a_1,\dots,a_m,t \mid t^{-1}a_1 t = a_1,\ t^{-1}a_i t = a_i a_{i-1}\ \text{for all } i>1\rangle$$
virtually special?

original_question: (N. Brady). Do there exist finitely presented subgroups of right-angled Artin groups whose Dehn functions are super-exponential, or sub-exponential but not polynomial? Such subgroups are known to exist in general CAT(0) groups, whereas the only Dehn functions currently realized for subgroups of right-angled Artin groups are exponential and polynomial of arbitrary degree.
self_contained_problem:
A right-angled Artin group is a group given, for some finite simplicial graph $\Gamma$ with vertex set $V(\Gamma)$ and edge set $E(\Gamma)$, by the presentation
$$A_\Gamma = \langle\, V(\Gamma) \mid [v,w] = 1 \text{ for all } \{v,w\} \in E(\Gamma)\,\rangle.$$
For a finitely presented group $G = \langle X \mid R\rangle$, the Dehn function $\delta_G : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ is defined by
$$\delta_G(n) = \max\{\operatorname{Area}(w) : w \text{ a null-homotopic word in } X^{\pm 1} \text{ with } |w| \le n\},$$
where $\operatorname{Area}(w)$ is the minimal $N$ such that $w$ can be written in the free group on $X$ as a product of $N$ conjugates of elements of $R^{\pm 1}$. The growth type of $\delta_G$ (up to the standard equivalence of functions $f \simeq g$ given by mutual domination after affine reparameterization) is a quasi-isometry invariant of $G$.

A function $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ is called:
- polynomial if $f(n) \simeq n^d$ for some integer $d \ge 1$;
- exponential if $f(n) \simeq 2^n$;
- super-exponential if $f(n)$ grows strictly faster than every function of the form $n \mapsto 2^n$ (e.g.\ $2^{2^n}$, $n!$, etc.);
- sub-exponential but not polynomial if $f(n)$ is bounded above by every function of exponential type up to equivalence, yet is not equivalent to any polynomial $n^d$ (e.g.\ $n^{\log n}$).

Question: Does there exist a finite simplicial graph $\Gamma$ and a finitely presented subgroup $H \le A_\Gamma$ of the corresponding right-angled Artin group whose Dehn function $\delta_H$ is either super-exponential, or sub-exponential but not polynomial?

However, no examples with super-exponential or with sub-exponential non-polynomial Dehn functions are known among finitely presented subgroups of RAAGs, and the problem appears to remain open.

original_question: Let G be a right-angled Artin group. Is the stable commutator length scl(g) a rational number for every g ∈ [G, G]? For free groups this is true by Calegari’s Rationality Theorem. (See 18.40 for the definition of scl(g).)
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Gamma$ be a finite simple graph with vertex set $V$ and edge set $E$. The right-angled Artin group on $\Gamma$ is the group
$$G = \langle V \mid [v,w] = 1 	ext{ for all } \{v,w\}\in Eangle.$$
For an element $g$ in the commutator subgroup $[G,G]$, the commutator length $\mathrm{cl}(g)$ is the least integer $n\ge 0$ such that $g$ can be written as a product of $n$ commutators in $G$. The stable commutator length is
$$\mathrm{scl}(g) = \lim_{n	o\infty}  rac{\mathrm{cl}(g^n)}{n},$$
which exists in $[0,\infty)$ by subadditivity. (For free groups it is a theorem of Calegari that $\mathrm{scl}(g)\in\mathbb{Q}$ for every $g\in [F,F]$.)

Question: Is it true that for every right-angled Artin group $G$ (i.e., for every finite simple defining graph $\Gamma$) and every $g\in [G,G]$, the stable commutator length $\mathrm{scl}(g)$ is a rational number?
status_search_result: The question of whether scl is rational on the commutator subgroup of every right-angled Artin group appears to remain open. Recent work of Chen and Heuer (2020) on scl in RAAGs and Coxeter groups establishes spectral gaps and shows every rational $q\ge 1$ is realized as scl of some integral chain in a RAAG, and proves that computing scl in RAAGs is NP-hard, but does not establish (nor refute) rationality of scl for all elements of $[G,G]$ in an arbitrary RAAG.

original_question: Two groups G1 and G2 are said to be commensurable if there exist finiteindex subgroups H1 ⩽ G1 and H2 ⩽ G2(not necessarily of the same index) such that H1 ∼= H2. Let A[F4 ] and A[H4 ] denote the Artin groups of spherical types F4 and H4, respectively. Are these two groups commensurable? This is the most difficult case in the classification of Artin groups of spherical type up to commensurability.
self_contained_problem:
Two groups G₁ and G₂ are called commensurable if there exist finite-index subgroups H₁ ≤ G₁ and H₂ ≤ G₂ (the indices need not be equal) such that H₁ ≅ H₂.

For a Coxeter graph Γ of spherical type with vertex set S = {s₁, …, sₙ} and edge labels m(sᵢ, sⱼ) ∈ {2, 3, 4, …} (with m(sᵢ, sⱼ) = 2 meaning no edge), the associated Artin group A[Γ] is defined by the presentation
   A[Γ] = ⟨ s₁, …, sₙ | sᵢsⱼsᵢ… = sⱼsᵢsⱼ… (each side of length m(sᵢ, sⱼ)) for all i ≠ j with m(sᵢ, sⱼ) < ∞ ⟩.

Let A[F₄] denote the Artin group whose Coxeter graph is the linear diagram on four vertices s₁ — s₂ =⁴ s₃ — s₄ (i.e., m(s₁,s₂) = m(s₃,s₄) = 3, m(s₂,s₃) = 4, and all other off-diagonal labels equal 2). Let A[H₄] denote the Artin group whose Coxeter graph is the linear diagram on four vertices t₁ =⁵ t₂ — t₃ — t₄ (i.e., m(t₁,t₂) = 5, m(t₂,t₃) = m(t₃,t₄) = 3, and all other off-diagonal labels equal 2).

Question: Are the Artin groups A[F₄] and A[H₄] commensurable?
status_search_result: Cumplido and Paris reduced the classification of Artin groups of spherical type up to commensurability to six undecided pairs, including (F₄, H₄). Soroko (2021) resolved (F₄, D₄) and (H₄, D₄) by showing those pairs are not commensurable, but the case (F₄, H₄) remains unresolved in the literature available through 2026.

original_question: If two Artin groups of spherical type are quasi-isometric, must they be commensurable? (This is not true for right-angled Artin groups.)
self_contained_problem:
Let $W$ be a finite Coxeter group with Coxeter system $(W,S)$ and Coxeter matrix $(m_{st})_{s,t\in S}$, where $m_{ss}=1$ and $m_{st}=m_{ts}\in\{2,3,\dots,\infty\}$ for $s\neq t$. The associated Artin group of spherical type is
$$A = \bigl\langle S \,\bigm|\, \underbrace{sts\cdots}_{m_{st}\text{ factors}} = \underbrace{tst\cdots}_{m_{st}\text{ factors}} \text{ for all } s\neq t \text{ with } m_{st}<\infty \bigr\rangle,$$
where $W$ is required to be finite (so the Coxeter diagram is a disjoint union of diagrams of types $A_n$, $B_n$, $D_n$, $E_6$, $E_7$, $E_8$, $F_4$, $G_2$, $H_3$, $H_4$, or $I_2(p)$).

Two finitely generated groups $G_1$ and $G_2$ are quasi-isometric if, equipped with word metrics from finite generating sets, there exist a map $f:G_1\to G_2$ and constants $K\geq 1$, $C\geq 0$ such that
$$\tfrac{1}{K} d(x,y) - C \le d(f(x),f(y)) \le K\, d(x,y) + C \quad\text{for all } x,y\in G_1,$$
and every point of $G_2$ lies within distance $C$ of $f(G_1)$. Two groups are commensurable if they contain isomorphic finite-index subgroups.

Question: If $A$ and $A'$ are two Artin groups of spherical type that are quasi-isometric as finitely generated groups, must $A$ and $A'$ be commensurable?
status_search_result: Recent work (Cumplido–Paris, 2019 and follow-ups through 2024) classifies spherical-type Artin groups up to commensurability almost completely, with a few exceptional pairs (e.g. (F4,D4), (H4,D4), (F4,H4), (E6,D6), (E7,D7), (E8,D8)) recently resolved to be non-commensurable. However, the quasi-isometric classification of spherical-type Artin groups, and in particular whether QI implies commensurability for them, does not appear to be established in the literature; the analogous question for RAAGs is known to fail in general. The problem appears to remain open.

self_contained_problem:

original_question: Does a group need to have a subnormal abelian series if every countable subgroup of it has such a series?
self_contained_problem:
A subnormal series of a group $G$ is a finite chain of subgroups
$$\{e\} = G_0 \trianglelefteq G_1 \trianglelefteq \cdots \trianglelefteq G_n = G$$
such that each $G_i$ is normal in $G_{i+1}$. The series is called abelian (or solvable) if every factor $G_{i+1}/G_i$ is abelian; equivalently, $G$ is solvable.

Question: Suppose $G$ is a group with the property that every countable subgroup of $G$ admits a subnormal abelian series (i.e., is solvable). Must $G$ itself admit a subnormal abelian series (i.e., be solvable)?

original_question: For a finite group G, let the type of G be the function on positive integers whose value at n is the number of solutions of the equation xn = 1 in G. a) Is it true that a group having the same type as a group with trivial solvable radical must also have trivial solvable radical? Note that there are solvable and nonsolvable groups with the same type(see 12.37). b) Is it true that a group having the same type as an almost simple group must be isomorphic to it? This is true for a group having the same type as a simple group, as follows from the affirmative answer to 12.39(in Archive).
self_contained_problem:
For a finite group $G$, define the type of $G$ to be the function $t_G:\mathbb{Z}_{>0}\to\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}$ given by
$$t_G(n) = |\{x\in G : x^n = 1\}|.$$
Two finite groups $G$ and $H$ are said to have the same type if $t_G(n) = t_H(n)$ for every positive integer $n$. Recall that the solvable radical of a finite group is its largest solvable normal subgroup, and a finite group is called almost simple if it has a non-abelian simple normal subgroup $S$ such that $S \le G \le \mathrm{Aut}(S)$.

Answer the following questions.

(a) Suppose $G$ and $H$ are finite groups of the same type. If $G$ has trivial solvable radical, must $H$ also have trivial solvable radical?

(b) Suppose $G$ is a finite group having the same type as a finite almost simple group $A$. Must $G$ be isomorphic to $A$?

original_question: Let G be a torsion-free group of type F∞ of infinite cohomological dimension. Must G contain a copy of Thompson’s group F?

original_question: (Well-known problem). Is Thompson’s group F automatic?
self_contained_problem:
Thompson's group $F$ is the group with the infinite presentation
$$F = \langle x_0, x_1, x_2, \ldots \mid x_i^{-1} x_n x_i = x_{n+1} \text{ for all } i < n \rangle,$$
which is finitely generated by $x_0, x_1$ (and admits a finite presentation on these two generators).

A finitely generated group $G$ with finite generating set $A$ is called automatic if there exists a regular language $L \subseteq A^*$ of words mapping onto $G$ such that:
(i) the evaluation map $L \to G$ is surjective, and
(ii) for each $a \in A \cup \{1\}$, the "fellow-traveler" set
$$L_a = \{(u,v) \in L \times L : \overline{u}\,a = \overline{v}\text{ in }G\}$$
is recognized by a synchronous two-tape finite automaton (equivalently, the paths in the Cayley graph of $G$ corresponding to $u$ and $v$ stay within a uniformly bounded distance of each other at all times).

Determine whether Thompson's group $F$ is automatic in this sense.
status_search_result: The question of whether Thompson's group $F$ is automatic in the classical sense remains open. Weaker or related properties have been established: $F$ is known to be 1-counter graph automatic (Burillo–Cleary–Taback / Elder–Taback, arXiv:1501.04313) and autostackable (Corwin et al.), and admits a bounded regular convergent prefix-rewriting system. However, classical automaticity has not been resolved and continues to be listed as a well-known open problem on Thompson's group problem lists.

original_question: (Well-known problem). A classifying space for a group G is a connected CW complex with fundamental group G and all higher homotopy groups trivial. A group is of type Fn if it has a classifying space with finite n-skeleton. For example, type F1 is equivalent to finite generation, and type F2 is equivalent to finite presentability. original_question: (V. M. Kopytov, N. Ya. Medvedev). A subgroup H of a right-orderable group G is said to be right-relatively convex if it is convex under some right ordering on G. Is the lattice of right-relatively convex subgroups of a right-orderable group always a sublattice of the lattice of its subgroups?
self_contained_problem: Let $G$ be a right-orderable group; that is, there exists a total order $\le$ on $G$ that is invariant under right multiplication ($x \le y \Rightarrow xg \le yg$ for all $g \in G$). A subgroup $H \le G$ is called right-relatively convex if there exists some right-invariant total order $\le$ on $G$ with respect to which $H$ is convex (i.e., whenever $a \le b \le c$ with $a, c \in H$, also $b \in H$). Let $\mathcal{C}(G)$ denote the set of all right-relatively convex subgroups of $G$, and let $\mathcal{L}(G)$ denote the lattice of all subgroups of $G$, with meet given by intersection and join by the subgroup generated by the union. Determine whether $\mathcal{C}(G)$, with the partial order given by inclusion, is always a sublattice of $\mathcal{L}(G)$. Equivalently: is it true that for every right-orderable group $G$ and any $H_1, H_2 \in \mathcal{C}(G)$, both $H_1 \cap H_2$ and $\langle H_1 \cup H_2 \rangle$ belong to $\mathcal{C}(G)$?
status_search_result: The question is recorded as a problem in the Kourovka Notebook (attributed to Kopytov and Medvedev). Antolín, Dicks and Šunić (2015) studied the analogous notion of left-relatively convex subgroups and showed that intersections of such subgroups are again left-relatively convex, but the corresponding join question (and hence the sublattice property) remains a research problem with no known general resolution. No publication found resolving the right-orderable case in full generality.

original_question: (V. M. Kopytov, N. Ya. Medvedev). Are there order automorphisms of Dlab groups that are not inner automorphisms?
self_contained_problem:
Let $(G,\le)$ be a right-ordered group, i.e. a group $G$ equipped with a total order $\le$ such that $a\le b$ implies $ac\le bc$ for all $a,b,c\in G$. An order automorphism of $(G,\le)$ is a group automorphism $\varphi:G\to G$ such that $a\le b$ if and only if $\varphi(a)\le\varphi(b)$. An inner automorphism is a map of the form $x\mapsto gxg^{-1}$ for some $g\in G$.

A Dlab group is a right-ordered group obtained by Dlab's construction: given a totally ordered set $\Omega$ and a subgroup $H$ of the group $A(\Omega)$ of order-preserving bijections of $\Omega$ that acts on $\Omega$ in such a way that for every $\alpha\in\Omega$ the stabilizer subgroup $H_\alpha=\{h\in H:h(\alpha)=\alpha\}$ is convex in $H$ for the right order induced by a fixed point $\alpha_0\in\Omega$ (i.e., the right order on $H$ defined by $h>1$ iff $h(\alpha_0)>\alpha_0$, extended via Dlab's lexicographic refinement using $\Omega$); equivalently, a right-ordered group whose right order arises from its faithful action on a totally ordered set in this canonical way.

Question: Does there exist a Dlab group $(G,\le)$ admitting an order automorphism that is not an inner automorphism of $G$?

original_question: Let G be an extension of a normal elementary abelian subgroup A by an elementary abelian group B ≅ G/A such that A contains an element a with C_B(a) = 1. Is it true that the rank of the subgroup Z(⟨a, B⟩) ∩ (⟨a, B⟩)′ is at most the rank of B?

original_question: Let M be a connected Riemannian manifold isometrically immersed in Euclidean (n+1)-space E^(n+1). original_question: Among compact surfaces immersed in Euclidean 3-space E^3, are the ordinary spheres the only compact surfaces whose immersion is of finite type, meaning that the position vector splits into finitely many Laplace eigensections?
self_contained_problem:

The immersion $x$ is said to be of finite type if the position vector field admits a finite spectral decomposition
$$x = x_0 + \sum_{i=1}^{k} x_i,$$
where $x_0 \in \mathbb{E}^3$ is constant and $x_1, \dots, x_k$ are non-constant $\mathbb{E}^3$-valued smooth maps on $M$ satisfying $\Delta x_i = \lambda_i x_i$ for pairwise distinct real eigenvalues $\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_k$.

original_question: Among compact hypersurfaces in Euclidean space, are the only finite type examples the ordinary hyperspheres?

$$x = x_0 + \sum_{i=1}^{k} x_i,$$

original_question: A hypersurface immersion is of 2-type when it is of finite type with exactly two distinct Laplace eigenvalues in its spectral decomposition. Study and classify 2-type hypersurfaces in a hypersphere of E^(n+2); in particular, classify 2-type hypersurfaces of S^4 in E^5.
self_contained_problem:
Let $x: M^n \to \mathbb{E}^{n+2}$ be an isometric immersion of a closed (compact, without boundary) smooth $n$-dimensional Riemannian manifold $M$ into Euclidean space $\mathbb{E}^{n+2}$, and assume that the image lies in a hypersphere $S^{n+1} \subset \mathbb{E}^{n+2}$ (so $x$ realizes $M$ as a hypersurface of $S^{n+1}$). Let $\Delta$ denote the Laplace–Beltrami operator of the induced metric on $M$, acting on $\mathbb{E}^{n+2}$-valued functions componentwise. Then the position vector admits a spectral decomposition
$$x = x_0 + \sum_{i \in I} x_i, \qquad \Delta x_i = \lambda_i x_i,$$
where $x_0$ is a constant vector in $\mathbb{E}^{n+2}$, the $\lambda_i$ are distinct nonzero real numbers, and the $x_i: M \to \mathbb{E}^{n+2}$ are nonzero smooth maps. The immersion (or the hypersurface $M$) is said to be of $k$-type if the index set $I$ has exactly $k$ elements, i.e., the spectral decomposition involves exactly $k$ distinct nonzero Laplace eigenvalues. In particular, $M$ is of 2-type if $|I| = 2$.

(a) Classify all 2-type hypersurfaces of a hypersphere $S^{n+1} \subset \mathbb{E}^{n+2}$ for general $n \ge 2$.

(b) In particular, classify all 2-type hypersurfaces of the standard 4-sphere $S^4 \subset \mathbb{E}^5$ (i.e., the case $n = 3$).
status_search_result: The classification of 2-type hypersurfaces in spheres is a long-standing problem of B.-Y. Chen. Partial results are known under additional hypotheses (e.g., constant mean curvature, or at most two distinct principal curvatures, leading to products of spheres), and local rigidity theorems have been established, but a complete classification—even in the specific case of 2-type hypersurfaces of $S^4 \subset \mathbb{E}^5$—does not appear in the literature, and the problem is still listed as open in recent surveys on Riemannian submanifolds and finite-type theory.

original_question: Classify finite type hypersurfaces of a hypersphere in E^(n+2). Here finite type means that the position vector of the immersed hypersurface is a finite sum of Laplace eigenmaps.
self_contained_problem:
Let $S^{n+1}(r) \subset \mathbb{E}^{n+2}$ denote the round hypersphere of radius $r$ in Euclidean space, and let $x : M^n \hookrightarrow S^{n+1}(r) \subset \mathbb{E}^{n+2}$ be an isometric immersion of a connected $n$-dimensional Riemannian manifold as a hypersurface of this hypersphere. Identify $x$ with its $\mathbb{E}^{n+2}$-valued position vector field on $M$, and let $\Delta$ denote the Laplace–Beltrami operator of the induced metric on $M$ (acting componentwise on $\mathbb{E}^{n+2}$-valued functions).

The immersion $x$ is said to be of finite type if there exists a decomposition
$$x = x_0 + x_{t_1} + x_{t_2} + \cdots + x_{t_k},$$
where $x_0 \in \mathbb{E}^{n+2}$ is a constant vector, $k$ is a positive integer, and each $x_{t_i}$ is a non-constant $\mathbb{E}^{n+2}$-valued smooth map on $M$ satisfying
$$\Delta x_{t_i} = \lambda_{t_i} x_{t_i}$$
for some real eigenvalue $\lambda_{t_i}$, with the $\lambda_{t_i}$ pairwise distinct. The smallest such integer $k$ is called the type number of the immersion.

Problem: Classify, up to congruence in $\mathbb{E}^{n+2}$, all finite type hypersurfaces $M^n$ of the hypersphere $S^{n+1}(r) \subset \mathbb{E}^{n+2}$.
status_search_result: The general classification problem remains open. Only partial results are known: Takahashi's theorem fully characterizes 1-type (minimal) cases; for 2-type, Chen and others showed such hypersurfaces have constant mean and scalar curvatures, and partial classifications exist for low dimensions and special classes (e.g., quadric hypersurfaces of finite type by Chen–Dillen–Song, 1992). No complete classification of finite type hypersurfaces in a hypersphere has been published.

original_question: Inside the unit 3-sphere S^3 subset E^4, are the only finite type surfaces the minimal surfaces, the standard 2-spheres, and the products of two plane circles?
self_contained_problem:
Let $S^3 \subset \mathbb{E}^4$ denote the unit 3-sphere in Euclidean 4-space, and let $M \subset S^3$ be a connected smooth surface, regarded (via the inclusion $S^3 \hookrightarrow \mathbb{E}^4$) as a submanifold of $\mathbb{E}^4$. Let $\Delta$ denote the Laplace–Beltrami operator on $M$ with respect to the induced metric, acting componentwise on the position vector $x: M \to \mathbb{E}^4$. The surface $M$ is said to be of finite type if its position vector admits a finite spectral decomposition
$$x = x_0 + \sum_{i=1}^{k} x_i,$$
where $x_0 \in \mathbb{E}^4$ is a constant vector and each non-constant $\mathbb{E}^4$-valued map $x_i$ satisfies $\Delta x_i = \lambda_i x_i$ for some real eigenvalue $\lambda_i$, with $k$ a positive integer. 

Prove or disprove: the only finite-type surfaces $M \subset S^3$ are
(i) the minimal surfaces of $S^3$,
(ii) the totally umbilical 2-spheres (i.e., intersections of $S^3$ with affine hyperplanes of $\mathbb{E}^4$ that yield round 2-spheres), and
(iii) the products $S^1(r_1) \times S^1(r_2) \subset S^3$ of two plane circles, with $r_1^2 + r_2^2 = 1$.
status_search_result: Searches indicate this is a long-standing conjecture of B.-Y. Chen on finite-type surfaces in $S^3$, generally referred to as still open. Surveys on finite-type submanifolds and Chen-type problems list partial classifications (e.g., for ruled surfaces, surfaces with constant mean curvature, tubes, etc.) but no general proof or counterexample has been reported.

original_question: A hypersurface M of S^(n+1) is called a Dupin hypersurface when the multiplicities of its principal curvatures are constant and each principal curvature is constant along its principal directions. Determine when such a Dupin hypersurface is of finite type, and determine when a finite type Dupin hypersurface of a hypersphere must be isoparametric.
self_contained_problem:
Let $S^{n+1}$ denote the unit sphere in Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^{n+2}$, and let $M\subset S^{n+1}$ be a smooth hypersurface. Recall that:

(a) $M$ is called a Dupin hypersurface if the multiplicities of the principal curvatures of $M$ are constant on $M$ and each principal curvature is constant along the leaves of its corresponding principal foliation.

(b) $M$ is called isoparametric if all principal curvatures of $M$ are constant on $M$.

(c) Viewing the inclusion $x:M\hookrightarrow S^{n+1}\subset\mathbb{R}^{n+2}$ as an $\mathbb{R}^{n+2}$-valued map and letting $\Delta$ denote the Laplace–Beltrami operator of the induced metric on $M$, the hypersurface $M$ is said to be of finite type if $x$ admits a finite spectral decomposition
$$x = x_0 + \sum_{i=1}^{k} x_i,\qquad \Delta x_i = \lambda_i\, x_i,$$
where $x_0\in\mathbb{R}^{n+2}$ is a constant vector, $x_1,\dots,x_k$ are non-constant $\mathbb{R}^{n+2}$-valued eigenfunctions of $\Delta$ with pairwise distinct eigenvalues $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_k\in\mathbb{R}$, and $k$ is finite.

Solve the following two questions:

(1) Characterize precisely those Dupin hypersurfaces $M\subset S^{n+1}$ which are of finite type.

(2) Determine necessary and sufficient conditions under which a finite type Dupin hypersurface $M\subset S^{n+1}$ must be isoparametric.
status_search_result: No characterization of finite type Dupin hypersurfaces of a sphere appears in the literature. Related work continues on the Cecil–Ryan and Chern conjectures concerning when Dupin hypersurfaces are isoparametric (e.g., recent results in 2025 on Chern's conjecture in the Dupin case, and constructions of compact Dupin hypersurfaces with non-constant Lie curvatures), but the specific finite-type problem does not appear to be resolved.

original_question: Do there exist 2-type surfaces lying fully in S^4 whose immersion is not mass-symmetric, where mass-symmetric means that the center of gravity of the surface in E^5 coincides with the center of the ambient hypersphere?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathbb{E}^m$ denote Euclidean $m$-space with its standard inner product, and let $S^{m-1}_c \subset \mathbb{E}^m$ denote a hypersphere of center $c \in \mathbb{E}^m$. For an isometric immersion $x : M \to \mathbb{E}^m$ of a compact Riemannian manifold $M$ with Laplace–Beltrami operator $\Delta$, decompose the position vector as $x = x_0 + \sum_{t} x_t$, where $x_0$ is the center of gravity of $M$ in $\mathbb{E}^m$ and the nonconstant components $x_t$ satisfy $\Delta x_t = \lambda_t x_t$ for distinct eigenvalues $\lambda_t$ of $\Delta$. The immersion is said to be of $k$-type if exactly $k$ of the components $x_t$ are nonzero. A spherical isometric immersion $x : M \to S^{m-1}_c \subset \mathbb{E}^m$ is called mass-symmetric in $S^{m-1}_c$ if the center of gravity $x_0$ of $M$ in $\mathbb{E}^m$ coincides with the center $c$ of the hypersphere. An immersion of a surface into $S^4 \subset \mathbb{E}^5$ is said to lie fully in $S^4$ if its image is not contained in any totally geodesic $S^3 \subset S^4$.

Question: Does there exist a 2-type surface lying fully in $S^4 \subset \mathbb{E}^5$ whose isometric immersion into $S^4$ is not mass-symmetric?
status_search_result: No published resolution of this question was found via web search. The problem is recorded as still unsolved in the relevant survey-style problem list on finite-type submanifolds, and no later paper indexed in standard sources appears to settle the existence of non-mass-symmetric 2-type surfaces lying fully in $S^4$.

original_question: Do there exist 2-type surfaces lying fully in an even-dimensional hypersphere of a Euclidean space? In particular, do there exist mass-symmetric 2-type surfaces lying fully in an even-dimensional hypersphere?
self_contained_problem:
Let $x: M \to \mathbb{E}^m$ be an isometric immersion of a compact surface $M$ into Euclidean $m$-space. The immersion is said to be of finite type if its position vector admits a finite spectral decomposition
$$x = x_0 + x_{t_1} + x_{t_2} + \cdots + x_{t_k},$$
where $x_0$ is a constant vector and $\Delta x_{t_i} = \lambda_{t_i} x_{t_i}$ for distinct eigenvalues $\lambda_{t_i}$ of the Laplace operator $\Delta$ of $M$. The immersion is of 2-type if $k = 2$, that is,
$$x = x_0 + x_p + x_q, \qquad \Delta x_p = \lambda_p x_p, \quad \Delta x_q = \lambda_q x_q, \quad \lambda_p \neq \lambda_q.$$
The surface lies fully in $\mathbb{E}^m$ if its image is not contained in any affine hyperplane, and lies fully in a hypersphere $S^{m-1} \subset \mathbb{E}^m$ if it lies in $S^{m-1}$ but not in any totally geodesic hypersphere of $S^{m-1}$. A 2-type surface contained in a hypersphere centered at $x_0$ is called mass-symmetric (with respect to that hypersphere) if the constant vector $x_0$ in its spectral decomposition coincides with the center of the hypersphere.

Determine whether the following hold:
(a) Does there exist a 2-type surface that lies fully in an even-dimensional hypersphere $S^{2n} \subset \mathbb{E}^{2n+1}$ for some $n \geq 1$?
(b) Does there exist a mass-symmetric 2-type surface that lies fully in an even-dimensional hypersphere $S^{2n}$?
status_search_result: The problem of whether 2-type (in particular mass-symmetric 2-type) surfaces can lie fully in an even-dimensional hypersphere is a long-standing question of B.-Y. Chen. Known partial results (Barros–Chen, Garay, and others) show that compact stationary or Chen-type mass-symmetric 2-type surfaces lie fully in $S^3$, $S^5$ or $S^7$, and that no mass-symmetric 2-type surface lies fully in $S^4$. No general resolution for arbitrary even-dimensional spheres was found in the available literature, so the problem appears to remain open.

original_question: Suppose a k-type immersion x : M -> E^m has spectral decomposition x = c + x1 + ... + xk, and for each i the subspace Ei is spanned by the values x_i(p) as p ranges over M. The immersion is called linearly independent when E1, ..., Ek are linearly independent. Study and classify linearly independent 2-type immersions.
self_contained_problem:
Let $x : M \to \mathbb{E}^m$ be an isometric immersion of a (connected) Riemannian manifold $M$ into Euclidean $m$-space, and let $\Delta$ denote the Laplace–Beltrami operator of $M$. The immersion $x$ is said to be of finite type $k$ if its position vector admits a spectral decomposition
$$ x = c + x_1 + x_2 + \cdots + x_k, $$
where $c \in \mathbb{E}^m$ is a constant vector and $x_1,\dots,x_k : M \to \mathbb{E}^m$ are non-constant smooth maps satisfying $\Delta x_i = \lambda_i x_i$ for pairwise distinct real eigenvalues $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_k$. For each $i \in \{1,\dots,k\}$, let $E_i \subseteq \mathbb{E}^m$ denote the linear subspace spanned by $\{x_i(p) : p \in M\}$. The immersion $x$ (and the submanifold $M$) is called linearly independent if the subspaces $E_1, \dots, E_k$ are linearly independent, i.e. $\dim(E_1 + \cdots + E_k) = \dim E_1 + \cdots + \dim E_k$.

Problem: Study and classify all linearly independent 2-type isometric immersions $x : M \to \mathbb{E}^m$, i.e. give a complete geometric classification of submanifolds $M$ of Euclidean space that are of 2-type and whose two associated spectral subspaces $E_1$ and $E_2$ are linearly independent.
status_search_result: Partial classification results exist for linearly independent 2-type submanifolds of Euclidean space (e.g., results characterizing such hypersurfaces and spherical submanifolds, and showing in various settings that linear independence forces the immersion to lie in a product of two spheres or related configurations). However, a complete general classification of all linearly independent 2-type immersions does not appear to be available, so the problem remains open in full generality.

original_question: Using the same notion of linearly independent immersion, study and classify linearly independent submanifolds of codimension 2.
self_contained_problem:
Let $x:M^n\to\mathbb{E}^m$ be an isometric immersion of a connected Riemannian $n$-manifold into Euclidean $m$-space, and let $\Delta$ denote the Laplace–Beltrami operator of the induced metric on $M$. Assume $x$ is of finite type $k$, i.e., the position vector admits a finite spectral decomposition
$$x = x_0 + x_{t_1} + x_{t_2} + \cdots + x_{t_k},$$
where $x_0\in\mathbb{E}^m$ is a constant vector and $x_{t_1},\ldots,x_{t_k}:M\to\mathbb{E}^m$ are non-constant smooth maps satisfying $\Delta x_{t_i}=\lambda_{t_i}x_{t_i}$ for pairwise distinct real eigenvalues $\lambda_{t_1},\ldots,\lambda_{t_k}$. For each $p\in M$, let
$$E_i(p) := \operatorname{span}_{\mathbb{R}}\{x_{t_i}(p)\}\subset\mathbb{E}^m,\qquad i=1,\ldots,k.$$
The immersion $x$ (equivalently, the submanifold $M$) is called \emph{linearly independent} if for every $p\in M$ the one-dimensional subspaces $E_1(p),\ldots,E_k(p)$ are linearly independent in $\mathbb{E}^m$.

original_question: A 2-type immersion is called null when one of its two Laplace eigenvalues is zero; equivalently, a non-null 2-type immersion has two nonzero eigenvalues. If an n-dimensional submanifold of Euclidean (n+2)-space is non-null 2-type and has constant mean curvature, must it be spherical?
self_contained_problem:
Let $x: M^n \to \mathbb{E}^{n+2}$ be an isometric immersion of a connected $n$-dimensional Riemannian manifold into Euclidean $(n+2)$-space. Let $\Delta$ denote the Laplace–Beltrami operator of $M^n$ acting componentwise on $\mathbb{E}^{n+2}$-valued maps. The immersion $x$ is said to be of finite type if the position vector admits a finite spectral decomposition
$$x = x_0 + x_1 + x_2 + \cdots + x_k,$$
where $x_0 \in \mathbb{E}^{n+2}$ is a constant vector and $x_1, \dots, x_k$ are non-constant $\mathbb{E}^{n+2}$-valued maps satisfying $\Delta x_i = \lambda_i x_i$ for real numbers $\lambda_i$. The immersion is of $2$-type when exactly two such non-constant components $x_1, x_2$ appear, with eigenvalues $\lambda_1, \lambda_2$. A $2$-type immersion is called null if one of $\lambda_1, \lambda_2$ equals zero, and non-null otherwise (equivalently, $\lambda_1 \lambda_2 \neq 0$). The mean curvature function of $M^n$ is the norm of the mean curvature vector $H$, and $M^n$ is said to have constant mean curvature when $\|H\|$ is constant on $M^n$. The submanifold $M^n$ is called spherical if $x(M^n)$ lies in some round hypersphere of $\mathbb{E}^{n+2}$.

Question: Must every $n$-dimensional non-null $2$-type submanifold of $\mathbb{E}^{n+2}$ with constant mean curvature be spherical?
status_search_result: Searches turn up Chen's surveys on Riemannian submanifolds and finite-type theory in which this question is repeatedly listed as an open problem; no published result resolving the codimension-2 case in full generality was found. Partial results exist (e.g., for hypersurfaces, for surfaces, and under additional curvature/Chen-type assumptions), but the general statement appears to remain unresolved.

original_question: A null 2-type submanifold is one whose mean curvature vector H satisfies Delta H = lambda H for some nonzero real constant lambda. Study and classify null 2-type submanifolds. In particular, classify all null 2-type surfaces in 4-dimensional Euclidean space and in 4-dimensional pseudo-Euclidean spaces.
self_contained_problem:
Let $M$ be an isometrically immersed submanifold of a (pseudo-)Euclidean space $\mathbb{E}^m_s$, and let $H$ denote its mean curvature vector field. Let $\Delta$ be the Laplace–Beltrami operator of the induced metric on $M$, acting componentwise on vector-valued functions. The submanifold $M$ is called null 2-type if its position vector admits a spectral decomposition into exactly two non-constant components, one harmonic and one an eigenfunction of $\Delta$ with non-zero eigenvalue; equivalently, $M$ is non-minimal and its mean curvature vector satisfies
$$\Delta H = \lambda H$$
for some non-zero real constant $\lambda$.

(a) Develop a structure theory for null 2-type submanifolds in (pseudo-)Euclidean spaces.

(b) Give a complete classification of all null 2-type surfaces in the Euclidean 4-space $\mathbb{E}^4$.

(c) Give a complete classification of all null 2-type surfaces in the pseudo-Euclidean 4-spaces $\mathbb{E}^4_s$ for $s = 1, 2$ (i.e., in Minkowski 4-space and in the neutral pseudo-Euclidean 4-space).

original_question: An isometric immersion x : M -> E^m is biharmonic when Delta^2 x = 0, equivalently Delta H = 0 for the mean curvature vector H. Other than minimal submanifolds, which submanifolds of Euclidean space E^m are biharmonic?
self_contained_problem:
Let $x : M \to \mathbb{E}^m$ be an isometric immersion of a (smooth, connected) Riemannian manifold $M$ into Euclidean $m$-space $\mathbb{E}^m$. Let $\Delta$ denote the Laplace–Beltrami operator of the induced metric on $M$, acting componentwise on $\mathbb{E}^m$-valued maps, and let $H$ denote the mean curvature vector field of the immersion. The immersion is called biharmonic if
$$\Delta^2 x \equiv 0,$$
which is equivalent to $\Delta H \equiv 0$. The immersion is called minimal if $H \equiv 0$; every minimal submanifold is therefore biharmonic.

Problem. Determine all biharmonic submanifolds of $\mathbb{E}^m$ that are not minimal. Equivalently, decide whether every biharmonic submanifold of $\mathbb{E}^m$ must be minimal, and if not, classify the non-minimal biharmonic submanifolds.
status_search_result: This is Chen's biharmonic conjecture (1991), which asserts that every biharmonic submanifold of Euclidean space is minimal. It remains open in general. Confirmed cases include: surfaces in $\mathbb{E}^m$ (Chen, Jiang, ~1987), hypersurfaces in $\mathbb{E}^4$ (Hasanis–Vlachos, 1995), hypersurfaces in $\mathbb{E}^5$ (Koiso–Umehara/Fu–Hong–Zhan, 2020/2021), and hypersurfaces with at most three distinct principal curvatures (Fu). Higher-codimension and higher-dimensional cases (including surfaces $M^2 \hookrightarrow \mathbb{E}^4$ in full generality and hypersurfaces in $\mathbb{E}^n$ for $n \geq 6$) remain unresolved.

original_question: Are the only biharmonic submanifolds of Euclidean spaces the minimal ones?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\phi:M^n \to \mathbb{R}^m$ be an isometric immersion of a Riemannian manifold into Euclidean $m$-space, and let $\Delta$ denote the (rough/Laplace–Beltrami) Laplacian acting on $\mathbb{R}^m$-valued functions on $M$ (componentwise). The submanifold $M$ is called biharmonic if its position vector field $\phi$ satisfies $\Delta^2 \phi = 0$, equivalently $\Delta H = 0$, where $H$ is the mean curvature vector field of $M$ in $\mathbb{R}^m$. The submanifold is called minimal if $H \equiv 0$.

Prove or disprove: every biharmonic submanifold $M^n$ of a Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^m$ is minimal.

It is verified in several special cases—surfaces in $\mathbb{R}^3$ (Chen, Jiang), hypersurfaces in $\mathbb{R}^4$ (Hasanis–Vlachos, 1995), and hypersurfaces in $\mathbb{R}^5$ (Fu–Hong–Zhan, 2021)—as well as under various curvature or boundedness hypotheses. original_question: Is every biharmonic hypersurface of a Euclidean space minimal?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ denote Euclidean $(n+1)$-space with its standard flat metric, and let $M^n \subset \mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ be an isometrically immersed smooth hypersurface with mean curvature vector field $\mathbf{H}$. Write $\Delta$ for the (rough/Laplace–Beltrami) Laplacian acting on $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$-valued maps via the induced metric on $M$. The immersion $\mathbf{x}: M^n \to \mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ is called biharmonic if $\Delta^2 \mathbf{x} = 0$, equivalently $\Delta \mathbf{H} = 0$, and minimal if $\mathbf{H} \equiv 0$.

Prove or disprove the following statement: every biharmonic hypersurface $M^n$ of $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ (for all $n \ge 1$) is minimal.
status_search_result: Chen's biharmonic conjecture for hypersurfaces in Euclidean space remains open in full generality. It is known to hold for surfaces in $\mathbb{R}^3$ (Chen, Jiang, 1987), for hypersurfaces in $\mathbb{R}^4$ (Hasanis–Vlachos, 1995), for hypersurfaces in $\mathbb{R}^5$ (Fu–Hong–Zhan, 2021), and for hypersurfaces with at most three distinct principal curvatures in arbitrary dimension. No proof or counterexample is known in general dimensions.

original_question: Is every complete biharmonic submanifold of a Euclidean space minimal?
self_contained_problem:
Let $M$ be a smooth submanifold of Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^n$ via an isometric immersion $\phi: M \to \mathbb{R}^n$, and assume that $M$ is complete with respect to the induced Riemannian metric. The immersion $\phi$ is called biharmonic if it satisfies $\Delta^2 \phi = 0$, where $\Delta$ denotes the (componentwise) Laplace–Beltrami operator on $M$ associated with the induced metric. Equivalently, by Beltrami's formula $\Delta \phi = -n\, \mathbf{H}$, where $\mathbf{H}$ is the mean curvature vector field of the immersion, biharmonicity is equivalent to $\Delta \mathbf{H} = 0$. The submanifold $M$ is called minimal if $\mathbf{H} \equiv 0$.

Question: Must every complete biharmonic submanifold of a Euclidean space necessarily be minimal?
status_search_result: Chen's biharmonic conjecture (and its global/complete version) remains open in general. Partial results are known: it has been confirmed for properly immersed complete biharmonic submanifolds in Euclidean spaces (Akutagawa–Maeta), for hypersurfaces in low dimensions (including $\mathbb{R}^4$ and recently $\mathbb{R}^5$), and under various curvature or finiteness assumptions, but the full conjecture for arbitrary complete biharmonic submanifolds is still unresolved.

original_question: In recovery problems with noisy data, why do semidefinite-programming relaxations of maximum-likelihood estimators often remain tight beyond the exact-recovery regime? More concretely, when noise is large enough that the maximum-likelihood estimator cannot exactly recover the ground truth, under what structural or probabilistic conditions does the SDP relaxation still return a solution that lies in the original nonconvex model class, or equivalently matches the lower-rank quasi-maximum-likelihood solution instead of requiring a rounding step?
self_contained_problem:
Consider statistical recovery problems of the following form. A ground-truth object $x_0$ lies in a nonconvex set $\mathcal{M}$ (for example, the set of phase vectors $\{z\in\mathbb{C}^n:|z_i|=1\}$, the orthogonal group $O(d)$, or a discrete partition class). One observes a noisy datum $Y$ obtained from $x_0$ through a known statistical model, and considers the maximum-likelihood estimator
$$\hat{x}_{\mathrm{MLE}} \in \arg\max_{x\in\mathcal{M}} \, \ell(x;Y),$$
where $\ell(\cdot;Y)$ is a quadratic (or otherwise lift-able) log-likelihood. By writing $\ell(x;Y) = \langle C(Y), xx^{\!*}\rangle$ and lifting the variable to $X = xx^{\!*}$, one obtains the standard semidefinite programming (SDP) relaxation
$$\hat{X}_{\mathrm{SDP}} \in \arg\max_{X\succeq 0,\ X\in\mathcal{C}} \, \langle C(Y), X\rangle,$$
where $\mathcal{C}$ encodes linear constraints (e.g., diagonal entries equal to $1$, or block-orthogonality constraints) that are satisfied by every lift $xx^{\!*}$ with $x\in\mathcal{M}$.

The SDP relaxation is said to be tight if any optimizer $\hat{X}_{\mathrm{SDP}}$ has the rank that lifts of elements of $\mathcal{M}$ have (e.g., rank $1$ in the phase case), so that $\hat{X}_{\mathrm{SDP}} = \hat{x}\,\hat{x}^{\!*}$ for some $\hat{x}\in\mathcal{M}$.

Empirically, in many such problems (angular synchronization, multireference alignment, global registration, $\mathbb{Z}/2$ synchronization, community detection, camera-motion estimation, $k$-means clustering, etc.) the SDP relaxation remains tight with high probability in noise regimes where exact recovery is information-theoretically impossible, i.e., where $\hat{x}_{\mathrm{MLE}} \neq x_0$. In particular, $\hat{X}_{\mathrm{SDP}}$ coincides with the lifted MLE rather than producing a higher-rank optimizer that would require rounding.

Problem. Provide a unified theoretical explanation, with provable sufficient conditions, for the following rank-recovery phenomenon: identify general structural and probabilistic hypotheses on the model class $\mathcal{M}$, the constraint set $\mathcal{C}$, and the noise distribution generating $Y$, under which, with high probability, every optimizer of the SDP relaxation has the form $\hat{x}\,\hat{x}^{\!*}$ for some $\hat{x}\in\mathcal{M}$ (equivalently, equals the lifted MLE), throughout a noise regime that strictly extends the exact-recovery regime where $\hat{x}_{\mathrm{MLE}} = x_0$.
status_search_result: The general phenomenon remains an open problem with no unified theory. However, problem-specific progress has been made: tightness of the SDP relaxation beyond the exact-recovery regime has been established for angular synchronization (Bandeira–Boumal–Singer, 2014/2017), for $\mathbb{Z}/2$ synchronization and stochastic block models, for k-means clustering (Iguchi–Mixon and others, 2015+), and for related QCQPs. A general unifying explanation across all such recovery problems has not been established.

original_question: Let d > 1, n > 2, and m >= d + 1. Let A in R^(d x m) be a point cloud whose m columns are random points in R^d with i.i.d. uniform coordinates in [0,1]^d, and let O_1, ..., O_n be orthogonal transformations in R^d. Suppose the observed data are matrices A_i = O_i A + sigma eta_i in R^(d x m), where each eta_i has i.i.d. standard Gaussian entries. Form the generalized orthogonal Procrustes quasi-maximum-likelihood problem of maximizing Tr(CX) over block matrices X with X >= 0, X_ii = I_(d x d), and rank(X) <= d, and its semidefinite relaxation obtained by dropping the rank constraint. Does there exist a threshold sigma* > 0 such that whenever sigma < sigma*, with high probability the SDP relaxation has rank d and therefore exactly matches the quasi-maximum-likelihood solution?
self_contained_problem:
Fix integers d > 1, n > 2, and m ≥ d + 1, and a noise level σ > 0. Let A ∈ ℝ^{d×m} be a random point cloud whose entries are i.i.d. uniform on [0,1], and let O_1, …, O_n ∈ O(d) be arbitrary orthogonal d×d matrices (O_i O_i^T = I_d). The observations are

   A_i = O_i A + σ η_i,   i = 1, …, n,

where the η_i ∈ ℝ^{d×m} have i.i.d. standard Gaussian entries, mutually independent. The (quasi) maximum-likelihood estimator of (O_1, …, O_n) (up to a global orthogonal transformation) can be cast as the rank-constrained program

   maximize  Tr(C X)
   subject to  X ⪰ 0,  X_{ii} = I_d for i = 1, …, n,  rank(X) ≤ d,

where X is an nd × nd block matrix with d×d blocks X_{ij}, and C is the nd × nd block matrix whose (i,j) block equals A_i A_j^T. Its semidefinite programming relaxation is obtained by dropping the rank constraint:

   maximize  Tr(C X)
   subject to  X ⪰ 0,  X_{ii} = I_d for i = 1, …, n.   (*)

Question: Does there exist a constant σ* > 0 (possibly depending on d, n, m) such that for all σ < σ*, with high probability (over A and the η_i) every optimal solution of (*) has rank exactly d, and hence (*) recovers the quasi-maximum-likelihood solution?
status_search_result: The conjecture, posed by Bandeira, Khoo, and Singer in 2014, asks for a noise threshold below which the SDP relaxation of the generalized orthogonal Procrustes problem is tight (rank d). Subsequent work, in particular Ling's "Near-optimal bounds for generalized orthogonal Procrustes problem via generalized power method" (2022/2023) and follow-ups including the adversarial setting (SIMAX 2025), establishes sufficient signal-to-noise conditions under which the SDP relaxation is tight and matches the MLE, nearly matching information-theoretic limits up to a factor of d and a log term. These works substantially advance, but do not fully close, the original conjecture's regime; thus the problem is partially solved.

original_question:
For the modified focusing nonlinear Schrodinger equation on R^d, with d = 2 in the no-group-velocity-dispersion case or d = 3 in the anomalous-group-velocity-dispersion case,

 i partial_t v + Delta v + (1 + f(epsilon^r |v|^2)) |v|^2 v = 0,

where f models high-intensity corrections such as a cubic-quintic or saturated nonlinearity, can one rigorously prove the oscillatory dynamics reported in experiments and numerics, in which a solution focuses, then defocuses, then refocuses, in an almost periodic or recurrent way rather than simply collapsing once?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the modified focusing nonlinear Schrödinger equation on $\mathbb{R}^d$,
$$ i\,\partial_t v + \Delta v + \bigl(1 + f(\varepsilon^r |v|^2)\bigr)|v|^2 v = 0, \qquad t>0,\ x \in \mathbb{R}^d, $$
where $\varepsilon>0$ and $r>0$ are fixed parameters, and $f:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R}$ is a smooth saturation-type correction modeling high-intensity effects (for instance the cubic–quintic correction $f(s)=-s$ or a saturated correction such as $f(s)=-s/(1+s)$), with $f(0)=0$ and $f$ chosen so that the total nonlinearity $(1+f(\varepsilon^r|v|^2))|v|^2 v$ prevents finite-time blow-up. The dimension is taken to be $d=2$ (the no-group-velocity-dispersion case) or $d=3$ (the anomalous-group-velocity-dispersion case).

Physical experiments and numerical simulations indicate that for suitable initial data $v(0,\cdot) \in H^1(\mathbb{R}^d)$ whose unmodified cubic dynamics would lead to focusing/blow-up, the solution $v(t,\cdot)$ of the modified equation does not simply concentrate once but rather undergoes an oscillatory cycle: it focuses toward a high-amplitude state, then defocuses, then refocuses, and so on, in an almost-periodic or recurrent fashion.

Problem: Prove rigorously that there exist a class of nontrivial initial data and an admissible nonlinearity $f$ for which the corresponding global solution $v$ exhibits this oscillatory focus–defocus–refocus dynamics (in a precise, quantitative sense such as recurrence of the $L^\infty$ or $H^1$ norm to within a fixed factor of repeated peak values, or almost-periodicity of a suitable concentration profile), as opposed to monotone dispersion or single-event focusing.
status_search_result: Recent rigorous work on the cubic–quintic NLS in $\mathbb{R}^3$ and saturated NLS focuses on global well-posedness, orbital stability of solitary waves, and scattering beyond virial thresholds. None of these results establishes the experimentally and numerically observed almost-periodic focus/defocus/refocus oscillations rigorously; such oscillatory dynamics are still only observed numerically and remain unproven.
