context_brief: lower bounds for two-dimensional digital base-2 sequences
original_question: Can one show that every two-dimensional digital sequence in base 2 satisfies the lower discrepancy bound D_N >= c (log N)^2 / N for infinitely many N, or at least prove this for a substantial class such as NUT sequences or finite-row sequences?
self_contained_problem:
Background and definitions. For an infinite sequence $\mathbf{x}_1,\mathbf{x}_2,\ldots$ in the unit square $[0,1)^2$, let
$$D_N(\mathbf{x}) \;=\; \sup_{B}\left|\frac{\#\{1\le n\le N:\mathbf{x}_n\in B\}}{N} - \lambda(B)\right|,$$
where the supremum runs over all axis-aligned boxes $B=[0,a_1)\times[0,a_2)\subset[0,1)^2$ and $\lambda$ is Lebesgue measure. This is the star discrepancy of the first $N$ terms.

A two-dimensional digital sequence in base $2$ is constructed as follows. Choose two infinite matrices $C^{(1)},C^{(2)}\in\mathbb{F}_2^{\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}}$ (called generating matrices). For an integer $n\ge 0$ with binary expansion $n=\sum_{r\ge 0} a_r(n)\,2^r$, $a_r(n)\in\{0,1\}$, define the $j$-th coordinate of the $n$-th term by
$$x_n^{(j)} \;=\; \sum_{i\ge 1} \frac{y_{n,i}^{(j)}}{2^{i}}, \qquad y_{n,i}^{(j)} \;=\; \sum_{r\ge 0} C^{(j)}_{i,r+1}\, a_r(n) \pmod 2,$$
provided each coordinate is well defined (all column sums are finite). The sequence $(\mathbf{x}_n)_{n\ge 0}$ in $[0,1)^2$ thus produced is called a two-dimensional digital sequence in base $2$.

Two important subclasses are:
\begin{itemize}
\item NUT (non-singular upper triangular) digital sequences: each $C^{(j)}$ is upper triangular with non-zero diagonal entries.
\item Finite-row digital sequences: every row of each $C^{(j)}$ has only finitely many non-zero entries.
\end{itemize}

It is known that any such sequence can satisfy $D_N \le c'(\log N)^2/N$ for all $N\ge 2$, and a corresponding lower bound of order $(\log N)^2/N$ infinitely often is conjectured but not proved.

Problem. Prove that there exists an absolute constant $c>0$ such that for every two-dimensional digital sequence $(\mathbf{x}_n)_{n\ge 0}$ in base $2$ one has
$$D_N(\mathbf{x}) \;\ge\; c\,\frac{(\log N)^2}{N} \qquad \text{for infinitely many } N\in\mathbb{N}.$$
Or, failing the general statement, establish the same lower bound for the restricted class of NUT digital sequences, or for the class of finite-row digital sequences in base $2$.
status_search_result: Web search did not surface a proof of the conjectured $(\log N)^2/N$ lower bound for the star discrepancy of general two-dimensional digital base-2 sequences, nor for the NUT or finite-row subclasses. The closest progress concerns matching $L_p$-discrepancy lower bounds (Proinov; Dick–Pillichshammer 2014; later optimal $L_p$ results for order-2 digital sequences), but these address $L_p$-discrepancy rather than the star discrepancy lower bound asked here. The problem appears to remain open.

context_brief: lower bounds for the two-dimensional Halton sequence
original_question: Can one obtain a better lower bound for the discrepancy of the two-dimensional Halton sequence, and ideally determine whether its true order is (log N)^2 / N or not?
self_contained_problem:
For an integer N ≥ 1 and a finite sequence of points x_1, …, x_N in the unit square [0,1)^2, define the star discrepancy
  D*_N = sup_{B} | #{1 ≤ n ≤ N : x_n ∈ B}/N − λ(B) |,
where the supremum is taken over all axis-aligned boxes B = [0,a_1) × [0,a_2) ⊂ [0,1)^2 and λ denotes the Lebesgue measure.

The two-dimensional Halton sequence (with bases 2 and 3) is the sequence (x_n)_{n ≥ 1} ⊂ [0,1)^2 defined by x_n = (φ_2(n), φ_3(n)), where for a prime p the radical-inverse function φ_p is given by
  φ_p(n) = Σ_{k ≥ 0} a_k p^{−k−1}   when   n = Σ_{k ≥ 0} a_k p^k,   a_k ∈ {0,1,…,p−1}.

It is known that the star discrepancy of the two-dimensional Halton sequence satisfies D*_N = O((log N)^2 / N).

Problem: Prove an improved lower bound for the star discrepancy of the two-dimensional Halton sequence. In particular, decide whether
  limsup_{N → ∞}  N · D*_N / (log N)^2  >  0,
i.e. whether the true order of magnitude of the star discrepancy of this sequence is exactly (log N)^2 / N.
status_search_result: M. B. Levin proved exact lower bounds for the star discrepancy of Halton's sequence, establishing in particular that limsup N (log N)^{-s} D*_N > 0 for the s-dimensional Halton sequence. For s = 2 this matches the known O((log N)^2/N) upper bound, so the true order of the discrepancy of the two-dimensional Halton sequence is (log N)^2/N. A survey of Levin's proofs (Kritzer, 2017) confirms these as exact lower discrepancy bounds. The problem therefore appears to be solved.

original_question: In a two-queue polling system with cyclic service, where arrivals to both queues are independent Poisson processes, service times and switch-over times are independent, and the first queue uses gated service while the second queue uses 1-limited service, determine the joint probability generating function of the steady-state queue-length vector at polling instants. Equivalently, determine the joint queue-length PGFs F1(z1, z2) and F2(z1, z2) for this G/1-L polling system.
self_contained_problem:
Consider a polling system with a single server and two queues $Q_1, Q_2$ operating in continuous time. Customers arrive at $Q_i$ according to a Poisson process with rate $\lambda_i > 0$, $i = 1, 2$, and the two arrival processes are independent. Service times at $Q_i$ are i.i.d. with distribution $B_i$ (Laplace–Stieltjes transform $\beta_i$ and finite mean), independent across queues and of the arrival processes. The server visits the queues in cyclic order $Q_1, Q_2, Q_1, Q_2, \ldots$ . Between a visit to $Q_i$ and the next visit to $Q_{i+1 \bmod 2}$, the server incurs an i.i.d. switch-over time with distribution $S_i$ (LST $\sigma_i$, finite mean), independent of everything else.

The service disciplines are mixed:
- $Q_1$ uses the gated discipline: upon arrival of the server at $Q_1$, exactly those customers present at that polling instant are served, while customers arriving during the visit are deferred to the next cycle.
- $Q_2$ uses the 1-limited discipline: at each visit to $Q_2$, the server serves exactly one customer if $Q_2$ is non-empty, and otherwise leaves immediately.

Assume the system is stable. Let $(X_1^{(i)}, X_2^{(i)})$ denote the steady-state vector of queue lengths at the polling instant of $Q_i$ ($i = 1, 2$), and define the joint probability generating functions
$$F_i(z_1, z_2) = \mathbb{E}\!\left[ z_1^{X_1^{(i)}} z_2^{X_2^{(i)}} \right], \qquad |z_1|, |z_2| \le 1, \quad i = 1, 2.$$

Determine $F_1(z_1, z_2)$ and $F_2(z_1, z_2)$ in closed form (or as the explicit solution of a tractable functional/boundary value problem) for this two-queue gated/1-limited polling system with general service and switch-over time distributions.

No published solution was located in the search.

context_brief: Renewal arrivals with large deterministic switch-overs
original_question: Consider a cyclic polling system with a fixed cyclic order of N queues and general renewal arrival processes at the queues. When the switch-over times are deterministic and all deterministic switch-over times grow without bound while their ratios remain fixed, provide a rigorous proof that the system converges to a deterministic cyclic system.
self_contained_problem:
Consider a cyclic polling system with $N \geq 2$ queues $Q_1, \dots, Q_N$ served by a single server that visits the queues in the fixed cyclic order $Q_1 \to Q_2 \to \cdots \to Q_N \to Q_1 \to \cdots$. Customers arrive at $Q_i$ according to an independent renewal process with finite mean inter-arrival time $1/\lambda_i$ and a generally distributed service requirement with finite mean. The server uses a fixed work-conserving service discipline (e.g. exhaustive or gated) at each queue. Between completing service at $Q_i$ and starting service at $Q_{i+1}$, the server incurs a deterministic switch-over time $s_i > 0$. Assume the system is stable, i.e. $\rho := \sum_{i=1}^N \lambda_i \mathbb{E}[B_i] < 1$, where $B_i$ is the service time at $Q_i$.

Fix positive constants $\alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_N$ with $\sum_i \alpha_i = 1$, and consider the family of systems indexed by $S > 0$ in which the switch-over times are $s_i = s_i(S) = \alpha_i S$. Let the corresponding stationary cycle behavior (e.g. the joint distribution of cycle lengths, visit times, and queue lengths at polling instants, suitably normalized by $S$) be denoted $\mathcal{P}(S)$.

Prove rigorously that as $S \to \infty$, $\mathcal{P}(S)$ converges (in an appropriate distributional sense) to the behavior of the corresponding "deterministic cyclic system" — namely the limiting cyclic system in which inter-arrival times act as their means and all randomness in the polling dynamics vanishes, yielding a deterministic periodic schedule of visit times, cycle lengths, and workload trajectories determined solely by the means $1/\lambda_i$, $\mathbb{E}[B_i]$, and the ratios $\alpha_i$.
status_search_result: The problem is posed as an open problem (a conjecture asking for a rigorous proof) in the polling systems literature. original_question: Let A be a nonnegative tensor of order m and dimension n. Define the majorization matrix by M(A)_{ij} = a_{ij...j}. For a fixed j in [n], call A j-primitive if there exists a positive integer k such that (M(A^k))_{u j} > 0 for every u in [n]. Call A irreducible if there is no nonempty proper subset I of {1, ..., n} such that a_{i_1...i_m} = 0 whenever i_1 is in I and i_2, ..., i_m are all outside I. Is it true that A is primitive if and only if A is irreducible and there exists some j in [n] for which A is j-primitive?
self_contained_problem:
Let $m \ge 2$ and $n \ge 2$ be integers, and let $[n] = \{1, 2, \ldots, n\}$. A tensor of order $m$ and dimension $n$ is an array $A = (a_{i_1 i_2 \cdots i_m})$ with entries indexed by $i_1, \ldots, i_m \in [n]$. Such a tensor is called nonnegative if all entries $a_{i_1 \cdots i_m}$ are nonnegative real numbers.

For a nonnegative tensor $A$ of order $m$ and dimension $n$, define the majorization matrix $M(A)$ to be the $n \times n$ matrix whose $(i, j)$ entry is
$$M(A)_{ij} = a_{i j j \cdots j}, \qquad i, j \in [n].$$

The tensor product $A^k$ is defined recursively so that $A^k$ is again a nonnegative tensor of order $m$ and dimension $n$ via the standard tensor product associated with the Perron–Frobenius theory of nonnegative tensors: the entries of $A^k$ are the iterated polynomial expressions in the entries of $A$ obtained from $k$-fold composition (equivalently, from the map $x \mapsto Ax^{m-1}$).

The tensor $A$ is said to be primitive if there exists a positive integer $k$ such that every entry of $A^k$ is strictly positive. For a fixed $j \in [n]$, the tensor $A$ is said to be $j$-primitive if there exists a positive integer $k$ such that
$$\bigl(M(A^k)\bigr)_{u j} > 0 \quad \text{for every } u \in [n].$$

The tensor $A$ is said to be reducible if there exists a nonempty proper subset $I \subsetneq [n]$ such that
$$a_{i_1 i_2 \cdots i_m} = 0 \quad \text{whenever } i_1 \in I \text{ and } i_2, \ldots, i_m \in [n] \setminus I.$$
Otherwise $A$ is called irreducible.

Prove or disprove: a nonnegative tensor $A$ of order $m$ and dimension $n$ is primitive if and only if $A$ is irreducible and there exists some $j \in [n]$ such that $A$ is $j$-primitive.

context_brief: Extremal j-primitive degree for nonprimitive tensors
original_question: Fix integers m >= 3 and n >= 2. Let A be a nonnegative tensor of order m and dimension n, and let M(A) denote its majorization matrix, defined by M(A)_{ij} = a_{ij...j}. For a fixed j in [n], call A j-primitive if there exists a positive integer k such that (M(A^k))_{u j} > 0 for every u in [n], and let γ_j(A) be the least such k. Among tensors A that are j-primitive for at least one j but are not primitive tensors, define r(m, n) to be the maximum possible value of γ_j(A). Determine r(m, n), and characterize the tensors that attain this extremal value.
self_contained_problem:
Fix integers $m \ge 3$ and $n \ge 2$. A tensor $A = (a_{i_1 i_2 \ldots i_m})$ of order $m$ and dimension $n$ has entries indexed by $i_1, \ldots, i_m \in [n] := \{1, 2, \ldots, n\}$, and is called nonnegative if all entries are $\ge 0$. For two order-$m$ dimension-$n$ tensors $A$ and $B$, their product $A B$ is the order-$m$ dimension-$n$ tensor whose $(i, i_2, \ldots, i_m)$ entry is
$$ (AB)_{i\, i_2 \cdots i_m} \;=\; \sum_{j_2,\ldots,j_m \in [n]} a_{i\, j_2 \cdots j_m}\, b_{j_2\, i_2 \cdots i_m} \cdot \mathbf{1}[j_3=\cdots=j_m]\text{ along the standard tensor product convention,} $$
so that powers $A^k$ are defined recursively by $A^1 = A$ and $A^{k+1} = A \cdot A^k$ in the standard way used for nonnegative tensors. The majorization matrix $M(A)$ of $A$ is the $n \times n$ matrix with entries
$$ (M(A))_{ij} \;=\; a_{i\, j\, j\, \cdots\, j}, \qquad i,j \in [n]. $$
The tensor $A$ is called primitive if there exists a positive integer $k$ such that every entry of $M(A^k)$ is positive. For a fixed $j \in [n]$, $A$ is called $j$-primitive if there exists a positive integer $k$ such that $(M(A^k))_{u\, j} > 0$ for every $u \in [n]$; the smallest such $k$ is the $j$-primitive degree $\gamma_j(A)$.

Define
$$ r(m, n) \;=\; \max\bigl\{\, \gamma_j(A) \,:\, A \text{ is a nonnegative order-}m\text{ dimension-}n\text{ tensor},\ A \text{ is not primitive},\ \exists\, j \in [n] \text{ with } A \text{ being } j\text{-primitive} \,\bigr\}. $$

original_question: Let A be a nonnegative tensor of order m and dimension n. original_question: When can a non-trivial virtual knot arise as the connected sum of two trivial virtual knots? Equivalently, for long virtual knots whose closure is the unknot, classify which non-isotopic long virtual knots can close to the same trivial compact knot and thereby explain when different connected-sum choices for closed virtual knots can produce a non-trivial result.
self_contained_problem:
Background and definitions. A virtual knot diagram is a 4-valent planar graph whose vertices are decorated as either classical crossings (with over/under information) or virtual crossings (drawn as a small circle). Two virtual knot diagrams are equivalent if they are related by a finite sequence of planar isotopies, the three classical Reidemeister moves, the three virtual Reidemeister moves, and the mixed (semi-virtual) move. A virtual knot is an equivalence class of virtual knot diagrams. The unknot is the equivalence class of the diagram with no crossings.

A long virtual knot diagram is a virtual knot diagram in which one strand is cut at a generic point to produce two free ends going to infinity (a 1-1 tangle in the plane); equivalence of long virtual knot diagrams is generated by all the moves above performed away from the two ends. The closure of a long virtual knot is the (closed) virtual knot obtained by reconnecting the two ends in the plane.

The connected sum of two closed virtual knots K_1 and K_2 is defined by cutting each at a chosen arc and splicing them; in general this operation depends on the chosen arcs. For long virtual knots, concatenation gives a well-defined (but in general non-commutative) connected sum.

Problems.
(a) Classify all non-trivial virtual knots K that arise as a connected sum K = K_1 # K_2 in which both K_1 and K_2 are equivalent to the unknot.
(b) Classify all long virtual knots whose closure is equivalent to the (closed) unknot, up to equivalence of long virtual knots, and use this classification to describe precisely which choices of cutting arcs in two unknotted closed virtual knots can yield a non-trivial closed virtual connected sum.
status_search_result: The phenomenon that a non-trivial virtual knot (e.g., the Kishino knot) can be a connected sum of two unknotted virtual knots is well known, and many invariants (surface bracket, biquandle, parity, arrow polynomials) detect specific examples of non-triviality. However, no general classification of such virtual knots, nor of the long virtual knots whose closure is the unknot, appears in the literature; the question is listed among unsolved problems in virtual knot theory and remains open.

original_question: Find new combinatorial invariants of flat virtual knots, and determine richer algebraic structures that can detect flat virtual-knot phenomena beyond mod 2 linking numbers despite the fact that the flat biquandle algebra is isomorphic to the Weyl algebra and has no non-trivial finite-dimensional representations.
self_contained_problem:
A virtual knot diagram is a 4-valent plane graph whose vertices are decorated as either classical crossings (with over/under information) or virtual crossings (drawn as a small circle), considered up to the generalized Reidemeister moves (the three classical Reidemeister moves, the three purely virtual moves, and the mixed semivirtual move). A flat virtual knot (equivalently, a virtual string) is the equivalence class of a virtual knot diagram in which the over/under information at every classical crossing is forgotten, so that classical crossings are simply transverse double points; the equivalence relation is generated by the corresponding flat versions of the generalized Reidemeister moves.

The flat biquandle algebra is the unital associative algebra generated by two invertible elements A and B subject to the relations obtained from the flat Reidemeister moves; it is known to be isomorphic to the Weyl algebra (the algebra generated by x, y with [x, y] = 1 over a field of characteristic zero), and consequently it admits no nontrivial finite-dimensional representations.

To date, the principal nontrivial combinatorial invariant of flat virtual knots is the mod 2 linking number (and small refinements thereof).

Problem: Construct new combinatorial invariants of flat virtual knots that distinguish pairs of flat virtual knots not separated by mod 2 linking numbers, and identify richer algebraic structures (beyond the flat biquandle / Weyl algebra) capable of detecting flat virtual-knot phenomena despite the absence of nontrivial finite-dimensional representations of the Weyl algebra.
status_search_result: The problem is posed as part of a list of unsolved problems in virtual knot theory. Subsequent work has produced partial advances—e.g., semiquandle counting invariants, chord-index based invariants, and polynomial invariants from affine flat biquandles—but flat virtual knots remain difficult to classify and the search for richer algebraic invariants beyond the Weyl-algebra setting continues. No source indicates the problem has been fully resolved.

original_question: For the flat hierarchy in which flat crossings are labeled by elements of an ordinal alpha and a flat third Reidemeister move allows a strand with two labels a to slide across a crossing labeled b only when a is greater than b, classify the resulting diagrams and determine how this hierarchy generalizes ordinary flat virtual-knot theory.
self_contained_problem:
Fix an ordinal $\alpha$. Define the *flat $\alpha$-hierarchy of diagrams* as follows. A diagram is a 4-valent planar graph (with the usual virtual-crossing convention) whose classical-type crossings are flat (i.e. unsigned, with no over/under information) and each such flat crossing carries a label drawn from $\alpha$. Two diagrams are considered equivalent if they are related by a finite sequence of the following local moves, performed in any region of the plane:

(i) Planar isotopy and the standard detour move for virtual crossings (so virtual crossings behave as in flat virtual knot theory).

(ii) A flat first Reidemeister move that adds or removes a flat kink with an arbitrary label from $\alpha$.

(iii) A flat second Reidemeister move that creates or destroys a bigon whose two flat crossings carry the same label.

(iv) A *labeled flat third Reidemeister move*: a strand both of whose crossings on the boundary of a triangular region are labeled by the same element $a \in \alpha$ may be slid across a flat crossing labeled $b \in \alpha$ to the opposite side of that crossing if and only if $a > b$ in $\alpha$.

When $\alpha = 1$ this reduces to ordinary flat virtual knot theory (virtual strings).

Problem: Classify the equivalence classes of diagrams under these moves for an arbitrary ordinal $\alpha$, and describe in what precise sense the resulting theory generalizes flat virtual knot theory (e.g., construct complete or computable invariants distinguishing the classes, identify nontrivial elements arising at each level $a \in \alpha$, and determine the relationship between the hierarchies for $\alpha < \alpha'$).
status_search_result: The flat hierarchy indexed by ordinals appears in Kauffman's list of unsolved problems in virtual knot theory, where the classification of its diagrams is explicitly posed as an open question. Even the base case (ordinary flat virtual knots / virtual strings) is known to be difficult and is not fully classified, and no complete classification of the hierarchy for general ordinals appears in the literature.

original_question: Clarify the relationship between flat virtual-knot theories and theories of doodles, including doodles with virtual crossings, and determine the resulting structures for cobordism, associated groups, and free-abelian cobordism classes of immersed surfaces without triple points.
self_contained_problem:
Background and definitions.

(a) A flat virtual knot/link diagram is a 4-valent planar diagram whose crossings are of two kinds: flat (unoriented, undecorated) crossings and virtual crossings (drawn with a small circle). Two diagrams are equivalent as flat virtual links if they are related by a finite sequence of: (i) the flat Reidemeister moves on flat crossings, (ii) the virtual Reidemeister moves on virtual crossings, and (iii) the mixed "detour" move that allows an arc passing only through virtual crossings to be replaced by any other such arc with the same endpoints. (Crucially, the detour move is allowed for virtual crossings relative to flat crossings, but not vice versa.)

(b) A doodle is a finite collection of closed curves immersed in the 2-sphere (or in a closed oriented surface) having only transverse double points and no triple points, considered up to ambient isotopy and the doodle Reidemeister moves that exclude any move creating or destroying a triple point. One may also enlarge this category to "virtual doodles" by allowing, in addition to ordinary double points, virtual crossings subject to the virtual Reidemeister moves and the detour move.

(c) A cobordism between two doodles D_0 and D_1 is a compact immersed surface S in (surface)×[0,1] whose boundary is D_0⊔D_1, whose singular set consists only of double-point curves (i.e. S has no triple points and no branch points). Doodle cobordism is an equivalence relation, and the set of cobordism classes of doodles forms an abelian group under disjoint union; this group is conjectured/observed to be free abelian.

Problem. Develop a precise dictionary between the theory of flat virtual knots and links and the theory of (possibly virtual) doodles. Specifically:

1. Construct a well-defined map (or pair of mutually inverse maps) between equivalence classes of flat virtual links and equivalence classes of (virtual) doodles, and determine its kernel and image.

2. Define cobordism in both categories so that the dictionary of (1) descends to a homomorphism between the corresponding cobordism groups, and identify this homomorphism.

3. Determine the structure of the free-abelian cobordism group of doodles whose cobordisms are immersed surfaces without triple points: produce an explicit set of free generators (e.g. in terms of double-point–count invariants or homotopy classes of immersions), and compute the analogous group for virtual doodles.

4. For each of the categories above (flat virtual links, doodles, virtual doodles), describe the naturally associated group invariant (the analogue of the knot group / fundamental group of the complement / quandle-type group), and exhibit how these groups correspond under the dictionary of (1).
status_search_result: The problem of relating flat virtual knot theory to doodle theory (with or without virtual crossings) and describing the associated cobordism groups and group invariants appears in collections of unsolved problems on virtual knot theory and is the subject of ongoing research. Recent works (e.g. on free-knot invariants by Manturov, on doodle groups and twin groups, and on virtual knot cobordism) develop pieces of the picture but no complete dictionary or full computation of the free-abelian doodle-cobordism group has been established.

original_question: Do the two equivalence relations on ordinary 3-manifolds presented by surgery on framed links - homeomorphism and virtual equivalence via generalized Kirby moves - actually coincide? More generally, give a geometric-topological interpretation of virtual 3-manifolds, and determine whether the alternative construction obtained by doing surgery on links in thickened surfaces S_g x R up to stabilization yields the same theory.
self_contained_problem:
Background. A classical closed orientable 3-manifold can be presented by integral Dehn surgery on a framed link in S^3, and two such links present homeomorphic 3-manifolds if and only if they are related by a finite sequence of Kirby moves (handle slides and stabilizations). A virtual link diagram is a 4-valent planar graph whose crossings are labeled as classical (over/under) or virtual, considered up to the classical Reidemeister moves and the virtual Reidemeister moves. By extending the Kirby calculus to framed virtual link diagrams via "generalized Kirby moves," one obtains an equivalence relation on framed virtual links; the equivalence classes are called virtual 3-manifolds. Every classical framed link is in particular a virtual one, so this gives an equivalence relation on classical (ordinary) 3-manifolds (two ordinary 3-manifolds are virtually equivalent if their framed-link presentations are related through the virtual Kirby calculus).

Alternatively, for each closed orientable surface Σ_g one may consider framed links in the thickened surface Σ_g × ℝ and perform Dehn surgery on them; identifying surfaces and links under stabilization (adding a handle to Σ_g together with the corresponding inclusion of links) produces another candidate notion of "virtual 3-manifold."

Problems.
(a) Do the two equivalence relations on ordinary closed orientable 3-manifolds — homeomorphism, and virtual equivalence via generalized Kirby moves — coincide? Equivalently, if two framed links K, L ⊂ S^3 are equivalent via the virtual Kirby calculus, must they be equivalent via the classical Kirby calculus?

(b) Give a geometric-topological interpretation of the equivalence classes of framed virtual links under the virtual Kirby calculus: that is, identify what kind of geometric object a "virtual 3-manifold" is.

(c) Does the theory of virtual 3-manifolds defined via surgery on framed links in thickened surfaces Σ_g × ℝ, taken up to surface stabilization, coincide with the theory defined by virtual Kirby calculus on framed virtual link diagrams?
status_search_result: Web search did not surface a published resolution. The notion of virtual 3-manifolds via virtual Kirby calculus is established in work of Dye and Kauffman, and a thickened-surface/stabilization viewpoint is well known in virtual knot theory, but no source found explicitly proves that virtual Kirby equivalence of classical links implies classical Kirby equivalence, gives a definitive geometric-topological interpretation of virtual 3-manifolds, or proves equivalence of the two constructions. Status appears to remain open, but this could not be conclusively verified.

original_question: Develop effective invariants and, if possible, a classification theory for welded knots. In particular, determine whether Satoh's map from welded knots or links to ambient-isotopy classes of ribbon torus embeddings in four-space is faithful, and determine whether a welded knot with trivial fundamental group must itself be trivial as a welded knot.
self_contained_problem:
Background and definitions.

A welded knot diagram is a generic immersion of a circle in the plane whose double points are decorated as either classical crossings (with over/under information) or welded (virtual) crossings. Two welded knot diagrams are equivalent if they are related by a finite sequence of the classical Reidemeister moves R1, R2, R3, the virtual Reidemeister moves V1, V2, V3, the mixed move M (a classical strand passes through a welded crossing), and the over-commute (forbidden-overpass, F1) move in which an over-strand may slide past a virtual crossing. (The under-commute move F2 is NOT allowed.) A welded knot is an equivalence class of welded knot diagrams under these moves; welded links are defined analogously with several components.

The welded knot group of a welded knot K is the group with Wirtinger presentation read off from any of its diagrams (one generator per arc, one relation per classical crossing); this is a welded invariant.

Satoh's Tube map Tube assigns to every welded knot K an ambient isotopy class Tube(K) of an oriented embedded ribbon torus in S^4, by "inflating" each arc of a diagram into an annulus and resolving classical and welded crossings as ribbon singularities in 4-space. The map is well defined on welded equivalence classes, surjects onto ambient-isotopy classes of ribbon torus knots, and induces an isomorphism between the welded knot group of K and the fundamental group π_1(S^4 ∖ Tube(K)).

Problems. Provide answers to each of the following.

(a) Construct effective invariants of welded knots that, ideally, suffice to classify them up to welded equivalence.

(b) Decide whether the Tube map
      Tube : { welded knots } / (welded equivalence)  →  { ribbon torus knots in S^4 } / (ambient isotopy)
(and its analogue for welded links) is injective.

(c) Decide whether every welded knot K with trivial welded knot group (i.e. π_1 isomorphic to Z) is welded-equivalent to the unknot.
category_tag: welded knots and ribbon torus knots
status_search_result: Recent work shows Satoh's Tube map is not injective: there exist non-trivial welded knots and links mapped to the same ribbon torus knot, and Y-type local moves on welded links have been identified as part of the kernel, though the kernel of Tube is not yet completely understood. It is also known that having welded knot group Z does not force a welded knot to be trivial; non-trivial welded knots with trivial group exist. The broader problem of constructing a complete set of invariants and a full classification of welded knots remains open.

context_brief: Long virtual and long flat knots
original_question: Strengthen the invariant theory for long virtual knots and long flat virtual knots, especially by combining the long-knot approach of [160] with biquandle constructions, by extracting useful classical-knot invariants from that framework, and by seeking a full classification of long flat knots using the descending-diagram construction D(F) associated to a long flat virtual knot F.
self_contained_problem:
A virtual knot diagram is a 4-valent plane graph whose vertices are decorated as classical crossings (with over/under information) or as virtual crossings (drawn with a small circle), considered up to the generalized Reidemeister moves (the classical Reidemeister moves R1, R2, R3 together with the virtual moves V1, V2, V3 and the mixed move M). A long virtual knot is the analogous object for a properly embedded oriented arc with a generic projection to the plane (one input and one output strand at infinity), again considered up to generalized Reidemeister moves performed in a compact region. A long flat virtual knot is obtained by forgetting the over/under information at every classical crossing, so that classical crossings are replaced by transverse double points and one works modulo the flat versions of R2, R3 and the virtual/mixed moves.

A biquandle is a set X equipped with two binary operations (a,b) ↦ a^b and (a,b) ↦ a_b satisfying the axioms ensuring invariance under the classical and virtual Reidemeister moves: each map x ↦ x^y and x ↦ x_y is a bijection, the "sideways" map S(a,b) = (b^a, a_b) is invertible, and the operations satisfy the exchange laws making the biquandle coloring of any virtual knot diagram well defined.

For a long flat virtual knot F, one may form its descending diagram D(F): traverse the long arc from input to output and at each double point encountered for the first time declare the strand to pass over the strand met later, producing a long virtual (non-flat) knot D(F).

Solve the following research program:

(a) Construct a strengthened invariant theory for long virtual knots that unifies the long-knot invariant framework (in which a long virtual knot is encoded by the algebraic word read along its strand, modulo relations corresponding to long-knot Reidemeister moves) with the biquandle coloring construction, and produce invariants of long virtual knots strictly stronger than those obtained from either framework alone.

(b) From this combined framework, extract new invariants of classical knots (long classical knots, viewed as long virtual knots whose diagrams have no virtual crossings) that are not equivalent to previously known classical invariants, or prove that no such new classical invariants arise.

(c) Using the descending-diagram assignment F ↦ D(F), give a complete classification of long flat virtual knots: namely, decide whether two long flat virtual knots F1 and F2 are equivalent if and only if D(F1) and D(F2) are equivalent as long virtual knots, and if not, determine the precise equivalence relation on long virtual knots induced by this assignment so as to obtain a full set of invariants classifying long flat virtual knots.
status_search_result: The problem is a research program combining long virtual knot invariants, biquandle constructions, and the descending-diagram approach for long flat knots. No published work appears to fully classify long flat virtual knots or to establish the requested unified invariant framework; work on biquandle invariants and flat virtual knots continues but the classification problem for long flat virtual knots remains an acknowledged open problem.

original_question: Construct explicit presentations of a virtual biquandle that uses the given linear non-commutative representation at classical crossings together with a genuinely informative algebraic structure at virtual crossings.
self_contained_problem:
A virtual link diagram is a 4-valent planar graph whose vertices are decorated either as classical crossings (with over/under information) or as virtual crossings (drawn with a small circle). A virtual biquandle is a set X equipped with two binary operations ▷, ▷* : X×X → X (for the classical crossings) and a bijection f : X → X (for the virtual crossings), satisfying:

(i) the biquandle axioms at classical crossings, ensuring invariance under the classical Reidemeister moves R1, R2, R3;
(ii) the conditions making f compatible with the virtual Reidemeister moves V1, V2, V3 and the mixed move M, namely that f is a bijection and that the operations ▷, ▷* commute appropriately with f so that labeling rules at virtual crossings (where the outgoing labels are obtained by applying f and f⁻¹ to the incoming labels) yield an invariant of virtual links.

Given a unital (possibly non-commutative) ring R, a linear (non-commutative) representation of the classical biquandle operations on a free R-module M is a pair of formulas of the form
   a ▷ b = α·a + β·b ,    a ▷* b = γ·a + δ·b ,
with fixed elements α, β, γ, δ ∈ R chosen so that the biquandle axioms hold; these specify how the labels in M propagate through classical crossings.

Problem. Exhibit an explicit virtual biquandle (X, ▷, ▷*, f) of the following form:
 • X = M is a free module over a (non-commutative) ring R, with classical operations ▷, ▷* given by a fixed linear formula as above (a non-commutative analogue of the Alexander/Burau-type biquandle);
 • the virtual-crossing map f : M → M is given by a non-trivial algebraic operation (i.e., not equal to the identity and not reducible to a permutation that trivializes the virtual structure) producing a genuinely informative invariant of virtual links;
 • all virtual biquandle axioms (compatibility with the classical, virtual and mixed Reidemeister moves) are verified.

Provide the ring R, the module M, the constants α, β, γ, δ, and the map f explicitly.

The problem appears to remain a stated open direction in surveys of unsolved problems in virtual knot theory.

original_question: Determine whether there exists a birack whose induced action on virtual braids is faithful, and determine whether the invariant for virtual braids cited in [150] is faithful. More broadly, decide whether the known linear actions fail precisely because the corresponding linear invariants of virtual knots and links are not faithful.
self_contained_problem:
Background and definitions.

The virtual braid group VB_n is the group with generators σ_1, …, σ_{n−1} (classical braid generators) and τ_1, …, τ_{n−1} (virtual generators) subject to:
• σ_i σ_j = σ_j σ_i and τ_i τ_j = τ_j τ_i for |i−j| ≥ 2;
• σ_i σ_{i+1} σ_i = σ_{i+1} σ_i σ_{i+1};
• τ_i^2 = 1, τ_i τ_{i+1} τ_i = τ_{i+1} τ_i τ_{i+1};
• σ_i τ_j = τ_j σ_i for |i−j| ≥ 2;
• τ_i τ_{i+1} σ_i = σ_{i+1} τ_i τ_{i+1}.

A birack is a set X equipped with a bijection S : X × X → X × X, written S(a,b) = (b^a, a_b), satisfying the set-theoretic Yang–Baxter equation
   (S × id)(id × S)(S × id) = (id × S)(S × id)(id × S)
on X × X × X, together with the invertibility/sideways conditions that make the maps a ↦ a_b and b ↦ b^a bijections (so that S yields a well-defined assignment for each generator σ_i of the virtual braid group, with τ_i acting by the transposition).

Given a birack (X, S), the assignments σ_i ↦ id^{i−1} × S × id^{n−i−1} and τ_i ↦ id^{i−1} × T × id^{n−i−1} (where T is the swap on X × X) define a homomorphism
   ρ_{X,S} : VB_n → Sym(X^n).

A linear biquandle is a birack arising from a pair of commuting invertible linear maps on a module, giving the Burau-like (Alexander) representation of VB_n.

Problems.

(1) Does there exist a birack (X, S) (allowing X infinite) such that the induced homomorphism ρ_{X,S} : VB_n → Sym(X^n) is faithful for every n ≥ 2?

(2) For the standard birack/biquandle invariant of virtual braids defined by a generic biquandle structure (in particular the "universal" birack invariant assigning to a virtual braid the tuple of output labels as a function of input labels), determine whether this invariant distinguishes all distinct virtual braids — i.e., whether it is faithful as an invariant on VB_n.

(3) Show that every linear biquandle action on VB_n fails to be faithful precisely because the induced linear invariant of the closure (a virtual link invariant) is not a complete invariant of virtual links; equivalently, identify whether the failure of faithfulness of linear biquandle actions on virtual braids comes from, and is equivalent to, the non-faithfulness of the corresponding linear invariant of virtual knots and links.

The questions therefore appear to remain open.

original_question: Does the fundamental biquandle classify virtual links up to mirror images, including the known ambiguity that the biquandle has the same value on the orientation-reversed mirror image obtained by reflection in a plane perpendicular to the diagram plane?
self_contained_problem:
A virtual link diagram is a 4-valent planar diagram whose crossings are marked as classical (with over/under information) or virtual (drawn with a small circle). Virtual links are equivalence classes of oriented virtual link diagrams under the generalized Reidemeister moves (the three classical Reidemeister moves together with the four virtual Reidemeister moves).

A biquandle is a set X equipped with four binary operations a^b, a_b, a^{\bar b}, a_{\bar b} (right actions) satisfying:
(i) for all a,b in X, the maps b \mapsto a^b and b \mapsto a_b are bijections, and the operations with bars are their inverses;
(ii) for every a, there exists x with x^a = a and a_x = x, and a^a = a_a;
(iii) the exchange/biquandle axioms
   (a^b)^{c^b} = (a^c)^{b_c}, \quad (a_b)_{c_b} = (a_c)_{b_c}, \quad (a^b)_{c^b} = (a_c)^{b_c},
hold for all a,b,c in X.

The fundamental biquandle FB(L) of an oriented virtual link diagram L is the biquandle presented by one generator for each semi-arc of the diagram (a semi-arc is an edge between two consecutive under/virtual breaks) together with two relations at each classical crossing encoding the biquandle operations between incoming and outgoing semi-arcs (with no relations at virtual crossings beyond the identification of semi-arcs as one passes through). Up to isomorphism, FB(L) is an invariant of the oriented virtual link.

Given a virtual link L, let L^* denote the mirror image of L (obtained, say, by switching every classical crossing). It is known that FB(L) equals FB(L^{*r}), where L^{*r} denotes the orientation-reversed mirror image obtained by reflecting the diagram in a line in the diagram plane (equivalently, reflecting in a plane perpendicular to the diagram plane and reversing orientation).

Question: Does the fundamental biquandle classify oriented virtual links up to this known mirror-image ambiguity? That is, if L_1 and L_2 are oriented virtual links with FB(L_1) \cong FB(L_2) as biquandles, must L_1 be equivalent either to L_2 or to the orientation-reversed mirror image of L_2?
status_search_result: The question is listed as one of the unsolved problems in virtual knot theory and remains an active research direction. Recent work continues to investigate biquandle invariants of virtual links and their ability to distinguish links and their mirror images, but no proof of the conjectured classification (nor a counterexample) appears in the literature.

original_question: Give concrete examples of weak biquandles that are not strong.
self_contained_problem:
A biquandle structure on a set $X$ consists of two binary operations $\underline{\triangleright}, \overline{\triangleright}: X\times X\to X$ satisfying the following axioms:

(B1) For every $a\in X$, $a\,\underline{\triangleright}\,a = a\,\overline{\triangleright}\,a$.

(B2) The maps $\alpha_b: X\to X$, $\alpha_b(a)=a\,\underline{\triangleright}\,b$, and $\beta_b: X\to X$, $\beta_b(a)=a\,\overline{\triangleright}\,b$, are bijections of $X$ for every $b\in X$, and the map $S: X\times X\to X\times X$ defined by $S(a,b)=(b\,\overline{\triangleright}\,a,\, a\,\underline{\triangleright}\,b)$ is a bijection.

(B3, exchange / Yang–Baxter type identities) For all $a,b,c\in X$,
$$(a\,\underline{\triangleright}\,b)\,\underline{\triangleright}\,(c\,\underline{\triangleright}\,b) = (a\,\underline{\triangleright}\,c)\,\underline{\triangleright}\,(b\,\overline{\triangleright}\,c),$$
$$(a\,\overline{\triangleright}\,b)\,\overline{\triangleright}\,(c\,\underline{\triangleright}\,b) = (a\,\overline{\triangleright}\,c)\,\overline{\triangleright}\,(b\,\overline{\triangleright}\,c),$$
$$(b\,\overline{\triangleright}\,a)\,\underline{\triangleright}\,(c\,\overline{\triangleright}\,a) = (b\,\underline{\triangleright}\,c)\,\overline{\triangleright}\,(a\,\underline{\triangleright}\,c).$$

Call $(X,\underline{\triangleright},\overline{\triangleright})$ a weak biquandle if it satisfies (B1), (B3), and the bijectivity of $\alpha_b,\beta_b$ together with the requirement that $S$ is a bijection, but where the additional "strong" condition
$$\text{for all } a,b\in X,\ \alpha_b(a)=a \iff \beta_a(b)=b$$
(equivalently, $a\,\underline{\triangleright}\,b=a$ if and only if $b\,\overline{\triangleright}\,a=b$) is not required. Call it a strong biquandle if this additional condition does hold.

Problem: Construct an explicit example of a weak biquandle $(X,\underline{\triangleright},\overline{\triangleright})$ that is not a strong biquandle, i.e., exhibit a set $X$ with operations $\underline{\triangleright},\overline{\triangleright}$ satisfying the weak biquandle axioms together with elements $a,b\in X$ such that exactly one of $a\,\underline{\triangleright}\,b=a$ and $b\,\overline{\triangleright}\,a=b$ holds.
status_search_result: Search results indicate that explicit examples of weak biquandles that are not strong have been constructed, in particular in the work "On axioms of biquandles," where a weak biquandle (using a construction involving the Prüfer group) is shown to fail the strong-biquandle axiom. Thus the problem is considered solved.

original_question: Suppose a non-trivial classical knot K is modified by virtualizing some crossings so that the resulting virtual knot K~ is non-trivial and has unit Jones polynomial. Must K~ be non-classical, or could it still be virtually equivalent to a classical knot? More generally, if a virtual knot has unit Jones polynomial, is it equivalent to a classical diagram after virtual equivalence together with crossing virtualization, and if one classical knot can be obtained from another by crossing virtualization plus virtual Reidemeister moves, must the two classical knots already be classically equivalent?
self_contained_problem:
Background and setup. A classical knot diagram is a 4-valent planar graph whose vertices are decorated with over/under crossing information. A virtual knot diagram is a 4-valent graph in the plane in which each vertex is marked either as a classical crossing (with over/under information) or as a virtual crossing (drawn with a small circle). Two virtual knot diagrams are said to be virtually equivalent if one can be obtained from the other by a finite sequence of the classical Reidemeister moves R1, R2, R3 together with the virtual Reidemeister moves V1, V2, V3 and the mixed move (a virtual triangle move involving one classical and two virtual crossings). A classical knot is called non-trivial if it is not virtually equivalent to the unknot.

The crossing virtualization operation replaces a chosen classical crossing c in a diagram by the local tangle obtained by switching c and then surrounding the resulting crossing by two virtual crossings on the two strands; equivalently, it is the local move that replaces a classical crossing by a "virtualized" crossing. This operation is known to preserve the Jones polynomial V (defined for virtual knots via the Kauffman bracket extended by setting the bracket of virtual crossings as identity) but can change the virtual isotopy class.

Say that a virtual knot K has unit Jones polynomial if V(K) = 1.

Questions. 

(a) Let K be a non-trivial classical knot, and let K̃ be the virtual knot obtained from K by virtualizing some non-empty subset of its classical crossings. Suppose K̃ is non-trivial and has V(K̃) = 1. Must K̃ be non-classical (i.e. not virtually equivalent to any classical knot diagram), or is it possible for K̃ to be virtually equivalent to a classical knot?

(b) Suppose K is an arbitrary virtual knot diagram with V(K) = 1. Is K necessarily equivalent, under the combination of virtual equivalence and crossing virtualization, to a classical knot diagram?

(c) Suppose K and K′ are two classical knots such that K can be obtained from K′ by a finite sequence of crossing virtualizations and virtual Reidemeister moves (including the classical Reidemeister moves and the mixed move). Must K and K′ then be classically equivalent (i.e. ambient isotopic as classical knots in S³)?
category_tag: virtual knot theory and Jones polynomial
status_search_result: The questions concern detecting non-classicality of virtual knots with unit Jones polynomial obtained by virtualization. Examples of virtual knots with unit Jones polynomial that are not equivalent to any classical knot have been produced (notably using Manturov's parity bracket), but the general questions—whether every virtual knot with unit Jones polynomial reduces to a classical diagram via virtualization, and whether crossing virtualization plus virtual Reidemeister moves between classical knots forces classical equivalence—appear to remain open in the surveyed literature on virtual knot theory.

original_question: Develop a theory of virtual quandle homology parallel to existing quandle homology theories and determine what new invariants of virtual knots and links it provides.
status_search_result: Virtual quandles were introduced by Manturov and quandle cocycle invariants have been extended to virtual knots in several works (e.g., Carter–Elhamdadi–Saito on twisted quandle homology, and follow-ups computing cocycle invariants of virtual knots). original_question: Construct a Khovanov complex for arbitrary virtual-knot diagrams over the integers, understand the existing constructions that work for large classes of virtual links, and determine structural consequences such as which knots are K-full or Kho-full, whether optimal diagrams are minimal in classical crossing number, and which diagram moves preserve that optimality.
self_contained_problem:
A virtual knot diagram is a 4-valent plane graph whose vertices are decorated as either classical crossings (with over/under information) or virtual crossings (drawn as a small circle), considered up to the generalized Reidemeister moves (the classical Reidemeister moves R1, R2, R3 together with the virtual moves V1, V2, V3 and the mixed move M). Classical Khovanov homology assigns to each oriented classical link diagram L a bigraded chain complex C(L) of free abelian groups whose homotopy type is a link invariant; its homology Kh(L) categorifies the Jones polynomial.

Problem. Construct, in a combinatorial and diagrammatic way, a Khovanov-type chain complex C(D) of free abelian groups associated to an arbitrary virtual knot (or link) diagram D, defined over the ring of integers Z, such that:

(a) C(D) is invariant up to chain homotopy equivalence under the generalized Reidemeister moves, so that its homology Kh(D) is a virtual link invariant;
(b) when D is a classical diagram, C(D) is chain-homotopy equivalent to the classical Khovanov complex, and Kh(D) recovers the classical Khovanov homology;
(c) the construction extends, or is compatible with, existing partial constructions of Khovanov homology defined for those virtual diagrams whose associated abstract surface (atom) is orientable.

Using such a theory, address the following structural questions. Call a virtual knot K-full (respectively Kho-full) if it attains the maximal possible rank of an associated Kauffman-bracket-based (respectively Khovanov) invariant in a suitable sense made precise by the construction. Call a diagram D of a virtual knot K optimal if it realizes the maximum possible bigraded support of Kh(K).

(i) Classify all K-full virtual knots and all Kho-full virtual knots.
(ii) Determine whether every optimal diagram of a virtual knot is minimal with respect to the number of classical crossings.
(iii) Determine which diagrammatic moves preserve optimality of a diagram.
status_search_result: Manturov constructed a Khovanov-type homology for virtual knots over arbitrary coefficient rings (including Z), agreeing with classical Khovanov homology on classical diagrams. Subsequent works (Dye–Kaestner–Kauffman, Tubbenhauer, Rushworth, etc.) have extended and refined such constructions. However, the full package of structural questions (classification of K-full/Kho-full knots, minimality of optimal diagrams in classical crossing number, and characterization of optimality-preserving moves) remains open in general.

original_question: Describe the structure of Jones-Wenzl-type projectors inside the Brauer algebra that arises from adding virtual crossings to the Temperley-Lieb algebra, and determine whether that setting supports a useful algebraic generalization of classical recoupling theory.
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathrm{TL}_n(d)$ denote the Temperley–Lieb algebra on $n$ strands with loop value $d$, generated by identity and elements $U_1,\dots,U_{n-1}$ subject to $U_i^2 = dU_i$, $U_iU_{i\pm 1}U_i = U_i$, and $U_iU_j = U_jU_i$ for $|i-j|\ge 2$. Inside $\mathrm{TL}_n(d)$, the Jones–Wenzl projector $p_n$ is the unique nonzero idempotent satisfying $p_n U_i = U_i p_n = 0$ for all $1\le i\le n-1$ (when $d$ avoids the relevant roots of unity).

Adjoin to $\mathrm{TL}_n(d)$ "virtual crossing" generators $v_1,\dots,v_{n-1}$, where each $v_i$ is an involution corresponding to a transposition of strands $i$ and $i+1$, satisfying the symmetric group relations $v_i^2 = 1$, $v_iv_{i+1}v_i = v_{i+1}v_iv_{i+1}$, $v_iv_j = v_jv_i$ for $|i-j|\ge 2$, together with the mixed relations
$$v_i U_j = U_j v_i \quad (|i-j|\ge 2), \qquad v_i v_{i+1} U_i = U_{i+1} v_i v_{i+1}, \qquad v_i U_i = U_i v_i = U_i$$
that make the resulting algebra isomorphic to the Brauer algebra $B_n(d)$.

(a) Determine the structure of the virtual analogues of the Jones–Wenzl projectors inside $B_n(d)$: explicitly describe idempotents $\tilde p_n \in B_n(d)$ characterized by $\tilde p_n U_i = U_i \tilde p_n = 0$ and $\tilde p_n v_i = v_i \tilde p_n = \tilde p_n$ for all $i$, and give a recursive or closed-form construction analogous to the Wenzl recursion.

(b) Decide whether classical Temperley–Lieb recoupling theory (the trivalent spin network calculus producing $6j$-symbols, theta nets, and the Kauffman–Lins evaluation of closed networks) admits a useful algebraic generalization to this Brauer-algebraic setting with virtual crossings, and if so formulate the corresponding recoupling identities (orthogonality, Biedenharn–Elliott, fusion).
status_search_result: A 2021 paper by Kauffman, Mehrabi and Radmanesh, "Projectors in the Virtual Temperley–Lieb Algebra" (arXiv:2103.11355), constructs idempotents in the virtual Temperley–Lieb algebra (which is isomorphic to the Brauer algebra) that generalize Jones–Wenzl projectors and satisfy the property that multiplication by a virtual generator is trivial. This addresses part (a) of the question. A complete development of a virtual recoupling theory (full $6j$-symbol calculus, fusion identities, etc.) does not appear to be fully established, so the second half remains partially open.

original_question: Define a notion of alternating virtual knot, classify alternating virtual knots and alternating weaves on surfaces without stabilization, and formulate and prove the virtual analogue of the Tait flyping conjecture.
self_contained_problem:
A virtual knot may be presented either as a virtual knot diagram (a 4-valent planar diagram whose crossings are marked as classical over/under or virtual) modulo the generalized Reidemeister moves, or equivalently as a knot in a thickened orientable surface Σ × [0,1] modulo ambient isotopy and stabilization/destabilization of Σ. A "weave" on a surface Σ is the image of an immersed circle in Σ that gives a knot diagram on Σ (i.e. a knot in Σ × [0,1] together with its projection).

(a) Give a definition of "alternating virtual knot" and classify alternating virtual knots up to equivalence.

(b) Classify all alternating weaves on closed orientable surfaces, considered up to homeomorphism of the surface and Reidemeister moves on the surface, but without allowing stabilization (adding/removing handles to the surface).

(c) Formulate a virtual analogue of the Tait flyping conjecture — i.e. a statement asserting that any two reduced alternating diagrams (in the appropriate virtual or surface sense) representing the same virtual knot are related by a sequence of flypes — and prove it.
status_search_result: Substantial progress has been made. Boden and Karimi developed a theory of alternating virtual knots, and Boden–Karimi–Sikora proved Tait's first two conjectures for alternating links in thickened surfaces. A "virtual flyping theorem" was established (arXiv:2210.03720), proving the virtual analogue of Tait's flyping conjecture for alternating virtual links / links in thickened surfaces. The complete classification of alternating weaves on surfaces without stabilization does not appear to be fully resolved in a single comprehensive statement, so the program is best characterized as partially solved.

original_question: For a virtual link with minimal classical crossing number C, minimal virtual crossing number V, and minimal total crossing number T, determine how C, V, and T are related, whether T = V + L in the notation of the paper, how the virtual unknotting number behaves, how V relates to minimal genus in a surface representation, and what effective algorithms or polynomial bounds exist for computing or estimating these quantities.
self_contained_problem:
Let L be a virtual link, i.e., an equivalence class of virtual link diagrams (4-valent planar graphs whose vertices are either classical crossings, marked with over/under information, or virtual crossings, marked with a small circle) under the generalized Reidemeister moves. For a virtual link L define:

- C(L) = the minimum, over all diagrams of L, of the number of classical crossings;
- V(L) = the minimum, over all diagrams of L, of the number of virtual crossings;
- T(L) = the minimum, over all diagrams of L, of the total number of crossings (classical plus virtual).

Investigate the following questions:

(a) Determine the relationships among C(L), V(L), and T(L). In particular, decide whether the equality
        T(L) = C(L) + V(L)
holds for every virtual link L, or exhibit virtual links for which T(L) is strictly smaller than C(L) + V(L).

(b) Define the virtual unknotting number u_v(L) as the minimum number of classical crossing changes (in any diagram of L) needed to transform L into the unknot in the virtual category, and study its basic properties (additivity under connected sum, lower bounds in terms of invariants, computability).

(c) Every virtual knot can be represented as a knot in a thickened oriented closed surface up to stabilisation; let g(L) denote the minimal genus of such a surface representative. Determine the precise relationship between V(L) and g(L) (e.g., whether V(L) ≥ 2g(L), or sharper bounds).

(d) Provide effective algorithms or polynomial-time bounds for computing or estimating C(L), V(L), T(L), u_v(L), and g(L) from a given virtual link diagram.
status_search_result: The questions remain largely open. Work by Manturov and others (e.g., "On Virtual Crossing Numbers for Virtual Knots", arXiv:1107.4828) shows that V(L) can grow quadratically in C(L), refuting earlier linear conjectures, but the exact relationship among C, V, T is not determined; the virtual unknotting number is poorly understood; and no general polynomial-time algorithms for these invariants are known. Recent work (e.g., arXiv:2312.03994 on flat virtual knots) continues to study connected-sum/crossing-number relations without resolving the general problems.

original_question: Formulate a category of wild virtual knots together with an appropriate axiom system, and prove a criterion describing when a wild equivalence between tame virtual links already implies tame equivalence.
self_contained_problem:
A virtual link diagram is a 4-valent plane graph each of whose vertices is decorated either as a classical crossing (with over/under information) or as a virtual crossing (drawn as a small circle). Two virtual link diagrams are called tamely equivalent if they are related by a finite sequence of classical Reidemeister moves and the detour (virtual) moves; the resulting equivalence classes are the (tame) virtual links.

By analogy with the classical theory, where wild knots are obtained from tame knots by allowing limit points of "infinitely many shrinking crossings", one wishes to enlarge the class of virtual link diagrams so as to permit diagrams with infinitely many crossings accumulating at limit points (and possibly with limit points of limit points, etc.), together with a notion of "wild Reidemeister/detour equivalence" allowing infinite sequences of moves whose supports shrink to such limit points.

The problem has two parts:

(1) Define a category WVK of wild virtual knots: specify precisely the objects (a class of generalized virtual link diagrams admitting wild behavior), the morphisms or equivalence relation (a wild analogue of the classical and detour Reidemeister moves), and a complete list of axioms making this into a well-defined category that contains the category of tame virtual links as a full subcategory and that reduces to the classical theory of wild knots in the absence of virtual crossings.

(2) Within the category WVK so constructed, formulate and prove a criterion (a "tameness theorem") giving necessary and sufficient conditions on two tame virtual links L_1 and L_2 under which the existence of a wild equivalence between L_1 and L_2 in WVK implies that L_1 and L_2 are already tamely equivalent as virtual links.
status_search_result: The construction of a category of wild virtual knots with axiomatics, and a criterion for when wild equivalence of tame virtual links forces tame equivalence, is listed among unsolved problems in virtual knot theory. No subsequent paper appears to have established such a categorical framework or proved the requested tameness criterion; related literature on wild and non-compact knot theory exists but does not resolve the virtual case.

original_question: Understand how virtual-knot polynomials relate to Vassiliev invariants for virtual knots, and determine whether every finite-type Vassiliev invariant of classical knots extends to a finite-type invariant of long virtual knots in the sense described by the paper, while also clarifying the alternate finite-type notion for virtual knots mentioned there.
self_contained_problem:
Background. A virtual knot diagram is a knot diagram in the plane in which each double point is labelled either as a classical crossing (over/under) or as a virtual crossing (a small circle). Virtual knots are equivalence classes of such diagrams under the generalized Reidemeister moves (the classical Reidemeister moves together with the virtual and mixed moves of Kauffman). A long virtual knot is the analogous notion for a 1-1 tangle: a virtual knot diagram with two free ends going to infinity, considered up to generalized Reidemeister moves fixing the ends.

Singular extension and finite-type (Vassiliev) invariants. A singular (virtual) knot is a (virtual) knot diagram allowed to have finitely many transverse classical double points. Any invariant v of (virtual) knots with values in an abelian group is extended to singular (virtual) knots by the Vassiliev skein relation
   v(D_×) = v(D_+) − v(D_−),
where D_+, D_− denote the two classical resolutions of a transverse double point D_×. The invariant v is said to be of finite type of order ≤ n (a Vassiliev invariant of order ≤ n) if its extension vanishes on every singular (virtual) knot with more than n double points. For long virtual knots one uses the same definition with singular long virtual diagrams.

Polynomial invariants. Let P denote the collection of polynomial-type invariants of virtual knots (for example, Kauffman's f-polynomial / bracket polynomial for virtual knots, the Sawollek / Alexander-type polynomial of a virtual knot, the arrow polynomial, and similar invariants).

Problems.
(a) Determine the precise relationship between the polynomial invariants in P and the Vassiliev (finite-type) invariants of virtual knots in Kauffman's sense: specifically, characterize which coefficients, evaluations, or derived numerical functions of these polynomials are finite-type invariants, and identify the order of each such finite-type invariant.

(b) Decide whether every finite-type (Vassiliev) invariant of classical knots extends to a finite-type invariant of long virtual knots of the same order. That is, for every Vassiliev invariant v of order ≤ n on classical knots (valued in an abelian group), does there exist a finite-type invariant V of order ≤ n on long virtual knots whose restriction to classical long knots equals v?

(c) An alternate notion of finite-type invariant for virtual knots may be formulated using moves other than the standard Vassiliev double-point resolution (for instance, by replacing the local change D_+ − D_− with a virtualization move or another local replacement on virtual diagrams). Investigate this alternate finite-type theory: compare the resulting filtration on the space of virtual-knot invariants with the Kauffman/Goussarov–Polyak–Viro filtrations, and determine which classical Vassiliev invariants extend in this alternate sense.
status_search_result: Significant partial progress is documented but the problems are not fully resolved. Goussarov–Polyak–Viro introduced a finite-type theory for virtual and long virtual knots and showed that classical Vassiliev invariants extend to long virtual knots via Gauss-diagram formulas, addressing part of (b); however, a complete equivalence between Kauffman's finite-type theory and the GPV theory, and a full classification of which polynomial-invariant coefficients are Vassiliev of given order, remains an active area of research with ongoing recent work (e.g., on V_1 and V_2 polynomials of long virtual knots, and Vassiliev invariants for knotoids and virtual knotoids).

original_question: Do there exist classical knots that are not slice in the ordinary classical sense but become slice either in Kauffman's notion of virtual-knot sliceness or in Turaev's notion of sliceness for knots in thickened surfaces, and if a knot in a thickened surface is slice in Turaev's sense, must it stabilize to a virtual knot that is slice in Kauffman's sense?
self_contained_problem:
Background and definitions.

(a) A classical knot is a smooth embedding $K\colon S^1\hookrightarrow S^3$, considered up to ambient isotopy. Such a knot is (smoothly) slice in the classical sense if it bounds a smoothly embedded disk in the 4-ball $B^4$.

(b) A virtual knot (in Kauffman's sense) is an equivalence class of Gauss diagrams, equivalently a knot in a thickened surface $\Sigma\times[0,1]$ modulo orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms of $\Sigma$ and stabilization/destabilization (adding or removing handles to $\Sigma$ disjoint from the knot). A virtual knot is slice in the sense of Kauffman if its representative bounds an immersed disk realizable by a sequence of births, saddles, deaths and virtual moves whose total Euler characteristic equals $1$, equivalently if it is concordant to the unknot in the virtual concordance category.

(c) For a closed oriented surface $\Sigma$, a knot $K\subset \Sigma\times[0,1]$ is slice in the sense of Turaev if there exists a compact oriented $3$-manifold $W$ with $\partial W=\Sigma$ and a smoothly (properly) embedded disk $D\hookrightarrow W\times[0,1]$ with $\partial D=K\subset \Sigma\times\{0\}\subset \partial(W\times[0,1])$.

Stabilization. Given $K\subset \Sigma\times[0,1]$, attaching a $1$-handle to $\Sigma$ disjoint from $K$ yields a knot in $\Sigma'\times[0,1]$; the equivalence class under all such stabilizations and destabilizations is the underlying virtual knot of $K$.

Questions. 
(1) Does there exist a classical knot $K\subset S^3$ that is not slice in the classical sense, but, when regarded as a virtual knot via the standard inclusion $S^2\hookrightarrow \Sigma$, is slice in the sense of Kauffman, or, when regarded as a knot in a thickened surface, is slice in the sense of Turaev?

(2) If a knot $K\subset \Sigma\times[0,1]$ is slice in the sense of Turaev, must its associated virtual knot (obtained by stabilization) be slice in the sense of Kauffman?
status_search_result: Question (1) has been resolved in the negative for Kauffman's notion of virtual sliceness: Boden and Nagel (2017, "Concordance group of virtual knots") proved that a classical knot is virtually slice in Kauffman's sense if and only if it is classically slice, so the classical concordance group injects into the virtual concordance group. The status of the Turaev variant of (1) and of question (2) (whether Turaev-sliceness in a fixed thickened surface implies Kauffman-sliceness after stabilization) does not appear to be conclusively settled in the searched literature.

original_question: For the virtual braid group V B_n, determine whether it is linear for all n greater than 3, whether the representation rho: V B_n -> Aut(F_{n+1}) described in the paper is faithful for all n greater than 2, and whether there exist non-equivalent virtual links whose braid closures become equivalent after applying the welded-braid representation rho_A.
self_contained_problem:
Let $VB_n$ denote the virtual braid group on $n$ strands, defined as the group with generators $\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_{n-1}$ (classical braid generators) and $\rho_1,\dots,\rho_{n-1}$ (virtual generators) subject to the relations:
- $\sigma_i\sigma_{i+1}\sigma_i = \sigma_{i+1}\sigma_i\sigma_{i+1}$ and $\sigma_i\sigma_j = \sigma_j\sigma_i$ for $|i-j|\ge 2$;
- $\rho_i^2 = 1$, $\rho_i\rho_{i+1}\rho_i = \rho_{i+1}\rho_i\rho_{i+1}$, $\rho_i\rho_j=\rho_j\rho_i$ for $|i-j|\ge 2$;
- $\sigma_i\rho_j=\rho_j\sigma_i$ for $|i-j|\ge 2$ and $\rho_i\rho_{i+1}\sigma_i = \sigma_{i+1}\rho_i\rho_{i+1}$.

Let $F_{n+1}$ be the free group of rank $n+1$ with basis $x_1,\dots,x_n,y$, and let $\rho:VB_n\to \operatorname{Aut}(F_{n+1})$ be the homomorphism given by
$$\sigma_i:\ x_i\mapsto x_ix_{i+1}x_i^{-1},\ x_{i+1}\mapsto x_i,\ x_k\mapsto x_k\ (k\ne i,i+1),\ y\mapsto y,$$
$$\rho_i:\ x_i\mapsto y x_{i+1} y^{-1},\ x_{i+1}\mapsto y^{-1} x_i y,\ x_k\mapsto x_k\ (k\ne i,i+1),\ y\mapsto y.$$

Let $WB_n$ denote the welded braid group, obtained from $VB_n$ by additionally imposing the mixed relation $\sigma_i\sigma_{i+1}\rho_i = \rho_{i+1}\sigma_i\sigma_{i+1}$, and let $\rho_A:VB_n\to WB_n$ be the natural projection. Virtual links are equivalence classes of closures of virtual braids modulo the virtual Reidemeister moves; welded links are obtained by additionally allowing the forbidden over-crossing move.

Settle the following:

(a) Is $VB_n$ a linear group (i.e., does it admit a faithful finite-dimensional representation over a field) for every $n>3$?

(b) Is the homomorphism $\rho:VB_n\to\operatorname{Aut}(F_{n+1})$ described above faithful for every $n>2$?

(c) Do there exist non-equivalent virtual links $L_v$ and $L'_v$, realized as closures of virtual braids $\beta,\beta'\in VB_n$, such that the welded links obtained as the closures of $\rho_A(\beta)$ and $\rho_A(\beta')$ in $WB_n$ are equivalent as welded links?
status_search_result: Recent literature (2021–2025) on virtual and welded braid groups continues to list the linearity of $VB_n$ for $n>3$ and the faithfulness of the standard representation $\rho:VB_n\to\operatorname{Aut}(F_{n+1})$ as open problems; partial linearity results exist only for certain quotients (e.g., crystallographic quotients $VB_n/VP_n'$). The question on distinguishing virtual from welded link equivalence via braid closures also remains unresolved in the literature surveyed.

context_brief: Prime decomposition of long virtual knots
original_question: Prove existence and uniqueness of prime decompositions for long virtual knots, and determine whether the concatenation of two non-classical prime long virtual knots can also be expressed through any essentially different decomposition into the same factors.
self_contained_problem:
A long virtual knot is an equivalence class of immersed oriented arcs in the plane, with finitely many double points each marked as either a classical crossing (with over/under information) or a virtual crossing, that coincide with a fixed horizontal line outside a compact region, taken modulo planar isotopy and the generalized Reidemeister moves of virtual knot theory. The set of long virtual knots forms a monoid under the concatenation operation #, in which two long virtual knots are joined end to end; the unit is the trivial long knot. A long virtual knot K is called prime if K is non-trivial and whenever K ≅ A # B, then either A or B is trivial. A long virtual knot is called classical if it admits a diagram with no virtual crossings, and non-classical otherwise.

(a) Prove that every non-trivial long virtual knot K admits a decomposition K ≅ P₁ # P₂ # ⋯ # Pₙ as a finite concatenation of prime long virtual knots.

(b) Prove that such a prime decomposition is unique in the following sense: if P₁ # ⋯ # Pₙ ≅ Q₁ # ⋯ # Qₘ where all Pᵢ and Qⱼ are prime long virtual knots, then n = m and Pᵢ ≅ Qᵢ for every i (note that # is not commutative on long virtual knots, so the order matters).

(c) Determine whether, when A and B are prime non-classical long virtual knots, the concatenation A # B can ever admit an essentially different decomposition into the same prime factors A and B (for instance A # B ≅ B # A or any other rearrangement realized in the monoid).
status_search_result: A uniqueness theorem for prime decompositions of long virtual knots in the non-classical regime was established by M. Chrisman (arXiv:1311.5748): if A, B, C, D are prime non-classical long virtual knots with A#B non-classical and A#B ≅ C#D, then A ≅ C and B ≅ D. The monoid of long virtual knots is known to be non-commutative. A complete existence-and-uniqueness theorem for prime decompositions of arbitrary long virtual knots (covering mixed classical/non-classical factors and arbitrary lengths) does not appear to have been fully established, so the problem is partially solved.

original_question: Extend the theory of virtual covers so that it applies effectively to classical knots in S^3, relate virtual-cover invariants to Milnor mu-invariants and possibly to one-component links, understand how virtual covers behave under local moves such as crossing changes, self-Delta moves, and Z-moves, determine whether virtual covers can detect mutations, and characterize exactly which moves on two-component links preserve the associated virtual-knot type.
self_contained_problem:
Background. Let L = K ∪ J be an oriented two-component link in S^3 with J a (possibly trivial) component such that the linking number lk(K, J) = 0. Choose a Seifert surface Σ for J, push it off to obtain a thickened surface neighborhood N(Σ) ≅ Σ × [−1, 1] disjoint from K, and let Σ_g be a closed orientable surface obtained by capping or stabilizing Σ. The "virtual cover" construction associates to (K, J) (together with a choice of Σ) a virtual knot v(K, J) ∈ Σ_g × I, well defined up to a controlled set of stabilizations and isotopies of Σ in S^3 \ K. This produces a map from a class of two-component classical links in S^3 to the set of virtual-knot types.

Problem. Develop and resolve the following items concerning the virtual-cover construction.

(a) Knot extension. Formulate an effective extension of the virtual-cover construction that takes as input a one-component link (i.e. a classical knot) K ⊂ S^3 and produces an associated virtual-knot invariant, in such a way that nontrivial classical information about K is detected.

(b) Relation to Milnor invariants. For an oriented link L = K ∪ J in S^3 with lk(K, J) = 0, exhibit an explicit relation between Milnor's μ-invariants μ_L(I) of L and invariants (e.g. polynomial, quandle, or concordance invariants) of the virtual knot v(K, J). In particular, identify which μ-invariants of L are recovered from v(K, J).

(c) Behavior under local moves. Determine how the virtual-knot type of v(K, J) changes when L is altered by each of the following local operations applied to the classical link L: (i) a single crossing change, (ii) a self-Δ-move on K, (iii) a Z-move. In each case, give a sharp description of the resulting change in v(K, J) (invariance, controlled stabilization, or specific virtual local move).

(d) Mutation. Decide whether the virtual-knot type v(K, J) can distinguish a link L = K ∪ J from any of its Conway mutants L'; equivalently, exhibit a pair (L, L') of mutant two-component classical links whose associated virtual knots are not virtually isotopic, or prove that no such pair exists.

(e) Complete move set. Find a finite list M_1, …, M_n of local moves on the class of two-component oriented links L = K ∪ J ⊂ S^3 with lk(K, J) = 0 such that, for two such links L and L', the associated virtual knots v(K, J) and v(K', J') are virtually isotopic if and only if L can be transformed into L' by a finite sequence of ambient isotopies and the moves M_1, …, M_n.

A complete solution consists of precise definitions making (a)–(e) well posed and proofs of the corresponding statements.

The behavior of virtual covers under crossing changes, self-Δ-moves and Z-moves, and the mutation-detection question, do not appear settled. The cluster of questions is therefore open, with partial progress on the Milnor-invariant side.

original_question: Let F be a distribution on R or R^d that is n-completely mixable, meaning there exist random variables X1, ..., Xn all having distribution F and satisfying X1 + ··· + Xn = nµ for some center µ. Must that center be unique? Equivalently, if µ and ν are distinct real numbers, is it impossible for the same distribution to belong to both M_n(µ) and M_n(ν)?
self_contained_problem:
For an integer $n\ge 2$ and a real number $\mu$, let $\mathcal{M}_n(\mu)$ denote the set of all probability distributions $F$ on $\mathbb{R}$ (respectively on $\mathbb{R}^d$, with $\mu\in\mathbb{R}^d$) for which there exist random variables $X_1,\dots,X_n$, each having distribution $F$, such that
$$X_1+X_2+\cdots+X_n = n\mu \quad \text{almost surely}.$$
A distribution $F$ is called $n$-completely mixable if $F\in\mathcal{M}_n(\mu)$ for some $\mu$, and any such $\mu$ is called a center of mixability of $F$.

Question: Is the center of mixability necessarily unique? Equivalently, prove or disprove that for every $n\ge 2$ and every pair of distinct real numbers (or vectors) $\mu\ne\nu$,
$$\mathcal{M}_n(\mu)\cap\mathcal{M}_n(\nu)=\varnothing.$$
status_search_result: A survey on open questions in complete mixability notes that uniqueness of the center holds whenever the distribution F has a finite first moment (in which case the center must equal the mean), but the question remains unresolved in general for distributions with infinite mean. No full resolution has been located.
