paper_title: Recent Progress and Open Problems in Algorithmic Convex Geometry
original_question: Which broader classes of distributions or geometric spaces admit efficient random-walk sampling algorithms? In particular, can one give a sufficient condition, phrased in terms of isoperimetry together with a suitable local regularity property of the target density, that guarantees efficient sampling, and can such a framework cover manifolds of nonnegative curvature?
self_contained_problem:
Let $(M,g)$ be a complete connected Riemannian manifold equipped with a probability density $f:M\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ (with respect to the Riemannian volume measure). For a Markov chain on $M$ with stationary distribution proportional to $f$, define the mixing time $\tau_{\mathrm{mix}}(\varepsilon)$ as the smallest $t$ such that the total variation distance between the distribution at step $t$ (from any starting point in a set of large measure) and the target is at most $\varepsilon$. Call a sampling algorithm "efficient" if $\tau_{\mathrm{mix}}(\varepsilon)$ is bounded by a polynomial in $\dim M$, $\log(1/\varepsilon)$, and natural geometric/analytic parameters of $(M,f)$.

Recall that $(M,f)$ satisfies an isoperimetric inequality with constant $\psi>0$ if for every measurable $S\subseteq M$,
$$\int_{\partial S} f \;\ge\; \psi\,\min\bigl(\mu_f(S),\,1-\mu_f(S)\bigr),$$
where $\mu_f$ is the probability measure with density $f$.

Problem. Identify a broad class of pairs $(M,f)$ that admit efficient random-walk sampling. Specifically:

(a) Formulate a sufficient condition, expressed as the conjunction of (i) an isoperimetric inequality for $\mu_f$ and (ii) a local regularity property of $f$ (for instance, a quantitative bound on how fast $f$ varies over balls of a controlled radius), under which there exists a Markov chain whose mixing time is polynomial in the dimension and the relevant parameters, and prove that this condition implies efficient sampling.

(b) Apply such a framework to Riemannian manifolds of nonnegative sectional (or Ricci) curvature, for which isoperimetric inequalities are known, and determine for which such manifolds $M$ and target densities $f$ an efficient sampling process can be defined.
status_search_result: Substantial progress has been made. Mangoubi–Smith (2018) proved rapid mixing of geodesic walks on manifolds with positive sectional curvature bounded above and below, with mixing time independent of dimension. Goyal–Shetty (2019) gave a polynomial-time random-walk-based sampling and optimization algorithm on convex sets in Riemannian manifolds of non-negative curvature. Recent work (e.g. Riemannian proximal samplers, 2025) further develops high-accuracy sampling on manifolds. A fully general sufficient condition combining isoperimetry with a local regularity property covering all such settings has not been definitively established, so the problem is partially solved rather than fully closed.

paper_title: Recent Progress and Open Problems in Algorithmic Convex Geometry
context_brief: Sampling lattice points in convex bodies
original_question: Can one sample lattice points in a convex body under substantially weaker geometric assumptions than the currently known large-inscribed-ball condition? For example, is efficient sampling possible for lattice points of a near-isotropic convex body, or for a body that contains at least half of a ball of radius O(sqrt(n))?
self_contained_problem:
Let $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ be a convex body specified by a membership oracle, and let $\mathbb{Z}^n$ denote the integer lattice. The "lattice point sampling problem" asks for a randomized algorithm that, given access to $K$, outputs a (nearly) uniformly random point of $K \cap \mathbb{Z}^n$ in time polynomial in $n$ and the relevant input parameters. Existing efficient algorithms require strong geometric assumptions, most notably that $K$ contains a ball of radius polynomial in $n$ (a large inscribed ball condition).

The problem is to determine whether efficient (random polynomial time) sampling of lattice points in $K$ is possible under substantially weaker geometric assumptions. In particular:

(a) Suppose $K$ is in near-isotropic position, meaning that, after translation to put its centroid at the origin, the covariance matrix $\mathbb{E}_{x \sim \mathrm{Unif}(K)}[x x^\top]$ has all eigenvalues within a constant factor of each other (equivalently, $K$ has been affinely transformed so that its inertia tensor is close to the identity). Is there an efficient algorithm to sample (almost) uniformly from $K \cap \mathbb{Z}^n$?

(b) More weakly, suppose that $K$ contains at least half of some Euclidean ball of radius $O(\sqrt{n})$ (i.e., there exists a ball $B$ of radius $c\sqrt{n}$ such that $\mathrm{vol}(K \cap B) \geq \tfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{vol}(B)$). Is efficient (almost) uniform sampling from $K \cap \mathbb{Z}^n$ possible under this assumption?
category_tag: Lattice point sampling in convex bodies
status_search_result: Web search did not return any specific result resolving the question of efficient lattice-point sampling in near-isotropic convex bodies or under the weaker "half a ball of radius O(√n)" condition. Known efficient grid-walk algorithms still rely on the assumption that $B_n \subseteq K$, and no relaxation under the proposed weaker assumptions could be confirmed. Status appears unresolved based on available evidence.

paper_title: Recent Progress and Open Problems in Algorithmic Convex Geometry
original_question: Is there a substantially faster random-walk-based optimization method for logconcave optimization whose analysis tracks direct progress toward the optimum, rather than relying on the intermediate task of producing nearly random samples from changing distributions?
self_contained_problem:
Let f : K → R_{>0} be a logconcave function on a convex body K ⊂ R^n given by a membership oracle, and suppose we wish to compute a point x ∈ K with f(x) ≥ (1−ε) max_{y∈K} f(y) (equivalently, to minimize a convex function on K). The known approaches based on random walks proceed indirectly: they generate (approximately) random samples from a sequence of slowly changing logconcave distributions (e.g. via simulated annealing on f^{β} as β increases), and their analyses bound the total cost by bounding the mixing time of each walk plus the warm-start distance between consecutive distributions. This yields oracle complexities of order n^{4.5} to n^{5} (up to polylogarithmic factors and dependence on ε and geometric parameters).

Question: Does there exist a random-walk-based optimization algorithm for logconcave functions whose oracle complexity is substantially smaller than the best sampling-based bounds, and whose correctness analysis directly tracks a progress measure toward the optimum (such as the gap f* − f(X_t), or a distance from X_t to argmax f) rather than passing through the intermediate step of bounding mixing to near-stationarity for a sequence of distributions?
status_search_result: A web search did not turn up a definitive resolution. The state of the art for random-walk-based logconcave optimization (hit-and-run / simulated annealing approaches by Lovász–Vempala and successors) still analyzes algorithms via sampling/mixing-time arguments, with complexities around O*(n^{4.5})–O*(n^5). No algorithm appears to be widely recognized as achieving a substantially faster bound through a direct optimization-progress analysis that bypasses the sampling step. The question is best classified as unknown / likely still open.

paper_title: Recent Progress and Open Problems in Algorithmic Convex Geometry
context_brief: Volume from random samples of a polytope
original_question: Can the volume of a polytope with a bounded number of facets be computed efficiently from a random sample drawn from the polytope, without using an annealing sequence of changing sampling distributions?
self_contained_problem:
Let $P \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ be a full-dimensional bounded polytope described as the intersection of $m$ closed half-spaces, where $m$ is bounded by a fixed polynomial in $n$ (so the number of facets is "small"). Suppose one is given as input the polytope $P$ together with $N$ independent samples drawn from the uniform distribution on $P$, where $N$ is polynomial in $n$.

Question: Does there exist a randomized algorithm that, for every $\varepsilon > 0$, runs in time polynomial in $n$, $m$, and $1/\varepsilon$, and outputs (with high probability) a $(1\pm\varepsilon)$-approximation of $\mathrm{vol}(P)$, using only such uniform samples from $P$ itself — that is, without constructing or sampling from an "annealing" sequence of auxiliary distributions (e.g., a sequence of progressively rescaled bodies, telescoping ratios of nested convex bodies, or cooling Gaussians/exponentials) whose densities or supports change over the course of the algorithm?

Equivalently: can the volume of a polytope with a polynomially bounded number of facets be approximated efficiently directly from uniform random samples on the polytope, bypassing the standard multiphase Monte Carlo (annealing) paradigm?
status_search_result: A web search did not return any result establishing a positive or negative resolution of whether the volume of a polytope with a bounded number of facets can be efficiently approximated from uniform random samples without an annealing sequence. Subsequent practical and theoretical work on volume computation (Sequence of Balls, Cooling Gaussians, Cooling Bodies, Billiard Walk, etc.) continues to rely on multiphase / annealing schemes, and no source clearly resolves the specific question.

paper_title: Recent Progress and Open Problems in Algorithmic Convex Geometry
context_brief: Learning a polytope with m facets
original_question: Let P be a polytope in R^n with m facets. Is there an algorithm with complexity polynomial in m, n, and 1/ε that learns P from either uniform random points sampled from P or from samples drawn from a Gaussian distribution restricted as described in the source?
self_contained_problem:
Let $n, m \geq 1$ and let $P \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ be an unknown convex polytope with at most $m$ facets (i.e., $P$ is a bounded intersection of at most $m$ closed halfspaces). A learning algorithm is given access to one of the following sample oracles:

(a) i.i.d. samples drawn from the uniform distribution on $P$, or
(b) i.i.d. samples drawn from the standard Gaussian distribution on $\mathbb{R}^n$ conditioned to lie in $P$ (the standard Gaussian measure restricted to $P$ and renormalized).

Given a tolerance parameter $\varepsilon \in (0,1)$, the algorithm must output, with probability at least $2/3$, a set $\hat{P} \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ such that $\mu(P \triangle \hat{P}) \leq \varepsilon$, where $\mu$ is the corresponding sampling distribution and $\triangle$ denotes symmetric difference.

Question: Does there exist such a learning algorithm whose running time and sample complexity are bounded by a polynomial in $m$, $n$, and $1/\varepsilon$?
status_search_result: Search results indicate that learning intersections of $k$ halfspaces under Gaussian distributions has been studied, with the best known algorithms (e.g., Vempala 2010, Klivans–O'Donnell–Servedio) having running times such as $\mathrm{poly}(n,1/\varepsilon,k) + n\cdot\min((k/\varepsilon)^k, k^{O(\log k/\varepsilon^4)})$, which are super-polynomial in the number of facets $m=k$. No fully $\mathrm{poly}(m,n,1/\varepsilon)$ algorithm is known for learning a polytope with $m$ facets from uniform or restricted-Gaussian samples, and the problem is still considered open.

paper_title: Open problems in microscopic theory of large-amplitude collective motion
original_question: When oblate and prolate Hartree-Fock-Bogoliubov shape minima coexist in the same nucleus without an exact discrete symmetry relating them, what are the correct collective degree or degrees of freedom that mediate the large-amplitude shape-mixing dynamics between those two configurations, and how can a microscopic theory identify and describe those coordinates?
self_contained_problem:
Consider an even-even atomic nucleus described in the mean-field framework of Hartree–Fock–Bogoliubov (HFB) theory. Suppose that the HFB energy surface, viewed as a function of the quadrupole deformation parameters (β, γ), possesses (at least) two distinct local minima: one corresponding to an oblate shape and one corresponding to a prolate shape, and that there is no exact discrete symmetry of the underlying Hamiltonian that maps one minimum onto the other (so the two minima are dynamically inequivalent and the standard one-dimensional reflection-symmetric tunneling picture does not apply).

The nucleus is expected to undergo large-amplitude collective shape-mixing dynamics between these two HFB minima. The task is to formulate and solve, on a fully microscopic basis (i.e. starting from a many-body nucleonic Hamiltonian without assuming a phenomenological collective Hamiltonian), the following:

1. Identify the correct collective degree(s) of freedom — i.e. a collective coordinate q (or a small set of collective coordinates) embedded in the high-dimensional HFB configuration manifold — along which the wave function must extend in order to mediate the mixing of the oblate and prolate configurations.

2. Provide a microscopic prescription that determines this collective subspace self-consistently from the many-body Hamiltonian (for example by selecting a decoupled collective submanifold of TDHFB phase space), and derive the associated collective Hamiltonian, including its kinetic (inertia) and potential parts, governing the large-amplitude shape-mixing motion between the two minima.

3. Demonstrate how the resulting theory yields the low-lying spectrum and shape-mixing wave functions in the (β, γ) plane for nuclei exhibiting such oblate–prolate coexistence without exact symmetry.
status_search_result: The question has been substantially addressed via the Adiabatic Self-Consistent Collective Coordinate (ASCC) method, which microscopically extracts a one-dimensional collective path connecting oblate and prolate HFB minima and derives a five-dimensional quadrupole collective Hamiltonian; applications to proton-rich Se isotopes (e.g., 68,70,72Se) reproduce coexisting rotational bands. Related approaches use local QRPA-derived inertial functions and analyses of the Er-Pt region. However, a fully general microscopic identification of the relevant collective coordinates in arbitrary asymmetric oblate-prolate coexistence cases (especially beyond quadrupole degrees of freedom and including pairing dynamics consistently) remains an active topic, so the broader problem is only partially solved.

paper_title: Open problems in microscopic theory of large-amplitude collective motion
original_question: For the unusually low first excited 0+ states observed in nuclei such as 72Ge, what is the correct microscopic interpretation of those states, and how should one reconcile or distinguish the boson-expansion picture based on coupling between quadrupole anharmonic vibration and neutron pairing vibration from the phenomenological shape-coexistence interpretation?
self_contained_problem:
In certain even-even nuclei, notably $^{72}$Ge, the first excited $0^+$ state lies at an unusually low excitation energy compared with neighboring isotopes. Two microscopic/phenomenological pictures have been proposed for such states:

(a) A boson-expansion description in which the low-lying $0^+$ state arises from the coupling between an anharmonic quadrupole vibrational mode and a neutron pairing vibrational mode built on the correlated ground state.

(b) A phenomenological shape-coexistence description, in which the state is interpreted as the band-head of a configuration with a different intrinsic deformation (e.g., a spherical/oblate state coexisting with a prolate or triaxial ground-state configuration), often modeled via two-state or multi-state configuration mixing.

Provide a microscopic interpretation of the anomalously low first excited $0^+$ state in $^{72}$Ge (and analogous nuclei) that determines:

1. Which collective and single-particle degrees of freedom dominate its wave function.
2. The precise relationship between interpretation (a) and interpretation (b): in particular, whether they correspond to equivalent descriptions in different bases, complementary aspects of the same underlying many-body state, or genuinely distinct physical scenarios that can be distinguished by observables (e.g., $E2$ and $E0$ matrix elements, monopole transition strengths $\rho^2(E0)$, two-neutron transfer cross sections, Kumar–Cline shape invariants, $g$ factors).
3. Quantitative criteria, expressible in terms of measurable nuclear-structure observables, that allow one to discriminate between the quadrupole-anharmonic-vibration $\otimes$ neutron-pairing-vibration coupling scenario and the shape-coexistence-with-configuration-mixing scenario.

However, a definitive reconciliation between the boson-expansion (anharmonic-quadrupole-vibration coupled to neutron-pairing-vibration) interpretation and the phenomenological shape-coexistence interpretation has not been established, and the microscopic nature of the state continues to be debated. The problem therefore appears to remain open, with partial progress.

paper_title: Open problems in microscopic theory of large-amplitude collective motion
original_question: What microscopic mechanism produces the oblate-prolate asymmetry in nuclear structure, meaning the empirical tendency for prolate shapes to be energetically favored over oblate shapes in many nuclei, especially in gamma-soft situations where large-amplitude shape mixing can easily wash out separate rotational-band identities?
self_contained_problem:
In the context of nuclear structure theory, the equilibrium quadrupole deformation of an even–even atomic nucleus can be characterized by the sign of the axial deformation parameter β₂ (or equivalently by the Hill–Wheeler angle γ): β₂>0 (γ=0°) corresponds to a prolate (cigar-shaped) intrinsic shape, while β₂<0 (γ=60°) corresponds to an oblate (pancake-shaped) intrinsic shape. Empirically, among deformed even–even nuclei across the nuclear chart, prolate ground-state shapes occur far more frequently than oblate ones, and this asymmetry persists even in γ-soft regions where large-amplitude collective shape mixing tends to blur the distinction between rotational bands built on different intrinsic shapes.

Identify, from a microscopic many-body standpoint starting from realistic nucleon–nucleon (and possibly three-nucleon) interactions or from a self-consistent mean-field plus beyond-mean-field treatment that includes large-amplitude collective dynamics, the mechanism responsible for this prolate-over-oblate energetic preference. Specifically, derive in a controlled microscopic framework the dependence of the prolate/oblate ground-state energy difference on (i) the spin–orbit and orbit–orbit terms of the effective single-particle potential, (ii) the surface diffuseness of the mean field, (iii) pairing correlations, and (iv) shape-mixing fluctuations associated with γ-soft potential energy surfaces, and explain quantitatively why prolate shapes are systematically favored.
status_search_result: Several partial microscopic explanations have been proposed and quantitatively explored. Nilsson–Strutinsky studies (Takahara–Tajima–Onishi, Phys. Rev. C 64, 037301) attribute prolate dominance to interference between the spin–orbit and l² terms together with surface diffuseness. Bonatsos et al. (Eur. Phys. J. A, 2017, arXiv:1707.03763) derive prolate-over-oblate dominance from SU(3) symmetry combined with the Pauli principle. A 2023 deformed relativistic Hartree–Bogoliubov-in-continuum study (Phys. Rev. C 108, 014319) reproduces the empirical pattern from microscopic single-particle spectra. However, no single fully ab-initio derivation explains the asymmetry across all mass regions, and especially in γ-soft nuclei the question of why prolate still wins remains under active investigation. The problem is therefore best classified as partially solved.

paper_title: Open problems in microscopic theory of large-amplitude collective motion
original_question: In the generator coordinate method for quadrupole collective phenomena, how reliable are the collective masses or inertia functions computed using real generator coordinates, and how should one choose or determine the generator coordinates so that the resulting collective description captures both the coordinates and the momenta needed for correct large-amplitude dynamics?
self_contained_problem:
Setup. Let $|\Phi(q)angle$ be a family of normalized many-body Slater-determinant (or HFB) states on a fermionic Fock space, parametrized smoothly by a finite set of real generator coordinates $q=(q_1,\dots,q_n)\in\mathbb{R}^n$. The generator coordinate method (GCM) defines collective wave functions through the Hill–Wheeler ansatz
$$|\Psiangle=\int f(q)\,|\Phi(q)angle\,dq,$$
whose weight $f(q)$ is determined by the Hill–Wheeler equation
$$\int igl[\mathcal{H}(q,q')-E\,\mathcal{N}(q,q') igr]f(q')\,dq'=0,$$
with kernels $\mathcal{N}(q,q')=\langle\Phi(q)|\Phi(q')angle$ and $\mathcal{H}(q,q')=\langle\Phi(q)|\hat H|\Phi(q')angle$. After a Gaussian-overlap (or equivalent local) approximation, one extracts a collective Hamiltonian of the form
$$H_{m coll}=	frac{1}{2}\sum_{ij}B^{ij}(q)\,p_i p_j+V(q),$$
where $B^{ij}(q)$ is the inverse collective inertia (mass) tensor and $V(q)$ the collective potential.

Problem. Restricting attention to quadrupole collective phenomena (i.e. generator coordinates associated with quadrupole shape degrees of freedom):
(a) Determine quantitatively the reliability of the collective masses/inertia functions $B^{ij}(q)$ obtained from purely real generator coordinates $q$, by comparing them with the exact inertia tensor that would correctly reproduce large-amplitude collective dynamics; in particular, characterize the systematic errors introduced by omitting momentum-like (conjugate) generator coordinates.
(b) Provide a constructive prescription for selecting or self-consistently determining the generator coordinates $q$ (and any conjugate variables) so that the resulting collective subspace $\{|\Phi(q)angle\}$ simultaneously captures the relevant collective coordinates and their conjugate momenta, yielding a collective Hamiltonian $H_{m coll}$ whose dynamics agrees with the exact large-amplitude time-dependent mean-field evolution within a controlled approximation.
status_search_result: The reliability of GCM collective inertias computed with real generator coordinates and the optimal choice of generator coordinates are widely acknowledged long-standing open problems in nuclear large-amplitude collective dynamics. Recent literature (e.g. extensions involving complex/time-odd generator coordinates, the adiabatic self-consistent collective coordinate method, and ongoing work on GCM with momentum-like coordinates) continues to address but has not definitively resolved either issue.

paper_title: Open problems in microscopic theory of large-amplitude collective motion
context_brief: Time-odd mean-field contributions to collective mass
original_question: How large are the contributions of time-odd mean-field components induced by the time evolution of the mean field to the collective mass in large-amplitude collective motion, and how can those effects be evaluated reliably within modern nuclear energy density functionals rather than being omitted as they are in the usual cranking mass?
self_contained_problem:
In the microscopic theory of large-amplitude collective motion of atomic nuclei, consider a self-consistent mean-field description (e.g., time-dependent Hartree–Fock or Hartree–Fock–Bogoliubov dynamics) derived from a nuclear energy density functional. As the mean field evolves with a collective coordinate q, time-odd components of the one-body density and of the associated mean-field potential (terms odd under time reversal, such as those coupling to spin, current, and spin-current densities) are induced; these terms are required for Galilean invariance and are absent from the standard Inglis–Belyaev cranking formula for the collective mass.

Let M_cr(q) denote the cranking collective mass (computed without the time-odd response of the mean field) and let M_full(q) denote the collective mass obtained from a fully self-consistent adiabatic treatment that includes the dynamically induced time-odd mean-field components (for instance via the adiabatic self-consistent collective coordinate method or adiabatic time-dependent HFB).

Provide the following:
(a) A quantitative estimate, within a modern nuclear energy density functional (e.g., a Skyrme or covariant density functional with pairing), of the magnitude of the contribution ΔM(q) := M_full(q) − M_cr(q) arising from the time-odd mean-field components, for representative collective modes (low-lying quadrupole vibrations, large-amplitude shape coexistence, fission, and rotational moments of inertia).
(b) A reliable, practical computational scheme to evaluate ΔM(q) consistently within the chosen energy density functional, including all time-odd coupling constants (spin, spin-current, current, and pairing time-odd channels) without ad hoc omission, and an analysis of how M_full(q) depends on those coupling constants.
category_tag: Nuclear collective mass and time-odd mean fields
status_search_result: Subsequent work has demonstrated, in specific settings, that time-odd mean-field components substantially enhance collective masses and moments of inertia relative to the Inglis–Belyaev cranking formula (e.g., ATDHFB and ASCC computations show sizable quadrupole-pairing time-odd contributions, and recent 2025 work on rare-earth moments of inertia within exact adiabatic theory). However, a comprehensive, systematic evaluation across modern energy density functionals and across all relevant collective modes is still ongoing, so the problem is best classified as partially solved.

paper_title: Open problems in microscopic theory of large-amplitude collective motion
original_question: What microscopic mechanism determines the collective mass along a large-amplitude collective path, in particular how do pairing correlations, repeated level crossings near the Fermi surface, nucleon-pair hopping, and smooth changes of single-particle wave functions combine to set the inertia against changing the collective coordinate?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a self-bound finite many-fermion system (a nucleus) described by a microscopic Hamiltonian acting on a Hilbert space of A nucleons with two-body interactions including a pairing channel. Suppose one parametrizes a one-dimensional manifold of time-even Slater determinants (or generalized HFB quasiparticle vacua) {|Φ(q)⟩ : q ∈ ℝ}, called a large-amplitude collective path, together with a conjugate momentum direction giving a collective coordinate q and momentum p. Within an adiabatic self-consistent collective coordinate framework, the collective Hamiltonian takes the form H_coll(q,p) = (1/2) M(q) p^2 + V(q), where M(q) is the collective inertia (mass) along the path.

Problem. Determine, from first principles, the microscopic mechanism that fixes the collective mass M(q) along such a path. In particular, give a quantitative decomposition of M(q) into contributions arising from
(i) pairing correlations among nucleons near the Fermi surface,
(ii) repeated single-particle level crossings near the Fermi surface as q varies,
(iii) nucleon-pair hopping between single-particle orbitals across these crossings, and
(iv) the smooth q-dependence of the single-particle wave functions defining the mean field,
and explain how these four mechanisms combine to determine the inertia against changing q. The answer should produce a closed microscopic expression for M(q) in which each of (i)–(iv) appears as an identifiable term, and should reduce, in suitable limits, to known approximations such as the Inglis–Belyaev cranking mass and the adiabatic self-consistent collective coordinate (ASCC) mass.
status_search_result: The microscopic determination of the collective mass for large-amplitude collective motion remains an actively studied open problem in nuclear many-body theory. Approximate frameworks (Inglis–Belyaev cranking, ATDHFB, ASCC, generator-coordinate-method with Gaussian overlap approximation) give partial answers, and recent works show that pairing fluctuations and level-crossing dynamics substantially enhance the inertia, but no complete first-principles decomposition has been established.

paper_title: Open problems in microscopic theory of large-amplitude collective motion
original_question: How can one microscopically derive the full five-dimensional Bohr-Mottelson quadrupole collective Hamiltonian by extending a one-dimensional collective path to a two-dimensional collective hypersurface that can be mapped onto the beta-gamma plane, while also evaluating rotational moments of inertia at non-equilibrium points in a fully self-consistent way?
self_contained_problem:
Let a nucleus be described in the time-dependent Hartree-Fock-Bogoliubov (TDHFB) framework, in which the self-consistent mean-field state |φ(t)⟩ evolves on the TDHFB phase-space manifold. A standard goal of nuclear large-amplitude collective motion theory is to derive, microscopically and self-consistently, the five-dimensional (5D) quadrupole collective Hamiltonian of Bohr and Mottelson,

  H_coll = T_vib(β,γ) + T_rot(β,γ,ω) + V(β,γ),

where (β,γ) are the intrinsic quadrupole deformation parameters, ω = (ω_1, ω_2, ω_3) are the angular velocities about the body-fixed principal axes, T_vib is a quadratic form in (β̇, γ̇) with three vibrational mass parameters, T_rot = (1/2) Σ_k J_k(β,γ) ω_k^2 with three rotational moments of inertia J_k(β,γ), and V(β,γ) is the collective potential.

Formulate and solve the following problem:

(a) Starting from a microscopic many-body Hamiltonian and the TDHFB equations, construct an extension of a one-dimensional collective reaction path |φ(q)⟩ to a two-dimensional collective hypersurface {|φ(q_1, q_2)⟩} embedded in the TDHFB manifold, determined self-consistently by a local-harmonic (e.g., local QRPA) condition, such that the surface admits a smooth diffeomorphism onto the (β,γ) plane.

(b) Derive, on this 2D hypersurface, the three vibrational mass parameters and the collective potential V(β,γ) entering H_coll, together with the three rotational moments of inertia J_k(β,γ) evaluated at every (non-equilibrium) point of the surface in a fully self-consistent way (i.e., respecting the local mean-field and pairing self-consistency, beyond Inglis-type or constrained cranking prescriptions evaluated only at the equilibrium shape).

(c) Show that the resulting 5D collective Schrödinger equation reproduces large-amplitude quadrupole shape dynamics such as shape coexistence and shape-mixing phenomena.

The problem is to give such a microscopic derivation that produces all seven functions {three vibrational masses, three rotational moments of inertia, V(β,γ)} of the 5D Bohr-Mottelson Hamiltonian self-consistently from the underlying nucleonic Hamiltonian.
status_search_result: Substantial progress has been reported. Subsequent work by Matsuyanagi and collaborators (Physica Scripta 91 (2016) 063014, arXiv:1606.08547) develops a local QRPA method on a 2D collective hypersurface mapped to (β,γ), yielding the 5D Bohr-Mottelson Hamiltonian with self-consistent vibrational masses, moments of inertia, and potential, and applies it to quadrupole shape coexistence. However, a fully self-consistent microscopic derivation valid in general (including realistic interactions and full pairing self-consistency at all non-equilibrium points) remains an active research program rather than a closed problem.

paper_title: Open problems in microscopic theory of large-amplitude collective motion
original_question: How can a microscopic theory of large-amplitude collective motion be extended to high-spin states so that it self-consistently includes the variation of intrinsic structure caused by rapid rotation, rather than remaining limited to low-spin states where those rotationally induced intrinsic changes can be neglected?
self_contained_problem:
In the microscopic theory of nuclear large-amplitude collective motion (LACM), one starts from a many-nucleon Hamiltonian and seeks a low-dimensional collective subspace, typically constructed via the adiabatic self-consistent collective coordinate (ASCC) method or related time-dependent mean-field schemes, in which slow shape-coordinate dynamics is decoupled from fast intrinsic excitations on top of a mean-field (Hartree–Fock–Bogoliubov) reference. Existing formulations are derived under the assumption that the intrinsic mean-field configuration does not change appreciably with rotation, restricting their applicability to low-spin states.

Formulate a microscopic theory of LACM that is valid at high angular momentum, with the following requirements:

(i) The theory should be defined on top of a rotating mean-field reference such as the cranked or tilted-axis cranked HFB state, parametrized by one or more rotational frequency vectors ω.

(ii) Collective coordinates {q^α(t)} and their conjugate momenta should be introduced through a moving-frame self-consistent decoupling condition that determines, jointly and self-consistently, both the collective subspace and the variation of the intrinsic HFB structure (single-particle alignments, pairing correlations, deformation, etc.) induced by rapid rotation.

(iii) The resulting collective Hamiltonian should reduce, in the small-amplitude limit, to the quasiparticle random-phase approximation built on the rotating mean field, and, in the limit ω → 0, to the standard ASCC theory for low-spin LACM.

(iv) The construction should be invariant (or transform covariantly) under the choice of rotating frame and should preserve, at the appropriate level, the constraints associated with angular momentum and particle number.

The problem is to construct such a theory, derive its basic equations (moving-frame LACM equations together with the cranked HFB equations and self-consistency conditions), and demonstrate its consistency in the two limiting cases above.
status_search_result: A literature search returns established components (cranked/tilted-axis cranked HFB, self-consistent cranking, ASCC at low spin, QRPA on rotating mean fields, microscopic analyses of wobbling) but no unified microscopic LACM theory at high spin that self-consistently incorporates rotation-induced variation of intrinsic structure. The problem appears to remain an outstanding challenge.

paper_title: Open problems in microscopic theory of large-amplitude collective motion
original_question: How can large-amplitude collective-motion calculations be made systematic with improved nuclear energy density functionals while also developing numerical algorithms efficient enough to solve the moving-frame HFB and moving-frame QRPA equations iteratively along one-dimensional collective paths and especially over two-dimensional collective hypersurfaces?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the microscopic theory of large-amplitude collective motion (LACM) in self-bound many-fermion systems described by a nuclear energy density functional (EDF). In this framework the quasi-stationary mean field is determined by Hartree–Fock–Bogoliubov (HFB) theory, and small fluctuations around it are described by the quasiparticle random-phase approximation (QRPA). The adiabatic self-consistent collective coordinate (ASCC) / constrained-HFB-plus-local-QRPA approach generalizes these to a collective subspace by introducing, along a collective path parametrized by coordinates q=(q^1,…,q^d), the moving-frame HFB equation
   δ⟨φ(q)| Ĥ − Σ_i λ_i(q) N̂_i − Σ_a μ_a(q) Q̂_a(q) |φ(q)⟩ = 0,
together with the moving-frame QRPA (local harmonic) equations that determine the infinitesimal generators P̂_a(q), Q̂_a(q) and the collective inertia tensor M_{ab}(q) and collective potential V(q) on the d-dimensional collective hypersurface.

Formulate and address the following two-part problem:

(a) Construct a systematic procedure by which LACM calculations in this moving-frame HFB + moving-frame QRPA formalism can be carried out using improved nuclear EDFs (beyond standard Skyrme- or Gogny-type functionals), in such a way that the chosen functional, the treatment of pairing, and the truncation of the quasiparticle space yield convergent, well-defined collective Hamiltonians H_coll(q,p) = (1/2)Σ M^{ab}(q) p_a p_b + V(q).

(b) Develop numerical algorithms that solve the coupled moving-frame HFB and moving-frame QRPA equations iteratively at every point of the collective manifold, and that remain computationally tractable not only along a one-dimensional collective path (d=1) but also over a two-dimensional collective hypersurface (d=2), producing the inertia tensor M_{ab}(q), the potential V(q), and the associated collective wave functions for low-lying excited states of medium-heavy and heavy nuclei.
category_tag: large-amplitude collective motion in nuclear DFT
status_search_result: No web evidence indicates this two-fold program has been fully resolved. Recent work has implemented ASCC / multi-dimensional QRPA-based collective Hamiltonians in 1D and progressed toward 2D collective surfaces with Skyrme and covariant EDFs, but a systematic, EDF-improved framework with scalable iterative moving-frame HFB+QRPA solvers over 2D hypersurfaces remains an active research direction rather than a settled result.

paper_title: Open problems in microscopic theory of large-amplitude collective motion
original_question: What non-perturbative microscopic framework can describe large-amplitude collective motion in odd-A nuclei, or more generally in systems with several quasiparticles present, while treating the interplay between single-particle motion and collective motion in a unified way rather than starting from a small-amplitude particle-vibration-coupling approximation?
status_search_result: A non-perturbative microscopic framework for LACM in odd-A nuclei (and configurations with several blocked quasiparticles) that unifies single-particle and collective motion beyond particle–vibration coupling has not been established. Existing ASCC/TDHFB-based LACM theories are formulated for even-even systems; recent generator-coordinate and beyond-mean-field extensions to odd-mass nuclei (e.g., projected GCM with self-consistently blocked one-quasiparticle HFB states) address related aspects but do not provide a fully non-perturbative LACM treatment with self-consistent collective submanifolds in the presence of multiple quasiparticles. The problem appears to remain open.

paper_title: Open problems in microscopic theory of large-amplitude collective motion
original_question: How should one build a microscopic theory of large-amplitude collective motion at finite temperature, and what microscopic mechanisms govern damping and dissipation of those motions as one moves from yrast states toward the compound-nucleus regime?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a many-fermion quantum system (e.g. an atomic nucleus) described by a microscopic Hamiltonian H acting on a fermionic Fock space. At zero temperature, large-amplitude collective motion (LACM) can be formulated by selecting, within the time-dependent Hartree–Fock(–Bogoliubov) manifold of generalized Slater determinants, a low-dimensional collective submanifold M parametrized by collective coordinates q = (q^1, …, q^n) and conjugate momenta p, on which the dynamics is approximately self-consistent (e.g. via the adiabatic self-consistent collective coordinate method or the constrained HFB + local QRPA approach). The collective Hamiltonian H_coll(q,p) is then derived from H by requiring decoupling of collective and non-collective modes.

Develop an analogous microscopic theory at finite temperature T > 0. Concretely:

(a) Replace pure Slater determinants by thermal (mixed) states ρ(q,p;T) — for instance generalized thermal HFB density operators — and define a finite-temperature collective submanifold M_T in the space of such density operators that is invariant (to a controlled approximation) under the Liouville–von Neumann evolution iℏ∂_t ρ = [H, ρ]. Provide a self-consistent variational principle that determines M_T and the collective coordinates (q,p) as functions of T, reducing to the zero-temperature theory as T → 0.

(b) From this construction, derive a transport equation for the collective variables of the form
   M_{ij}(q,T) q̈^j + Γ_{ij}(q,T) q̇^j + ∂V(q,T)/∂q^i = ξ_i(t),
identifying microscopically the collective inertia M_{ij}, the friction (dissipation) tensor Γ_{ij}, the collective potential V, and the random force ξ_i, together with a fluctuation–dissipation relation linking Γ and the covariance of ξ.

(c) Identify and quantify the microscopic mechanisms responsible for the damping of collective motion — couplings of the collective degrees of freedom to non-collective one-particle–one-hole, two-particle–two-hole, …, and to thermally excited quasiparticles — and describe how the dominant mechanism evolves as the excitation energy increases from yrast (cold, near-ground) configurations toward the compound-nucleus regime (high level density, statistical equilibrium).

A complete solution consists of: (i) a mathematically well-posed definition of M_T and the finite-T collective Hamiltonian; (ii) explicit microscopic formulas for M_{ij}, Γ_{ij}, V, with proof of the appropriate fluctuation–dissipation relation; and (iii) a classification of damping mechanisms with quantitative criteria for their relative importance as a function of temperature.
status_search_result: The problem is posed as a long-term, largely unexplored research program: constructing a microscopic finite-temperature theory of large-amplitude collective motion and identifying the microscopic mechanisms of damping/dissipation between yrast and compound-nucleus regimes. While various partial approaches exist (finite-temperature HFB, linear response, dissipative TDHF, Kramers-type modeling of fission), no comprehensive, generally accepted microscopic theory has been established, so the problem is considered open.

paper_title: Open problems in microscopic theory of large-amplitude collective motion
context_brief: Competing decay paths for high-K isomers
original_question: For tunneling decay from high-K to low-K isomers, which decay path dominates: the path through large-amplitude collective motion in the triaxial shape degree of freedom or the path through motion in the orientation degree of freedom of the angular-momentum vector relative to the principal axes of the body-fixed frame?
self_contained_problem:
In the microscopic theory of large-amplitude collective motion (LACM) in atomic nuclei, consider the tunneling decay of a high-K isomeric state to states of lower K, where K denotes the projection of the total angular momentum on the body-fixed symmetry axis of a deformed nucleus. Two competing collective decay pathways have been proposed:

(i) a path that proceeds through large-amplitude collective motion in the triaxial shape degree of freedom (i.e., tunneling through the γ degree of freedom of the nuclear shape, via shapes departing from axial symmetry);

(ii) a path that proceeds through large-amplitude collective motion in the orientation degree of freedom of the angular-momentum vector with respect to the principal axes of the body-fixed frame (i.e., reorientation of the angular momentum at fixed intrinsic shape, associated with K-mixing).

Determine which of these two pathways dominates the tunneling decay rate from a high-K isomer to low-K states. More precisely, identify the conditions (in terms of nuclear deformation parameters, the softness of the potential energy surface in γ, the height and shape of the relevant collective barriers, and the angular momentum) under which one pathway dominates over the other, and provide a microscopic, self-consistent description of the dominant collective tunneling mode and the associated decay rate.
status_search_result: Recent literature (e.g., reviews on K isomers in deformed nuclei and superfluid tunneling models, 2018–2024) continues to discuss both competing mechanisms — tunneling in the triaxial (γ) shape degree of freedom and reorientation/Coriolis K-mixing — as candidate pathways for high-K isomer decay, without a definitive microscopic resolution of which dominates in general. The question of identifying the dominant LACM path therefore appears to remain open.

paper_title: Open problems in microscopic theory of large-amplitude collective motion
original_question: What happens when the amplitude of the wobbling mode in a rapidly rotating nucleus grows beyond the small-amplitude regime and the uniformly rotating nucleus becomes unstable with respect to that collective rotational degree of freedom, and how can microscopic large-amplitude collective-motion theory be applied to that regime as well as to chiral vibrations connecting right-handed and left-handed triaxial configurations?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a rapidly rotating atomic nucleus with a triaxial shape, modeled microscopically (e.g., by a cranked mean-field plus quasiparticle description). In the small-amplitude limit, fluctuations of the angular-momentum vector around the uniformly rotating axis give rise to the wobbling mode, a collective rotational excitation describable within the random-phase approximation built on the cranked mean field. Two regimes lie outside this small-amplitude treatment:

(a) Large-amplitude wobbling. Suppose the amplitude of the wobbling mode grows so large that linear-response (small-amplitude) theory ceases to be valid, and the uniformly rotating mean-field state becomes unstable with respect to this collective rotational degree of freedom.

(b) Chiral vibrations. In a triaxially deformed rotating nucleus, the angular-momentum vector may tunnel between two configurations of opposite handedness (left-handed and right-handed orientations of the angular-momentum vector relative to the three principal axes), producing a collective vibrational mode that connects these two chiral configurations.

Develop a microscopic large-amplitude collective-motion (LACM) theory — that is, a theory of self-consistent collective coordinates and momenta extracted from the time-dependent mean-field (TDHF/TDHFB) dynamics in the rotating frame, valid beyond the harmonic/RPA regime — and apply it to:

1. Describe the dynamics of the wobbling degree of freedom beyond the small-amplitude regime, including the fate of the uniformly rotating state once it becomes unstable against large-amplitude wobbling.
2. Describe chiral vibrations as large-amplitude collective motion connecting the left- and right-handed triaxial rotating configurations.

Provide a microscopic determination of the relevant collective coordinate(s), the corresponding collective potential and inertia, and the resulting spectra and transition properties for both phenomena.
status_search_result: Substantial progress has been made since the problem was posed: microscopic angular-momentum-projection calculations from cranked triaxial mean fields now describe wobbling and chiral bands (e.g., 2018 microscopic study of wobbling motion, and 2024 reports of "chiral wobbling" in triaxial nuclei). However, a fully microscopic large-amplitude collective-motion treatment of the unstable/large-amplitude wobbling regime and of chiral vibrations as nonlinear LACM remains incomplete; recent work continues to refine these approaches rather than closing the problem.

paper_title: Realistic shell-model calculations: current status and open problems
context_brief: Three-body forces in shell-model effective interactions
original_question: How should realistic shell-model effective interactions for medium- and heavy-mass nuclei be extended to include the contribution of three-body forces, given that most current shell-model calculations derive the effective interaction from two-body low-momentum nucleon-nucleon interactions alone even though calculations for systems with more than two nucleons depend on omitted induced and genuine many-body components?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the nuclear shell model in which an effective Hamiltonian acts in a truncated valence model space and is derived from an underlying microscopic nucleon-nucleon (NN) interaction (for example, a low-momentum NN potential obtained by renormalization-group decimation of a realistic high-precision NN force). The standard derivation (e.g., via the Q-box folded-diagram expansion or many-body perturbation theory in the valence space) produces a two-body effective interaction V_eff that, when applied to A>2 valence nucleons, omits two distinct kinds of many-body contributions:

(i) "induced" three- and higher-body forces in the valence space generated by the medium and by the projection onto the model space (i.e., effective many-body operators that arise from the NN interaction even when the underlying free-space Hamiltonian contains only two-body terms), and

(ii) "genuine" three-nucleon forces (3NFs) present in the underlying free-space Hamiltonian (for instance, the chiral N2LO 3NF), together with the effective valence-space operators they induce.

Problem. Develop a systematic and tractable framework for constructing realistic shell-model effective Hamiltonians for medium- and heavy-mass nuclei that consistently incorporates both induced and genuine three-body (and, where relevant, higher-body) contributions. Specifically:

(a) Give a perturbative or non-perturbative procedure (analogous to the folded-diagram / Q-box expansion for the two-body case) that produces an effective three-body interaction in the chosen valence space starting from a given NN + 3N free-space Hamiltonian, and prove or numerically demonstrate its convergence.

(b) Quantify, for representative medium-mass and heavy-mass isotopic chains, the size and structure (monopole, multipole, isospin dependence) of the induced and genuine three-body contributions to V_eff, and determine to what extent shell evolution, single-particle energies, spin-orbit splittings, drip-line locations, and spectra computed from the resulting Hamiltonian agree with experiment and with ab initio benchmarks.

(c) Identify under what conditions the three-body effective interaction can be accurately replaced by a density-dependent (normal-ordered two-body) approximation, and bound the error of such a reduction.

status_search_result: Substantial progress has been made since the question was posed. Three-body forces have been included in shell-model effective interactions for p-shell and sd-shell nuclei using chiral N2LO 3NFs and Q-box/folded-diagram techniques (e.g., Phys. Rev. C 98, 044305 (2018); Prog. Part. Nucl. Phys. review (2023)). Valence-space in-medium SRG and coupled-cluster methods now include 3NFs (often via normal-ordered two-body approximation) for nuclei up to mass A~100 and recently A~208. However, fully consistent inclusion of both induced and genuine three-body components in shell-model effective interactions for general medium- and heavy-mass nuclei, beyond the normal-ordered two-body approximation, remains an active area of research and is not fully solved.

paper_title: Realistic shell-model calculations: current status and open problems
original_question: For low-momentum shell-model effective interactions derived from phase-shift equivalent nucleon-nucleon potentials, how sensitive are the resulting shell-model observables to moderate variations of the cutoff momentum Λ, and how should that cutoff dependence be characterized or controlled?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the framework of low-momentum nucleon-nucleon interactions $V_{\mathrm{low}\text{-}k}$ obtained by integrating out high-momentum modes (above a sharp or smooth cutoff $\Lambda$) of a realistic, phase-shift equivalent two-nucleon potential $V_{NN}$, so that all $V_{\mathrm{low}\text{-}k}(\Lambda)$ reproduce the same on-shell two-nucleon data and the deuteron binding energy below $\Lambda$. Let $V_{\mathrm{eff}}(\Lambda)$ denote the shell-model effective interaction in a chosen valence space, derived from $V_{\mathrm{low}\text{-}k}(\Lambda)$ via a many-body perturbation expansion of the $\hat{Q}$-box (e.g., the Kuo–Lee–Ratcliffe folded-diagram series), and let $\mathcal{O}(\Lambda)$ stand for resulting shell-model observables (binding energies relative to a closed core, low-lying excitation spectra, electromagnetic transition matrix elements, etc.) computed by diagonalizing $V_{\mathrm{eff}}(\Lambda)$ in the valence space.

(a) Quantify, as a function of $\Lambda$ varied over a physically reasonable window (e.g., $\Lambda \in [1.8, 3.0]\ \mathrm{fm}^{-1}$), the variation $\Delta\mathcal{O}(\Lambda)$ of representative shell-model observables, and determine to what extent this variation is suppressed when only two-nucleon forces are retained at the $V_{\mathrm{low}\text{-}k}$ level versus when induced three- and higher-body forces generated by the renormalization-group transformation are systematically included.

(b) Provide a principled characterization or control scheme of the residual $\Lambda$-dependence: identify the dominant operator structures responsible for it, propose a method (e.g., consistent inclusion of induced many-body forces, smooth regulators, or order-by-order perturbative resummation) that renders shell-model observables approximately $\Lambda$-independent within a quantified theoretical uncertainty, and give an estimate of the residual cutoff sensitivity that should be attributed as a systematic theoretical error to realistic shell-model predictions.
status_search_result: Empirical and theoretical work indicates that for cutoffs near $\Lambda \approx 2\ \mathrm{fm}^{-1}$, low-lying shell-model spectra derived from $V_{\mathrm{low}\text{-}k}$ depend only weakly on $\Lambda$, and the residual cutoff dependence is understood to originate from omitted short-range induced three- and higher-body forces generated by the renormalization-group transformation. Including such induced many-body forces (or using SRG-evolved consistent NN+3N interactions) substantially reduces the dependence, but a fully systematic, quantitative characterization and control of the residual cutoff sensitivity for shell-model observables across mass regions remains an active research problem.

paper_title: Realistic shell-model calculations: current status and open problems
original_question: How can one establish the convergence properties of the Qˆ-box expansion used to derive shell-model effective interactions, especially the size and necessity of contributions beyond second order and the extent to which folded-diagram summations compensate higher-order Qˆ-box terms?
self_contained_problem:
Setup. In the derivation of effective shell-model interactions from a realistic nucleon–nucleon potential, one decomposes the full Hilbert space into a model space P and its complement Q = 1 − P. Following the Kuo–Lee–Ratcliffe folded-diagram formalism, the energy-independent effective interaction V_eff acting in P can be written as

   V_eff = Q̂ − Q̂' ∫ Q̂ + Q̂' ∫ Q̂ ∫ Q̂ − Q̂' ∫ Q̂ ∫ Q̂ ∫ Q̂ + … ,

where Q̂(ε) is the so-called Q̂-box, defined as the sum of all linked, non-folded, irreducible valence-linked Goldstone diagrams with at least one Q-space intermediate state, evaluated as a function of the starting energy ε; Q̂' denotes the Q̂-box with the zeroth-order term removed; the integral symbols stand for the folded-diagram operation (energy derivatives evaluated on shell); and the alternating series sums folded diagrams to all orders. In practice Q̂ is itself computed perturbatively in the residual interaction (typically the Brueckner G-matrix) and truncated at some finite order n in the interaction.

Problem. Establish rigorous convergence properties of the perturbative Q̂-box expansion used to construct V_eff. Specifically:

(a) Determine whether, for realistic low-momentum nucleon–nucleon interactions, the order-by-order expansion of Q̂(ε) (in powers of the residual interaction) converges, and characterize quantitatively the magnitude and operator structure of contributions beyond second order.

(b) Quantify the extent to which the all-orders folded-diagram resummation appearing in the formula above attenuates the differences between V_eff computed from Q̂-boxes truncated at different perturbative orders; in particular, prove or disprove that this resummation is sufficient to render second-order Q̂-box truncations adequate, or alternatively establish that third-order (and higher) Q̂-box terms produce non-negligible residual effects on V_eff.

(c) Provide criteria (on the model-space choice, the single-particle spectrum, and the underlying interaction) under which the combined Q̂-box plus folded-diagram series for V_eff is convergent, together with bounds on the truncation error.
status_search_result: Recent literature on realistic shell-model effective interactions continues to treat the convergence of the Q̂-box perturbative expansion as an unresolved issue: practical calculations are limited to third order because going beyond is computationally very difficult and no rigorous proof of convergence exists. Studies indicate that folded-diagram resummation attenuates differences between Q̂-boxes computed at different orders, but third-order contributions remain non-negligible, supporting the view that the problem remains open.

paper_title: Realistic shell-model calculations: current status and open problems
context_brief: Validity of omitting U and bubble diagrams
original_question: When the auxiliary one-body potential U in realistic shell-model calculations is taken to be a harmonic-oscillator potential rather than a Hartree-Fock self-consistent potential, is it justified to omit diagrams containing U and bubble insertions on the assumption that they cancel, or do those omitted terms make a significant contribution to the effective interaction?
self_contained_problem:
In the microscopic derivation of the nuclear shell-model effective interaction, one starts from an A-nucleon Hamiltonian
H = T + V = (T + U) + (V − U) ≡ H_0 + H_1,
where T is the intrinsic kinetic energy, V is a realistic nucleon–nucleon interaction, and U is an auxiliary one-body potential introduced so that H_0 = T + U defines a convenient single-particle basis. The effective interaction V_eff acting in a chosen valence model space is then obtained as a perturbative (folded-diagram) expansion in H_1 = V − U, whose Goldstone-type diagrams include both "V-insertions" and "−U-insertions," together with self-energy ("bubble") insertions on internal and external single-particle lines.

It is a standard observation that if U is chosen to be the Hartree–Fock self-consistent one-body potential, then to each order in the expansion the diagrams containing explicit −U vertices exactly cancel the corresponding bubble (Hartree–Fock self-energy) insertions, so that both classes of diagrams may be omitted from V_eff without loss.

Suppose instead that U is taken to be a harmonic-oscillator potential U(r) = (1/2) m ω² r² (the conventional choice for generating the single-particle basis in shell-model calculations), so that U is no longer the Hartree–Fock potential of V in the chosen model space. In the perturbative expansion of V_eff with this non-self-consistent U:

(a) Determine whether the omission of all diagrams containing −U vertices and all bubble self-energy insertions remains a justified approximation, i.e. whether the sum of these omitted diagrams still cancels (exactly or to a controlled accuracy) order by order.

(b) If the cancellation fails, quantify the size of the contribution of the omitted U- and bubble-insertion diagrams to V_eff and assess whether this contribution is significant compared with the diagrams that are retained.
status_search_result: Reviews of realistic shell-model effective interactions note that the cancellation between −U vertex diagrams and bubble (Hartree–Fock) self-energy insertions is exact only when U is the Hartree–Fock self-consistent potential. With a harmonic-oscillator U—the standard choice in practice—the justification of omitting these diagrams is acknowledged as not established, and a systematic quantitative assessment has not been reported in the available literature, so the question appears to remain open.

paper_title: Realistic shell-model calculations: current status and open problems
original_question: As the number of valence nucleons increases away from a doubly magic core, why do realistic shell-model calculations increasingly overestimate ground-state energies in long isotopic or isotonic chains, and to what extent is that overbinding caused by missing many-body forces, especially three-body forces, versus missing higher-order contributions such as third-order Qˆ-box diagrams?
self_contained_problem:
Setting. In the nuclear shell model, one starts from a doubly magic closed-shell core and treats nucleons in a finite valence model space outside the core. From an underlying realistic nucleon–nucleon (and possibly three-nucleon) interaction, an effective shell-model Hamiltonian H_eff is derived for the valence space using many-body perturbation theory, typically through the Kuo–Lee–Suzuki Q̂-box folded-diagram expansion. The Q̂-box is a sum of irreducible, valence-linked diagrams whose external lines lie in the valence space; one usually truncates the Q̂-box at second order in the residual interaction, retaining all folded diagrams to all orders. Diagonalizing H_eff in the valence space yields binding energies, level schemes, and other observables along isotopic (fixed Z, varying N) or isotonic (fixed N, varying Z) chains.

Empirical observation. For two-valence-nucleon systems near a doubly magic core, ground-state energies are accurately reproduced. As one moves along an isotopic or isotonic chain by adding valence nucleons, the calculated ground-state energies become progressively more bound than experiment, producing a systematic overbinding that grows with the number of valence nucleons.

Problem. Provide a quantitative theoretical explanation of this systematic overbinding by determining the relative contributions of:
(a) genuine three-nucleon forces in the underlying interaction;
(b) effective (induced) three-body forces generated by the many-body interaction of valence nucleons with core excitations and excluded states;
(c) higher-order terms of the Q̂-box, in particular third- and higher-order diagrams beyond the standard second-order truncation.

Specifically, decompose the discrepancy between calculated and experimental ground-state energies along long isotopic/isotonic chains into the contributions (a), (b), and (c), and identify which mechanism is dominant in producing the growth of overbinding with valence-nucleon number.

However, residual overbinding (up to ~1 MeV/nucleon by Sn with some chiral interactions) persists, and a systematic, fully quantitative separation between 3N-force effects and higher-order Q̂-box (third-order and beyond) contributions has not been definitively established. The problem is therefore partially solved but remains an active area of investigation.

paper_title: Realistic shell-model calculations: current status and open problems
original_question: Why is the agreement between theory and experiment generally worse for nuclei in which hole-hole interaction matrix elements are relevant than for nuclei dominated by particle-particle or particle-hole matrix elements, and what physical or methodological origin explains this asymmetry?
self_contained_problem:
In the realistic nuclear shell model, an effective two-body interaction acting within a chosen valence space is derived from a realistic nucleon-nucleon potential (typically via a $\hat{Q}$-box / folded-diagram or similar perturbative construction). For a given doubly-closed-shell core, valence nucleons can be classified as particles (occupying single-particle orbitals above the Fermi surface of the core) or holes (occupying single-hole orbitals below it). Accordingly, the matrix elements of the effective interaction split into three classes: particle-particle (pp), particle-hole (ph), and hole-hole (hh).

Empirically, when realistic shell-model calculations are compared to experimental spectra and other observables across chains of nuclei, the level of agreement is systematically of high quality for nuclei whose low-lying structure is dominated by pp or ph matrix elements, but is noticeably and consistently worse for nuclei in which hh matrix elements play a significant role.

Problem. Identify and justify the physical and/or methodological origin of this asymmetry. Specifically, determine whether the discrepancy stems from (a) the perturbative derivation of the effective interaction (e.g. truncations of the $\hat{Q}$-box, treatment of folded diagrams, or core-polarization contributions) treating hole orbitals less accurately than particle orbitals, (b) intrinsic features of the underlying realistic nucleon-nucleon (and possibly three-nucleon) interaction in hole channels, (c) limitations of the chosen model space when hole excitations are involved, or (d) some combination thereof, and provide a quantitative explanation that accounts for the observed systematic degradation of agreement in hh-dominated nuclei.
status_search_result: This is posed as an open conceptual/methodological question in realistic shell-model theory. No search result was found indicating a definitive resolution; subsequent reviews of realistic shell-model calculations continue to discuss difficulties in hole-hole channels (often linked to missing three-nucleon force contributions and to the perturbative derivation of the effective interaction) without providing a settled explanation of the asymmetry.

paper_title: Realistic shell-model calculations: current status and open problems
original_question: How should realistic shell-model calculations incorporate coupling to the scattering continuum for nuclei near the drip lines, where continuum effects are expected to play an important role in the structure and spectroscopy of weakly bound systems?
self_contained_problem:
Develop a framework for realistic shell-model calculations of atomic nuclei near the proton and neutron drip lines that explicitly incorporates the coupling of bound single-particle configurations to the scattering continuum. More precisely:

(i) Starting from a realistic nucleon–nucleon interaction V (e.g., derived from a high-precision potential or chiral effective field theory) and using a many-body renormalization procedure to construct an effective two-body (and, where needed, three-body) interaction H_eff in a chosen model space, formulate a configuration-interaction shell-model scheme in which the single-particle basis includes bound states, narrow resonances (Gamow states), and non-resonant scattering states on equal footing — for instance via a Berggren completeness relation 
   1 = Σ_b |b⟩⟨b| + Σ_r |r⟩⟨r̃| + ∫_{L^+} dk |k⟩⟨k̃|,
where L^+ is a contour in the complex momentum plane enclosing the selected resonances.

(ii) Specify how the effective Hamiltonian H_eff, originally constructed for a discrete bound-state model space, must be modified (renormalized) to remain consistent when the model space is extended to include resonant and continuum single-particle states, ensuring that the resulting many-body eigenvalue problem yields physically meaningful (complex) energies and widths for weakly bound and unbound nuclear states.

(iii) Demonstrate that the resulting realistic continuum-coupled shell model reproduces, in a controlled and systematic way, the known structure and spectroscopy of weakly bound or unbound nuclei near the drip lines (binding energies, one- and two-nucleon separation energies, resonance widths, decay thresholds, and threshold-related effects on spectra), and provides predictive power for nuclei beyond current experimental reach.

Provide such a construction, prove (or numerically establish) its convergence with respect to the truncation of the Berggren contour and many-body model space, and quantify the impact of continuum coupling on observables relative to standard bound-state shell-model calculations using the same realistic interaction.
category_tag: Nuclear shell model with continuum coupling
status_search_result: Substantial progress has been made via the Realistic Gamow Shell Model, which uses the Berggren basis to incorporate bound, resonant, and scattering states on equal footing together with effective interactions derived from realistic potentials (e.g., CD-Bonn, chiral EFT). Calculations for neutron-rich oxygen, calcium, and other drip-line isotopes have been published, showing that continuum coupling significantly affects spectra and separation energies. However, a fully systematic, convergent ab initio treatment for heavier drip-line systems and a complete renormalization of three-body and higher continuum couplings remain active research; the broader program is partially solved rather than closed.

paper_title: Open problems in nuclear structure near drip lines
context_brief: Halo and skin constraints on dilute matter
original_question: What information about dilute neutron matter and asymmetric nuclear matter can be inferred from finite neutron-rich nuclei near the neutron drip line? In particular, can observed neutron halos and neutron skins be used to extract properties of dilute neutron matter, determine the symmetry energy of asymmetric nuclear matter, and quantify how strongly low-density matter properties are manifested in finite nuclei whose outer neutron density is far below normal nuclear saturation density?
self_contained_problem:
Consider neutron-rich atomic nuclei lying near the neutron drip line, whose outermost neutron density extends to values far below the saturation density of normal nuclear matter (ρ₀ ≈ 0.16 fm⁻³). Such nuclei exhibit two characteristic features: (i) a neutron halo, in which one or a few weakly bound neutrons form a low-density tail extending well beyond the nuclear core, and (ii) a neutron skin, defined as the difference Δr_np = ⟨r²⟩_n^{1/2} − ⟨r²⟩_p^{1/2} between the root-mean-square radii of the neutron and proton density distributions. The symmetry energy S(ρ) of asymmetric nuclear matter is the coefficient governing the isospin-asymmetry dependence of the energy per particle, E(ρ,δ)/A = E(ρ,0)/A + S(ρ)δ² + O(δ⁴), where δ = (ρ_n − ρ_p)/ρ.

Address the following:

1. Determine to what extent the observed properties of neutron halos and neutron skins in finite drip-line nuclei can be used to infer the equation of state of dilute (sub-saturation) pure neutron matter.

2. Determine whether, and how quantitatively, measurements of neutron skin thicknesses and halo structures can constrain the symmetry energy S(ρ) of asymmetric nuclear matter, especially at sub-saturation densities, including its magnitude S(ρ₀) and slope L = 3ρ₀ (dS/dρ)|_{ρ₀}.

3. Quantify the degree to which low-density nuclear matter properties are manifested in the structural observables of finite neutron-rich nuclei whose outer neutron density is far below ρ₀, and identify the observables most sensitive to this dilute regime.
category_tag: nuclear structure and equation of state
status_search_result: The question of extracting the dilute-neutron-matter equation of state and the symmetry energy (and its slope L) from neutron skins and halos remains an active and unresolved research problem. Recent work (2024–2025), including analyses reconciling PREX-II (208Pb) and CREX (48Ca) parity-violating measurements, dipole polarizability data, and EDF studies, continues to debate how tightly such observables constrain S(ρ) at sub-saturation densities. No consensus determination has been achieved.

paper_title: Open problems in nuclear structure near drip lines
original_question: Do the correlations predicted for dilute nuclear or neutron matter actually occur in finite nuclei, and if so how are they connected to observed finite-nucleus phenomena such as spatial di-neutron correlation in two-neutron-halo nuclei, surface di-neutron correlation in neutron-rich isotopes, and low-density alpha clustering in the Hoyle state of carbon-12? The open problem is to establish whether these finite-nucleus signatures are manifestations of the same exotic low-density correlations expected in dilute matter.
self_contained_problem:
Consider infinite dilute nuclear matter and infinite dilute neutron matter at very low density. In such systems, theory predicts characteristic low-density correlations, including BCS–BEC crossover behavior of nucleon pairs, strong di-neutron spatial correlations at low density, and alpha-particle (four-nucleon) clustering when the density falls below a critical value of order one fifth of nuclear saturation density.

Now consider finite nuclei in which similar low-density regions or low-density limits occur, such as:
(i) two-neutron-halo nuclei (e.g. ^6He, ^11Li, ^14Be), where the two valence neutrons inhabit a dilute halo and exhibit a spatially compact "di-neutron" configuration;
(ii) neutron-rich isotopes whose surfaces and skins constitute a low-density neutron environment, in which a "surface di-neutron correlation" is conjectured;
(iii) the second 0^+ state of ^12C (the Hoyle state), interpreted as a dilute three-alpha cluster configuration.

Establish whether the exotic low-density correlations predicted in dilute infinite nuclear/neutron matter (di-neutron pairing in the BCS–BEC crossover regime and low-density alpha condensation) are actually realized in finite nuclei, and if so, give a quantitative theoretical and experimental link between these infinite-matter correlations and the observed finite-nucleus signatures listed above. Specifically:

(a) Define a precise correlation observable (e.g. the two-neutron pair-density or the alpha-particle four-body density correlation) that interpolates between the dilute-matter and finite-nucleus regimes.
(b) Determine whether the observed di-neutron spatial correlations in halo and neutron-rich nuclei, and the observed dilute alpha-cluster structure of the Hoyle state, are manifestations of the same low-density correlations expected in dilute infinite matter.
status_search_result: Recent literature on di-neutron correlations in halo and neutron-rich nuclei and on alpha clustering / alpha condensation in the Hoyle state continues to investigate—but has not conclusively established—their identification with the low-density correlations of dilute infinite nuclear/neutron matter (BCS–BEC crossover and alpha condensation). Studies through the mid-2020s still treat the connection as an active research question.

paper_title: Open problems in nuclear structure near drip lines
context_brief: Microscopic drip-line structure and halo physics
original_question: What is the correct microscopic description of nuclei at the neutron or proton drip lines when weak binding, short-range nucleon-nucleon correlations, long-range many-body correlations, and continuum coupling all matter at once? Within that description, does pairing suppress the spatial halo of weakly bound neutrons through an anti-halo effect, and how important are three-body interactions, such as Fujita-Miyazawa-type forces, in determining drip-line structure and isotope limits?
self_contained_problem:
Consider an atomic nucleus consisting of A nucleons (Z protons and N = A − Z neutrons) governed by a non-relativistic many-body Hamiltonian of the form

  H = Σ_i T_i + Σ_{i<j} V_{ij}^{(2)} + Σ_{i<j<k} V_{ijk}^{(3)},

where T_i is the single-nucleon kinetic energy, V^{(2)} is a realistic two-nucleon interaction containing both short-range repulsion and intermediate/long-range attraction, and V^{(3)} is a genuine three-nucleon interaction (e.g. of the Fujita–Miyazawa type, arising from intermediate Δ-isobar excitation in two-pion exchange). Suppose the nucleus lies at the neutron (or proton) drip line, meaning that the separation energy of the last nucleon(s) is positive but small enough that coupling to the single-particle continuum is non-negligible.

Formulate, and analyze, a microscopic many-body framework that simultaneously incorporates:

  (i) short-range nucleon–nucleon correlations induced by the hard core of V^{(2)};
  (ii) long-range collective/many-body correlations involving particle–hole excitations into the continuum (resonant and non-resonant scattering states);
  (iii) pairing correlations among weakly bound nucleons; and
  (iv) the three-body force V^{(3)}.

Within this framework, address the following:

(a) Anti-halo effect. Let ρ_n(r) denote the one-body density of the valence weakly bound neutrons, and let ⟨r^2⟩^{1/2} be its rms radius. Determine, as a function of the pairing gap Δ and the single-particle separation energy ε, whether switching on the pairing interaction reduces ⟨r^2⟩^{1/2} relative to the unpaired (Hartree–Fock) value. In particular, identify the regime (in Δ, ε, and orbital angular momentum ℓ of the valence orbit) in which pairing produces a localizing "anti-halo" effect versus the regime in which a spatially extended halo persists.

(b) Role of three-body forces. Quantify the extent to which the three-nucleon interaction V^{(3)} shifts the position of the neutron and proton drip lines (i.e., the largest N for fixed Z, and the largest Z for fixed N, with positive one- and two-nucleon separation energies), and the extent to which it modifies halo structure, spatial distributions, and continuum coupling at the drip line.

Provide either rigorous results, controlled approximations, or a precise conjecture with supporting analysis.
category_tag: nuclear drip-line structure and halo nuclei
status_search_result: The microscopic description of drip-line nuclei combining short-range correlations, continuum coupling, pairing, and three-nucleon forces remains an active research frontier. Ab initio approaches (no-core shell model, coupled-cluster, Gorkov–Green's function, in-medium SRG with chiral 2N+3N forces) and Gamow shell-model / continuum-shell-model techniques have made substantial progress, and three-nucleon forces are known to significantly affect drip-line locations (e.g. for oxygen and calcium isotopes). The anti-halo effect of pairing has been demonstrated in specific cases but is not universal. No complete, unified solution exists; the problem is considered open.
