(i) restores good total angular momentum quantum numbers J and M (i.e. yields eigenstates of J^2 and J_z in the laboratory frame),
(ii) describes the quantum tunneling between left-handed and right-handed chiral intrinsic configurations and produces the resulting energy splitting between the two chiral partner bands as a function of spin, and
(iii) reduces, in an appropriate semiclassical limit, to the tilted-axis cranking mean-field picture of two degenerate aplanar solutions.

Provide such a microscopic theory, derive from it the spin dependence of the chiral partner-band splitting and the in-band and inter-band electromagnetic transition probabilities, and demonstrate that it reproduces the observed properties of chiral doublet bands in triaxial odd-odd and odd-A nuclei.

paper_title: Open Problems in Understanding the Nuclear Chirality
original_question: How can the particle-rotor model for nuclear chirality be extended beyond a rigid triaxially deformed core so that the quadrupole deformation parameters β and γ and the particle-hole configuration are not fixed inputs, but instead change self-consistently with nuclear rotation and feed back on whether chiral doublet bands appear?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the particle-rotor model used to describe chiral doublet bands in atomic nuclei. In its standard form, the Hamiltonian couples a small number of valence nucleons (particles and/or holes occupying fixed single-particle orbitals) to a rigid triaxially deformed rotor core characterized by fixed quadrupole deformation parameters (β, γ) and three rotational moments of inertia. The total Hamiltonian has the schematic form

  H = H_core(β, γ; I) + H_sp(β, γ) + H_pair,

where H_core describes the rotational kinetic energy of a rigid triaxial rotor with angular momentum operator \hat{R} = \hat{I} − \hat{j}, H_sp is a deformed mean-field single-particle Hamiltonian (e.g. of Nilsson or Woods–Saxon type) for the valence particle/hole configuration with definite occupations, and H_pair is a pairing interaction. Chiral doublet bands appear, in this framework, as nearly degenerate ΔI = 1 partner bands of the same parity, arising from left- and right-handed couplings of the angular-momentum vectors of the core, the valence particle, and the valence hole.

Problem. Construct an extension of the particle-rotor model in which:
(i) the deformation parameters β and γ are dynamical variables rather than fixed inputs, allowed to depend on the total angular momentum I (and possibly to fluctuate quantum-mechanically about their equilibrium values);
(ii) the particle–hole configuration is not imposed by hand but is determined self-consistently together with the deformation, so that occupations of single-particle orbitals can change with rotation;
(iii) the deformation and the configuration are coupled back to the rotational dynamics through a self-consistency condition (for example, by minimizing the total energy or by solving coupled mean-field plus collective equations at each I).

Formulate explicit equations of motion or a variational principle yielding (β(I), γ(I), configuration(I)) jointly with the rotational wave functions, and determine, within this extended framework, under what conditions on the nucleon number, single-particle spectrum, and rotational frequency the spectrum exhibits a pair of nearly degenerate chiral doublet bands. In particular, characterize how the response of β and γ to rotation modifies, enhances, or destroys the chirality predicted by the rigid-core particle-rotor model.

original_question: How can microscopic energy-density-functional calculations of candidate chiral nuclei include rotational motion self-consistently, for example through three-dimensional cranking or angular-momentum projection, and then determine the deformation by minimizing the energy at fixed total angular momentum, rather than studying deformation with the rotational degree of freedom switched off?

Within a microscopic energy-density-functional (EDF) framework for atomic nuclei, develop and carry out self-consistent calculations of candidate chiral nuclei (i.e., triaxially deformed nuclei in which the total angular momentum vector lies outside any principal plane of the density distribution, giving rise to pairs of nearly degenerate rotational bands of the same parity). (a) Incorporate the rotational degree of freedom into the EDF self-consistent mean-field equations by means of three-dimensional (tilted-axis) cranking, in which a Lagrange constraint −ω·Ĵ is added to the single-particle Hamiltonian with a cranking-frequency vector ω that is allowed to point in an arbitrary direction relative to the principal axes of the deformed density, and/or by means of angular-momentum projection, in which the mean-field state |Φ⟩ is projected onto an eigenstate of total angular momentum Ĵ² and Ĵ_z via the standard projection operator P^J_{MK} = (2J+1)/(8π²) ∫ dΩ D^{J*}_{MK}(Ω) R̂(Ω).

(b) For each fixed value of the total angular momentum J, determine the equilibrium intrinsic deformation parameters (β, γ) by minimizing the (cranked or projected) total energy E(β,γ;J) under the constraint ⟨Ĵ²⟩ = J(J+1) (or, in the cranking version, ⟨Ĵ⟩ = √{J(J+1)}), rather than determining (β, γ) from a non-rotating constrained calculation and only afterwards imposing rotation.

(c) Demonstrate that this procedure yields a controlled, self-consistent prediction of the triaxial deformation, the orientation of the angular-momentum vector, and the chiral-doublet spectrum of the nucleus as functions of J.

Provide a computationally tractable implementation of this scheme and apply it to identify and describe nuclear chirality microscopically.

original_question: What model-independent experimental fingerprints can identify chiral doublet bands in atomic nuclei unambiguously, especially in electromagnetic transitions, so that the diagnosis of chirality does not depend on subjective near-degeneracy criteria or on selection rules derived only from a specific rigid triaxial rotor plus one-particle-one-hole model?
self_contained_problem:
In an atomic nucleus, chiral doublet bands are pairs of nearly degenerate rotational bands of the same parity that are interpreted as arising from the left- and right-handed couplings of three mutually perpendicular angular momentum vectors (typically those of a valence proton, a valence neutron, and the triaxial core). The standard theoretical framework used to predict their properties is the rigid triaxial rotor coupled to one or more particle/hole configurations (the particle-rotor model), which yields specific selection rules and staggering patterns for M1 and E2 electromagnetic transition probabilities along and between the doublet bands.

Identify a set of experimental fingerprints — formulated without reference to any particular microscopic Hamiltonian, mean field, or rigid triaxial rotor plus one-particle-one-hole assumption, and not relying on subjective judgments of near-degeneracy of the two band energies — whose simultaneous observation in measured electromagnetic transition probabilities (e.g., B(M1), B(E2), and their ratios or staggering with spin) and other observables would unambiguously establish the chiral character of a given pair of bands in a nucleus. Equivalently, derive a model-independent selection rule (or family of selection rules) for electromagnetic transitions in chiral bands that follows solely from the assumed chiral geometry and its underlying symmetries, and specify the experimental signatures by which this selection rule can be tested.
status_search_result: Selection rules for electromagnetic transitions in chiral geometry have been proposed and refined, including a quantum number derived from Hamiltonian invariance giving M1/E2 staggering patterns (Koike–Starosta–Hamamoto PRL 2004; Chen et al., arXiv:1102.0163), and have been extended to chirality-parity violation cases (Chinese Sci. Bull./Sci. Bulletin 2020). Compilations of >60 candidate chiral doublet bands exist. However, these rules still rest on specific (triaxial particle-rotor) models, and a fully model-independent fingerprint that removes reliance on near-degeneracy criteria has not been universally established; the question is therefore partially solved.

paper_title: Open Problems in Understanding the Nuclear Chirality
original_question: Can a microscopic and self-consistent nuclear-structure calculation reproduce both the near-degenerate energy spectra and the electromagnetic transition properties of the doublet bands in 134Pr, and thereby decide whether those bands are better understood as a manifestation of chirality or of shape coexistence rather than treating the two interpretations separately?
self_contained_problem:
In the odd-odd nucleus $^{134}$Pr, two nearly degenerate $\Delta I = 1$ rotational bands ("doublet bands") have been observed and have been interpreted in two competing ways: (i) as a chiral doublet, arising from spontaneous breaking of chiral symmetry by a triaxial nuclear shape together with the angular momenta of an unpaired proton particle, an unpaired neutron hole, and the collective core, which couple in a left- or right-handed aplanar geometry; or (ii) as a manifestation of shape coexistence, in which the two bands are built on intrinsic configurations associated with different (e.g. distinct triaxial) nuclear shapes.

Construct a single microscopic and self-consistent nuclear-structure framework — for example a covariant or non-relativistic energy-density-functional approach with cranking and beyond-mean-field correlations (such as projection on angular momentum and parity, configuration mixing via the generator coordinate method, or fully three-dimensional tilted-axis cranking) — that, without phenomenological adjustment to $^{134}$Pr data, simultaneously reproduces:

(a) the observed near-degeneracy of the energies of the two partner bands of $^{134}$Pr as a function of spin, including the energy staggering $S(I) = [E(I) - E(I-1)]/2I$; and

(b) the in-band and inter-band electromagnetic transition properties, namely the $B(M1)$ and $B(E2)$ strengths and their $I$-dependence and staggering patterns.

Using this calculation, determine which physical picture — chiral geometry of angular momenta on a (possibly soft) triaxial shape, or coexistence of distinct shapes — provides the correct microscopic interpretation of the doublet bands of $^{134}$Pr, or whether both mechanisms must be combined within one framework.
status_search_result: Recent work has applied microscopic self-consistent methods (3D tilted-axis cranking covariant density functional theory, adiabatic and configuration-fixed constrained triaxial CDFT) to chiral candidate nuclei in the A≈130 region, including neighbors such as 129Cs, 131La and other N=75 isotones, and chiral vibration interpretations are discussed for 134Pr. However, no published calculation appears to have simultaneously reproduced both the near-degenerate spectra and the full electromagnetic transition properties of the 134Pr doublet bands in a fully microscopic and self-consistent way that conclusively distinguishes chirality from shape coexistence; the question therefore appears to remain open.

paper_title: Open Problems in Understanding the Nuclear Chirality
context_brief: Microscopic collective Hamiltonian extension of PRM
original_question: Can the particle-rotor description of chiral doublet bands be reformulated so that the rigid core is replaced by a collective Hamiltonian whose parameters are extracted microscopically from constrained triaxial mean-field calculations, thereby incorporating vibration-rotation coupling into chirality studies in a genuinely microscopic way?
self_contained_problem:
In the standard particle-rotor model (PRM) of nuclear structure, one or more valence nucleons are coupled to a rigid triaxial rotor that represents the collective core. Chiral doublet bands arise in odd-odd (or odd-mass multi-quasiparticle) triaxial nuclei when the angular momenta of the valence proton, valence neutron, and the triaxial core are mutually perpendicular, producing left-handed and right-handed configurations whose quantum mixing yields a pair of nearly degenerate ΔI=1 rotational bands of the same parity.

Replace the rigid triaxial rotor in the PRM by a collective Bohr-type Hamiltonian
$$H_{\mathrm{coll}}(\beta,\gamma) = T_{\mathrm{vib}}(\beta,\gamma) + T_{\mathrm{rot}}(\beta,\gamma,\Omega) + V(\beta,\gamma),$$
in which the collective potential $V(\beta,\gamma)$, the three moments of inertia $\mathcal{J}_k(\beta,\gamma)$ ($k=1,2,3$), and the vibrational mass parameters $B_{\beta\beta},B_{\beta\gamma},B_{\gamma\gamma}$ are all determined microscopically from constrained self-consistent triaxial mean-field calculations (e.g. constrained Hartree-Fock-Bogoliubov or relativistic mean-field with cranking) as functions of the deformation parameters $(\beta,\gamma)$. Couple this collective Hamiltonian to the valence quasiparticles through the standard particle-core interaction, and diagonalize the resulting Hamiltonian in a basis labeled by $(\beta,\gamma)$ and quasiparticle quantum numbers.

Question: Can such a microscopically founded particle plus collective-Hamiltonian framework be formulated and implemented so that vibration-rotation coupling (fluctuations in $\beta$ and $\gamma$, including soft-triaxial dynamics) is incorporated into the description of chiral doublet bands, and so that the resulting energies, $B(M1)$ and $B(E2)$ transition probabilities, and chiral partner splittings are obtained without phenomenological adjustment of core parameters?
status_search_result: Subsequent work has implemented closely related programs: a collective Hamiltonian for the chiral modes has been derived from particle-triaxial-rotor and tilted-axis-cranking input, and a two-dimensional collective Hamiltonian on azimuth/polar motions with potential and mass parameters extracted from 3D TAC calculations has been used to describe chiral and wobbling modes. A rotation-vibration model for chiral and wobbling bands in transitional nuclei has also appeared. These represent partial realizations of the proposed microscopic extension, although a fully microscopic particle plus (β,γ)-collective Hamiltonian description of chiral doublets with parameters drawn entirely from constrained triaxial mean-field calculations remains an active research direction rather than a definitively settled problem.

paper_title: Bayesian predictive densities for linear regression models under α-divergence loss: some results and open problems
context_brief: Shrinkage versus invariant prediction under α-divergence
original_question: In the normal linear regression prediction setting considered in the paper, assume the design matrices satisfy assumption (AS1): m ≥ k ≥ 3, n = mN for some positive integer N, and X = 1_N ⊗ X̃ so that the observed and future design matrices have the repeated-design structure used by Komaki (2001). Under α-divergence loss D_α with −1 < α < 1, does the predictive density based on the shrinkage prior π_S,1(β, σ²) = (β′X̃′X̃β)^{1−k/2}(σ²)^{−2} improve on the best invariant predictive density, namely the generalized Bayes predictive density based on the right invariant prior π_I,1(β, σ²) = (σ²)^{−1}?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the normal linear regression prediction problem with unknown variance. Let k ≥ 3 and m ≥ k be positive integers, let N be a positive integer, and set n = mN. Let X̃ be a fixed m × k matrix of full column rank, and let the observed design matrix be X = 1_N ⊗ X̃ (an n × k matrix), where 1_N is the N-vector of ones. The observed data Y is an n-vector with

   Y | β, σ² ∼ N_n(Xβ, σ² I_n),

and the future observation Ỹ is an m-vector independent of Y with

   Ỹ | β, σ² ∼ N_m(X̃β, σ² I_m).

The unknown parameter is ψ = (β, σ²) ∈ R^k × (0, ∞). For a fixed α with −1 < α < 1, the α-divergence loss between a true density p(ỹ | ψ) and a predictive density p̂(ỹ | y) is

   D_α(p, p̂) = (4 / (1 − α²)) ∫ [1 − (p̂/p)^{(1−α)/2}] p(ỹ | ψ) dỹ,

with associated risk obtained by integrating over Y. For a (possibly improper) prior π(β, σ²), let p_π(ỹ | y) denote the corresponding generalized Bayes predictive density.

Define two priors:

   π_S(β, σ²) = (β′ X̃′ X̃ β)^{1 − k/2} (σ²)^{−2},     (shrinkage prior)
   π_I(β, σ²) = (σ²)^{−1}.                              (right-invariant prior)

The generalized Bayes predictive density p_{π_I} is the best invariant predictive density. Determine whether, under the design assumption above, the predictive density p_{π_S} dominates p_{π_I} under the α-divergence risk for every −1 < α < 1; that is, whether

   R_α(ψ, p_{π_S}) ≤ R_α(ψ, p_{π_I})   for all ψ,

with strict inequality for some ψ.
status_search_result: The problem was posed as an open problem in 2010. Subsequent work by Ghosh–Kubokawa, Boisbunon–Maruyama, and others has extended dominance results for shrinkage predictive densities under α-divergence loss, mostly in the known-variance setting or related but distinct setups. We did not find a definitive published resolution for the specific unknown-variance regression problem with the stated shrinkage prior π_S and design assumption AS1 across the full range −1 < α < 1.

paper_title: Bayesian predictive densities for linear regression models under α-divergence loss: some results and open problems
context_brief: Bayesian improvement for k equals 1 or 2 under D1
original_question: Under D_1 loss in the same predictive-density estimation problem for normal linear regression with unknown variance, and in the low-dimensional cases k = 1 or k = 2, the paper notes that the best invariant predictive density is still inadmissible because a better non-Bayesian predictive density can be constructed. The open question is whether one can construct improved Bayesian predictive densities that dominate the best invariant predictive density in these cases k = 1 and k = 2.
self_contained_problem:
Setup. Consider the normal linear regression model in which one observes
\[ X = A\beta + \sigma \varepsilon_X, \qquad \varepsilon_X \sim N_n(0, I_n), \]
where $A$ is a known $n\times k$ design matrix of full rank $k$, $\beta\in\mathbb{R}^k$ and $\sigma^2>0$ are unknown. A future observation
\[ Y = B\beta + \sigma \varepsilon_Y, \qquad \varepsilon_Y \sim N_m(0, I_m), \]
is to be predicted, where $B$ is a known $m\times k$ matrix and $\varepsilon_Y$ is independent of $\varepsilon_X$. Let $p(y\mid\beta,\sigma)$ denote the density of $Y$ given $(\beta,\sigma)$.

Loss. For two densities $p,q$ on $\mathbb{R}^m$, the $D_1$ (Kullback–Leibler) divergence is
\[ D_1(p, q) = \int p(y)\,\log\!\frac{p(y)}{q(y)}\,dy, \]
and a predictive density $\hat p(y; X)$ is evaluated by the risk
\[ R(\beta,\sigma; \hat p) = E_{(\beta,\sigma)}\bigl[D_1\bigl(p(\cdot\mid\beta,\sigma),\, \hat p(\cdot;X)\bigr)\bigr]. \]

Best invariant predictive density. The problem is invariant under the group of location–scale transformations acting jointly on $(X,Y,\beta,\sigma)$. Among all equivariant predictive densities, there is a (unique) best invariant predictive density $\hat p_{I}(y;X)$, which coincides with the formal Bayes predictive density obtained from the right-invariant prior $\pi(\beta,\sigma)\propto 1/\sigma$.

Question. In the low-dimensional cases $k=1$ and $k=2$, $\hat p_{I}$ is known to be inadmissible under $D_1$ loss (an improved non-Bayesian predictive density can be exhibited). Construct a proper-Bayes (or generalized-Bayes with respect to a prior other than $\pi(\beta,\sigma)\propto 1/\sigma$) predictive density $\hat p_{\pi}(y;X)$ such that
\[ R(\beta,\sigma;\hat p_{\pi}) \le R(\beta,\sigma;\hat p_{I}) \quad \text{for all } (\beta,\sigma), \]
with strict inequality for some $(\beta,\sigma)$, in each of the cases $k=1$ and $k=2$.
status_search_result: The source itself indicates that an exact solution to this particular problem is given within the same work, suggesting it is resolved there. However, web searches did not return an independent, verifiable construction or follow-up confirming the solution, so the broader status (in particular whether such improved Bayesian predictive densities have been firmly established in the literature) could not be confirmed from accessible sources.

paper_title: Bayesian predictive densities for linear regression models under α-divergence loss: some results and open problems
original_question: When the parameter dimension is k = 1 or k = 2 and the loss is α-divergence D_α with −1 ≤ α < 1, does the best invariant predictive density remain inadmissible? If it does, which Bayesian predictive density or class of Bayesian predictive densities improves upon it?
self_contained_problem:
Let $X \mid \mu \sim N_k(\mu, v_x I_k)$ be an observation and $Y \mid \mu \sim N_k(\mu, v_y I_k)$ a future independent observation, with the unknown location parameter $\mu \in \mathbb{R}^k$ and known variances $v_x, v_y > 0$. A predictive density for $Y$ given $X$ is a measurable function $\hat p(y \mid x)$ such that $\hat p(\cdot \mid x)$ is a probability density on $\mathbb{R}^k$ for each $x$.

For $\alpha \in [-1, 1)$, define the $\alpha$-divergence between two densities $p$ and $q$ on $\mathbb{R}^k$ by
$$D_\alpha(p, q) \;=\; \frac{4}{1 - \alpha^{2}} \left( 1 - \int p(y)^{(1-\alpha)/2} q(y)^{(1+\alpha)/2}\, dy \right),$$
with the standard limiting interpretations at $\alpha = \pm 1$ (so $\alpha = -1$ gives the Kullback–Leibler divergence $\mathrm{KL}(p \,\|\, q)$). The risk of a predictive density $\hat p$ at $\mu$ is
$$R_\alpha(\mu, \hat p) \;=\; \mathbb{E}_\mu\!\left[ D_\alpha\!\big( p(\cdot \mid \mu),\, \hat p(\cdot \mid X) \big) \right],$$
where $p(y \mid \mu)$ denotes the $N_k(\mu, v_y I_k)$ density.

The best location-invariant predictive density $\hat p_{\mathrm{BI}}^{(\alpha)}(y \mid x)$ is the predictive density that minimizes $R_\alpha(\mu, \hat p)$ within the class of predictive densities depending on $(x, y)$ only through $y - x$; equivalently, it is the formal Bayes predictive density under the right-invariant (Lebesgue) prior on $\mu$, suitably defined for the given $\alpha$.

Question. Suppose $k \in \{1, 2\}$ and $-1 \le \alpha < 1$.

(a) Is $\hat p_{\mathrm{BI}}^{(\alpha)}$ inadmissible under the risk $R_\alpha$? That is, does there exist a predictive density $\hat p$ with $R_\alpha(\mu, \hat p) \le R_\alpha(\mu, \hat p_{\mathrm{BI}}^{(\alpha)})$ for all $\mu \in \mathbb{R}^k$ and strict inequality for some $\mu$?

(b) If so, exhibit a (generalized) Bayesian predictive density, or a class of such Bayesian predictive densities corresponding to specified prior distributions on $\mu$, that dominates $\hat p_{\mathrm{BI}}^{(\alpha)}$ under $R_\alpha$.
status_search_result: Subsequent literature on predictive density estimation under $\alpha$-divergence loss (e.g., work by Maruyama–Ohnishi on harmonic Bayesian prediction and a 2019 paper "On Predictive Density Estimation under $\alpha$-Divergence Loss") establishes domination of the best invariant predictive density by harmonic-prior Bayes rules in dimensions $k \ge 3$, and gives improvements in special cases. However, the available abstracts and accessible portions do not confirm a complete resolution of inadmissibility, or identification of an improving Bayesian predictive density, for the low-dimensional cases $k = 1, 2$ across the full range $-1 \le \alpha < 1$. Status could not be definitively verified.

paper_title: Bayesian predictive densities for linear regression models under α-divergence loss: some results and open problems
context_brief: Analogue of KL risk-reduction identity for general α
original_question: For predictive density estimation under α-divergence loss D_α with |α| < 1 in the canonical normal model, is there an identity or structural relationship analogous to the one George, Liang, and Xu (2006) used for Kullback-Leibler loss, namely a relationship linking predictive-risk reduction to the risk-reduction theory for estimating a multivariate normal mean vector?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the canonical Gaussian prediction setup: observe $X \sim N_d(\theta, \sigma_X^2 I_d)$ and seek a predictive density $\hat p(\,\cdot\,;X)$ for the independent future observation $Y \sim N_d(\theta, \sigma_Y^2 I_d)$, where $\theta \in \mathbb R^d$ is unknown and $\sigma_X^2,\sigma_Y^2>0$ are known. For $\alpha \in (-1,1)$, define the $\alpha$-divergence between two densities $p,q$ on $\mathbb R^d$ by
$$D_\alpha(p,q) \;=\; \frac{4}{1-\alpha^2}\left(1-\int p^{(1-\alpha)/2}(y)\,q^{(1+\alpha)/2}(y)\,dy\right),$$
and let the predictive risk be $R_\alpha(\theta,\hat p) = \mathbb E_\theta\, D_\alpha\!\big(p(\,\cdot\,\mid\theta),\hat p(\,\cdot\,;X)\big)$, where $p(\,\cdot\,\mid\theta)$ is the $N_d(\theta,\sigma_Y^2 I_d)$ density.

For Kullback–Leibler loss (the limit $\alpha\to -1$), there is a known identity expressing the difference of predictive risks of two Bayesian predictive densities $\hat p_{\pi_1}$ and $\hat p_{\pi_2}$ (associated with priors $\pi_1,\pi_2$ on $\theta$) as an integral, over a range of variances, of the difference of mean-squared-error risks of the corresponding posterior-mean estimators of $\theta$. This identity directly connects predictive-risk reduction to the Stein-type theory of risk reduction for estimating a multivariate normal mean.

Question: For $\alpha \in (-1,1)$ with $\alpha \neq -1$, does there exist an analogous identity or structural relationship that links the reduction in $\alpha$-divergence predictive risk between two Bayes predictive densities $\hat p_{\pi_1}$ and $\hat p_{\pi_2}$ to the reduction in risk for estimating the mean vector $\theta$ of a multivariate normal distribution? Establish such a relationship or prove that none exists.
category_tag: Bayesian predictive density estimation under α-divergence
status_search_result: Subsequent work has made substantial progress on connecting α-divergence predictive risk to multivariate normal mean estimation. Maruyama–Ohnishi-type results, Boisbunon–Maruyama, and the Kubokawa–Marchand–Strawderman line of work (including "Optimal Shrinkage Estimation of Predictive Densities under α-Divergences", Bayesian Analysis 2022, and the 2019 paper "On Predictive Density Estimation under α-Divergence Loss") obtain dominance and improvement results for |α|<1 by reducing the problem to expanded-variance plug-in densities and Stein-type unbiased risk estimates, providing a partial analogue of the George–Liang–Xu KL identity. A clean, fully general identity matching the KL case is not clearly stated; the structural link exists but its strongest form appears not to have been definitively established.

original_question: Let X and X' be hyperkahler manifolds of the same dimension. If there is a Hodge isometry lambda: H^2(X, Z) -> H^2(X', Z), determine what geometric relationship between X and X' follows, and whether one can force X and X' to be isomorphic by requiring lambda to preserve additional structure beyond the Hodge structure itself.
self_contained_problem:
A compact Kähler manifold $X$ is called hyperkähler (irreducible holomorphic symplectic) if it is simply connected and $H^0(X,\Omega_X^2)$ is generated by an everywhere non-degenerate holomorphic 2-form. On the second integral cohomology of such an $X$ there is a canonical integral symmetric bilinear form $q_X$ of signature $(3,b_2-3)$, the Beauville–Bogomolov–Fujiki form, together with the weight-two Hodge structure on $H^2(X,\mathbb{Z})$.

A Hodge isometry $\lambda : H^2(X,\mathbb{Z}) \to H^2(X',\mathbb{Z})$ between two hyperkähler manifolds of the same complex dimension is a $\mathbb{Z}$-linear isomorphism that preserves the Beauville–Bogomolov–Fujiki forms and sends $H^{2,0}(X)$ to $H^{2,0}(X')$.

(a) Given that $X$ and $X'$ are hyperkähler manifolds of the same dimension and that such a Hodge isometry $\lambda$ exists, what geometric relationship between $X$ and $X'$ can be deduced (e.g.\ deformation equivalence, bimeromorphic equivalence, or isomorphism)?

(b) Identify additional structural conditions on $\lambda$ (for instance, that $\lambda$ be a parallel transport operator along a smooth family, or that $\lambda$ map the Kähler cone, or some specific Kähler/ample class, of $X$ to that of $X'$) under which one may conclude that $X$ and $X'$ are bimeromorphic, and under which one may further conclude that they are isomorphic.
status_search_result: Verbitsky's global Torelli theorem (2009, published 2013) gives a definitive answer in the deformation-equivalent setting: if $\lambda$ is a parallel transport operator that is a Hodge isometry, then $X$ and $X'$ are bimeromorphic, and if in addition $\lambda$ maps a Kähler class of $X$ to a Kähler class of $X'$, then $X \cong X'$. However, examples of Debarre and Namikawa show that the naive Hodge-isometric Torelli statement (without the parallel transport hypothesis) fails: there exist non-bimeromorphic hyperkähler manifolds with Hodge-isometric $H^2$, and non-isomorphic birational hyperkähler manifolds with the same periods. Thus the question is partially solved: a complete answer is known under the parallel-transport hypothesis, but the precise geometric relationship implied by an arbitrary Hodge isometry remains subtle.

original_question: Determine whether there are only finitely many hyperkahler manifolds, up to deformation, in each dimension.
self_contained_problem:
A compact connected complex manifold $X$ of complex dimension $2n$ is called an irreducible holomorphic symplectic (hyperkähler) manifold if $X$ is simply connected and $H^0(X,\Omega_X^2)$ is spanned by an everywhere non-degenerate holomorphic 2-form. Two such manifolds are called deformation equivalent if they occur as fibers of a smooth proper holomorphic family over a connected base.

Prove or disprove: for every positive integer $n$, there are only finitely many deformation equivalence classes of irreducible holomorphic symplectic manifolds of complex dimension $2n$.
status_search_result: The conjecture that there are only finitely many deformation types of irreducible compact hyperkähler manifolds in each fixed (complex) dimension remains open in general. Partial finiteness results are known: Huybrechts proved finiteness when the underlying smooth manifold or the second cohomology lattice is fixed; finiteness has been established for hyperkähler manifolds with prescribed cohomological invariants, for polarized cases, and recent topological/Betti-number bounds have been obtained. Only finitely many deformation classes are currently known in each dimension (K3$^{[n]}$, generalized Kummer, and O'Grady's two exceptional examples).

original_question: For a hyperkahler fourfold X, determine whether additional values of the second Betti number b2 can be excluded beyond the currently known cases, especially whether b2 = 3 can occur at all; and if b2 = 23, determine whether X must be deformation equivalent to the Hilbert square S^[2] of a K3 surface.
self_contained_problem:
A hyperkähler manifold is a simply connected compact Kähler manifold X such that H^0(X, Ω_X^2) is generated by an everywhere non-degenerate holomorphic 2-form. Let X be a hyperkähler fourfold (i.e. of complex dimension 4), and let b_2(X) denote its second Betti number. It is known that either b_2(X) = 23, or 3 ≤ b_2(X) ≤ 8.

(a) Determine which values of b_2(X) in {3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 23} can actually occur for some hyperkähler fourfold X. In particular, can the value b_2(X) = 3 be excluded?

(b) Suppose b_2(X) = 23. Must X be deformation equivalent to the Hilbert square S^{[2]} of a K3 surface S?
status_search_result: The classification of possible second Betti numbers for hyperkähler fourfolds remains open. Guan's bounds (2001) restrict b_2 to {3,...,8} ∪ {23}, but no further values have been excluded in general; in particular, whether b_2 = 3 occurs is still unresolved. For b_2 = 23, it is known that the Hodge diamond agrees with that of S^{[2]}, but the question whether such X must be deformation equivalent to a Hilbert square of a K3 surface remains a well-known open problem; only partial results (e.g., under additional polarization or geometric hypotheses) are available.

original_question: Let X be a hyperkahler manifold of dimension 2r. If L is a nontrivial nef line bundle on X with Beauville-Bogomolov square q(L) = 0, determine whether there must exist a Lagrangian fibration f: X -> P^r such that L = f^* O_{P^r}(k) for some integer k >= 1. More generally, determine whether X is birational to a hyperkahler manifold X' admitting a Lagrangian fibration X' -> P^r exactly when X carries a nontrivial line bundle L with q(L) = 0.
self_contained_problem:
Let X be a compact hyperkähler manifold of complex dimension 2r; that is, X is a simply connected compact Kähler manifold such that H^0(X, Ω_X^2) is generated by an everywhere nondegenerate holomorphic 2-form. Recall that the second cohomology H^2(X, Z) carries a canonical nondegenerate integral quadratic form q, the Beauville–Bogomolov–Fujiki form. For a line bundle L on X, write q(L) := q(c_1(L)).

A Lagrangian fibration on X is a surjective holomorphic map f : X → B onto a normal projective variety B with 0 < dim B < 2r, whose general fiber is a connected Lagrangian submanifold with respect to the holomorphic symplectic form. (When X is projective and admits such a fibration, B is necessarily of dimension r and, in all known cases, isomorphic to P^r.)

Prove or disprove the following two statements:

(a) If L is a nontrivial nef line bundle on X with q(L) = 0, then there exists a Lagrangian fibration f : X → P^r and an integer k ≥ 1 such that L ≅ f^* O_{P^r}(k).

(b) There exists a compact hyperkähler manifold X' bimeromorphic to X admitting a Lagrangian fibration X' → P^r if and only if X carries a nontrivial line bundle L with q(L) = 0.
status_search_result: The conjecture (often called the hyperkähler SYZ conjecture) remains open in general. Substantial partial results are known: Matsushita proved structural results on Lagrangian fibrations; Verbitsky established semiampleness statements under deformation hypotheses; and the birational (part b) version has been verified for all currently known deformation types of hyperkähler manifolds (K3^[n], generalized Kummer, OG6, OG10) by combining work of Matsushita, Markman, Bayer–Macrì, Yoshioka and others. A general proof for arbitrary hyperkähler manifolds has not been given.

original_question: Does every hyperkahler manifold admit a deformation that carries a Lagrangian fibration?
self_contained_problem: A hyperkähler manifold is a simply connected compact Kähler manifold $M$ such that $H^0(M, \Omega_M^2)$ is generated by a holomorphic symplectic form $\sigma$ that is everywhere non-degenerate. A holomorphic Lagrangian fibration on a hyperkähler manifold $(M, \sigma)$ of complex dimension $2n$ is a surjective holomorphic map $\pi : M \to B$ with connected fibers onto a normal complex variety $B$ of dimension $n$ such that the smooth fibers of $\pi$ are Lagrangian with respect to $\sigma$ (equivalently, by results of Matsushita, the generic fiber is a complex torus of dimension $n$). A deformation of $M$ is a smooth proper holomorphic family $\mathcal{M} \to \Delta$ over a connected complex base $\Delta$ such that one fiber is biholomorphic to $M$; the other fibers are again hyperkähler manifolds.\n\nQuestion: Does every hyperkähler manifold $M$ admit a deformation $\mathcal{M} \to \Delta$ such that some fiber $M_t$ carries a holomorphic Lagrangian fibration?
status_search_result: This is the well-known hyperkähler SYZ conjecture, formulated independently by Tyurin, Bogomolov, Hassett–Tschinkel, Sawon, and Huybrechts. It remains open in general. Partial results are known: density/openness in Teichmüller space of deformations admitting Lagrangian fibrations under hypotheses on line bundles (Markman, Verbitsky, and others), positive answers for all known deformation types in a birational form, and verification for hyperkähler fourfolds in various cases. No general solution is known.

original_question: Let X be a hyperkahler manifold and let T subset X be a Lagrangian submanifold that is a complex torus. Must T occur as a fibre of a Lagrangian fibration X -> P^r, or at least of a birational model of such a fibration?
self_contained_problem:
Let $X$ be a compact hyperkähler manifold, that is, a simply connected compact Kähler manifold whose space of global holomorphic 2-forms is spanned by a single everywhere non-degenerate holomorphic symplectic form $\sigma$. A complex submanifold $T \subset X$ of dimension $\tfrac{1}{2}\dim_{\mathbb{C}} X$ is called Lagrangian if $\sigma|_T \equiv 0$. Suppose $T \subset X$ is a Lagrangian submanifold which, as a complex manifold, is biholomorphic to a complex torus.

(a) Must there exist a surjective holomorphic map $f : X \to \mathbb{P}^r$ with connected fibres (necessarily $r = \tfrac{1}{2}\dim_{\mathbb{C}} X$ and $f$ a Lagrangian fibration) such that $T$ is a fibre of $f$?

(b) If not, must there at least exist a compact hyperkähler manifold $X'$ bimeromorphic to $X$ and a surjective holomorphic Lagrangian fibration $X' \to \mathbb{P}^r$ for which (the proper transform of) $T$ appears as a fibre?
status_search_result: The question is partially resolved. Greb–Lehn–Rollenske (2011) settled the non-projective case affirmatively and, together with later work, established the existence of an almost holomorphic Lagrangian fibration in the projective case under additional hypotheses; Hwang–Weiss also addressed the projective setting producing an almost holomorphic Lagrangian fibration with fibre T. For hyperkähler fourfolds, a fully holomorphic Lagrangian fibration has been constructed. The general projective case in higher dimensions (existence of a holomorphic, not merely almost holomorphic/bimeromorphic, Lagrangian fibration) is not known to be fully resolved.

original_question: For a polarized K3 surface S of genus g, describe the general projective deformation of S[2], for some choice of polarization on S[2], or at least find more examples of locally complete projective families. Ask the same question for S[r] with r >= 3.
self_contained_problem:
Let $S$ be a smooth complex projective K3 surface, polarized by an ample line bundle $H$ with $H^2 = 2g-2$ for an integer $g \geq 2$ (so $S$ is a K3 surface of genus $g$). For an integer $r \geq 2$, let $S^{[r]}$ denote the Hilbert scheme of length-$r$ zero-dimensional subschemes of $S$; it is a smooth irreducible holomorphic symplectic (hyperkähler) variety of dimension $2r$ deformation-equivalent to the standard Hilbert scheme of points on a K3 surface.

A projective family $\pi : \mathcal{X} \to B$ of smooth $2r$-dimensional irreducible holomorphic symplectic varieties (with $B$ a smooth quasi-projective base) is called locally complete if for every $b \in B$ the Kodaira–Spencer map $T_b B \to H^1(\mathcal{X}_b, T_{\mathcal{X}_b})$ is surjective; equivalently, the family realizes an open subset of the moduli space of polarized hyperkähler manifolds of $K3^{[r]}$-type.

Address the following:

(a) For $r = 2$ and each $g \in \{2, 3, 4, \dots\}$, describe explicitly the general projective deformation of the Hilbert square $S^{[2]}$ of a polarized K3 surface of genus $g$, equipped with some natural choice of polarization on $S^{[2]}$. At minimum, exhibit further examples of locally complete projective families of hyperkähler fourfolds of $K3^{[2]}$-type beyond those previously known.

(b) Carry out the analogous task for $r \geq 3$: describe the general projective deformation of $S^{[r]}$ for polarized K3 surfaces $S$ (with appropriate choice of polarization on $S^{[r]}$), or at least produce more examples of locally complete projective families of hyperkähler $2r$-folds of $K3^{[r]}$-type.
category_tag: Hyperkähler manifolds and Hilbert schemes of K3 surfaces
status_search_result: The question remains an active research program. Further locally complete projective families of hyperkähler fourfolds of K3^[2]-type have been constructed since the question was posed (e.g., Debarre–Voisin twentyfolds and associated Hilbert-square models, and recent work giving projective models for Hilbert squares of K3 surfaces of genus 7 and 8 via Mukai models and degeneracy loci on homogeneous spaces). However, a complete description of the general projective deformation of S^[r] for arbitrary g and r ≥ 3 is not available; only partial results and isolated examples are known.

original_question: Let X be a projective hyperkahler manifold. If z in CH(X) is a Chow class that is a polynomial in divisor classes D1, ..., Dk from Pic(X) and in the Chern classes c_i(X), and if the cohomology class of z vanishes in H^*(X, Z), must z already vanish in the Chow ring?
self_contained_problem:
Let X be a projective hyperkähler manifold (i.e., a simply connected smooth projective complex variety such that H^0(X, Ω^2_X) is generated by an everywhere non-degenerate holomorphic 2-form). Let CH(X) denote the Chow ring of X with rational coefficients (or with integer coefficients), let Pic(X) ⊂ CH^1(X) be the Picard group, and let c_i(X) ∈ CH^i(X) denote the Chern classes of the tangent bundle of X. Let cl: CH(X) → H^*(X, Z) be the cycle class map.

Prove or disprove the following: for any divisor classes D_1, …, D_k ∈ Pic(X) and any class z ∈ CH(X) that can be written as a polynomial in D_1, …, D_k and the Chern classes c_i(X), if cl(z) = 0 in H^*(X, Z), then z = 0 in CH(X).

Equivalently, the restriction of cl to the subring of CH(X) generated by Pic(X) and the Chern classes c_i(X) is injective.
status_search_result: This is the Beauville–Voisin conjecture on the Chow ring of projective hyperkähler manifolds. It remains open in general but has been verified in numerous cases, including Hilbert schemes of points on K3 surfaces (in suitable ranges), generalized Kummer varieties, Fano varieties of lines on cubic fourfolds, LLSS eightfolds, and double EPW sextics.

original_question: Let X be a Fano complex manifold with a holomorphic Poisson structure, and for even s let X_{<=s} be the union of the loci X_k where the Poisson structure has rank k for k <= s. Must X_{<=s} contain a component of dimension greater than s?
self_contained_problem:
Let X be a Fano complex manifold (i.e., a smooth complex projective variety with ample anticanonical bundle), and let τ be a holomorphic Poisson structure on X, that is, a holomorphic bivector τ ∈ H^0(X, ∧²T_X) satisfying [τ,τ] = 0. The Poisson structure induces a skew-symmetric vector bundle map τ^♯ : Ω¹_X → T_X; for x ∈ X define the rank of τ at x to be rank τ^♯(x), which is necessarily an even integer. For each even integer k ≥ 0, set
   X_k := { x ∈ X : rk τ(x) = k },
so that X = ⨆_{k even} X_k. For an even integer s, let
   X_{≤s} := ⋃_{k ≤ s, k even} X_k,
the locus where τ has rank at most s.

Question: Must X_{≤s} contain an irreducible component of dimension strictly greater than s?
status_search_result: Known as Bondal's conjecture on degeneracy loci of Poisson structures on Fano manifolds. Polishchuk verified the conjecture in special cases (projective space, and the maximal nontrivial degeneracy locus when the Poisson structure has maximal generic rank). Gualtieri–Pym (2013) and later work (e.g., on flag varieties, and a 2026 note by Aza providing further evidence) establish partial results, but the full conjecture remains open.

original_question: Let X be a compact complex manifold with a holomorphic Poisson structure. If X_s, the locus where the Poisson structure has rank s, is non-empty, must it contain a component of dimension greater than s?
self_contained_problem:
Let $X$ be a compact complex manifold equipped with a holomorphic Poisson structure $\tau \in H^0(X, \wedge^2 TX)$. For each point $x \in X$, the bivector $\tau(x) \in \wedge^2 T_xX$ has a well-defined rank, which is necessarily an even integer. For each even integer $s \ge 0$, define the rank stratum
$$X_s := \{x \in X \mid \mathrm{rk}\,\tau(x) = s\},$$
so that $X = \bigsqcup_{s \text{ even}} X_s$.

Prove or disprove: whenever $X_s$ is non-empty, it contains an irreducible component of complex dimension strictly greater than $s$.
status_search_result: The conjecture (commonly attributed to Bondal, with refined formulations by Beauville, Polishchuk and Pym) that the rank-$s$ degeneracy locus of a holomorphic Poisson manifold contains a component of dimension $>s$ is known in several special cases—e.g., for Fano Poisson manifolds with rank $\le 2$ everywhere, for Fano $3$-folds and $4$-folds, for projective space, and for the maximal nontrivial degeneration locus when the rank is generically maximal—but the general statement remains open as of 2026, with recent works (Gualtieri–Pym 2013, Pym 2017, "A note on Bondal's conjecture" 2026, and the flag-variety case 2024) providing only partial progress.

original_question: Classify projective contact manifolds: is every projective contact manifold either the projectivized cotangent bundle P(T^*M) of a compact complex manifold M or the closed contact Fano orbit X_g associated with a simple complex Lie algebra g?
self_contained_problem:
A holomorphic contact structure on a complex manifold $X$ of dimension $2n+1$ is a corank-one holomorphic subbundle $F\subset TX$ such that the Frobenius (O'Neill) form $F\times F\to TX/F$, $(u,v)\mapsto [u,v]\bmod F$, is everywhere non-degenerate. A projective (compact, complex projective) manifold equipped with such a structure is called a projective contact manifold.

Two known classes of projective contact manifolds are:

(a) For any compact complex manifold $M$, the projectivized cotangent bundle $\mathbb{P}(T^*M)$ carries a canonical holomorphic contact structure given by the projectivization of the Liouville $1$-form.

(b) For any simple complex Lie algebra $\mathfrak{g}$, the adjoint group acts on $\mathbb{P}(\mathfrak{g})$ with a unique closed orbit $X_{\mathfrak{g}}$ (every other orbit contains $X_{\mathfrak{g}}$ in its closure). This $X_{\mathfrak{g}}$ is a contact Fano manifold (the adjoint variety of $\mathfrak{g}$).

Problem. Prove or disprove: every projective contact manifold is biholomorphic, as a contact manifold, either to $\mathbb{P}(T^*M)$ for some compact complex manifold $M$, or to the adjoint variety $X_{\mathfrak{g}}$ for some simple complex Lie algebra $\mathfrak{g}$.
status_search_result: The classification (LeBrun–Salamon conjecture) remains open in full generality. Partial results include verification for positive quaternion-Kähler manifolds of real dimension ≤ 16, contact Fano manifolds with Kähler–Einstein metric in dimension ≤ 9, and cases where the automorphism group has sufficiently high rank (Buczyński–Wiśniewski–Weber and others, 2018–2021).

original_question: Is every contact Fano manifold homogeneous?
self_contained_problem:
A complex contact manifold is a connected complex manifold $X$ of odd complex dimension $2n+1$ together with a corank-one holomorphic subbundle $D \subset TX$ such that the Frobenius (O'Neill) form $D \times D \to TX/D$ induced by the Lie bracket is everywhere non-degenerate. Equivalently, the line bundle $L := TX/D$ satisfies $K_X \cong L^{-(n+1)}$, and $X$ carries a holomorphic 1-form $\theta$ with values in $L$ whose differential is non-degenerate on $D$. The manifold $X$ is called Fano if it is projective and its anticanonical bundle $-K_X$ is ample; equivalently $L$ is ample.

A homogeneous complex contact Fano manifold is one on which a complex Lie group acts transitively by contact automorphisms; up to isomorphism such manifolds are exactly the closed orbits in the projectivizations of the adjoint representations of complex simple Lie groups (the so-called adjoint varieties).

Question: Is every contact Fano manifold homogeneous? That is, must every smooth Fano variety $X$ admitting a holomorphic contact structure be isomorphic to the adjoint variety of some complex simple Lie group?
status_search_result: The question is the algebraic-geometric form of the LeBrun–Salamon conjecture. It remains open in full generality. It has been verified in low dimensions (contact Fano manifolds of dimension at most 9, equivalently positive quaternion-Kähler manifolds of real dimension at most 16) and under various symmetry hypotheses, e.g. when the automorphism group is reductive of sufficiently high rank (work of Buczyński, Wiśniewski, Weber, Occhetta, Romano, Solá Conde, and others).

original_question: Are the only compact quaternion-Kahler manifolds with positive scalar curvature homogeneous?
self_contained_problem:
A Riemannian manifold $(M^{4n}, g)$ of real dimension $4n \geq 4$ is called a quaternion-Kähler manifold if its holonomy group is contained in $\mathrm{Sp}(n)\cdot \mathrm{Sp}(1) \subset \mathrm{SO}(4n)$. Equivalently, there exists a parallel rank-3 subbundle $\mathcal{Q} \subset \mathrm{End}(TM)$ that is locally spanned by three almost complex structures $I, J, K$ satisfying the quaternionic relations $I^2 = J^2 = K^2 = IJK = -\mathrm{Id}$, with $g$ Hermitian with respect to each. Such a manifold is automatically Einstein, so its scalar curvature is constant; assume this constant is positive. A homogeneous example is a Wolf space, i.e., a compact symmetric space of the form $G/(H\cdot \mathrm{Sp}(1))$ associated with a compact simple Lie group $G$; one such space exists for each compact simple $G$.

Prove or disprove: every compact quaternion-Kähler manifold with positive scalar curvature is homogeneous (equivalently, isometric to a Wolf space).
status_search_result: This is the well-known LeBrun–Salamon conjecture. It remains open in general. It has been verified in real dimension 4 (Hitchin), 8 (Poon–Salamon), and recently up to dimension 16. Active research continues, including a 2025 workshop devoted to the conjecture; no counterexamples are known.

paper_title: Open Problems in α Particle Condensation
context_brief: Experimental verification of the ¹⁶O condensate candidate
original_question: In ¹⁶O, is the sixth 0⁺ state at 15.1 MeV, about 700 keV above the four-α threshold, an α-particle condensate analogous to the Hoyle state, and can this be established experimentally through inelastic electromagnetic form factors and four-α coincidence measurements with invariant-mass reconstruction?
self_contained_problem:
Background and definitions. The Hoyle state is the second 0⁺ excited state of ¹²C (at about 7.65 MeV, just above the 3α threshold), which has been interpreted as a dilute, low-density configuration in which three α particles occupy a common lowest (0S) center-of-mass orbital — an "α-particle condensate." A natural generalization predicts that, in self-conjugate (N=Z) nuclei with mass number A=4n, an analogous nα condensate state should appear near the nα breakup threshold, characterized by (i) a strongly enhanced root-mean-square radius compared to the ground state, (ii) a large overlap with a product wave function of α particles in a common 0S orbit, and (iii) characteristic inelastic monopole transition strength to the ground state.

For ¹⁶O the four-α separation threshold lies at approximately 14.4 MeV of excitation, and the sixth 0⁺ state, denoted 0₆⁺, is observed near 15.1 MeV (about 700 keV above this threshold).

Problem. Determine, on the basis of nuclear structure theory and experiment, whether the 0₆⁺ state of ¹⁶O at ≈15.1 MeV is an α-particle condensate state — i.e. a four-α analogue of the Hoyle state in which the four α clusters predominantly occupy a common 0S orbit with a dilute, gas-like spatial distribution. In particular:

(a) Establish whether this state exhibits the dilute, large-radius structure predicted by the α-condensate hypothesis, for instance through the inelastic electromagnetic (monopole) form factor measured in (e,e′) scattering and through analyses of α + ¹²C and α + ¹⁶O elastic/inelastic scattering sensitive to its radius.

(b) Establish whether a four-α coincidence measurement of its decay, with full invariant-mass reconstruction of the 4α final state, reveals decay patterns (e.g. dominance of channels passing through the Hoyle state of ¹²C, or simultaneous/sequential α emission consistent with a condensate) that confirm or refute its identification as a 4α condensate analogue of the Hoyle state.
status_search_result: The question remains open and contested. Subsequent analyses of α+¹⁶O elastic and inelastic scattering did not confirm the predicted enhanced radius of the 0₆⁺ state at 15.1 MeV, weakening the condensate interpretation, while dedicated 4α coincidence/breakup searches over the past two decades have so far been unsuccessful or inconclusive. More recent work has identified narrow resonances just above 15.1 MeV decaying via α + ¹²C(Hoyle), suggesting Hoyle-like structure may instead lie above the 0₆⁺ state. No definitive experimental verification or refutation of the condensate nature of the 15.1 MeV 0₆⁺ state has been established.

paper_title: Open Problems in α Particle Condensation
context_brief: Cluster spectrum of ¹⁶O near 15–18 MeV
original_question: What cluster structures occur in ¹⁶O in the 15–18 MeV excitation-energy range, including possible excited states built on an α condensate and the known rotational band with I = 0⁺, 2⁺, 4⁺, and 6⁺ and a very large moment of inertia?
self_contained_problem:
In the nucleus ¹⁶O, consider the excitation-energy interval 15–18 MeV, which lies in the vicinity of the four-α-particle disintegration threshold. A rotational band is known in this region with members of spin-parity I^π = 0⁺, 2⁺, 4⁺, 6⁺ and an unusually large moment of inertia, whose band head sits near 15–17 MeV.

Determine, for the cluster spectrum of ¹⁶O in the 15–18 MeV excitation range:

(a) The full set of cluster configurations realized by the eigenstates in this window, including possible α + ¹²C molecular configurations and 4α-type configurations.

(b) Whether one or more of these states can be interpreted as excited states of a four-α Bose–Einstein condensate (i.e. states in which four α-particles predominantly occupy a common 0S-like single-particle orbit), and if so identify their excitation energies, spins, and microscopic structure.

(c) The precise excitation energies, spins, widths, and intrinsic deformation of all members of the observed rotational band with I^π = 0⁺, 2⁺, 4⁺, 6⁺ and large moment of inertia near 17 MeV, together with a microscopic cluster-model interpretation that explains the magnitude of the moment of inertia.

Provide either a microscopic many-body / cluster-model derivation or a definitive experimental determination of the cluster content of every level of ¹⁶O in this energy interval.
category_tag: Nuclear cluster structure and α-particle condensation
status_search_result: Subsequent theoretical and experimental work has identified candidate band members (e.g., 0⁺ at 15.1 MeV proposed as a 4α condensate-like state, and 2⁺(16.95), 2⁺(17.15), 4⁺(18.05), 6⁺(19.35) observed via ¹²C(α,⁸Be)), and α+¹²C molecular bands have been computed with predicted heads near 16.6 MeV. However, a definitive microscopic identification of all cluster states in the 15–18 MeV window and unambiguous confirmation of excited α-condensate states remains under active investigation, so the problem is partially solved.

paper_title: Open Problems in α Particle Condensation
context_brief: Hoyle-like α-gas states in heavier A = 4n nuclei
original_question: Which heavier self-conjugate A = 4n nuclei beyond ¹²C, such as ²⁰Ne, ²⁴Mg, ²⁸Si, or ⁴⁰Ca, possess dilute α-gas condensate states near their nα disintegration thresholds, and can experiments excite and identify them through large-amplitude breathing modes or soft Coulomb-explosion modes?
self_contained_problem:
Background. In nuclear physics, a self-conjugate A = 4n nucleus is one composed of n protons and n neutrons grouped into n α-particle units (so A = 4n with equal proton and neutron numbers). The Hoyle state of ¹²C, an excited 0⁺ state lying just above the 3α breakup threshold at about 7.65 MeV, has been interpreted as a dilute, weakly interacting "α-particle condensate": a state in which three α clusters occupy, with high probability, a common 0S single-particle orbital, forming a Bose–Einstein-like condensate of α particles. The nα disintegration (Ikeda) threshold for a self-conjugate A = 4n nucleus is the minimum energy required to dissociate it into n free α particles; for ²⁰Ne, ²⁴Mg, ²⁸Si, and ⁴⁰Ca it is approximately 19.17, 28.48, 38.46, and 45.4 MeV respectively.

Problem. For the self-conjugate A = 4n nuclei with n ≥ 4 (in particular ²⁰Ne (n=5), ²⁴Mg (n=6), ²⁸Si (n=7), and ⁴⁰Ca (n=10)):

(a) Determine which of these nuclei admit an excited 0⁺ "α-gas" eigenstate near the nα disintegration threshold whose intrinsic structure is well approximated by n α-particles condensed in a common 0S-like orbital (an analog of the Hoyle state).

(b) Identify a feasible experimental excitation mechanism — for example a large-amplitude monopole "breathing" mode or, when the Coulomb barrier vanishes for sufficiently large n (expected around n = 8–10), a coherent "soft Coulomb explosion" decay into n α particles — by which such condensate states could be populated and uniquely identified.

In particular, decide whether a 10α condensate state of ⁴⁰Ca exists and can in principle be observed via dissociation into 10 α particles.
status_search_result: As of 2023–2024, a candidate 5α condensate state in ²⁰Ne has been reported around ~22 MeV excitation, providing the first experimental evidence beyond ¹²C. For ²⁴Mg, a peak near ~34 MeV in 4α-decay events is consistent with predictions but not firmly identified as a condensate. For ²⁸Si and ⁴⁰Ca no condensate states have been experimentally identified; α-penetrability suppresses the n-α decay channel, so the question for n ≥ 6 (and especially ⁴⁰Ca → 10α) remains open.

paper_title: Open Problems in α Particle Condensation
context_brief: α condensates on inert nuclear cores
original_question: Can excited nuclei made of an inert core plus several α clusters, such as ³²S* = ¹⁶O + 4α or ⁵²Fe* = ⁴⁰Ca + 3α, host α-particle condensates, and what clear experimental fingerprint would verify such condensates?
self_contained_problem:
Consider an excited nucleus modeled as an inert doubly-closed-shell core plus several α-particles weakly bound on top of it (a "core + nα" system). Concrete examples of interest are
  ³²S* = ¹⁶O (core) + 4α,   and   ⁵²Fe* = ⁴⁰Ca (core) + 3α.
An α-particle condensate on top of a core is, by definition, a state in which the nα valence α-clusters preserve their internal structure and occupy, with high probability, a single 0S-like center-of-mass orbital in the mean field generated by the core (analogously to the THSR-type description of the Hoyle state in ¹²C as a 3α condensate, generalized to include an inert core).

Problem: 
(a) Determine whether such core + nα α-particle condensate states exist as identifiable excited states of nuclei such as ³²S* = ¹⁶O + 4α and ⁵²Fe* = ⁴⁰Ca + 3α; in particular, decide whether near the nα-decay threshold (above the core) there is an excited 0⁺ state whose dominant component is well approximated by an α-condensate wave function of the form
  Ψ ∝ A{ φ_core · ∏_{i=1}^{n} φ_α(i) · exp(−Σ_i (R_i − R_core)²/(2B²)) }
with a large extension parameter B compared to ordinary shell-model states.
(b) Identify a clear and experimentally accessible fingerprint that would unambiguously distinguish such a core + nα condensate from non-condensed cluster or shell-model excitations (for example: enhanced α-decay widths, anomalously large monopole transition strengths, characteristic n-α momentum/angular correlations, large radii, or specific reaction cross-section signatures), and verify the prediction experimentally.
status_search_result: Reviews on nuclear α-particle condensation (e.g., the 2017 review on alpha clusters and their condensation) and recent experimental work (such as the 2023 identification of a 5α condensate candidate in ²⁰Ne) indicate continuing theoretical interest in core + nα condensates, but no clear experimental fingerprint has been established for systems like ³²S* = ¹⁶O + 4α or ⁵²Fe* = ⁴⁰Ca + 3α. The question of unambiguous experimental verification of α-condensates on top of an inert core therefore remains open.

paper_title: Open Problems in α Particle Condensation
original_question: Do linear α-chain states exist as physical nuclear cluster states, and if they do, are their α clusters arranged in quasi-rigid Brink configurations with fixed inter-cluster distances or delocalized along the line as one-dimensional condensate-like systems?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a nucleus consisting of N alpha particles (4He clusters), modeled as a system of N composite bosons interacting via an effective nucleon-nucleon force. Two competing microscopic descriptions of a "linear alpha-chain state" are proposed:

(i) A Brink-type wave function in which the centers of the N alpha clusters are localized at equally spaced fixed points along a common axis, so that the chain behaves as a quasi-rigid one-dimensional arrangement with well-defined inter-cluster distances.

(ii) A delocalized one-dimensional condensate-type wave function (of Tohsaki-Horiuchi-Schuck-Röpke type, restricted to one spatial direction) in which all N alpha clusters occupy the same single-particle orbital extended along the axis, allowing the clusters to move freely along the line, in analogy with a one-dimensional Bose system in the Tonks-Girardeau regime.

Address the following:

(a) Do linear alpha-chain states exist as genuine physical nuclear cluster states (e.g., as resonances or near-threshold states in nuclei such as 12C, 16O, and heavier 4N nuclei)?

(b) If such states exist, determine which of the two descriptions (i) or (ii) is realized: are the alpha clusters arranged in a quasi-rigid Brink configuration with fixed inter-cluster spacings, or are they delocalized along the line as a one-dimensional condensate-like (Tonks-Girardeau-like) system?
status_search_result: Subsequent work has provided substantial evidence supporting both the existence of linear alpha-chain states and a delocalized (condensate-like) character. A 2014 PRL by Suhara, Funaki, Zhou, Horiuchi, and Tohsaki showed that linear-chain states in 12C and 16O constructed by superposing many Brink wave functions have nearly 100% overlap with a single THSR (one-dimensional condensate) wave function, supporting picture (ii) over the rigid Brink picture. More recent work (e.g., the 2023 Nature Communications report on the 5α condensate in 20Ne, and reviews of cluster models and α condensation) continues to develop the picture, but a fully definitive experimental confirmation of all linear-chain candidates remains open.

paper_title: Open Problems in α Particle Condensation
original_question: Does the short-range α–α repulsion remain dynamically active in a linear chain configuration of three or more α clusters, given that α clusters in such a one-dimensional condensate may behave as hard-core bosons?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a one-dimensional ("linear chain") configuration of N ≥ 3 α particles (i.e., ⁴He nuclei treated as compact bosonic clusters), modeled as a low-density Bose system in which the α clusters are taken to behave as hard-core bosons (each cluster excluding the others from its spatial location, so that in 1D they cannot pass one another). Independently of this hard-core constraint, two α particles in free space are known to interact via a potential whose low-energy s-wave part contains a strong short-range repulsive component (in addition to a longer-range attractive tail), reflecting the underlying Pauli antisymmetrization of the eight constituent nucleons.

Question: In the linear chain configuration of three or more α clusters, does this short-range α–α repulsion (beyond what is already enforced by the hard-core/impenetrability condition in 1D) remain dynamically active and produce observable effects on the many-body ground state and excitations, or is it effectively rendered inert by the hard-core structure of the 1D condensate?

Determine whether the residual short-range α–α repulsion contributes nontrivially to the energetics and correlations of an N-α linear-chain state, and quantify its effect.
status_search_result: No specific source addressing whether the short-range α–α repulsion remains dynamically active in a linear chain of three or more α clusters was located. General results on 1D hard-core bosons exist but do not directly resolve this nuclear-physics question, so the status remains unverified.

paper_title: Open Problems in α Particle Condensation
original_question: In neutron-rich linear-chain nuclei such as ¹⁶C, do extra neutrons stabilize α-chain geometries while partly or completely preventing α condensation among the α clusters?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a neutron-rich light nucleus modeled as a linear chain of three α particles (each α being a tightly bound spin–isospin-zero cluster of two protons and two neutrons) supplemented by additional valence neutrons localized between or around the α clusters; the prototypical case is ¹⁶C, viewed as three α's plus four valence neutrons. By "α condensation" one means a state in which all α clusters occupy a common 0S single-α orbital, in analogy with the bosonic condensate proposed for the Hoyle state of ¹²C (the THSR-type α-condensate wave function). 

Determine the following: in such neutron-rich linear α-chain configurations, do the extra valence neutrons (i) stabilize the linear-chain geometry of the α clusters against bending and dissociation, while simultaneously (ii) hindering—either partially or completely—the formation of an α-condensate among the α clusters? In particular, decide whether one can have a regime in which a stable α-chain structure coexists with a substantial reduction or total suppression of α-condensate character, and quantify the degree to which the presence of valence neutrons between α clusters destroys condensate occupancy of the lowest single-α 0S orbital.
status_search_result: Cluster-model studies (Itagaki et al. and follow-ups, plus AMD/covariant density functional analyses) provide evidence that valence neutrons in σ orbitals stabilize three-α linear-chain configurations in neutron-rich carbon isotopes such as ¹⁶C, ¹⁴C and ²⁰C, and recent experiments report chain-like resonances in ¹⁴C. paper_title: Open Problems in α Particle Condensation
context_brief: Existence and stability of α rings
original_question: Are α-particle ring configurations, such as a six-α ring in ²⁴Mg or an eight-α ring in ³²S, real nuclear cluster states after correcting mean-field artifacts, and when are rings more stable than chains as the number of α particles changes?
self_contained_problem:
Within nuclear cluster physics, model an even-even self-conjugate nucleus consisting of N alpha particles by a microscopic mean-field-type wave function (e.g., a Hartree–Fock or Tohsaki–Horiuchi–Schuck–Röpke type ansatz) at sufficiently low average density, in which the alpha particles localize at definite spatial positions. Two natural geometric arrangements are: (i) a planar regular ring, in which the N alpha clusters sit at the vertices of a regular N-gon, and (ii) a linear chain, in which the N alpha clusters are aligned along a common axis.

After projecting out spurious center-of-mass motion of the individual alpha particles (so as to remove mean-field artifacts), address the following:

1. Do ring configurations of alpha particles correspond to genuine intrinsic nuclear cluster states? In particular, is a six-alpha planar ring a real cluster configuration of ²⁴Mg, and is an eight-alpha planar ring a real cluster configuration of ³²S?

2. As a function of the number N of alpha particles, determine for which N the ring configuration is energetically more stable than the linear chain configuration of the same N alpha particles, and for which N the chain is more stable.

Provide either a proof of existence/stability of these ring states as resonant intrinsic configurations of the corresponding nuclei, or rigorous criteria, in terms of N and the inter-alpha effective interaction, that decide ring-versus-chain stability.
status_search_result: Recent reviews on nuclear clustering (2023–2024) continue to discuss alpha ring/chain configurations in light self-conjugate nuclei such as ²⁴Mg and ³²S as predicted but not experimentally established structures, with the relative stability of rings versus chains depending on N and on shell effects. paper_title: Open Problems in α Particle Condensation
context_brief: Hoyle analogues with extra neutrons or tritons
original_question: Do Hoyle-analogue cluster-gas states exist in non-self-conjugate nuclei with A ≠ 4n, for example ¹³C made of three α clusters plus one valence neutron or ¹¹B made of two α clusters plus one triton, and how do the extra neutrons or tritons alter the condensate character?
self_contained_problem:
Background and setup. In nuclear cluster physics, the Hoyle state of ¹²C is interpreted as a dilute gas-like state of three α particles, each occupying the lowest 0S single-cluster orbit, and is regarded as a finite-size analogue of an α-particle Bose–Einstein condensate. This picture is described, for example, by the Tohsaki–Horiuchi–Schuck–Röpke (THSR) wave function, in which all α clusters share a common 0S center-of-mass orbit near the cluster disintegration threshold.

Problem. For non-self-conjugate light nuclei with mass number A ≠ 4n, consider cluster-gas configurations consisting of α particles together with one or more additional valence nucleons or light clusters (neutrons, deuterons, tritons), all occupying their respective 0S orbits, located near the corresponding cluster disintegration threshold. Two prototype cases are:

(i) ¹³C, modeled as a four-body cluster system of three α particles plus one valence neutron (3α + n);
(ii) ¹¹B, modeled as a three-body cluster system of two α particles plus one triton (2α + t).

Determine:

(a) Whether such Hoyle-analogue cluster-gas states actually exist as resonant states (or near-threshold states) in the spectra of these A ≠ 4n nuclei, and if so, identify their quantum numbers Jπ, excitation energies, and widths;

(b) In what manner the presence of the extra valence neutron (in ¹³C) or triton (in ¹¹B) modifies the α-condensate character of the Hoyle state, in particular how it affects the diluteness, the single-cluster 0S occupation, the bosonic-condensate fraction, and the rms radius compared with the pure (0Sα)³ Hoyle configuration in ¹²C.

Provide criteria distinguishing genuine Hoyle-analogue (cluster-gas) states from ordinary cluster resonances in these systems.
status_search_result: Subsequent theoretical and experimental work has addressed Hoyle-analogue candidates in non-self-conjugate nuclei. Microscopic cluster-model and THSR-extended studies (e.g., Phys. Rev. C 98, 024325 (2018) on systematic Hoyle-analog states; α+α+t and 3α+n calculations for ¹¹B and ¹³C; recent 2024–2025 work on ¹³C 1/2⁻ resonances and a Hoyle-analog state in ¹³N) have proposed candidate states and analyzed how a valence neutron/triton perturbs the α-condensate character. However, definitive experimental confirmation of pure Hoyle-analogue cluster-gas states in ¹³C and ¹¹B, and a fully settled quantitative description of how extra nucleons alter the condensate, remain under active investigation. The problem is therefore best classified as partially solved.

paper_title: Open Problems in α Particle Condensation
context_brief: Wave-function description of neutron-rich Hoyle analogues
original_question: For ¹⁰Be-like systems with two α clusters and two valence neutrons, especially when the neutrons occupy a π orbit, is a fixed-cluster Brink wave function or a delocalized Tohsaki-Horiuchi-Schuck-Röpke (THSR) wave function more appropriate for a gas-like Hoyle analogue, and can the extra neutrons themselves occupy loosely bound 0S orbits without strongly disturbing α condensation?
self_contained_problem:
Consider an A=10 nuclear system consisting of two α clusters (each α being a tightly bound 4-nucleon S-wave configuration) plus two extra valence neutrons placed in a π molecular orbital around the two α cores (a ¹⁰Be-like configuration). Two candidate microscopic many-body trial wave functions are considered for describing a possible "gas-like" Hoyle-analogue excited state of this system:

(i) A Brink cluster wave function, in which the α clusters are localized Gaussian wave packets centered at fixed spatial positions R₁, R₂ (with R₁, R₂ subsequently projected onto good angular momentum), and the two valence neutrons are attached to the α centers in molecular-orbital fashion;

(ii) A Tohsaki–Horiuchi–Schuck–Röpke (THSR) wave function, in which each α cluster moves in a common delocalized 0S-like center-of-mass Gaussian of large width B (the α condensate ansatz), antisymmetrized over all nucleons:
   Ψ_THSR ∝ A { exp(−Σ_i (X_i² / B²)) · φ(α₁) φ(α₂) · χ_{2n} },
where X_i is the c.m. coordinate of the i-th α and φ(α) is its intrinsic 0s⁴ wave function, and χ_{2n} is a wave function for the two valence neutrons.

Determine:
(a) Which of the two ansätze (Brink-type localized cluster vs. delocalized THSR) gives a more appropriate description of a gas-like, weakly-bound, dilute Hoyle-analogue state of this 2α+2n system when the two neutrons occupy a π orbit around the α–α axis;
(b) Whether such a Hoyle-analogue state can be realized in which the two valence neutrons themselves occupy loosely bound 0S-type single-particle orbits in the dilute α-gas without significantly disturbing the α-particle condensate built from the two α clusters.
category_tag: Nuclear cluster wave functions / α-particle condensation
status_search_result: Subsequent work has extended THSR-type wave functions to neutron-rich systems including 10Be and to nuclei with valence nucleons (e.g., extensions including spin-orbit and pairing in A=10 nuclei), and reviews on α-condensation continue to discuss Hoyle analogues. However, no source definitively settles which ansatz (Brink vs. THSR) is more appropriate for a gas-like 10Be Hoyle analogue with π-orbit neutrons, nor confirms that valence neutrons occupy 0S orbits without disturbing the condensate. The question appears to remain open / partially explored.

paper_title: Open Problems in α Particle Condensation
original_question: Can nuclear structures that are stabilized by adding many neutrons to Hoyle-like, chain, or ring configurations still exhibit α-condensation aspects, despite Pauli-principle effects that may hinder formation of Hoyle-like states?
self_contained_problem:
Background and setup. In nuclear physics, an "α-particle condensate" refers to a low-density nuclear state in which N α-clusters (each a tightly bound 4-nucleon subunit of two protons and two neutrons) predominantly occupy a single 0S center-of-mass orbital, in analogy with Bose–Einstein condensation. The Hoyle state, identified with the second 0⁺ excited state of ¹²C at about 7.65 MeV, is the prototypical example: a dilute three-α state interpreted as a 3α condensate. Higher analogues ("Hoyle-like states") are conjectured to occur in self-conjugate nα nuclei such as ¹⁶O, ²⁰Ne, …, and exotic geometric arrangements of the α-clusters such as linear α-chains and planar α-rings have also been proposed.

Consider now nuclei obtained from such reference α-cluster configurations (Hoyle-like nα states, α-chains, or α-rings) by adding extra neutrons. In chain and ring geometries, neutron pairs placed between adjacent α-links can stabilize the geometric arrangement against breakup, but the Pauli exclusion principle, applied to the additional valence neutrons together with the nucleons inside the α-clusters, is expected to suppress the spatial overlap of the α-clusters with a single common 0S orbital and hence to hinder formation of a true Hoyle-like condensate.

Question. Determine whether nuclear bound or resonant states constructed by adding many extra neutrons to a Hoyle-like nα configuration, to a linear α-chain, or to a planar α-ring (where the added neutrons may stabilize the underlying α-skeleton) can still exhibit genuine α-particle condensation features — for instance, a dominant occupation of the lowest 0S orbital by the α-clusters and the associated dilute, weakly antisymmetrized α-cluster wave function — despite the Pauli-principle suppression induced by the additional neutrons. Identify the conditions on neutron number and geometry under which such α-condensation aspects survive, and quantify them through appropriate observables (e.g. α-cluster occupation numbers, cluster form factors, or Tohsaki–Horiuchi–Schuck–Röpke-type overlaps).
status_search_result: The question of whether neutron-rich extensions of Hoyle-like, chain, and ring α-cluster configurations retain α-condensation features remains an active research topic. Recent works (e.g. on α-clustering in dilute neutron-rich matter, the 5α condensate in ²⁰Ne, and reviews on the Hoyle family) continue to investigate the interplay between added neutrons, Pauli blocking, and α-condensation, but no definitive answer has been established for the general case posed here.

paper_title: Open Problems in α Particle Condensation
original_question: In compact-star matter or infinite nuclear matter with non-negligible α-particle mass fractions at certain density, temperature, and asymmetry ranges, do the α particles form a condensate?
self_contained_problem:
Consider infinite asymmetric nuclear matter (a uniform medium of neutrons and protons in thermal equilibrium) at finite temperature $T$, baryon number density $\rho$, and isospin asymmetry $\delta = (\rho_n - \rho_p)/\rho$, in regions of the $(\rho, T, \delta)$ parameter space relevant to the interior of compact stars where calculations indicate a non-negligible mass fraction of $\alpha$ clusters (bound four-nucleon states with quantum numbers of $^4\mathrm{He}$, treated as composite bosons).

Determine whether, in such phases, the $\alpha$ particles undergo Bose–Einstein condensation, i.e. whether there exists a macroscopically occupied zero-momentum bosonic mode for the $\alpha$-particle degree of freedom, and, if so, characterize the region of the $(\rho, T, \delta)$ parameter space in which this condensation occurs, taking into account in-medium effects (Pauli blocking, self-energy shifts, and Mott dissociation of the $\alpha$ cluster).
