original_question: Prove that every visibility graph of a point set with clique number omega(G) <= 4 has chromatic number chi(G) <= 5.
self_contained_problem:
Let $P \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ be a finite set of points in general position (no three collinear can be assumed when convenient, but more generally $P$ may be any finite point set). The visibility graph $G = G(P)$ of $P$ is the simple graph whose vertex set is $P$ and in which two distinct points $p, q \in P$ are joined by an edge if and only if the open line segment $pq$ contains no point of $P$. For a graph $G$, let $\omega(G)$ denote its clique number (the size of a largest complete subgraph) and $\chi(G)$ its chromatic number (the minimum number of colours needed for a proper vertex colouring).

Decide whether the following statement is true: for every finite point set $P$ in the plane, if $\omega(G(P)) \le 4$ then $\chi(G(P)) \le 5$. Either prove the implication, or exhibit a finite point set $P$ with $\omega(G(P)) \le 4$ and $\chi(G(P)) \ge 6$.

A point visibility graph with clique number 4 and chromatic number 6 has been constructed (Pach–Tóth-style / "On colouring point visibility graphs" by Diwan and others), so the original "prove χ ≤ 5 when ω ≤ 4" statement is false. Related results also show 5-colourability is NP-complete while 4-colourability is polynomial, but the broader question of whether χ is bounded by a function of ω for point visibility graphs remains open.

paper_title: Unsolved Problems in Visibility Graphs of Points, Segments and Polygons
original_question: For integers k >= 2 and ell >= 2, every sufficiently large planar point set should contain either ell collinear points or k mutually visible points. Prove this in the remaining open cases k = 6 or ell = 4.
self_contained_problem:
Let P be a finite set of points in the Euclidean plane. Two points p, q ∈ P are said to be mutually visible (with respect to P) if the open line segment joining p and q contains no other point of P. A subset S ⊆ P is called a visibility clique if every pair of points in S is mutually visible. A subset T ⊆ P is called collinear if all points of T lie on a common line.

Conjecture (Big-Line-Big-Clique): For every pair of integers k ≥ 2 and ℓ ≥ 2, there exists an integer N(k, ℓ) such that every set P of at least N(k, ℓ) points in the plane contains either ℓ collinear points or a visibility clique of size k.

Prove this conjecture in each of the following remaining cases:
(a) k = 6 (with ℓ ≥ 4 arbitrary), and
(b) ℓ = 4 (with k ≥ 6 arbitrary).

(It is already known that the conjecture holds whenever k ≤ 5 or ℓ ≤ 3.)
status_search_result: The big-line-big-clique conjecture remains open for finite planar point sets in all cases with k ≥ 6 and ℓ ≥ 4. Known partial results confirm the conjecture for k ≤ 5 (Kára–Pór–Wood proved k = 4; Abel et al. proved k = 5) and for ℓ ≤ 3. A strengthened "visible islands" variant was disproved in 2022 by Leuchtner–Nicolás–Suk, and the infinite version is also known to be false, but the original finite conjecture in the cases k = 6 or ℓ = 4 is still unresolved as of recent surveys.

original_question: Let b(P) be the minimum size of a blocking set Q for a finite point set P in general position, and let b(n) be the minimum of b(P) over all n-point sets with no three points collinear. Prove that b(n)/n tends to infinity as n tends to infinity.

Let P be a finite set of points in the plane in general position (no three collinear). A blocking set for P is a finite set Q of points in the plane, disjoint from P, such that for every pair of distinct points p, p' in P the open segment pp' contains at least one point of Q (equivalently, Q meets every line segment determined by two points of P, in its relative interior). Note that the points of Q themselves need not be in general position with respect to P.

Define b(P) to be the minimum cardinality of a blocking set for P, and define

Prove or disprove: b(n)/n → ∞ as n → ∞.

paper_title: Unsolved Problems in Visibility Graphs of Points, Segments and Polygons
original_question: Is every n-vertex graph representable by an obstacle representation that uses only O(n) polygonal obstacles, where vertices are points in the plane and two vertices are adjacent exactly when the segment joining the corresponding points avoids every obstacle?
self_contained_problem:
An obstacle representation of a simple graph $G=(V,E)$ consists of an injective placement of the vertices of $G$ as points in the Euclidean plane $\mathbb{R}^2$ together with a finite collection of pairwise disjoint simple polygons (called obstacles), none of which contains any vertex point, such that for any two vertices $u,v \in V$, the open straight line segment joining the points representing $u$ and $v$ is disjoint from every obstacle if and only if $\{u,v\} \in E$. The obstacle number $\mathrm{obs}(G)$ is the minimum number of obstacles in any obstacle representation of $G$.

Question: Does there exist an absolute constant $C>0$ such that every simple graph $G$ on $n$ vertices admits an obstacle representation using at most $Cn$ obstacles, i.e., is $\mathrm{obs}(G) = O(n)$?

original_question: Does every planar graph have obstacle number 1?
self_contained_problem:

original_question: Given the adjacency matrix of a graph G, determine whether there exists a set S of pairwise disjoint line segments in the plane whose segment visibility graph is G, where vertices correspond to segment endpoints and two endpoints are adjacent when the segment joining them avoids all segments of S, with the two endpoints of each original segment also adjacent.

The segment visibility graph $G(S)$ is the simple graph whose vertex set is the set of $2n$ endpoints of the segments in $S$, and in which two distinct endpoints $p$ and $q$ are joined by an edge if and only if either:
(i) $p$ and $q$ are the two endpoints of the same segment $s_i \in S$, or
(ii) the open line segment $\overline{pq}$ does not intersect any segment of $S$ (so $p$ sees $q$).

Design an algorithm that, given as input a finite simple graph $G$ specified by its adjacency matrix, decides whether there exists a set $S$ of pairwise disjoint line segments in $\mathbb{R}^2$ such that $G \cong G(S)$. self_contained_problem:

original_question: For k >= 5, determine whether there exist (2k + 2)-regular bar k-visibility graphs.
self_contained_problem:
A bar representation is a finite collection of pairwise disjoint horizontal closed line segments ("bars") in the plane, no two of which lie on the same horizontal line. For a nonnegative integer k, the bar k-visibility graph of such a representation has the bars as its vertices, and two bars u and v are adjacent if and only if there exists a vertical open line segment that joins a point of u to a point of v and that meets the interiors of at most k other bars. A graph is called a bar k-visibility graph if it can be realized as the bar k-visibility graph of some bar representation. A graph is r-regular if every vertex has degree r.

For each integer k ≥ 5, determine whether there exists a (2k+2)-regular bar k-visibility graph.
status_search_result: The problem appears still open. Literature on bar k-visibility graphs establishes that any regular bar k-visibility graph of degree less than 2k+2 must be complete, and (2k+2)-regular non-complete examples are known for small k (k ≤ 4), but no resolution for k ≥ 5 is reported in subsequent works.

original_question: Determine whether there exist d-regular bar k-visibility graphs with degree d >= 2k + 3.
self_contained_problem:
Let k be a nonnegative integer. A bar k-visibility representation of a graph G consists of an assignment of pairwise disjoint horizontal closed line segments ("bars") in the plane to the vertices of G such that two vertices u, v are adjacent in G if and only if there exists a vertical open line segment ("sightline") whose endpoints lie on the bars assigned to u and v and which crosses at most k other bars (no two bars are allowed to be collinear). A graph is called a bar k-visibility graph if it admits such a representation. A graph is d-regular if every vertex has degree exactly d.

Question: For which integers k ≥ 0 and d ≥ 2k + 3 does there exist a d-regular bar k-visibility graph? In particular, do there exist any d-regular bar k-visibility graphs with d ≥ 2k + 3?

paper_title: Unsolved Problems in Visibility Graphs of Points, Segments and Polygons
context_brief: Chromatic number of bar k-visibility graphs
original_question: Improve the current upper bound 6k + 6 on the chromatic number of a bar k-visibility graph.
self_contained_problem: A bar representation is a finite collection $\mathcal{B} = \{b_1, \ldots, b_n\}$ of pairwise disjoint horizontal closed line segments (bars) in the plane, with all bars lying on distinct horizontal lines. For a nonnegative integer $k$, the bar $k$-visibility graph of $\mathcal{B}$ is the graph $G$ on vertex set $\{b_1, \ldots, b_n\}$ in which two bars $b_i$ and $b_j$ are adjacent if and only if there exists a vertical open line segment $s$ with one endpoint on $b_i$ and the other endpoint on $b_j$ such that $s$ intersects the interiors of at most $k$ other bars in $\mathcal{B}$. A graph is called a bar $k$-visibility graph if it is isomorphic to the bar $k$-visibility graph of some such bar representation. The chromatic number $\chi(G)$ of a graph $G$ is the least integer $c$ such that the vertices of $G$ can be properly colored with $c$ colors. It is known that every bar $k$-visibility graph $G$ satisfies $\chi(G) \le 6k+6$. Determine whether this bound can be improved: that is, find the smallest function $f(k)$ such that $\chi(G) \le f(k)$ holds for every bar $k$-visibility graph $G$, and in particular establish an upper bound strictly smaller than $6k+6$ for general $k \ge 1$.
status_search_result: A search reveals follow-up work improving related parameters (e.g., the thickness upper bound for bar $k$-visibility graphs has been reduced from $2k(9k-1)$ to $6k$, and a chromatic bound of 12 has been shown for bar 1-visibility graphs), but no source verifies a general improvement of the $6k+6$ chromatic upper bound for arbitrary $k$. The problem appears to remain open.

paper_title: Unsolved Problems in Visibility Graphs of Points, Segments and Polygons
original_question: The thickness of a bar k-visibility graph is known to be at most 2k(9k - 1). Improve this upper bound.
self_contained_problem:
A horizontal bar is a non-degenerate closed line segment in the plane parallel to the x-axis. A bar layout is a finite collection B = {b_1, ..., b_n} of pairwise disjoint horizontal bars whose interiors lie on distinct horizontal lines. For a fixed nonnegative integer k, the bar k-visibility graph G(B) of such a layout has vertex set B, with two bars b_i and b_j adjacent if and only if there exists a vertical open line segment s connecting a point of b_i to a point of b_j such that the relative interior of s meets the interiors of at most k other bars in B. A graph G is called a bar k-visibility graph if it is isomorphic to G(B) for some bar layout B.

The thickness θ(G) of a graph G is the minimum number of planar subgraphs into which the edge set of G can be partitioned. Define T(k) to be the supremum of θ(G) over all bar k-visibility graphs G.

It is known that T(k) ≤ 2k(9k − 1) for every k ≥ 1. Improve this upper bound: determine the smallest possible function f(k) such that T(k) ≤ f(k) for all k ≥ 1, or otherwise establish a stronger asymptotic upper bound on T(k).
status_search_result: Subsequent work has improved the upper bound on the thickness of bar k-visibility graphs from 2k(9k − 1) to 6k, and established a lower bound of k + 1, using techniques analogous to those of Felsner and Massow for semi-bar k-visibility graphs. The exact maximum thickness remains undetermined, so the problem is partially solved.

paper_title: Unsolved Problems in Visibility Graphs of Points, Segments and Polygons
context_brief: Crossing numbers of bar k-visibility graphs
original_question: What is the largest possible crossing number of a bar k-visibility graph?
self_contained_problem:
A bar k-visibility graph is defined as follows. Let B be a finite set of pairwise disjoint horizontal closed line segments ("bars") in the plane, with all bars having distinct y-coordinates. The associated bar k-visibility graph G(B) has B as its vertex set, and two bars b, b' are adjacent in G(B) if and only if there exists a non-degenerate vertical open segment connecting a point of b to a point of b' that intersects the (open) interiors of at most k other bars of B. A graph is called a bar k-visibility graph if it is isomorphic to G(B) for some such collection B.

The crossing number cr(G) of a (simple) graph G is the minimum, over all drawings of G in the plane with vertices represented by distinct points and edges represented by simple curves between their endpoints, of the number of pairs of edges that cross (interior intersection points).

For fixed nonnegative integer k and positive integer n, define
   M(n, k) = max { cr(G) : G is a bar k-visibility graph on n vertices }.

Determine the value of M(n, k), or determine its asymptotic behavior as n → ∞ for each fixed k.
status_search_result: A web search surfaces literature establishing tight bounds on the number of edges, chromatic number, thickness, and clique size of bar k-visibility graphs (Dean et al.; Felsner; Hartke–Vandenbussche–Wenger), but no source directly resolves the maximum crossing number of bar k-visibility graphs. No paper found announces a solution to this specific question, so the status appears to remain unresolved, but this could not be confirmed conclusively.
